texts: O B S E R V A B I L I T Y Logs, Metrics, Traces & Visualization Building an observability stack with Loki, Prometheus and Grafana on Kubernetes LOKI · Logs PROMETHEUS · Metrics TRACES GRAFANA · Visualization

I N T R O D U C T I O N What is Observability? Observability is the ability to understand what is happening inside a system by examining the data it produces — without having to ship new code to ask a new question. Logs Discrete, timestamped records of events. “What happened, and what did it say?” Metrics Numeric measurements over time. “How much, how fast, how often?” Traces The path a single request takes across services. “Where did the time go?” Visualization Turns raw signals into dashboards a human can act on. Observability: Logs · Metrics · Traces · Visualization 2

T H I S L A B The Stack We're Deploying Loki + Promtail Loki stores and indexes logs. Promtail runs on every node, tails container logs, and ships them to Loki. Prometheus + Exporters Prometheus scrapes metrics from apps and infrastructure and stores them as time series. Grafana Connects to both Loki and Prometheus as data sources and renders everything in dashboards. Observability: Logs · Metrics · Traces · Visualization 3

L O G S Loki: Log Aggregation, Prometheus - Style • A horizontally - scalable, multi - tenant log aggregation system built by Grafana Labs. • Unlike Elasticsearch, Loki does NOT index the full text of every log line — only metadata (labels), which makes it far cheaper to run. • Logs are compressed into chunks and stored in cheap object storage (or a local filesystem in our lab). • You query it with LogQL, a query language deliberately similar to PromQL. Why Loki instead of ELK? ✓ 10 – 20x cheaper storage — index labels, not text ✓ Same label model as Kubernetes & Prometheus ✓ Native Grafana integration — no separate UI ✓ Simple to run for small/medium clusters Observability: Logs · Metrics · Traces · Visualization 4

L O G S Loki Architecture Promtail Ships logs from nodes Distributor Validates & hashes streams Ingester Batches into chunks, writes Store Chunks + index (object storage / local) Querier Executes LogQL queries Grafana (queries via LogQL) In our cluster: Promtail runs as a DaemonSet (one pod per node) and reads container log files directly from each node's files yst em. Observability: Logs · Metrics · Traces · Visualization 5

L O G S Promtail: How Logs Reach Loki 1 Discover Runs as a DaemonSet — one pod per Kubernetes node — and uses Kubernetes service discovery to find every pod on that node. 2 Tail Reads container log files from /var/log/pods on the node's filesystem, following them like `tail - f`. 3 Label Attaches Kubernetes metadata as labels: namespace, pod, container, node — the same labels Prometheus uses. 4 Ship Batches log lines and pushes them to Loki's distributor over HTTP. Observability: Logs · Metrics · Traces · Visualization 6

M E T R I C S Prometheus: Metrics & Time - Series • An open - source monitoring system that pulls (scrapes) metrics from targets on a regular interval — it does not wait for apps to push data. • Stores every measurement as a time series: a metric name + key/value labels + a sequence of timestamped values. • Comes with PromQL, a powerful query language for aggregating, filtering, and computing rates over time series. • Pairs with Alertmanager to turn PromQL conditions into routed alerts (Slack, email, PagerDuty, etc.). Example time series http_requests_total{ method="GET", status="200", pod="new - app - nti - 7d9" } => 1834 PromQL example: rate(http_requests_total[5m]) Observability: Logs · Metrics · Traces · Visualization 7

M E T R I C S Prometheus Architecture Node Exporter kube - state - metrics Your App /metrics scrape /metrics on an interval (pull model) Prometheus Server (scrape + TSDB storage) Alertmanager (routes alerts) Grafana (queries via PromQL) In our cluster: Prometheus finds targets automatically via Kubernetes service discovery and ServiceMonitor/PodMonitor custom res ources — no manual IP lists. Observability: Logs · Metrics · Traces · Visualization 8

M E T R I C S Where Kubernetes Metrics Come From node - exporter DaemonSet — one pod per node. Exposes host - level metrics: CPU, memory, disk, network. kube - state - metrics Watches the Kubernetes API and exposes object state as metrics: pod status, deployment replicas, restarts. cAdvisor (built into kubelet) Exposes per - container resource usage (CPU/memory actually consumed by each container). ServiceMonitor / PodMonitor Custom Resources (CRDs) that tell Prometheus which Services/Pods to scrape — this is how the Helm chart auto - wires everything. Observability: Logs · Metrics · Traces · Visualization 9

T R A C E S Traces: Following a Request A trace records the full journey of one request as it moves through multiple services — showing exactly where time was spent. API Gateway Auth Service Order Service → Database Query → Payment API Not deployed in this lab Tracing normally uses Grafana Tempo, Jaeger, or Zipkin, with apps instrumented via OpenTelemetry. We're focusing on logs + me tri cs + visualization first — tracing is a natural next step. Observability: Logs · Metrics · Traces · Visualization 10

V I S U A L I Z A T I O N Grafana: One Pane of Glass • Grafana doesn't store data itself — it connects to data sources (Prometheus, Loki, and many others) and queries them live. • A Data Source is a configured connection: URL + auth + the query language it should speak (PromQL for Prometheus, LogQL for Loki). • A Dashboard is a collection of Panels; each panel runs a query against a data source and renders it (graph, table, log stream , gauge...). • Explore mode lets you run ad - hoc PromQL/LogQL queries without building a dashboard — great for debugging. • Dashboards can be written as JSON and version - controlled, or imported from the community library (grafana.com/dashboards). Observability: Logs · Metrics · Traces · Visualization 11

P U T T I N G I T T O G E T H E R How Everything Fits Together App Pods (logs + /metrics) Nodes (node - exporter, Promtail) Loki Prometheus Grafana You (browser) All four components run inside the minikube cluster; only Grafana's port is forwarded out so you can view it from your browse r. Observability: Logs · Metrics · Traces · Visualization 12

D E P L O Y M E N T Deploying with Helm Charts kube - prometheus - stack One Helm chart that installs Prometheus, Alertmanager, Grafana, node - exporter, kube - state - metrics — plus a set of default dashboards. loki - stack One Helm chart that installs Loki and Promtail together, and can auto - register Loki as a Grafana data source. Helm A package manager for Kubernetes — a “chart” bundles all the manifests (Deployments, Services, ConfigMaps, CRDs) a piece of software needs. Full command - by - command deployment steps are in the companion guide (observability - deployment.md). Observability: Logs · Metrics · Traces · Visualization 13

D E P L O Y M E N T Opening Grafana in the Browser ▸ Helm installs Grafana as a ClusterIP Service inside minikube — not reachable directly from Windows/WSL. ▸ Run kubectl port - forward to tunnel Grafana's port 80 to your machine's localhost:3000. ▸ Open http://localhost:3000 in your browser and log in (default admin credentials from the chart). ▸ Both Prometheus and Loki are already wired up as data sources — open the pre - installed dashboards under Dashboards → Browse. kubectl port - forward -- address 0.0.0.0 svc/kube - prometheus - stack - grafana 3000:80 Observability: Logs · Metrics · Traces · Visualization 14
R e c a p Logs → Loki + Promtail Metrics → Prometheus + Exporters Traces → (next lab) Tempo/Jaeger Visualization → Grafana Questions?

We begin in Part 1 — What is Observability? : the ability to understand what's happening inside a system from the data it produces — without shipping new code to ask a new question — through four pillars: Logs , Metrics , Traces , and Visualization . (10–20× cheaper — it indexes labels, not text), Part 3·b the write/read path pipeline (Distributor → Ingester → Store ← Querier), and Part 3·c Promtail's DaemonSet workflow: Discover → Tail → Label → Ship. PART 01  What is Observability? — The Four Pillars  5 MIN Observability is the ability to understand what is happening inside a system by examining the data it produces — without having to ship new code to ask a new question . It relies on four core pillars: ▪ TASK [The Four Pillar s] and the question each answers  Logs "What happened, and what did it s ay?" Discrete, timestamped records of events — the error, the warning, the startup message.  Metrics "How much, ho w fast, ho w often?" Numeric measurements over time — CPU, requests per second, response latency.  Traces "Where did the time go?" The full path a single request takes as it moves across the different services.  Visualization "Can a human act on this?" Turns raw signals into dashboards a human can read and act upon. The first three pillars produce and store the signals — the fourth makes them understandable and actionable. KEY IDEA The pillars don't overlap — each answers a different kind of question : a Log tells you what happened in detail , a Metric tells you how much and how fast , a Trace tells you where the time went . A full investigation uses all three together. NOTE · Why the definition matters Notice the

PART 02 ⚖ Logs vs Metrics vs Traces  6 MIN The three signal types are complementary, not redundant . This table is the single most exam-worthy artifact in this guide:  Logs  Metrics  Traces Question What happened, and what did it say? How much, how fast, how often? Where did the time go? Nature Discrete, timestamped event records Numeric measurements over time Full journey of one request across services Shape Free-form text lines Time series (name + labels + values) Request path through service hops Stored by Loki Prometheus Not deployed in this lab (Tempo / Jaeger / Zipkin would be) Query language LogQL PromQL (trace UI) Best for Reading the exact content of an event ("show me the stack trace") Trends, rates, aggregation, alerting, dashboards Latency breakdown across a multi- service request ▪ TASK [How they w ork together] the classic debugging flow  A metric alert fires "error rate jumped" ── ►  a trace shows which hop got slow ── ►  a log line tells you the exact exception Grafana is the pane of glass where all of this comes together. KEY IDEA Because Loki uses the exact same label model as Pr ometheus and Kuber netes , you can pivot from a metric on a pod straight to th

PART 02·B 隣 The Core Stack — At a Glance  5 MIN ▪ TASK [Sev en components, sev en jobs] who does what Component Role Installed by Runs as  Loki Stores and indexes logs loki-stack Log backend  Promtail Tails container logs on every node and ships them to Loki loki-stack DaemonSet  Prometheus Scrapes and stores metrics as time series kube-prometheus- stack Metrics backend  node-expor ter Exposes host-level metrics kube-prometheus- stack DaemonSet  kube-stat e- metrics Exposes Kubernetes object state metrics kube-prometheus- stack Deployment  Alertmanager Routes PromQL alert conditions to Slack/email/P agerDuty kube-prometheus- stack DISABLED IN THIS LAB  Grafana Queries both backends, renders dashboards kube-prometheus- stack Deployment ▪ TASK [T wo transpor ts, one label model] the asymmetry  Promtail ── PUSH (HT TP batches) ── ►  Loki  Prometheus ◄ ── PULL (scrape interval) ──  targets /metrics KEY IDEA Key asymmetr y to remember : Promtail pushes logs to Loki; Prometheus pulls metrics from targets. T wo different transport models — one shar ed label model (namespace / pod / container / node) that makes the stack feel like a single system. KEY IDEA · Modularity These ar

PART 03 · LOGS 1/3  Why Loki? — The Philosophy & the Differences  6 MIN Loki is a horizontally-scalable, multi-tenant log aggregation system built by Grafana Labs . It stands apart from full-text systems like ELK for four essential reasons:  Cost-Effectiv e — the cheapest 10–20× cheaper for storage , because Loki indexes only metadata (labels) — not the full text of every log line. Light indexing = light storage bill.  Storage — cheap tier s Logs are compressed into chunks and stored in cheap object storage (or a local filesystem in labs) — no massive search nodes needed.  Querying — LogQL You query Loki with LogQL — a language deliberately designed to be similar to PromQL. Learn one and the other feels familiar.  Integration — nativ e fit Native Grafana integration (no separate UI needed), and it uses the exact same label model as Kubernetes and Prometheus . ▪ TASK [Loki vs ELK — the differ ence in one line] the trade-off ELK: indexes full text → powerful text search  ⇄ Loki: indexes labels only → 10–20× cheaper  KEY IDEA · The mental model + the philosophy Think of Loki as "Prometheus for logs." And the philosophy in one line: "don't index what y ou won't quer y." Indexin

PART 03·B · LOGS 2/3  Loki Architecture — Write Path & Read Path  6 MIN 3-A The fiv e-stage pipeline Logs travel through Loki's architecture along a specific path — writes flow down the pipeline, reads come back from the Store: 1️⃣ Promtail ships fr om the nodes ── ► 2️⃣ Distributor validat es & hashes str eams ── ► 3️⃣ Ingester batches int o chunks, writ es ▼ 4️⃣ Store chunks + index (object st orage / disk) ◄ ── 5️⃣ Querier execut es LogQL fr om Grafana WRITE: container log files → Promtail → Distributor → Ingester → Store · READ: Grafana —LogQL→ Querier → reads chunks + index from Store/Ingester Component Job 1. Promtail Ships logs from the nodes 2. Distributor Validates and hashes the incoming log streams 3. Ingester Batches the streams into chunks and writes them 4. Store Stores the chunks and the index (object storage or local disk) 5. Querier Executes the LogQL queries coming from Grafana KEY IDEA A log stream = a unique combination of labels . Every distinct label set is its own stream — which is exactly why the labels Promtail attaches matter so much ( Part 3·c ). NOTE · Reads vs writes Writes flow left→right down the pipeline (1→4). Reads never touch the write path's fr

PART 03·C · LOGS 3/3  Promtail Workflow — Why a DaemonSet + the 4 Steps  6 MIN Promtail runs as a DaemonSet — one pod per Kubernetes node . Why? Because container logs are files on each node's local filesystem . A Promtail pod on node A physically cannot read node B's /var/log/pods . Node-local data ⇒ node-local collector. ▪ TASK [The four st eps] discover → tail → label → ship 1️⃣ Discover Uses Kubernetes service discov ery to find every pod running on its node . 2️⃣ Tail Reads container log files directly from /var/log/pods — like a tail -f . 3️⃣ Label Attaches K8s metadata as labels: namesp ace, pod, container , node . 4️⃣ Ship Batches log lines and pushes t o Loki' s distributor over HTTP . KEY IDEA · Labels are the gear in the machine Step 3 matters more than it looks: because Promtail's labels are identical to Prometheus's labels , switching between logs and metrics in Grafana is seamless — same namespace, same pod, same language — and logs and metrics are cross-correlatable by default . See a CPU spike on pod X, namespace Y in a Prometheus panel → query {namespace="Y", pod="X"} in Loki → read the logs from exactly that window. Zero extra configuration produces this. WATCH

PART 04 · METRICS 1/2  Prometheus — Fundamentals  6 MIN Prometheus is an open-source monitoring system that uses a pull model : it scrapes metrics from targets on a regular interval, rather than waiting for applications to push data. ▪ TASK [The thr ee cor e concepts] storage · querying · alerting  Storage Every measurement is a Time Series : a metric name + key/value labels + a sequence of timestamped values . Example: container_cpu_usage_seconds_total{namespace="app", pod="api-7d9f"} — labels are the dimensions you aggregate by.  Querying — Pr omQL A powerful query language for aggregating , filtering , and computing rates over time series.  Alerting — Aler tmanager Pairs with Alertmanager to turn PromQL conditions into routed alerts — Slack, Email, PagerDuty. (Disabled in this lab — but the concept stands.) ▪ TASK [Why pulling matt ers] practical consequences CENTRAL CONTROL The Pull Model gives Prometheus full control: it knows when the last scrape happened and decides the cadence and the target list — apps don't need to know where Prometheus lives. Just expose a /metrics endpoint, nothing more. FAILURE IS VISIBLE A dead target doesn't just leave a gap in the data — its up

PART 04·B · METRICS 2/2  Metric Sources — Know Who Exposes What  7 MIN Component Where it runs What it exposes The question it answers  node- exporter DaemonSet (one pod per node) Host-level metrics: CPU, memory, disk, network "Is the machine itself healthy?"  kube-state- metrics Watches the Kubernetes API Object state : pod status, deployment replicas, restarts "Does Kubernetes think everything is fine?" ⚙ cAdvisor Built into the kubelet Per-container resource usage (actual CPU/memory each container consumes) "Which container is eating resources?"  ServiceMonitor / PodMonitor CRDs — not pods at all Declarative rules for which Services/Pods Prometheus should scrape "How does Prometheus find my app ?" KEY IDEA · Drill this distinction node-exporter = machine · kube-state-metrics = Kubernetes objects · cAdvisor = containers . Three layers of "is it healthy" — three different components. And the ServiceMonitor CRD is what wires your app into Prometheus with zero manual config. ▪ TASK [Who wat ches what ?] the layering  node-exporter → the node itself ⚙ cAdvisor → the containers  kube-state-metrics → K8s object state  ServiceMonitor → which targets get scraped NOTE · Why CRDs m

PART 05  Traces — The Journey of a Request  4 MIN A trace records the full journey of a single request as it moves through multiple services: ▪ TASK [The jour ney of one r equest] a worked example  API Gateway 2ms ── ►  Auth Service 15ms ── ►  Order Service 40ms ── ►  DB Query 120ms ⚠ The trace reveals instantly: most of the time went to the DB Query — no guessing, no manually checking every service. 5.1 The purpose Traces show exactly where time was spent during a request. Metrics tell you that requests are slow; traces tell you which hop made them slow — which service was slow, which call repeated, where the real bottleneck lives. 5.2 The tools Tracing typically uses Grafana Tempo , Jaeger , or Zipkin , with applications instrumented via OpenTelemetry . NOTE · In this lab Traces are not deployed in this specific lab — but they represent the natural next step once logs (Loki) and metrics (Prometheus) are in place. Two of the three signals are already running. KEY IDEA When someone tells you "the API is slow" — Logs tell you what happened , Metrics tell you how slow , but only the Trace tells you exactly where inside the request journey the time went.  EXAM A Trace = the jou

PART 06  Grafana — The Unified UI  7 MIN Grafana is the unified UI for observability — the pane of glass where logs and metrics meet. ▪ TASK [Four concepts] data · config · dashboards · explore  Data Handling Grafana does not store data itself — it connects to Data Sources (Prometheus, Loki) and queries them live on every panel refresh. Wipe the backends and Grafana has nothing to show — it's a lens, not a database . ⚙ Configuration Each Data Source requires: a URL + authentication + the query language it should speak ( PromQL or LogQL ).  Dashbo ards & P anels A Dashboard is a collection of Panels . Each panel runs a query and renders it as a graph, table, log stream, or gauge . Dashboards are JSON — version-controlled, or imported from grafana.com/dashboards by numeric ID.  Explor e Mode Run ad-hoc PromQL or LogQL queries without building a dashboard — the go-to tool for debugging ("just show me the errors from that namespace right now "). ▪ TASK [The hierar chy inside Grafana] the hierarchy  Dashboard ◂ contains 里 Panels ◄ query from  Data Source ◄ which is  Loki /  Prometheus KEY IDEA Grafana is deliberately memoryless: every panel = a liv e quer y at the moment of vie

PART 07 里 How It All Fits Together — in Kubernetes  6 MIN ▪ TASK [The complet e data f low] six steps, end to end 1. Application pods write logs and (optionally) expose /metrics . 2. On every node, Promtail (DaemonSet) tails /var/log/pods , labels each line with Kubernetes metadata, and pushes batches to Loki's distributor. 3. On every node, node-exporter (DaemonSet) exposes host metrics; cAdvisor (in the kubelet) exposes per- container metrics; kube-state-metrics exposes object state. 4. Prometheus pulls all of those metrics on a scrape interval, discovering targets via Kubernetes service discovery and CRDs (ServiceMonitor/PodMonitor). 5. Grafana holds both as data sources and queries Prometheus (PromQL) and Loki (LogQL) live. 6. You open Grafana in a browser through a port-forward tunnel and see everything. ▪ TASK [T wo transpor ts, one label model] the glue  Promtail ── pushes logs (HT TP) ── ►  Loki  Prometheus ◄ ── pulls metrics (scrape) ──  node-exporter · cAdvisor · kube-state-metrics · apps But both carry the same labels — namespace / pod / container / node — which is what makes the stack feel like one system. KEY IDEA Logs are pushed ; metrics are pulled . The transpo

PART 08 · DEPLOYMENT 1/2  Helm + kube-prometheus-stack  8 MIN Helm is a package manager for Kubernetes . It bundles all necessary manifests — Deployments, Services, ConfigMaps, CRDs — into "charts." Installing a chart creates a release . Charts live in repositories you add to your host. Instead of dozens of hand-written YAML files, two Helm commands deploy the entire platform — including default dashboards and wired-up data sources. Helm turned a week-long project into two commands. ▪ TASK [Setup — r epos + namesp ace] best practice: dedicated namespace # add both chart repositories, refresh indexes, create the namespace helm repo add prometheus-community https://prometheus-community.github.io/helm-charts helm repo add grafana https://grafana.github.io/helm-charts helm repo update kubectl create namespace observability # keeps monitoring separate from app workloads ▪ TASK [Char t 1: kube-pr ometheus-stack] one chart, many components INSTALLS Prometheus · Aler tmanager · Grafana · node-expor ter · kube-stat e-metr ics · Ser viceMonit or/PodMonit or CRDs · default Kuber netes dashbo ards — in one shot. ⚠ RESOURCE MANAGEMENT By default this chart requests mor e CPU and RAM than a sm

PART 08·B · DEPLOYMENT 2/2 ⚠ loki-stack + The Gotcha + Port-Forward  8 MIN helm upgrade --install loki-stack grafana/loki-stack \ -n observability \ --set grafana.sidecar.datasources.defaultDatasourceEnabled= false # ← THE critical flag ▪ TASK [ ⚠ The datasour ce provisioning conf lict] the one non-obvious gotcha 1. loki-stack ships its own Grafana data-source ConfigMap for Loki. 2. The Grafana sidecar (in the Grafana installed by kube-prometheus-stack ) auto-discovers datasource ConfigMaps and loads them — Loki appears with zero manual config. Nice. 3. The conflict: kube-prometheus-stack marks Prometheus as the default datasource. loki-stack also tries to mark Loki as default . 4. Grafana allows exactly one default datasource . Two defaults = "Datasource provisioning error" → Grafana crashes → restarts → crashes → CrashLoopBackOff . ✅ THE FIX Install Loki with --set grafana.sidecar.datasources.defaultDatasourceEnabled=false — Loki still becomes a datasource, just not the default (Prometheus stays default). 啕 EMERGENCY REPAIR Already broken? kubectl get configmap -n observability → find the extra datasource ConfigMap → remove isDefault: true → restart the Grafana pod. ▪ TASK [Acce

PART 09 · QUERYING 1/2  LogQL — Querying Loki  7 MIN Framing: two backends, two query languages, one UI. LogQL was deliberately designed t o be similar t o PromQL , and both select by the same labels — learn one, and the other feels familiar. ▪ TASK [S tart in Explor e mode] no dashboard needed Grafana → Explore → pick datasource → run ad-hoc queries  Loki: {namespace="observability"} → live streams  Prometheus: up → 1 = healthy, 0 = down ▪ TASK [LogQL — ev ery quer y has up t o three stages] selector → pipeline → wrapper 1️⃣ Stream select or Labels — indexed, fast . Picks which log streams to read. 2️⃣ Filter pipeline Line filters — evaluated at query time on the matched streams. 3️⃣ Metric wrapper Turns log counts into number s — logs become a metric. # 1) Stream selector: all logs from a namespace {namespace="observability"} # narrow by pod / container (the labels Promtail attached) {namespace="default", pod="my-app-7d9f8b6c-", container="app"} # 2) Line filters: keep / drop lines by content (Loki searches text HERE) {namespace="observability"} |= "error" {namespace="observability"} |= "error" != "timeout" # 3) Metric query: count matching log lines per pod over a 5m window

PART 09·B · QUERYING 2/2  PromQL — Querying Prometheus  6 MIN ▪ TASK [Cor e examples — annotat ed by sour ce component] know who exposes each metric # Health of every scrape target (1 = up, 0 = down) up # Only the observability stack itself up{namespace="observability"} # Per-container CPU rate over 5m — metric from cAdvisor (via kubelet) sum by (pod) ( rate ( container_cpu_usage_seconds_total [ 5m ])) # Container memory right now — cAdvisor sum by (pod) ( container_memory_usage_bytes ) # Node memory available, as a fraction — metric from node-exporter node_memory_MemAvailable_bytes / node_memory_MemTotal_bytes ▪ TASK [T wo mechanics w orth internalizing] range vectors & aggregation ⏱ [5m] = a range vector Selects many points ov er 5 minut es — functions like rate() require a range. A single instant value can't produce a rate. 燐 sum by (pod) = aggregation Aggregates across labels, keeping pod as the grouping dimension — the same labels Loki uses, so results line up across both backends. ▪ TASK [Instant vs tr end debugging] pick the right question "Right now, is it broken?" → up · raw stream {namespace="..."} "Trending toward broken?" → rate() over [5m] · errors/pod · memory fract

PART 10  Application Integration  6 MIN ▪ TASK [Logs — zer o configuration] it just works ✅ LOGS Promtail aut omatically collects logs fr om ev ery pod in the clust er — no annotations, no CRDs, nothing. Its DaemonSet + Kubernetes service discovery pick up new pods as they appear. Deploy an app, and its logs (already labeled with namespace/pod/container) are in Loki. ▪ TASK [Metr ics — tw o requirements] opt-in by design 1. The app must expose a /metrics endpoint on an http port (client libraries exist for every major language, publishing counters/gauges/histograms in Prometheus format). 2. Create a ServiceMonitor Custom Resource whose label selector matches your application — Prometheus discovers it through the CRD (Helm/operator auto-wires the rest). apiVersion : monitoring.coreos.com/v1 kind : ServiceMonitor metadata : name : my-app namespace : observability labels : release : kube-prometheus-stack # must match what the Prometheus operator selects spec : selector : matchLabels : app : my-app # selects YOUR app's Service by its labels namespaceSelector : matchNames : - default # where the app's Service lives endpoints : - port : http # the NAME of the Service port serving /metr

PART 11 · PLAYBOOK 1/2  Troubleshooting Playbook — Scenarios 1–3  8 MIN Reason from symptom → diagnosis → root cause → fix . The diagnostic command sequence matters more than memorizing fixes.  Scenar io 1 — P ods stuck in P ending Symptom kubectl get pods -n observability → pods sitting in Pending , not starting Diagnose kubectl describe pod <pod> -n observability → events show FailedScheduling: Insufficient cpu / memory Root cause Cluster lacks free CPU/memory — the chart's default resource requests don't fit on the Minikube node, and the scheduler will not place a pod whose requests don't fit Fix LOWER REQUESTS (the --set overrides from Part 8) or GROW MINIKUBE ( --cpus=... --memory=... ) Lesson Pending = scheduling problem = look at requests vs available before anything else  Scenar io 2 — Grafana OOMKilled Symptom Grafana restarts repeatedly; kubectl describe pod shows OOMKilled (exit code 137) Root cause The container ran out of memory — it exceeded its own memory limit Diagnose first Check the node's free memory first ( kubectl top nodes ) — do not blindly raise the Grafana limit Fix Node has headroom → RAISE LIMIT via --set ; node exhausted → FREE CAPACITY (disable comp

PART 11·B · PLAYBOOK 2/2  Scenarios 4–5 + Cleanup  6 MIN  Scenario 4 — "Connection refused" from Windows / WSL Symptom Browser on Windows can't reach localhost:3000 even though port-forward is running Root cause The forward was bound to loopback inside the WSL VM only — the --address 0.0.0.0 flag was missing Fix RE-RUN FULL COMMAND kubectl port-forward --address 0.0.0.0 -n observability svc/kube-prometheus-stack-grafana 3000:80 Lesson On WSL, your browser and your cluster live on different network boundaries — bind all interfaces so the port relay works  Scenario 5 — "Grafana shows no data" (general reasoning flow) Work the chain in order — the boring causes are the common ones: 1. Is the b ackend pod r unning? → kubectl get pods -n observability (a crashed Loki or Prometheus means no queries can succeed). 2. Is the datasour ce aliv e? → Explore → run up (Prometheus) or {namespace="observability"} (Loki). If Explore works but a dashboard doesn't, the problem is the dashboard's query/time-range — not the stack. 3. Missing app metr ics specifically ? → no /metrics endpoint, or the ServiceMonitor selector doesn't match — check up for the target. 4. Right namesp ace? Right time ran

PART 13  The Mental Model — Architecture on One Page  5 MIN YOUR HOST (Windows / WSL) ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ Browser ──► http://localhost:3000 (admin/admin123) │ │ ▲ │ │ └── kubectl port-forward --address 0.0.0.0 │ │ -n observability \ │ │ svc/kube-prometheus-stack-grafana 3000:80 │ └──────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────────┘ │ tunnel into the cluster ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ MINIKUBE CLUSTER ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ namespace: observability ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ GRAFANA (Deployment) │ │ the single UI — it stores NO data itself │ │ ▲ queries PromQL ▲ queries LogQL │ └─────┼────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────┘ │ │ ┌─────┴──────────────┐ ┌─────────┴────────────┐ │ PROMETHEUS │ │ LOKI │ │ pull model · TSDB │ │ label index + chunks │ │ time series store │ │ store (disk/object) │ └────────▲───────────┘ └──────────▲───────────┘ │ PULL /metrics │ PUSH (HTTP, batched) │ inside Loki: │ Promtail → Distributor → Ingester → Store │ ( Querier serves Grafana's LogQL) ┌────────┴──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ EVERY NODE (DaemonSets) │ │ ┌──────────────

PART 13·B  Quick Revision — The Terms Table  5 MIN Every term in this book, one line each. If you can define all of these without looking — you're ready. ▪ TASK [Signals + Logs] Term One-line definition Observability Understanding system state from its own data — without shipping new code to ask a new question Log Discrete, timestamped event record — "what happened, and what did it say" Metric Numeric measurement over time — "how much, how fast, how often" Trace Full journey of one request across services — "where did the time go" Visualization Dashboards turning raw signals into something a human can act on Loki Log aggregation backend; indexes labels only , stores compressed chunks Promtail DaemonSet tailing /var/log/pods on every node; pushes to Loki Distributor Validates & hashes incoming log streams Ingester Batches streams into chunks and writes them Store Keeps chunks + index (object storage or disk) Querier Executes LogQL queries coming from Grafana Log Stream A unique combination of labels — every distinct label set is its own stream LogQL Loki's query language: stream selector → line filters → metric wrapper Chunk Compressed batch of log lines in object storage / disk ▪

PART 14 · INTERVIEW PREP  Concept Questions — with Distilled Answers  10 MIN Q1 What is observability? Understanding what's happening inside a system from the data it produces — without shipping new code to ask a new question . Pillars: logs, metrics, traces, visualization. Q2 Logs vs metrics vs traces — when each? Logs = what happened (exact events). Metrics = how much/how fast (trends, alerting). Traces = where the time went (per hop). Debug flow: alert → trace → log. Q3 Why is Loki 10–20× cheaper than full-text systems? It indexes only metadata (labels) , not log text; text is searched at query time. Chunks are compressed into cheap object storage . Q4 Pull vs push — Prometheus vs Promtail? Prometheus pulls (scrapes on an interval — central cadence control; dead target visible via up=0 ). Promtail pushes HTTP batches to Loki's distributor. Q5 Why are Promtail & node-exporter DaemonSets? Their data is node-local : container logs live in each node's /var/log/pods ; host metrics are per-machine. One pod per node = full coverage. Q6 What makes up a Prometheus time series? A metric name + key/value labels + a sequence of timestamped values . Q7 node-exporter vs kube-state-metrics v

Metric name + k ey/value labels + a sequence o f timestamped v alues. 4. cAdvisor , built into the kubelet . 5. PART 03 · LOGS 1/3  Why Loki? — والفروق الفلسفة  6 MIN ز عن أنظمة ّ . يتمي Grafana Labs ، مبني من Multi-T enancy ( يدعم Horizontally-Scalable ع ) ّ أفقي التوس Logs هو نظام تجميع Loki لأربعة أسباب جوهر ية: ELK النص الكامل مثل — الأرخص Cost-Effectiv e  الـ ، لأنه يف هرس × في الت خزين 20 – 10 أرخ ص Metadata ف قط (Labels) — لا النص الكامل لكل سطر Log. ف هرسة خفيفة = فات ورة ت خزين خفيفة . ين رخيص — تخز Storage  الـ Logs ض غط إ لى ُ ت Chunks ن في َّ خز ُ وت Object Storage رخيص ( أو Filesystem مح لي في الـ Labs) — بلا Search Nodes ضخمة . Querying — LogQL  تستعلم Loki بـ LogQL — لتكون شبيهة بـ ا ً عمد لغة مصممة PromQL. م واحدة والثانية تبدو مألوفة ّ تعل . — تكامل أصلي Integration  أص لي مع تكامل Grafana ( بلا واجهة منفصلة )، نفس و يستخدم الـ Label Model الخاص بـ Kubernetes و Prometheus بالض بط . ▪ TASK [Loki vs ELK — الفرق في سطر واحد ] المقایضة  : يفھرس النص الكامل ← بحث نصي قوي ELK ⇄  × 20 – 10 فقط ← أرخص Labels : يفھرس الـ Loki س ما لا تستعلم »لا تفهر . والفلسفة في سطر: « Logs للـ Prometheus » كـ Loki ر في ّ فك الفلسفة + الذھني النموذج · KEY IDEA قر أ عند ُ ا ي ً ك النص خام ؟( تكفي لتصفية ملايين الأسطر، وتر Container ؟ أي Pod ؟ أي Namespace )أي Metadata . فهر سة الـ عنه« . دار

PART 03·B · LOGS 2/3  Loki Architecture — والقراءة الكتابة مسار  6 MIN احله الخمس بمر Pipeline الـ A - 3 الـ Logs تع بر معم ارية Loki ع بر مس ار محدد — الكتابة ت نزل ع بر الـ Pipeline، وال قراءة تعود من الـ Store: 1️⃣ Promtail يشحن من الـ Nodes ── ► 2️⃣ Distributor ق وي عمل ّ يحق Hash للـ Streams ── ► 3️⃣ Ingest er يدفعها دفعات Chunks و يكتبها ▼ 4️⃣ Store Chunks + Index (Object S torage / Disk) ◄ ── 5️⃣ Querier ذ ّ ينف LogQL القادم من Grafana Chunks + ← يقرأ Grafana —LogQL→ Querier · القراءة: Container Logs ← Promtail ← Distributor ← Ingester ← S tore الكتابة: ملفات Store/Ingester من Index ن ّ المكو مھمته Promtail . 1 Nodes من الـ Logs يشحن الـ Distributor . 2 الواردة Logs لتدفقات الـ Hash ويعمل ق ّ يحق Ingester . 3 ويكتبها Chunks دفعات Streams يدفع الـ Store . 4 مح لي( Disk أو Object Storage ) Index والـ Chunks يح فظ الـ Querier . 5 Grafana القادمة من LogQL ذ استعلامات ّ ينف ا الـ ً مستقلة بذاتها — ولهذا بالضبط تهم كثير Stream مختلفة هي Labels . كل مجموعة فر يد Labels مز يج = Log Stream الـ KEY IDEA .( c · 3 الجزء ) Promtail التي يلحقها Labels Querier اءة لا تلمس مقدمة مسار الكتابة: الـ . القر Pipeline (1←4) ا عبر الـ ً ا→يمين ً الكتابة تتدفق يسار الكتابة مقابل القراءة · NOTE غة

DAY 1 AGENDA  What is Ansible  Why Ansible  SSH overview  Ansible & SSH  Installing Ansible & preparing SSH  Ad - hoc commands  Inventory file  Ansible.cfg file  Ad - hoc commands escalation  Ansible playbook  Ansible modules

WHAT IS ANSIBLE ? ❖ Ansible is a software tool that provides simple but powerful automation for cross - platform computer support. ❖ It is used for updates on workstations and servers, cloud provisioning, configuration management, and nearly anything a systems administrator does on a daily basis.
C2 General server server server server server server server server server server server server

WHY ANSIBLE ? ❖ Idempotent : An operation is idempotent if the result of performing it once is exactly the same as the result of performing it repeatedly without any intervening actions. ❖ Agentless : Other tools like (Puppet & Chef) require an agent to be installed on the target device. Ansible only requires an SSH connection to the target device. ❖ Open - source : Ansible is an open - source community project sponsored by Red Hat.
SSH OVERVIEW ❖ OpenSSH is the premier connectivity tool for remote login with the SSH protocol. ❖ It encrypts all traffic to eliminate connection hijacking and other attacks.
C2 General PC 1 SSH PC 2
ANSIBLE & SSH How Ansible connects to servers ?
C2 General Ansible control machine SSH server server server

C2 General INSTALLING ANSIBLE & PREPARING SSH  Install ansible  Create a new user on control machine  Generate SSH key pair on control machine  Copy the public key to host 1  Make sure you can ssh into host 1
C2 General Controller Host 1 (ubuntu) My pc SSH (Master) SSH

AD - HOC COMMANDS Ad - hoc: Running Ansible to perform some quick command. An example of an ad hoc command might be rebooting 50 machines in your infrastructure. Structure: ansible [pattern] - i [inventory] -- private - key [/path/to/private/key] - u [ remote_user ] - m [ module_name ] Example: ansible all - i 3.87.24.251, -- private - key ~/. ssh / devops - u ubuntu - m ping SSH equivalent: ssh ubuntu@3.87.24.251 - i ~/. ssh / devops - o ' RemoteCommand echo hi; bash;' - t
INVENTORY FILE inventory file: A file that describes Hosts and Groups in Ansible. Examples: [ web_servers ] 3.87.24.251 [ database_servers ] 3.87.24.252 3.87.24.253

C2 General INVENTORY FILE  Create the inventory file  Put the IP of host 1 in the inventory file  Use the inventory file path in your ad - hoc command instead of using the IP hard - coded  Example: ansible all - i inventory -- private - key ~/. ssh / devops - u ubuntu - m ping

CONFIGURATION FILE ansible.cfg file: This is the brain and the heart of Ansible. The file that governs the behavior of all interactions performed by the control machine. Locations: ANSIBLE_CONFIG (environment variable if set) ansible.cfg (in the current directory) ~/. ansible.cfg (in the home directory) / etc /ansible/ ansible.cfg Example: [defaults] inventory = ./inventory private_key_file = ~/. ssh / devops remote_user = ubuntu
C2 General CONFIGURATION FILE  Create the configuration file  Insert some values in the configuration file  Run the minimized ad - hoc command  Example: ansible all - m ping

AD - HOC COMMANDS ESCALATION Ad - hoc: Running Ansible to perform some quick command with SUDO permissions. Structure: ansible [pattern] - m [ module_name ] -- become Example: ansible all - m command - a " whoami " -- become Example ansible.cfg : [ privilege_escalation ] become = true
C2 General AD - HOC COMMAND ESCALATION USING ROOT USER  Insert the correct values in the configuration file  Example: ansible all - m command - a " whoami "  What is the output of the command ?

PLAYBOOK • A playbook is a list of plays . • playbook: Playbook is the language Ansible uses to orchestrate, configure, administer, or deploy systems. • Play: is a mapping between a set of hosts (groups, hostnames, or IPs) and the tasks which run on those hosts to define the role that those systems will perform. • There can be one or many plays in a playbook. Examples: - name: your play name hosts: all tasks: - name: your task name ping:
C2 General PLAYBOOK  Write your first playbook file  Stop gather_facts and update cache

MODULES Modules: are units of code that can control system resources or execute system commands. Ansible provides a module library that you can execute directly on remote hosts or through playbooks. Playbook example: - name: your play name hosts: all tasks: - name: your task name ping: Ad - hoc command example: ansible all – m ping

C2 General MODULES  Explore some built - in modules like: ( apt, dnf , package, service, command, copy, user, group, lineinfile , authorized_key , etc .) ansible - builtin modules  Update cache  Install latest nginx  Copy index.html from controller to host 1  Restart nginx service  Can you see your index.html file when you hit host 1 on port 80 ?
THANK YOU Powered by TCPDF (www.tcpdf.org) Powered by TCPDF (www.tcpdf.org)
DAY 2 AGENDA  Tags  Variables  Loops  When  Register

TAGS Tags: Running only specific parts of a playbook instead of running the entire playbook . Example : - name: my play with tags hosts: all tasks : - name: my task1 with tags tags: my _first_tag ping: - name: my task2 with tags tags: my _second_tag ping : ansible - playbook my - playbook.yml -- tags my_first_tag

TAGS  Write simple playbook file  Add two tasks (apt update – apt install nginx )  Add tags to first task: update  Add tags to second task: install  Run only the (apt update) task  Example: ansible - playbook my - playbook.yml -- tags update  Add one task with “tags: always” and run the previous command again

VARIABLES V ariables: Ansible uses variables to manage differences between systems . L ocations: ➢ Playbooks ➢ Inventory ➢ Command Line ➢ Register ➢ Files or Roles example: - name: my play with variables hosts: all vars: package: nginx version: latest tasks: - name: my task with variables apt: name: "{{ package }}" state: "{{ varsion }}"

VARIABLES Define these variables ( package_name , package_version )  on playbook level  on inventory level  on command line level Use apt module with the package name and version from your variables

LOOPS Loops: Ansible uses loops to execute a task multiple times. example: - name: my play with loops hosts: all tasks: - name: my task with loops apt: name: "{{ item }}" state: latest loop: - nginx - mariadb - server - curl example: - name: my play with loops hosts: all tasks: - name: my task with loops apt: name: "{{ item.package_name }}" state: "{{ item.package _state }}" loop: - { package_name : " nginx ", package_state : “present"} - { package_name : “ mariadb - server", package_state : “latest"} - { package_name : “curl", package_state : “absent"}
LOOPS  Loop over a list of packages and install latest versions.  Loop over a list of packages and perform different actions as per input.

WHEN When: You want to execute different tasks depending on the value of a fact, a variable, or the result of a previous task. Example: - name : my play with conditions hosts: all tasks : - name: my task1 with conditions apt: name : nginx when : ansible_facts ['distribution'] == “Ubuntu“ - name: my task2 with conditions apt: name : httpd when : ansible_facts ['distribution'] == “CentOS“
WHEN  Install nginx or apache2 depending on distribution  Restart nginx service if distribution is ubuntu and variable value is true

REGISTER Register: Ansible register is a way to capture the output from task execution and store it in a variable . Example: - name: my play with register hosts: all tasks : - name: my task1 with register command: cat /var/www/html/index.html register: my_result - name: my task2 with register debug: var: my_result

REGISTER & WHEN  View the value of your register variable using debug module  R estart service if the installation task was changed or was not failed Powered by TCPDF (www.tcpdf.org) Powered by TCPDF (www.tcpdf.org)
DAY 3 AGENDA  Roles  Handlers  Templates “.j2”  Ansible - Vault  Ansible - Galaxy
ROLES Roles: pack related vars, files , templates, tasks , and handlers, based on a known file structure so you can easily reuse them and share them with other users .
roles web db tasks files vars main.yml main .yml

C2 General ROLES  Create your first role with name (web)  The task book will include: 1. installing a package (get the package name from vars ) 2. copying a list of files from controller to host using loop (get the list of file names from vars ) (the actual files will be stored in ./roles/web/files ) (will be executed only when the install task is in state: changed )  Restart the service of the installed package ( will be executed only when the copy task is in state: changed)

HANDLERS Handlers: Handlers are tasks that only run when notified . Example : - name: my play with handlers hosts : all tasks: - name: my task1 with handlers apt : name : nginx notify: my_handler handlers: - name: my_handler service: name : nginx state: restarted
roles web db tasks files vars main.yml main.yml main.yml

C2 General HANDLERS  Create your first role with name (web)  The task book will include: 1. installing a package (get the package name from vars) 2. copying a list of files from controller to host using loop (get the list of file names from vars) (the actual files will be stored in ./roles/web/files) (will be executed using Handlers)  Restart the service of the installed package (will be executed using Handlers chaining)

TEMPLATES Templates: Ansible uses Jinja2 templates to create dynamic content at the controller end, and render it as static content at the host end. index.html.j2 <html> <body> <h1> {{ my_message }} <h1> </body> < /html> index .html <html> <body> <h1> Hello from ansible < h1> </body> </html>
roles web db tasks files vars main.yml main.yml main.yml Index.html.j2

C2 General TEMPLATES  Create your first role with name (web)  The task book will include: 1. installing a package (get the package name from vars ) 2. Copying a file from controller to host using template (get the template name & template message from vars) (the actual template file will be stored in ./roles/web/templates ) (will also notify the restart handler) 3. copying a list of files from controller to host using loop (get the list of file names from vars) (the actual files will be stored in ./roles/web/files) (will be executed using Handlers )  Restart the service of the installed package (will be executed using Handlers chaining)

ANSIBLE - VAULT Ansible - Vault : provides a way to encrypt and manage sensitive data such as passwords . Example: - name: my play with vault hosts: all vars: user_name : ahmed var_files : - ./ passwords.yml tasks: - name: my task1 with vault user: name: " {{ user_name }} " password: "{{ user_pass }}" passwords .yml u ser_pass : 123456 Commands: $ ansible - vault encrypt ./ passwords.yml $ ansible - playbook my - playbook.yml -- ask - vault - pass

ANSIBLE - GALAXY Ansible - Galaxy: refers to the Galaxy website, a free site for finding, downloading, and sharing community developed roles and collections. C ommands: $ ansible - galaxy info username.role_ name $ ansible - galaxy install username . role_ name $ ansible - galaxy install username.role_ name ,1.0.0 $ ansible - galaxy list $ ansible - galaxy remove username . role_name Powered by TCPDF (www.tcpdf.org) Powered by TCPDF (www.tcpdf.org)

▶ CHAPTER 0 1 · FOUNDATIONS WHY AUTOMATION BEATS SCRIPTS 5 MIN ▸ WHAT — T he a utom a tion pro b lem Manual operation scales linearly with machines and fails quietly. Shell scripts capture *commands* but not *intent*: which machines, what state, what if state already exists, how to verify, how to retry. Configuration drifts. Knowledge lives in runbooks and heads. MANUAL LOOP VS DECLARATIVE CONVERGE MANUAL Operator → SSH for-loop → hosts one by one → drift accumulates → re-run repeats side effects DECLARATIVE Playbook → control node → inventory select → compare desired vs current → CHANGED or OK, audited Ansible addresses this by declaring desired stat e for selected targets and converging each target toward that state, reporting whether change was needed. ▸ WHY — W hy A nsi b le exists Problem it solves: repeatable, auditable, idempotent configuration and orchestration without per-host agents or custom orchestration code for simple cases. Where it fits: Provisioning (Terraform) → Configuration (Ansible) → Orchestration (K8s) → Verification (Observability) Ansible owns the configuration layer: OS, packages, files, services, users, application config — on bare metal, VMs, cloud insta

▶ CHAPTER 0 1 · FOUNDATIONS ( CONT . ) WHY AUTOMATION BEATS SCRIPTS 5 MIN ▸ WHERE DOES IT FIT — Ec osystem l a ne Script (Bash): "run this command again" → no convergence check Image baking (P acker): snapshot state → not day-2 config Provisioner (T erraform): creates infrastructure → hands off to Ansible for inside-OS config Orchestrator (K8s): schedules containers → Ansible can provision/configure K8s nodes themselves Decision tree (preview, detailed in PDF3): WHAT ARE YOU AUTOMATING? → Infrastructure → Terraform/OpenTofu → Host/app config → Ansible Same question, three answers — the comparison that decides the tool: QUESTION SHELL LOOP ANSIBLE Which machines? Hosts hardcoded in the loop Inventory selects by group and pattern Already correct? Runs again blindly Reports OK , changes nothing Proof it worked? Exit code of the last host Per-host recap, every host Repeat next week? Hope nothing changed Converge again with the same file F ound a tions · V ol 1 4 ok c h a nged f a iled = 0 TOC

▶ CHAPTER 0 1 · FOUNDATIONS ( CONT . ) WHY AUTOMATION BEATS SCRIPTS 5 MIN ▸ TERRAFORM VS ANSIBLE — P rovision vs c onfigure Terraform provisions infrastructure (creates it: VPCs, VMs, DNS, load balancers) and tracks it in a state file. Ansible configur es what already exists (OS, packages, files, services, users) and converges it on every run, keeping no state of its own. ASPECT TERRAFORM / OPENTOFU ANSIBLE Owns Infrastructure lifecycle (create, change, destroy) Inside-OS desired state (configure, converge) State State file ( terraform.tfstate ) maps config to real resources Stateless; compares desired vs current on the host each run Runs plan previews infra diff; apply changes infra --check --diff previews config diff; run converges hosts Re-run cost Re-plans against APIs; safe but slow Re-converges; OK where already correct, fast Secrets Provider creds + sensitive outputs Vault-encrypted vars, no_log , become scoping Combined workflow (the normal production shape): Terraform apply → outputs IPs/hostnames → generated inventory → Ansible configures OS/apps → services verified terraform output -json > tf-out.json # ips of new VMs ansible-playbook -i inventories/prod site.yml Handoff

▶ CHAPTER 0 1 · FOUNDATIONS ( CONT . ) WHY AUTOMATION BEATS SCRIPTS 5 MIN ▸ HOW IT WORKS — H igh - level loop USER → ansible-playbook → CONTROL NODE (inventory, vars, tasks) → SSH/WinRM → MANAGED NODE (module) → TARGET STATE → RESULT (OK/CHANGED/FAILED) ▸ PRACTICAL — N ot yet exe c ut ab le ( intention a l ) This chapter builds motivation. Execution begins in Ch 02–03. No commands to mis-run yet. ▸ WHAT CAN FAIL — M isunderst a nding a utom a tion SYMPTOM LIKELY CAUSE PREVENTION Automation reintroduces drift Scripts without idempotency Teach CHANGED vs OK early (Ch 05) Over-automation of infra as config Using Ansible to create VPCs Handoff callout: provision vs configure ▸ REAL - WORLD CONNECTION SRE uses Ansible to converge fleet after patch window: same playbook against staging then production, diff mode first, check mode for approval. ▸ I nterview c he c k Interview Why not just r un shell scr ipts via SSH loop? Scripts describe commands; automation must describe targets, desired state, convergence check, error handling, and audit result. Ansible's model adds selection, declaration, and verification around the transport that a loop lacks. [ NEXT ] We know *why* to automate. Next

▶ CHAPTER 0 2 · ARCHITECTURE AGENTLESS — CONTROL TO MANAGED 6 MIN ▸ WHAT — A gentless a r c hite c ture Ansible requires no permanently running agent on managed nodes. The control node holds automation content and initiates connections; managed nodes receive module payloads and execute them. AGENTLESS EXECUTION PATH CONTROL NODE playbook · inv entory · vars → SSH / WinRM connection plugin → MANAGED NODE module runs · JSON b ack Linux OpenSSH + Py thon 3 Windows WinRM + P owerShell ┌───────────────────┐ │ CONTROL NODE │ │ ansible-playbook │ │ inventory │ │ variables │ │ modules (FQCN) │ └─────────┬─────────┘ │ SSH / WinRM (connection plugins) ┌───────┴────────┐ ↓ ↓ HOST 01 (Linux) HOST 02 (Windows via WinRM) ▸ WHY — W hy a gentless Problem: agent lifecycle (install, upgrade, cert rotation) is its own fleet problem. Agentless trades persistent presence for on- demand execution: simpler bootstrap, no agent fleet to patch, works over standard transports already present. Tradeoff callout: [ WHY THIS EXISTS ] Agents give push-without-SSH but require ongoing fleet. Agentless gives immediate start but requires reachable transport + credentials per run. Choose agentless when SSH/WinRM alrea

▶ CHAPTER 0 2 · ARCHITECTURE ( CONT . ) AGENTLESS — CONTROL TO MANAGED 6 MIN ▸ WHERE DOES IT FIT — E xe c ution model COMMAND → LOAD CONFIG (ansible.cfg) → LOAD INVENTORY → SELECT HOSTS → LOAD VARIABLES/FACTS → PROCESS PLAY → EXECUTE TASK → RUN MODULE → RETURN RESULT → NEXT TASK This lane is the visual anchor reused every chapter. ▸ HOW IT WORKS Control node: where ansible / ansible-playbook runs. Needs Python 3.11+, collections, inventory, ansible.cfg . Managed node: target host. Needs Python (most modules) or P owerShell (Windows), SSH/WinRM reachable, privilege path ( become ). Transpor t: connection plugin. Default ssh (Linux), winrm / psrp (Windows). Data sent: module payload + args; result returned as JSON. Module ex ecution: module runs on managed node (or locally if delegate_to: localhost ), reports changed , failed , skipped . Config loading order (callout): ansible.cfg precedence: ANSIBLE_CONFIG env → ./ansible.cfg → ~/.ansible.cfg → /etc/ansible/ansible.cfg ▸ PRACTICAL — V erify c ontrol node $ ansible --version ansible [core 2.16.x] ... Meaning: confirms control node install. T arget: local. Internal: loads config, no inventory needed. Expected: version + config path. F

▶ CHAPTER 0 2 · ARCHITECTURE ( CONT . ) AGENTLESS — CONTROL TO MANAGED 6 MIN ▸ WSL SETUP — C ontrol node on W indows Windows cannot run Ansible natively. WSL2 + Ubuntu is the supported control node: a real Linux kernel where ansible- playbook , Python, and OpenSSH behave exactly like CI. wsl --install -d Ubuntu # Windows Terminal (admin): installs WSL2 + Ubuntu sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y python3 python3-pip pipx openssh-client git pipx install ansible # ansible + ansible-playbook on PATH pipx inject ansible ansible-lint ansible --version # expect: ansible [core 2.16.x], python 3.11+ Rules that prevent an entire class of failures: Keep the project inside WSL home ( ~/ansible/ ), not /mnt/c/ — Windows mounts are slow and cannot hold Linux permissions (SSH keys at 0600 silently break there) Use VS Code with the WSL Remote extension so editors save with LF endings; CRLF line endings corrupt Y AML and vault files Generate the SSH key inside WSL ( ssh-keygen -t ed25519 ), copy the public half to servers with ssh-copy-id One .venv or pipx per toolset; never sudo pip install (breaks system Python) ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "ansible-control" # ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 ssh-copy-id ansibl

▶ CHAPTER 0 2 · ARCHITECTURE ( CONT . ) AGENTLESS — CONTROL TO MANAGED 6 MIN Each maps to troubleshooting in PDF3 Ch 12. ▸ REAL - WORLD CONNECTION Fleet of 200 VMs: one control node (CI runner) holds inventory + V ault. No agent deployed to 200 hosts; rotation handled by SSH key management. ▸ I nterview c he c k Interview Why is Ansible called agentless? Managed nodes need no permanent Ansible daemon. Control node connects via SSH/WinRM per task and executes modules on demand. [ NEXT ] Architecture tells *how* Ansible reaches machines. Next: *which* machines — inventory and targeting. F ound a tions · V ol 1 1 0 ok c h a nged f a iled = 0 TOC

▶ CHAPTER 0 3 · INVENTORY INVENTORY — WHICH MACHINES 7 MIN ▸ WHAT — I nventory is t a rget de c l a r a tion Inventory lists managed nodes and organizes them into groups . Playbooks select from this list; ad hoc commands address it directly. INVENTORY HIERARCHY INVENT ORY FILE → GROUPS web · db · pr od → HOSTS web-01 · db-01 → VARS group_vars · host_v ars Static inventory example: [web] web-01 ansible_host=10.0.1.11 web-02 ansible_host=10.0.1.12 [db] db-01 ansible_host=10.0.1.21 [prod:children] web db Hierarchy: INVENTORY +-- groups (web, db, prod) +-- hosts (web-01, web-02) +-- group_vars / host_vars +-- variables (ansible_user, ansible_become) ▸ WHY — S ele c tion b efore de c l a r a tion Without inventory, automation has no audience. Inventory separates *which* from *what* — same playbook against web vs prod yields different blast radius. F ound a tions · V ol 1 1 1 ok c h a nged f a iled = 0 TOC

▶ CHAPTER 0 3 · INVENTORY ( CONT . ) INVENTORY — WHICH MACHINES 7 MIN ▸ HOW IT WORKS Static: INI or Y AML file, committed to repo, versioned. Dynamic: plugin queries cloud (A WS EC2, Azure) at runtime — generates inventory, not checked in. Patterns: web , web[0] , web:db , prod:&web , all:!db — composed at CLI/play hosts: . Variables: inventory vars flow into variable precedence (taught fully in PDF2 Ch 06) via group_vars/web.yml , host_vars/db-01.yml . ▸ PRACTICAL — A d ho c proof ( first exe c ution ) Ad hoc = single task without playbook. Proves inventory + transport before Y AML complexity. COMMAND ──────────────────────── ansible web -i inventory.ini -m ping Meaning: run ping module against group web . Target: web-01 , web-02 . Internal: control node loads inventory, selects hosts, sends ping.py via SSH, returns JSON. Expected: RESULT ──────────────────────── web-01 | SUCCESS => { "changed": false, "ping": "pong" } web-02 | SUCCESS => { "changed": false, "ping": "pong" } Why it matters: proves selection, transport, Python on target in 5 seconds. Common failure: UNREACHABLE → check ansible_user , ansible_host , key, ansible -m ping with -vvv changed: false surprise → ping is ch

▶ CHAPTER 0 3 · INVENTORY ( CONT . ) INVENTORY — WHICH MACHINES 7 MIN ▸ CONNECTING — SSH keys , users , IP s Inventory names the targets; connection variables explain how to reach them . Four variables do 95% of the work: [web] web-01 ansible_host=10.0.1.11 ansible_user=ansible ansible_port=22 web-02 ansible_host=10.0.1.12 ansible_user=ansible [web:vars] ansible_ssh_private_key_file=~/.ssh/id_ed25519 ansible_become=true ansible_host — real IP/hostname (the inventory name stays a stable alias even when IPs change) ansible_user — SSH login user; create a dedicated ansible user, never automate as root over SSH ansible_port — non-default SSH port where hardened ansible_ssh_private_key_file — which key; one key per environment ( prod_ed25519 vs staging_ed25519 ) Key bootstrap (once per server, from the control node): ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -f ~/.ssh/prod_ed25519 # private stays 0600, never leaves control node ssh-copy-id -i ~/.ssh/prod_ed25519 ansible@10.0.1.11 ssh -i ~/.ssh/prod_ed25519 ansible@10.0.1.11 # must log in with no password prompt Behind a bastion, hop transparently instead of copying keys around: F ound a tions · V ol 1 1 3 ok c h a nged f a iled = 0 TOC

▶ CHAPTER 0 3 · INVENTORY ( CONT . ) INVENTORY — WHICH MACHINES 7 MIN ▸ CONNECTING — Ba stions , first c ont ac t , trust [web:vars] ansible_ssh_common_args=-o ProxyJump=bastion.example.com First-contact checklist (in order, stop at the first red): ping -c2 10.0.1.11 # IP reachable at all? ssh ansible@10.0.1.11 # key auth works by hand? ansible web-01 -i inventory.ini -m ping # Ansible transport works? ansible web -i inventory.ini --list-hosts # pattern selects who you think? Host-key trust: first connection prompts Are you sure you want to continue connecting? . For known fleets, pre-seed ~/.ssh/known_hosts with ssh-keyscan ; setting host_key_checking=false in ansible.cfg silences the prompt but also silences real machine-in-the-middle warnings — scope it to ephemeral lab inventories only. ▸ WHAT CAN FAIL Pattern selects zero hosts → hosts: web matches nothing if group misspelled → --list-hosts verify Wrong vars file location → group_vars/ must sit beside inventory file Dynamic inventory creds → plugin fails silently if cloud creds missing ▸ REAL - WORLD CONNECTION Staging vs prod: same playbook, different inventories ( inventories/staging/ , inventories/prod/ ). Promotion = chang

▶ CHAPTER 0 3 · INVENTORY ( CONT . ) INVENTORY — WHICH MACHINES 7 MIN ▸ LAB — Ob serve / E xe c ute / V erify Objective: prove inventory selection. Prereqs: inventory.ini above. S teps: 1. ansible all -i inventory.ini --list-hosts → Observe all targets 2. ansible web -i inventory.ini -m ping → Execute + W atch CHANGED vs SUC CESS 3. Verify pong . Explain: ping validates transport, not config. Failure scenarios: wrong ansible_host → UNREA CHABLE; fix → correct IP. ▸ I nterview c he c k Interview Static vs dynamic inv entory? Static lists hosts in file; dynamic generates list at runtime from cloud API. S tatic for stable fleet, dynamic for elastic/autoscaling. [ NEXT ] We know *which* machines. Next: *what* state they should reach — playbooks. F ound a tions · V ol 1 1 5 ok c h a nged f a iled = 0 TOC

▶ CHAPTER 0 4 · PLAYBOOKS PLAYBOOK — DESIRED STATE IN YAML 8 MIN ▸ WHAT — P l a y b ook is desired - st a te do c ument A playbook maps hosts to tasks that invoke modules with arguments . It is Y AML, declarative: describe end state, not step- by-step shell. PLAY NESTS TASKS , TASKS INVOKE MODULES PLAY hosts · become → TASK name → MODULE ansible.builtin.* → ARGS name · stat e ▸ WHY — F rom a d ho c to repe a t ab le Ad hoc proves one module once. Playbooks repeat, order, and audit multiple tasks. They are the unit committed to Git and triggered by CI. ASPECT AD HOC COMMAND PLAYBOOK Shape One module call from the CLI Plays and tasks in a Y AML file Repeat Retype the command every time Run the file again, identical result Review Shell history on one laptop Git diff plus --check --diff Handoff Tell someone the command Commit site.yml ; CI runs it F ound a tions · V ol 1 1 6 ok c h a nged f a iled = 0 TOC

▶ CHAPTER 0 4 · PLAYBOOKS ( CONT . ) PLAYBOOK — DESIRED STATE IN YAML 8 MIN ▸ YAML — S ynt a x b efore sem a nti c s - name: Configure web server hosts: web become: true # privilege escalation tasks: - name: Install nginx ansible.builtin.package: name: nginx state: present - name: Ensure nginx running ansible.builtin.service: name: nginx state: started enabled: true Hierarchy: PLAY (hosts: web, become: true) +-- tasks +-- TASK (name: Install nginx) +-- MODULE (ansible.builtin.package, FQCN) +-- ARGUMENTS (name, state) Rule: FQCN always ( ansible.builtin.* ) — short names obsolete. Y AML whitespace matters; 2-space indent. ▸ HOW IT WORKS — E xe c ution PLAY (web) → TASK 1 (package) → SSH → managed node → check nginx absent → install → CHANGED → TASK 2 (service) → check stopped → start → CHANGED → RESULT per host → NEXT PLAY Play = which hosts; T ask = what module with which args; Module = implementation that converges state. F ound a tions · V ol 1 1 7 ok c h a nged f a iled = 0 TOC

▶ CHAPTER 0 4 · PLAYBOOKS ( CONT . ) PLAYBOOK — DESIRED STATE IN YAML 8 MIN ▸ PRACTICAL — R un it COMMAND ──────────────────────── ansible-playbook -i inventory.ini site.yml Meaning: execute playbook against inventory. T arget: web group. Internal: load site.yml , select hosts, for each task send module, collect changed/ok/failed . Expected: RESULT ──────────────────────── PLAY [Configure web server] *** TASK [Install nginx] *** changed: [web-01] TASK [Ensure nginx running] *** changed: [web-01] PLAY RECAP *** web-01 : ok=2 changed=2 failed=0 Why it matters: proves declarative convergence; re-run should yield ok=2 changed=0 . Common failure: Y AML parse error → ERROR! Syntax Error at line; fix indent or missing : . ▸ WHAT CAN FAIL hosts: web matches zero → skipping: no hosts matched → verify with --list-hosts become: true without sudo → Failed to escalate → ansible_become_user / sudoers Module args typo → unsupported parameter → check ansible-doc ansible.builtin.package F ound a tions · V ol 1 1 8 ok c h a nged f a iled = 0 TOC

▶ CHAPTER 0 4 · PLAYBOOKS ( CONT . ) PLAYBOOK — DESIRED STATE IN YAML 8 MIN ▸ REAL - WORLD CONNECTION Team commits site.yml to infra/ repo; reviewer sees state: present intent, not apt-get install imperative. ▸ LAB — Ob serve / E xe c ute / V erify Observe: nginx absent ( systemctl status nginx fails). Execute: ansible-playbook -i inventory.ini site.yml -- check --diff (dry run). V erify: --diff shows planned changes. Execute for real, verify ok with changed=2 , re-run verify changed=0 . ▸ I nterview c he c k Interview Play vs task vs module? Play selects hosts and holds tasks; task invokes one module with arguments; module does work on managed node and reports convergence. [ NEXT ] Playbooks declare state. Next: how modules enforce idempotency and report CHANGED vs OK. F ound a tions · V ol 1 1 9 ok c h a nged f a iled = 0 TOC

▶ CHAPTER 0 5 · IDEMPOTENCY MODULES AND IDEMPOTENCY ADV ▸ WHAT — M odule + ide a l result Module = unit of desired state. T akes args, checks current state, acts only if needed, returns JSON with changed , failed , msg . FIRST RUN — CHANGED Desired: nginx present ↓ Current: absent ↓ Install → CHANGED SECOND RUN — OK Desired: nginx present ↓ Current: present ↓ No action → OK Idempotency: same input applied twice → same end state, second run reports no change. ▸ WHY — D esired st a te ≠ re - run c omm a nds Scripts re-run commands blindly. Modules compare desired vs current: DESIRED STATE (state: present) ↓ CURRENT STATE (nginx absent? present?) ↓ COMPARE → CHANGE OR NO-OP → RESULT (CHANGED / OK) Without this, automation cannot be safely repeated for drift correction or retries. F ound a tions · V ol 1 2 0 ok c h a nged f a iled = 0 TOC

▶ CHAPTER 0 5 · IDEMPOTENCY ( CONT . ) MODULES AND IDEMPOTENCY ADV ▸ HOW IT WORKS — V isu a l First run: Desired: nginx present → Current: absent → Install → CHANGED Second run: Desired: nginx present → Current: present → No action → OK Result states (always labeled with symbol+color, not color alone): OK (green ●) — converged, no change CHANGED (blue ◐ ) — converged, did change FAILED (red ��) — did not converge SKIPPED (gray ○) — conditional skipped UNREACHABLE (amber ��) — transport failed DESIRED VS CURRENT DECIDES EVERYTHING DESIRED → CURRENT → COMPARE → CHANGE or NO-OP F ound a tions · V ol 1 2 1 ok c h a nged f a iled = 0 TOC

▶ CHAPTER 0 5 · IDEMPOTENCY ( CONT . ) MODULES AND IDEMPOTENCY ADV ▸ PRACTICAL — Ob serve idempoten c y - name: Idempotency demo hosts: web tasks: - name: Create app directory ansible.builtin.file: path: /opt/app state: directory mode: '0755' First run: changed: [web-01] . Second run: ok: [web-01] . Proof of desired-state model. Check and diff modes: $ ansible-playbook -i inventory.ini site.yml --check --diff --check dry-runs, --diff shows planned file/service changes. Use for approval gates. ▸ WHAT CAN FAIL — C ommon misre a ds OK misread as "nothing happened" → actually "already converged" (GO TCHA callout below) Module not idempotent by misuse → command: apt-get install always CHANGED vs package: converges → use package / file / template not command / shell where module exists changed_when abuse → masks real change signal [ GOTCHA ] "OK" does not mean Ansible did nothing meaningful. It means desired state already holds. Always read result state pair: ok vs changed count. F ound a tions · V ol 1 2 2 ok c h a nged f a iled = 0 TOC

▶ CHAPTER 0 5 · IDEMPOTENCY ( CONT . ) MODULES AND IDEMPOTENCY ADV ▸ COMMAND + RESULT PATTERN COMMAND ──────────────────────── ansible web -i inventory.ini -m ansible.builtin.file -a "path=/opt/app state=directory mode=0755" RESULT ──────────────────────── web-01 | CHANGED => { "changed": true, "path": "/opt/app", "state": "directory" } WHAT HAPPENED: file module ensured directory exists, created it. WHY IT MATTERS: proves CHANGED on creation, OK on repeat. COMMON FAILURE: path parent missing → use state=directory (creates parents), mode typo → permission drift. ▸ COMPARISON — M odule vs shell ASPECT MODULE ( F I L E , P A C K A G E ) C O M M A N D / S H E L L Intent desired state imperative command Idempotency built-in compare always CHANGED unless creates / removes Check mode supported skipped Audit diff friendly opaque ▸ REAL - WORLD CONNECTION Patch fleet: re-run same playbook weekly → CHANGED only where drift occurred. changed count becomes drift metric fed to observability. ▸ I nterview c he c k Interview What mak es a module idempot ent? It compares desired vs current state and acts only when different, reporting CHANGED when it acted and OK when already converged. [ NEXT ]

▶ APPENDIX · CHEATSHEET CHEATSHEET — FQCN AND FAILURES FINALE A FQCN — U se A lw a ys LEGACY FQCN yum , apt ansible.builtin.package template ansible.builtin.template service ansible.builtin.service file ansible.builtin.file B Fa ilure I ndex SYMPTOM FIX UNREA CHABLE SSH key / ansible_host Failed to escalate become + sudoers YAML error ansible-lint OK misread already converged ● OK — c onverged , no c h a nge ◐ CHANGED — c onverged , did c h a nge �� FAILED — did not c onverge F ound a tions · V ol 1 2 4 ok c h a nged f a iled = 0 TOC
