▶ CHAPTER 1 0 · SECURITY VAULT · BECOME · SECRETS 8 MIN   ي ب ر ع ح ر ش : S e c rets و ية ا م ح ل ا فع الامتياز عند الحاجة فقط . ار ّ ر السر ّ وشف Privilege ق ّ ا، فضي ً مع Secrets و Root ّ تمس Automation ) Ansible V ault ر ة بـ ّ مشف Secrets المناسب، وانسخ become_user ( مع sudo ا ً )غالب become عبر ها لحظة التشغيل بكلمة ّ ( وفك encrypt_str ing وقيم سطر ية بـ encrypt/decr ypt/view/edit/r ekey )تشفير ملفات داخل Ansible V ault ق بين ّ . فر no_log ، مع كتم المخرجات الحساسة بـ CI ّ سر أو ملف أو سر SELinux اجع ملكية الملفات وسياقات ر .( lookups )مخزن خارجي عبر HashiCorp V ault المستودع( و عند الأعطال. ansible_py thon_int erpreter ر ّ ومفس become · Ansible V ault · encrypt_str ing · no_log · SELinux · sudoer s ▸ WHAT — L e a st privilege + en c rypted se c rets become escalates privilege (typically sudo) per play, role, or task. Ansible V ault encrypts variables and files so secrets live in Git safely and decrypt only at run time. SECRETS STAY ENCRYPTED UNTIL RUN TIME PLAINTE XT VAR → VAULT ENCR YPT → COMMIT SAFE → DECRYPT AT RUN - name: Configure web fleet hosts: web become: true become_user: root vars_files: - group_vars/prod/vault.yml tasks: - name: Deploy TLS key ansible.builtin.co

▶ CHAPTER 1 0 · SECURITY ( CONT . ) VAULT · BECOME · SECRETS 8 MIN ▸ WHERE DOES IT FIT — S e c ure a fter org a nize Roles/collections (Ch 09) define vars → Vault encrypts the sensitive subset → become scopes who applies them → testing (Ch 11) verifies without leaking → CI/CD (Ch 12) injects vault password from CI secrets Do not confuse Ansible V ault (file/var encryption in-repo) with HashiCorp V ault (external secret store via lookup plugins). They compose: external vault supplies at run, Ansible V ault encrypts what must live in Git. ▸ HOW IT WORKS — E n c rypt , s c ope , inje c t Vault: ansible-vault encrypt|decrypt|view|edit|rekey per file; encrypt_string for inline values. Multiple vault IDs ( --vault-id prod@prompt ) separate environments. At run, password comes from prompt, file ( --vault-password-file ), or CI secret → file. no_log: true on secret-touching tasks suppresses output. Become: become: true + become_user + become_method: sudo (or su , runas on Windows). Scope narrowly: play default become: false , escalate only tasks needing root. --ask-become-pass for interactive sudo password; in CI use NOP ASSWD scoped sudoers or ephemeral privilege. - name: Read app status

▶ CHAPTER 1 0 · SECURITY ( CONT . ) VAULT · BECOME · SECRETS 8 MIN ▸ SUDO PITFALLS — P rivilege side : sudoers a nd b e c ome identity Most Ansible failures on Linux are not Ansible bugs — they are privilege, ownership, or interpreter mismatches. Learn the five usual suspects. 1. Sudoer s scope. Grant the automation user exactly what plays need, nothing more: ansible ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/systemctl *, /usr/bin/apt-get *, /usr/bin/yum * Blanket ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD: ALL works in labs and horrifies auditors; passworded sudo needs --ask-become-pass (interactive) or CI-managed credentials. Old RHEL/CentOS images also enforce Defaults requiretty — sudo over non- interactive SSH fails until that line is removed for the automation user. 2. Become identity . become_user decides *who you become*, default root . Database tasks often need the service account instead: - name: Vacuum app database community.postgresql.postgresql_query: query: VACUUM ANALYZE become: true become_user: postgres P rodu c tion · V ol 3 5 ok c h a nged f a iled = 0 TOC

▶ CHAPTER 1 0 · SECURITY ( CONT . ) VAULT · BECOME · SECRETS 8 MIN ▸ SUDO PITFALLS — H ost side : ownership , SEL inux , interpreter 3. Owner ship and modes. Files created by a root-run task belong to root. Serve them to an app user and reads fail: - name: Deploy app config ansible.builtin.template: src: app.conf.j2 dest: /etc/app/app.conf owner: app group: app mode: '0640' Always set owner/group/mode on security-relevant files; verify with a second task using ansible.builtin.stat when the service is picky. 4. SELinux cont exts. On enforcing systems, correct mode with wrong context still denies: ansible web -i inventory.ini -m ansible.builtin.command -a "getenforce" # Enforcing? ansible web -i inventory.ini -m ansible.builtin.command -a "ls -Z /etc/app/" Fix with community.general.sefcontext + restorecon , or ansible.posix.selinux booleans ( httpd_can_network_connect is the classic) — never blanket setenforce 0 in production. 5. Python int erpreter. Modules execute in Python on the target. Minimal images lack it, or ship two versions: [web:vars] ansible_python_interpreter=/usr/bin/python3 Symptom MODULE FAILURE: /bin/sh: python: command not found → install python3 via a raw bootstr

▶ CHAPTER 1 0 · SECURITY ( CONT . ) VAULT · BECOME · SECRETS 8 MIN ▸ PRACTICAL — E n c rypt a nd run without le a king COMMAND ──────────────────────── ansible-vault encrypt_string 's3cr3t-db-pass' --name 'vault_db_password' Expected: vault_db_password: !vault | $ANSIBLE_VAULT;1.1;AES256... — paste into group_vars/prod/vault.yml , commit safely. COMMAND ──────────────────────── ansible-playbook -i inventory.ini site.yml --ask-vault-pass --check --diff Why it matters: proves encrypted vars decrypt at run and dry-run shows structure without exposing values (with no_log: true ). Common failure: Attempting to decrypt but no vault secrets found → password file path wrong or -- vault-id label mismatch. ansible-vault view group_vars/prod/vault.yml # read without decrypting to disk ansible-vault edit group_vars/prod/vault.yml # decrypt, edit, re-encrypt in one step ansible-vault rekey group_vars/prod/vault.yml # rotate the password on existing files view for inspection, edit for changes, rekey for rotation — the file stays encrypted at every step except inside the editor. ▶ CHAPTER 1 0 · SECURITY ( CONT . ) VAULT · BECOME · SECRETS 8 MIN ▸ WHAT CAN FAIL SYMPTOM LIKELY CAUSE PREVENTION no vault secrets found Missing --ask-vault-pass / wrong password file CI secret → file → --vault-password-file ; test locally with prompt first Failed to escalate privilege sudoers denies or password needed Scoped NOP ASSWD for automation user; --ask-become- pass interactively Secret in logs Task echoes var without no_log no_log: true on secret tasks; audit with --check -vv in safe env Vault + HashiCorp V ault confused Same word, different tools Ansible V ault = encrypted files in repo; HCP V ault = lookup at run ( community.hashi_vault ) [ GOTCHA ] Encrypting a file does not fix over-broad privilege. V ault protects secrets at rest; become scoping protects hosts at run. Do both — one without the other leaves half the attack surface open. ▸ REAL - WORLD CONNECTION TLS key rotation: operator runs ansible-vault rekey per environment file, commits re-encrypted vault, opens PR showing only !vault blobs changed. Set become: false at play, become: true only on privileged task → V erify least-privilege scoping. CI ا وفي ً نفسها محلي molecule و lint 6+ ت إصدارات ّ ا. ثب ً ا متنكر ً ر سوب ّ عد ُ وي ansible-lint · --check --diff · Molecule · changed=0 · verify ▸ WHAT — T hree qu a lity g a tes ansible-lint enforces style, FQCN, and common mistakes statically. --check --diff dry-runs a playbook against real inventory without changing it. Molecule tests roles in ephemeral containers or VMs (create → converge → verify → destroy). THREE GATES BEFORE CI TRUSTS A ROLE LINT style + FQCN → CHECK + DIFF blast radius → MOLECULE converge twice → CI same gat es ansible-lint site.yml ansible-playbook -i inventories/staging site.yml --check --diff molecule test Molecule cycle: create (ephemeral host) → converge (apply role) → verify (assert state) → destroy . ▶ CHAPTER 1 1 · QUALITY ( CONT . ) LINT · CHECK · MOLECULE 7 MIN ▸ HOW IT WORKS — S t a ti c , dry - run , ephemer a l Lint: rule-based ( yaml , fqcn , name[prefix] , no-changed-when ). Pin ansible-lint 6+ in dev requirements; ansible-lint --fix for safe auto-fixes. Check mode: modules report would-change without acting ( --check ); --diff shows file/service deltas. Command/shell tasks skip check unless check_mode: true is handled — another reason to prefer modules. Molecule: molecule init role acme.web -d docker ; molecule.yml defines platform, provisioner ( ansible_playbook ), verifier ( ansible asserts). verify.yml asserts converged state: - name: Verify hosts: all tasks: - name: Nginx is running ansible.builtin.assert: that: - "'nginx' in ansible_facts.services" ▸ PRACTICAL — Ga te a role lo ca lly COMMAND ──────────────────────── ansible-lint roles/web/ && ansible-playbook -i inventories/staging site.yml --check --diff Meaning: static rules, then dry-run delta. Expected: lint clean, --diff shows only intended file lines. Any unexpected changed line blocks the commit. COMMAND ──────────────────────── molecule test Expected: create → converge (changed) → converge (ok, idempotent

▶ CHAPTER 1 1 · QUALITY ( CONT . ) LINT · CHECK · MOLECULE 7 MIN ▸ WHAT CAN FAIL SYMPTOM LIKELY CAUSE PREVENTION fqcn[action-core] lint errors Short module names ( copy , template ) FQCN everywhere; ansible-lint --fix once, then enforce --check shows nothing but real run changes command / shell tasks skip check mode Prefer modules; add check_mode: true handling or changed_when Molecule verify fails Role converged but assertion wrong Assert observable state (service, file, port), not task output Second converge still changed Non-idempotent content (timestamp, random) Remove volatile rendering; retest until changed=0 [ GOTCHA ] A green molecule run whose second converge still reports CHANGED is a failed idempotence test wearing a passing disguise. Gate on changed=0, not just exit code. ▸ REAL - WORLD CONNECTION PR pipeline: lint (30s) → check/diff against staging inventory (2min, artifact of --diff ) → molecule (5min). R eviewer approves the --diff artifact, not a description. Merge to main triggers staging converge; production requires manual approval + same gates with prod inventory in check mode. ▸ LAB — Ob serve / E xe c ute / V erify Objective: red → green quality loop. ▶ CHAPTER 1 1 · QUALITY ( CONT . ) LINT · CHECK · MOLECULE 7 MIN Failure drill: add {{ ansible_date_time.iso8601 }} to template → molecule second converge stays changed → remove volatile → green. ▸ I nterview c he c k Interview What does each gat e prove that the other s do not ? Lint proves style/FQCN correctness statically. Check/diff proves blast radius against real inventory without changing it. Molecule proves the role converges to testable state twice (idempotent) in a clean ephemeral host. [ NEXT ] Quality gates pass locally. ▶ CHAPTER 1 2 · DELIVERY CI / CD — COMMIT TO FLEET 9 MIN   D elivery ي ب ر ع ح ر ش : P rodu c tion و على check --diff ، معاينة Ephemeral يع، اختبار بأمان: فحص سر Fleet يقود Git push كل دفع واستر اتيجيتا serial/forks ) Production على Rolling ، اعتماد يدوي، ثم تقارب Staging Inventory aws_ec2 ا )مثل إضافة ً بنى ديناميكي ُ الواسع ي Inventory . CI من أسرار Vault ( مع كلمات سر linear/fr ee . عند العطل اقرأ ansible-inv entory --graph --v ars ، والفحص المسبق الدائم group_vars ( وطبقات . We start with an existential question: why do we bother logging into every server manually? The answer begins in Chapter 1 — Intro : Ansible is an Automation tool, Open-Source , Agentless , with simple YAML syntax, a Declarative approach, and safe repeatability — Idempotent . Then in Chapter 2 — Architecture we see the whole picture in just two components: a Control Node whispering over an SSH Connection with a Public/Private Key Pair to the Managed Nodes (Ubuntu / CentOS / DB). In Chapter 4 — Use Cases we tour the three domains: Configuration Management , Infrastructure Provisioning (where the Terraform conversation happens), and Network Automation . Now the practical gear: in Chapter 5 — Installation we install on macOS, Ubuntu, Pip and WSL, and set up the VS Code extensions. In Chapter 6 — SSH Keys we generate the Key Pair with ssh-keygen and pu

CHAPTER 01 烙 Intro — What is Ansible?  6 MIN Ansible is an Open-Source Automation tool used primarily for two things: 1️⃣ Configuration Management Managing settings — installing and updating software and configuring files across your servers. 2️⃣ Infrastr ucture Provisioning Building and preparing infrastructure — creating servers and cloud resources. ▸ TASK [Ansible 's Four Cor e Featur es] the four pillars 1.1 Agentless  No need to install any software or Agents on the target Managed Nodes .  Connection happens over SSH (on Linux systems) or WinRM/SSH (on Windows systems).  The only requirement on Linux servers is a Python environment. 1.2 Simple S yntax All configurations and automation scenarios are written in YAML — a language that is very simple to read and write, easy to learn and execute. No complex brackets, no semicolons; just spaces and order. 1.3 Declarativ e Approach You define the Desired State in the YAML file — like: "I want Apache and Git installed" — and Ansible executes the steps needed to reach that state on its own. It also supports the Imperative Approach when using Ad-hoc Commands . 1.4 Idempot ency ♻ Running the same script multiple times in a row change

CHAPTER 02  Architecture — Two Components  5 MIN Ansible's architecture consists of two main components — deliberate simplicity that is the secret of its power. [ Architecture — the two components and the channel ] Control Node Laptop / Linux Ser ver — Ansible liv es here ━━━ SSH Connection ── ► Managed Node Ubuntu / CentOS / DB The channel: a Public/Pr ivate Key Pair — secured connection, no passwords. 2.1 Control Node The machine or server where Ansible is installed, and through which the DevOps engineer runs commands and Playbooks . It can be a personal laptop or a Linux server in a lab or the cloud. 2.2 Managed Nodes (T argets) The servers targeted for applying changes and configurations. They receive instructions over SSH and execute them without needing Agents installed — that's why the architecture is called Agentless. [ KEY IDEA ] Notice what doesn't exist: no central database, no daemon constantly running on the targets, no agent to update. Ansible connects when needed, executes, then leaves. The footprint on Managed Nodes = zero. ▸ TASK [Component Map] who does what Component What is it? What's installed on it? Its role Control Node Laptop / Linux Server Ansible (only)

CHAPTER 03 ⚖ Comparison — Manual vs Bash vs Ansible  6 MIN Imagine you're an engineer managing 3 Linux servers with different distributions — Ubuntu, CentOS, Alpine — and you want to install Nginx on all of them. Three paths are open to you, and the difference between them is a whole philosophy: Aspect  Manual  Bash Scripts ▶ Ansible How it w orks SSH into every server and run commands by hand. Write a Bash script that detects the OS and runs the commands. Write one simple Y AML file defining the Desired S tate for everyone. Speed & effor t Slow and full of mistakes. Centralized but requires high scripting expertise. Fast, centralized, and Simple S yntax. Idempot ency Not available — manual double- checking. Not automatic — conditions written by hand. Automatically suppor ted ✓ Distribution suppor t Requires knowing every distro's commands ( apt , yum , apk ). Requires writing if/else for every OS. Modules handle all distr os automatically ✓ [ ASIDE · The paradox ] Notice that Bash scripts are smarter than Manual — but they accumulate: every new distribution = a new if/else branch, every update = reviewing every script. Ansible flips the equation: you don't write how to execute

CHAPTER 04  Use Cases — Where Ansible Shines  5 MIN Three major arenas where Ansible works today — the first is the most famous, the second carries a well-known industry debate. 4.1 Configuration Management The most famous and important use: installing and updating Packages , adjusting Files , and updating Servers from one place — whether the servers sit in a local Datacenter or on the Cloud. Hundreds of servers, one command. 4.2 Infrastr ucture Provisioning Creating and destroying cloud resources ( EC2, S3, Containers ) through the APIs of cloud services (AWS, Azure, GCP). [ ASIDE · Industry note ] Many people prefer using Terrafor m for Provisioning (building the infrastructure) and Ansible for Configuration Management (managing what's inside the servers). Division of labor: the contractor builds the house, the technician wires the electricity.   4.3 Network Aut omation Configuring and managing Routers , Switches , and Firewalls programmatically through automation protocols — instead of logging into every network device by hand through its interface. ▸ TASK [The Quick Decision Map] which tool when? Your task Right tool Why Install Nginx on 20 servers Ansible Configuration ins

CHAPTER 05 ⚙ Installation — Setup on Every OS  5 MIN Golden rule before we start: Ansible is installed only on the Control Node — a rule with no exceptions. Pick your path by OS:  macOS — Homebr ew $ brew install ansible  Ubuntu / Debian — apt $ sudo apt update && sudo apt install ansible -y  Any OS — Py thon Pip $ pip3 install ansible 犯 Windows — WSL Use WSL (Windows Subsystem for Linux) to run Ubuntu inside Windows and install Ansible on it naturally — then apply the Ubuntu command above. ▸ TASK [Verify the Installation] it works $ ansible --version ansible [core 2.16.3] config file = /etc/ansible/ansible.cfg python version = 3.10.12 A version number appeared = installation succeeded and you're ready. ▸ TASK [R ecommended V S Code Ext ensions] editor setup YAML Extension — Red Hat Ansible Extension — Red Hat Syntax highlighting and validation inside the editor — catches Indentation errors before they reach a Run. [ WATCH OUT ] Common mistake: installing Ansible on the Managed Nodes "just in case." Useless — they only receive commands over SSH. Installation belongs to the Control Node alone. [ DEBUG ] pip3 install is the shared option for every OS — especially useful if your d

CHAPTER 06 · PLAY  SSH Keys — Passwordless Secure Setup  8 MIN For the Control Node to connect to the Managed Nodes and execute instructions automatically , the connection should be set up over SSH keys — the Public/Private Key Pair . [ Play — three steps and the connection is done ] 1️⃣ ssh-keygen generate the Pair ── ► 2️⃣ ssh-copy-id push the Public K ey ── ► 3️⃣ Test no Password ✅ 6.1 Generat e the K ey Pair on the Contr ol Node $ ssh-keygen -t rsa -b 4096 This creates two files in the ~/.ssh/ folder:  id_rsa — Pr ivate Key The Private Key — kept strictly secret on the Control Node, never shared with anyone, ever.  id_rsa.pub — Public K ey The Public Key — this is the one that gets pushed to the Managed Nodes. Its lock opens nothing. 6.2 Copy the Public K ey to the Managed Node $ ssh-copy-id -i ~/.ssh/id_rsa.pub ubuntu@<MANAGED_NODE_IP> 6.3 Test the P asswordless Connection $ ssh ubuntu@<MANAGED_NODE_IP> Welcome to Ubuntu 22.04 LTS ... # logged in — no password asked ✅ $ exit [ DEBUG · AWS EC2 ] When using A WS EC2 machines, you don't generate a new key — use the .pem Private K ey file provided by A WS to format the first connection (the User is usually ubuntu or ec2-user d

CHAPTER 07 里 Modules — The Execution Units  6 MIN All of Ansible's work depends on Modules — ready-made software tools that perform specific functions. You don't write scripts; you call Modules and hand them the desired State. ▸ TASK [The most famous cor e Modules] know these five Module What it does apt / yum Managing, installing, updating, and removing Packages (depending on the distribution). ping Testing connectivity and readiness between the Control Node and the Managed Nodes. service Managing Services — start, stop, restart. copy Copying files from the Control Node to the Managed Nodes. command / shell Running direct system commands on the servers. There are hundreds of Modules covering almost everything — and you can always refer to the official Ansible Documentation to find the right Module and its options for each task. ▸ TASK [The thr ee Modules y ou'll use fir st] start here ping The first Module you'll try — proves the connection works. The success response is always: "pong" . apt / yum The heart of package management. With state=present it becomes Idempotent automatically. service Controls a Service's life: started , stopped , restarted — plus enabled at boot. [ KEY I

CHAPTER 08  Inventory — Your Server Map  5 MIN The Inventory file is the file that holds the IPs of the Managed Nodes — divided into Groups that you target in commands. ▸ TASK [Example hosts.ini file] inventory example # hosts.ini [web] 192.168.1.101 ansible_user=ubuntu 192.168.1.102 ansible_user=ubuntu [db] 192.168.1.201 ansible_user=ubuntu [ DEBUG · File anatomy ] [web] and [db] = group names in square brackets · the lines under them = member IPs · ansible_user=ubuntu = the SSH user used to connect to that server — defined once here instead of repeated in every command. ▸ TASK [How do w e target?] targeting [web] → 2 Servers [db] → 1 Server all → 3 Servers ansible web ... hits the web servers only · ansible all ... hits everyone · target by group instead of stuffing IPs manually every time. [ KEY IDEA ] The Inventory is the "source of truth" for your infrastructure map: added a server? One line in the file. Changed a user? One edit. Every command and Playbook coming next will refer to this file via -i hosts.ini . [ WATCH OUT ] Group names are strictly case-sensitive: [web] is not [webs] and not [Web] . One wrong letter in targeting = "no matching hosts" — and the error message

CHAPTER 09 ⚡ Ad-hoc Commands — Instant Execution  7 MIN Ad-hoc Commands are used to run a quick task without writing a full Playbook — a single line straight from the terminal. This is the Imperative side we mentioned in Chapter 1. ▸ TASK [The general syntax] anatomy ansible <group_or_all> -i <inventory_file> -m <module_name> -a "<module_arguments>" ▸ TASK [Thr ee practical examples] from ping to install 1️⃣ Test connectivity — ping all servers: $ ansible all -i hosts.ini -m ping 192.168.1.101 | SUCCESS => { "ping" : "pong" } 192.168.1.102 | SUCCESS => { "ping" : "pong" } 192.168.1.201 | SUCCESS => { "ping" : "pong" } 2️⃣ Get the Uptime of web servers — the web group: $ ansible web -i hosts.ini -a "uptime" [ DEBUG ] Smart note: when -m is omitted, the command Module is used by default — that's why we wrote uptime directly in -a without naming a module. 3️⃣ Ensure Nginx is installed on all servers: $ ansible all -i hosts.ini -m apt -a "name=nginx state=present" --become [ KEY IDEA ] --become = root privileges (like sudo) — installation always needs them. And state=present is the language of Idempotency: "make sure it exists" — already exists? Nothing happens at all. [ WATCH OUT ] A

CHAPTER 10  YAML Basics — The Language  7 MIN YAML is a declarative language that depends entirely on Indentation — not a programming language, just an orderly way to describe data. Mastering its rules = writing Playbooks without headaches. [ WATCH OUT · The most important rule ] Never use Tab — always use two Spaces . Mixing T ab with Spaces is the #1 cause of failed Y AML files for beginners, and the error appears far from its real line, making it hard to trace. ▸ TASK [The fir st rule] document start Files always start with three dashes --- — declaring the start of the YAML document: --- ▸ TASK [The thr ee data str uctures] everything is built from these ① Key-Value name: Ahmed Key and value — the simplest structure. ② Dictionar y employee: name: Mohamed age: 30 is_manager: true Dictionary — multiple keys under a parent key. ③ List skills: - Linux - Ansible - Docker List — a dash per item. [ KEY IDEA ] The Playbook we'll write in the next chapter is nothing new — it's exactly a List of Dictionar ies (structure ④ ): each Play is an item in a List, and each T ask inside it is a Dictionary. Whoever understands these three structures understands all of Ansible. [ WATCH OUT ] In th

CHAPTER 11 · PLAY  Playbooks — Write & Run  9 MIN A Playbook is a YAML file containing a set of Plays , and each Play contains a set of Tasks — to execute a complete automation scenario against a specific group of servers. This is Ansible's beating heart. [ Hierarchy ] Playbook site.yml ◂ contains Plays hosts · become ◂ contain Tasks steps ◂ call Modules apt · service ▸ TASK [Example: Playbook t o install & r un Apache] create site.yml --- - name: Install and Start Apache Web Server hosts: web become: yes tasks: - name: Install Apache Package apt: name: apache2 state: present - name: Ensure Apache Service is Running and Enabled service: name: apache2 state: started enabled: yes ▸ TASK [Running the Playbook] execute it $ ansible-playbook -i hosts.ini site.yml PLAY [Install and Start Apache Web Server] TASK [Gathering Facts] ok: [192.168.1.101] TASK [Install Apache Package] changed: [192.168.1.101] TASK [Ensure Apache Service is Running and Enabled] changed: [192.168.1.101] PLAY RECAP 192.168.1.101 : ok=3 changed=2 failed=0 [ DEBUG · Line by line ] hosts: web → target the web group from the Inventory · become: yes → run with root privileges · every T ask = a descriptive Name + a Mo

CHAPTER 11·B 粒 Playbooks — Removal & Results  7 MIN The same power that installs also removes — just by flipping the State. Then we master reading the three result indicators. ▸ TASK [Playbook t o stop & remove Apache] reverse order --- - name: Stop and Remove Apache Web Server hosts: web become: yes tasks: - name: Stop Apache Service service: name: apache2 state: stopped - name: Remove Apache Package apt: name: apache2 state: absent [ KEY IDEA ] The reverse logical order: we stop the Ser vice fir st , then remove the P ackage — deleting a package while its service is running = unpredictable behavior. And the whole secret is in state : present / absent / started / stopped — four values that rule the world. ▸ TASK [R esult indicat ors] the three colors Indicator Color Meaning ok Green The server is already in the Desired S tate — no change was required. changed Yellow The Change was applied successfully to the server. failed Red An Error occurred in the T ask — execution stopped on that server. [ RESCUED · If you see failed ] Read the red T ask name first — it tells you which st ep failed, then the line under it — it tells you why (network? permissions? wrong package name?). 90% of

CHAPTER 12  Roles & Galaxy — Organization & Sharing  7 MIN As automation projects grow, keeping all tasks and instructions in one Playbook file becomes hard to maintain . Ansible Roles give you a standard folder structure to organize the project and split it into Modular & Reusable components. ▸ TASK [The R ole's folder str ucture] role anatomy my_role/ ├── tasks/ # main.yml — the main tasks ├── handlers/ # conditional tasks (Handlers) ├── templates/ # Jinja2 templates ├── files/ # static files to be transferred ├── vars/ # variables specific to the Role ├── defaults/ # default variables (overridable) └── meta/ # info about the Role & dependencies [ KEY IDEA ] A Role = Encapsulation . Instead of a 200-line Playbook, you call a R ole by name — and everyone reading the project understands the structure instantly, because everyone knows this standard layout. ▸ TASK [The Ansible Galaxy platfor m] community hub An official open-source repository that lets you share and download ready-made Roles and Collections built by the Ansible community — to speed up development and automation. Instead of building an Apache Role from scratch: search Galaxy, download, and adjust to your needs. gala

STEPS 1–4  Skeleton · ansible.cfg · Inventory · Defaults  8 MIN 1 Create pr oject sk elet on and folder tr ee $ mkdir -p roles/generic_package/{tasks,handlers,templates,defaults,vars,meta} [ DEBUG · Paths ] Windows: C:\Users\eslam\OneDrive\Desktop\ansible · WSL: /mnt/c/Users/eslam/OneDrive/Desktop/ansible · For Linux permissions: copy to ~/ansible then chmod 644 ansible.cfg — this avoids the "world writable directory" warning on NTFS /mnt/c. 2 Write ansible.cfg [defaults] inventory = inventory.ini roles_path = roles host_key_checking = False retry_files_enabled = False stdout_callback = yaml private_key_file = /home/eslam/.ssh/id_ed25519 [privilege_escalation] become = True become_method = sudo become_ask_pass = False 3 Write inv entory.ini [web] web1 ansible_host=192.168.1.10 ansible_user=ubuntu web-server1 ansible_host=98.88.29.132 ansible_user=ubuntu [local] localhost ansible_connection=local [web:vars] ansible_become= true 4 Write role defaults — r oles/gener ic_p ackage/defaults/main.yml Lowest-priority variables — easy to override: --- package_name: nginx service_name: "{{ package_name }}" service_state: started service_enabled: true package_state: present app_port: 80 temp

STEPS 5–7 ⚙ vars Lock · Tasks · Handlers  8 MIN 5 Write role v ars — r oles/gener ic_p ackage/v ars/main.yml High-priority lock — commented out = nothing locked in this lab, so playbook vars win: --- # package_name: nginx # service_name: nginx [ WATCH OUT ] Uncomment those two lines and nothing in the playbook can ov erride them — vars/ beats playbook vars in precedence. That's the lock's power and its danger: use it only when a value must never be tuned. 6 Write role tasks — tasks/main.yml (order matt ers) --- - name: Update apt cache (Debian/Ubuntu) apt: update_cache: yes cache_valid_time: 3600 when: ansible_os_family == "Debian" - name: Install package {{ package_name }} package: name: "{{ package_name }}" state: "{{ package_state }}" notify: Restart service - name: Ensure service {{ service_name }} is {{ service_state }} and enabled={{ service_enabled }} service: name: "{{ service_name }}" state: "{{ service_state }}" enabled: "{{ service_enabled }}" when: service_name is defined and service_name | length > 0 ignore_errors: true 1️⃣ apt cache (Debian only, valid 1h) → 2️⃣ install {{ package_name }} with {{ package_state }} , notify Restart → 3️⃣ service task guarded by when so

STEPS 8–10  Templates · meta · site.yml  8 MIN 8 Write the thr ee t emplat es app.c onf.j2 — nginx-specific config when package_name == "nginx" , generic comment otherwise: {% if package_name == "nginx" %} user www-data; worker_processes auto; pid /run/nginx.pid; events { worker_connections {{ worker_connections | default (1024) }}; } http { sendfile on; include /etc/nginx/mime.types; default_type application/octet-stream; server { listen {{ app_port | default (80) }}; root /var/www/html; index index.html; location / { try_files $uri $uri/ =404; } } } {% else %} # Generic config for {{ package_name }} {% endif %} index.html.j2 — styled landing page showing package name, service name, host, port, and a live "Service Active & Enabled" status badge (gradient CSS, info boxes, pulse animation). nginx.conf.j2 — plain distro-style variant using worker_connections | default(1024) and app_port | default(80) . 9 Write role metadata — meta/main.yml --- galaxy_info: author: ansible description: Generic package installer - install any package (nginx, apache2, redis, etc.) license: MIT min_ansible_version: 2.9 platforms: - name: Ubuntu versions: [focal, jammy] - name: Debian versions: [bullsey

STEPS 11–13 離 Check · Dry Run · Real Run  8 MIN 11 Syntax and inv entory checks $ ansible-playbook site.yml -i inventory.ini --syntax-check $ ansible -i inventory.ini all --list-hosts $ ansible-inventory -i inventory.ini --graph ① Playbook parses without errors · ② every host listed · ③ groups render as [web] / [local] trees. 12 Dry run — no changes, show diff $ ansible-playbook site.yml -i inventory.ini --limit localhost --check --diff -v Expected: install/template/index tasks report changed (dry), the config template task reports skipping — because template_enabled: false . 13 Real r un # localhost with sudo prompt $ ansible-playbook site.yml -i inventory.ini --limit localhost --ask-become-pass -v # as root in WSL (no password) $ sudo ansible-playbook site.yml -i inventory.ini --limit localhost -v [ PROOF · Run it TWICE ] The second run must report ok everywhere — idempot ency pr oof . First run: changed (things installed) · second run: ok (nothing left to do). If the second run still says changed, something in the tasks is non-idempotent — fix before continuing. [ The three-gate testing ladder ] ① syntax-check parses ✓ ── ► ② --check --diff predicts, touches nothing ── ► ③ real

STEPS 14–15 ✅ Verify nginx ·  Prove Reusability  7 MIN 14 Verify nginx — six ways $ service nginx status # must be active (running) $ ss -tlnp | grep 80 # port 80 listening $ nginx -t # config test ok $ curl -s http://localhost/ | head -20 # styled index page $ cat /var/www/html/index.html $ curl -s http://127.0.0.1/ -H "Host: eslam.com" | head # vhost test 15 Prove reusability — a second p ackage, zer o role edits - role: generic_package vars: package_name: redis-server service_name: redis-server template_enabled: false Same role, different vars — redis installs. The role code was never touched . That's Objective 2 closed. [ Objective 4 — what green looks like ] service: active (running) ss: port 80 LISTEN nginx -t: ok curl: styled page ✓ [ KEY IDEA ] Step 14 is deliberately six checks, not one: service aliv e , por t bound , config v alid , cont ent ser ved , file landed , vhost answ ers . Each proves a different layer — systemd, network, syntax, rendering, file placement, name-based routing. One green curl alone could hide a broken config. [ DEBUG · The vhost test ] -H "Host: eslam.com" fakes the browser's Host header without DNS. It tests name-based routing locally — the answ

DEEP DIVE 溺 Variable Precedence + Role Anatomy  7 MIN Objective 3's trickiest concept: who wins when the same variable is set in several places? Ansible's answer is a precedence ladder — and this role uses every rung of it. [ The precedence ladder — lowest to highest ] defaults/ LOWEST — the fallb ack ◄ loses to vars/ HIGH — the lock ◄ loses to playbook r ole v ars: the tuning ◄ loses to -e extra v ars HIGHEST In this lab: defaults set nginx/80 · site.yml's role vars: confirm them · vars/ is commented out (the lock is open) · and -e could flip anything at run time. A The r ole's anat omy — folder by folder , in this pr oject Folder In this task tasks/ Cache update (Debian-only) · install via package · service guard · template/index deploys handler s/ Restart + R eload — once at end of play, only if notified, both ignore_errors templat es/ app.conf.j2 (nginx if/fork) · index.html.j2 (styled page) · nginx.conf.j2 (distro variant) defaults/ The 8 tunables — including service_name referencing package_name vars/ The high-precedence lock — commented out in this lab meta/ galaxy_info: author, MIT license, Ubuntu/Debian platforms, tags · dependencies: [] ▸ TASK [The exper iment y ou can r

DEEP DIVE  The Ansible Concepts — All in Play  6 MIN Objective 3 requires every concept "used correctly." Here's the map: each concept, where it lives in this project, and the rule it demonstrates. Concept Where it lives here The rule it proves Variables pr iority defaults/main.yml · vars/main.yml · site.yml vars: · potential -e defaults lowest → -e highest; vars/ = the lock (page 11) Handler s handlers/main.yml — R estart + R eload, notified by the install task Run once at end o f play , only if notified · ignore_errors so one bad service doesn't abort Templat es (Jinja2) app.conf.j2 (if/fork by package) · index.html.j2 (styled page) · nginx.conf.j2 {{ var }} holes + {% if %} logic + | default(1024) fallbacks Idempot ency The whole run — proven in S tep 13 Run twice → second reports ok , not changed Conditionals when: ansible_os_family == "Debian" · when: service_name is defined... · template_enabled | bool Guards make one role behave differently per OS, package, and flag Loose coupling Role code contains zero package names Everything arrives via variables (Objective 2) Role conv ention The standard 7-folder tree + meta Any engineer navigates it without a guide [ DEBUG · Reading

OBJECTIVE 5 ✅ The Expected Result — Proven  the four checks "Verified with the full command loop" — here is what each of the four gates looks like when it's green:   ✔ 1 · syntax-check p asses $ ansible-playbook site.yml -i inventory.ini --syntax-ch playbook: site.yml No errors — the YAML and structure parse cleanly. ✔ 2 · dr y-run shows expect ed counts $ ansible-playbook ... --check --diff -v changed: install / index tasks skipping: config template (template_enabled: false) Predicts changes without touching the system. ✔ 3 · r eal r un installs + star ts $ ansible-playbook site.yml ... changed: Install package nginx changed: Ensure service nginx... PLAY RECAP — second run: ok=N changed=0 failed=0 First run applies; second run proves idempotent. ✔ 4 · curl r etur ns the styled p age $ curl -s http://localhost/ | head -20

...Deployed via generic_package...

package · host · service · port shown The rendered index.html.j2, served live by nginx. ▸ TASK [The full gr een bo ard] all objectives at once O1 structure ✓ O2 generic ✓ O3 concepts ✓ O4 nginx proof ✓ O5 verified ✓ Five green chips = task complete. Any red → the T roubleshooting table (page 15) is ordered by likeliho

SECTION 05  Completion Checklist ☑ all 6 or it's not done The task's own completion gate. Tick every box — a single unchecked one means the task isn't finished, no matter how green the runs look. ☑ Syntax check ansible-playbook --syntax-check returns playbook: site.yml without errors. ☑ Idempot ent dr y + r eal r un Dry run --check --diff shows changed on first run, ok on second — the idempotency proof. ☑ Ser vice is liv e service nginx status shows active (running) . ☑ The styled p age ser ves curl http://localhost/ returns the styled page from index.html.j2 . ☑ Reusability pr oven Same role installs a second package (redis, apache2...) with only var changes . ☑ Everything explained and committ ed ansible.cfg , inventory.ini , site.yml , roles/generic_package/* — all explained and committed to git . [ KEY IDEA ] Read the six boxes as the task's definition o f done — structure, idempotency, service, content, reuse, version control. The last box matters most and fails most often: a working project that isn't in git doesn't satisfy the spec. [ DEBUG · Suggested commit ] git add -A && git commit -m "generic_package role: install+configure any package via vars; nginx deploy verified;

SECTION 06  Troubleshooting — Symptom → Cause → Fix  rescue kit Five failures this task actually produces, each with its root cause and exact fix — ordered by how likely you are to hit them: Symptom Cause Fix config file = None + "world writable directory" warning /mnt/c NTFS mounted 777 Copy project to ~/ansible , chmod 644 ansible.cfg , run with ANSIBLE_CONFIG=~/ansible/ansible.cfg sudo: a password is required become needs sudo Add --ask-become-pass — or run wsl --user root / sudo curl still shows the old eslam.com page eslam.com vhost is the default site Role already writes /var/www/eslam/index.html ; enable default site: sudo ln -s /etc/nginx/sites- available/default /etc/nginx/sites-enabled/ Handler "R estart service" fails on a non-service package That package has no service ignore_errors: true on handlers (already set) — or set service_name: "" to skip the service task entirely Role not found Wrong roles_path Confirm roles_path = roles in ansible.cfg — and that the role directory name matches the playbook reference [ WATCH OUT · The #1 trap, expanded ] The /mnt/c issue is environmental, not code: OneDrive + NTFS makes everything 777, and Ansible refuses t o tr ust it for c

texts: R E D L I N E D A Y L I G H T · A U T O M A T I O N H A N D B O O K The Complete Guide to Learning Ansible Your complete reference to Ansible — the Architecture, installing on every OS, setting up SSH K eys, Modules and the Inventory, Ad-hoc Commands, Y AML fundamentals, full Playbooks with result reading, and a deep dive into R oles, Templates, Handlers and the Galaxy platform. Based on the course by the Cloud Code channel — transcribed, corrected, expanded, and organized into a complete written reference. By Nabawy AUTHOR & COMPILER REDLINE EDITION Daylight · A4-Fix ed SSH Secur e Access YAML Playbook Language Roles Deep Div e  ▶ _ A G E N T L E S S · D E C L A R A T I V E · I D E M P O T E N T — V 9 E N · B Y N A B A W Y

CONTENTS  Table of Contents 12 chapters + extras  The Map — Executive Summary 3 01 Intro — What is Ansible? 4 02 Architecture — T wo Components 5 03 Comparison — Manual vs Bash vs Ansible 6 04 Use Cases — Where Ansible Shines 7 05 Installation — Every OS 8 06 SSH Keys — P asswordless Access 9 07 Modules — The Execution Units 10 08 Inventory — Y our Server Map 11 09 Ad-hoc Commands — Instant Execution 12 10 YAML Basics — The Language 13 11 Playbooks — Write & Run 14 11·b Playbooks — R emoval & R esults 15 12 Roles — The Concept & Anatomy 16 12·b Templates & Handlers 17 12·c Ansible Galaxy — Use & Share 18  Test Yourself — 12 Questions 19 ✅ Answer K ey 20  Cheat Sheet 21 ▸ TASK [Status Color Legend] how to read results ok — ser ver alr eady in the desir ed stat e, no change changed — a change was applied successfully failed — a task err ored out RED — headings & structur e (visual identity) [ DEBUG ] How to use this book : 12 connected chapters — each opens from the previous and sets up the next. The R oles topic gets a full three-page deep dive (concept → templates & handlers → Galaxy hands-on), because that's where beginners stall. Every line from the source course is here — co

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY  The Map — The Whole Route start here Before touching a single command, here's the whole story — every sentence below is a link that takes you to its chapter. We start with an existential question: why do we bother logging into every server manually? The answer begins in Chapter 1 — Intro : Ansible is an Automation tool, Open-Source , Agentless , with simple YAML syntax, a Declarative approach, and safe repeatability — Idempotent . Then in Chapter 2 — Architecture we see the whole picture in just two components: a Control Node whispering over an SSH Connection with a Public/Private Key Pair to the Managed Nodes (Ubuntu / CentOS / DB). In Chapter 3 — Comparison we weigh Ansible against the Manual way and Bash scripts on 3 different-distribution servers to install Nginx. In Chapter 4 — Use Cases we tour the three domains: Configuration Management , Infrastructure Provisioning , and Network Automation . Now the practical gear: Chapter 5 — Installation on every OS, then Chapter 6 — SSH Keys — the foundation every automation stands on. In Chapter 7 — Modules we meet the execution units, in Chapter 8 — Inventory we map our servers, and in Chapter 9 — Ad-hoc Commands we

CHAPTER 01 烙 Intro — What is Ansible?  6 MIN Ansible is an Open-Source Automation tool used primarily for two things: 1️⃣ Configuration Management Managing settings — installing and updating software and configuring files across your servers. 2️⃣ Infrastr ucture Provisioning Building and preparing infrastructure — creating servers and cloud resources. ▸ TASK [Ansible 's Four Cor e Featur es] the four pillars 1.1 Agentless  No need to install any software or Agents on the target Managed Nodes .  Connection happens over SSH (on Linux systems) or WinRM/SSH (on Windows systems).  The only requirement on Linux servers is a Python environment. 1.2 Simple S yntax All configurations and automation scenarios are written in YAML — a language that is very simple to read and write, easy to learn and execute. No complex brackets, no semicolons; just spaces and order. 1.3 Declarativ e Approach You define the Desired State in the YAML file — like: "I want Apache and Git installed" — and Ansible executes the steps needed to reach that state on its own. It also supports the Imperative Approach when using Ad-hoc Commands . 1.4 Idempot ency ♻ Running the same script multiple times in a row change

CHAPTER 02  Architecture — Two Components  5 MIN Ansible's architecture consists of two main components — deliberate simplicity that is the secret of its power. [ Architecture — the two components and the channel ] Control Node Laptop / Linux Ser ver — Ansible liv es here ━━━ SSH Connection ── ► Managed Node Ubuntu / CentOS / DB The channel: a Public/Pr ivate Key Pair — secured connection, no passwords. 2.1 Control Node The machine or server where Ansible is installed, and through which the DevOps engineer runs commands and Playbooks . It can be a personal laptop or a Linux server in a lab or the cloud. 2.2 Managed Nodes (T argets) The servers targeted for applying changes and configurations. They receive instructions over SSH and execute them without needing Agents installed — that's why the architecture is called Agentless. [ KEY IDEA ] Notice what doesn't exist: no central database, no daemon constantly running on the targets, no agent to update. Ansible connects when needed, executes, then leaves. The footprint on Managed Nodes = zero. ▸ TASK [Component Map] who does what Component What is it? What's installed on it? Its role Control Node Laptop / Linux Server Ansible (only)

CHAPTER 03 ⚖ Comparison — Manual vs Bash vs Ansible  6 MIN Imagine you're an engineer managing 3 Linux servers with different distributions — Ubuntu, CentOS, Alpine — and you want to install Nginx on all of them. Three paths, and the difference is a whole philosophy: Aspect  Manual  Bash Scripts ▶ Ansible How it w orks SSH into every server and run commands by hand. Write a Bash script that detects the OS and runs the commands. Write one simple Y AML file defining the Desired S tate for everyone. Speed & effor t Slow and full of mistakes. Centralized but requires high scripting expertise. Fast, centralized, and Simple S yntax. Idempot ency Not available — manual double- checking. Not automatic — conditions written by hand. Automatically suppor ted ✓ Distribution suppor t Requires knowing every distro's commands ( apt , yum , apk ). Requires writing if/else for every OS. Modules handle all distr os automatically ✓ [ ASIDE · The paradox ] Bash scripts are smarter than Manual — but they accumulate: every new distribution = a new if/else branch. Ansible flips the equation: you don't write how to execute — you write what you want, and it knows the How for every distro inside the Modu

CHAPTER 04  Use Cases — Where Ansible Shines  5 MIN Three major arenas where Ansible works today — the first is the most famous, the second carries a well-known industry debate. 4.1 Configuration Management The most famous and important use: installing and updating Packages , adjusting Files , and updating Servers from one place — whether the servers sit in a local Datacenter or on the Cloud. Hundreds of servers, one command. 4.2 Infrastr ucture Provisioning Creating and destroying cloud resources ( EC2, S3, Containers ) through the APIs of cloud services (AWS, Azure, GCP). [ ASIDE · Industry note ] Many prefer Terrafor m for Provisioning and Ansible for Configuration Management. Division of labor: the contractor builds the house, the technician wires the electricity.   4.3 Network Aut omation Configuring and managing Routers , Switches , and Firewalls programmatically through automation protocols — instead of logging into every network device by hand. ▸ TASK [The Quick Decision Map] which tool when? Your task Right tool Why Install Nginx on 20 servers Ansible Configuration inside machines — its first domain Create a VPC and 10 instances on A WS Terrafor m Cloud provisioning ov

CHAPTER 05 ⚙ Installation — Setup on Every OS  5 MIN Golden rule: Ansible is installed only on the Control Node — a rule with no exceptions. Pick your path by OS:  macOS — Homebr ew $ brew install ansible  Ubuntu / Debian — apt $ sudo apt update && sudo apt install ansible -y  Any OS — Py thon Pip $ pip3 install ansible 犯 Windows — WSL Use WSL to run Ubuntu inside Windows and install Ansible on it naturally — then apply the Ubuntu command above. ▸ TASK [Verify the Installation] it works $ ansible --version ansible [core 2.16.3] config file = /etc/ansible/ansible.cfg python version = 3.10.12 ▸ TASK [R ecommended V S Code Ext ensions] editor setup YAML Extension — Red Hat Ansible Extension — Red Hat [ WATCH OUT ] Common mistake: installing Ansible on the Managed Nodes "just in case." Useless — they only receive commands over SSH. Installation belongs to the Control Node alone. [ DEBUG ] pip3 install is the shared option for every OS — especially useful if your distro's package manager ships an outdated version.  EXAM Three install methods + Windows: brew · apt · pip3 · WSL . And "Where is Ansible installed?" — the Contr ol Node only . ⏭ Tool ready — connections need securing: →

CHAPTER 06 · PLAY  SSH Keys — Passwordless Secure Setup  8 MIN For the Control Node to connect to the Managed Nodes and execute instructions automatically , the connection should be set up over SSH keys — the Public/Private Key Pair . [ Play — three steps and the connection is done ] 1️⃣ ssh-keygen generate the Pair ── ► 2️⃣ ssh-copy-id push the Public K ey ── ► 3️⃣ Test no Password ✅ 6.1 Generat e the K ey Pair on the Contr ol Node $ ssh-keygen -t rsa -b 4096 This creates two files in the ~/.ssh/ folder:  id_rsa — Pr ivate Key The Private Key — kept strictly secret on the Control Node, never shared.  id_rsa.pub — Public K ey The Public Key — this is the one that gets pushed to the Managed Nodes. 6.2 Copy the Public K ey to the Managed Node $ ssh-copy-id -i ~/.ssh/id_rsa.pub ubuntu@<MANAGED_NODE_IP> 6.3 Test the P asswordless Connection $ ssh ubuntu@<MANAGED_NODE_IP> Welcome to Ubuntu 22.04 LTS ... # no password asked ✅ $ exit [ DEBUG · AWS EC2 ] On AWS EC2 machines, don't generate a new key — use the .pem Private K ey file provided by A WS for the first connection (User is usually ubuntu or ec2-user ). [ WATCH OUT ] Two common mistakes: copying id_rsa (Private) instead of id_r

CHAPTER 07 里 Modules — The Execution Units  6 MIN All of Ansible's work depends on Modules — ready-made software tools that perform specific functions. You don't write scripts; you call Modules and hand them the desired State. ▸ TASK [The most famous cor e Modules] know these five Module What it does apt / yum Managing, installing, updating, and removing Packages (depending on the distribution). ping Testing connectivity and readiness between the Control Node and the Managed Nodes. service Managing Services — start, stop, restart. copy Copying files from the Control Node to the Managed Nodes. command / shell Running direct system commands on the servers. Hundreds of Modules cover almost everything — always refer to the official Ansible Documentation to find the right Module and its options for each task. ▸ TASK [The thr ee Modules y ou'll use fir st] start here ping The first Module you'll try — proves the connection works. The success response is always: "pong" . apt / yum The heart of package management. With state=present it becomes Idempotent automatically. service Controls a Service's life: started , stopped , restarted — plus enabled at boot. [ KEY IDEA ] The Module hides th

CHAPTER 08  Inventory — Your Server Map  5 MIN The Inventory file is the file that holds the IPs of the Managed Nodes — divided into Groups that you target in commands. ▸ TASK [Example hosts.ini file] inventory example # hosts.ini [web] 192.168.1.101 ansible_user=ubuntu 192.168.1.102 ansible_user=ubuntu [db] 192.168.1.201 ansible_user=ubuntu [ DEBUG · File anatomy ] [web] and [db] = group names in square brackets · the lines under them = member IPs · ansible_user=ubuntu = the SSH user used to connect to that server — defined once here instead of repeated in every command. ▸ TASK [How do w e target?] targeting [web] → 2 Servers [db] → 1 Server all → 3 Servers ansible web ... hits the web servers only · ansible all ... hits everyone · target by group instead of stuffing IPs manually. [ KEY IDEA ] The Inventory is the "source of truth" for your infrastructure map: added a server? One line. Changed a user? One edit. Every command and Playbook coming next refers to this file via -i hosts.ini . [ WATCH OUT ] Group names are strictly case-sensitive: [web] is not [webs] and not [Web] . One wrong letter in targeting = "no matching hosts" — and the error message won't hint at your typo. 

CHAPTER 09 ⚡ Ad-hoc Commands — Instant Execution  7 MIN Ad-hoc Commands run a quick task without writing a full Playbook — a single line straight from the terminal. This is the Imperative side we mentioned in Chapter 1. ▸ TASK [The general syntax] anatomy ansible <group_or_all> -i <inventory_file> -m <module_name> -a "<module_arguments>" ▸ TASK [Thr ee practical examples] from ping to install 1️⃣ Test connectivity — ping all servers: $ ansible all -i hosts.ini -m ping 192.168.1.101 | SUCCESS => { "ping" : "pong" } 192.168.1.102 | SUCCESS => { "ping" : "pong" } 192.168.1.201 | SUCCESS => { "ping" : "pong" } 2️⃣ Get the Uptime of web servers: $ ansible web -i hosts.ini -a "uptime" [ DEBUG ] When -m is omitted, the command Module is used by default — that's why we wrote uptime directly in -a . 3️⃣ Ensure Nginx is installed on all servers: $ ansible all -i hosts.ini -m apt -a "name=nginx state=present" --become [ KEY IDEA ] --become = root privileges (like sudo) — installation always needs them. And state=present is the language of Idempotency: "make sure it exists" — already exists? Nothing happens. [ WATCH OUT ] Ad-hoc or Playbook? Ad-hoc is for a task that's quick and w on't repeat

CHAPTER 10  YAML Basics — The Language  7 MIN YAML is a declarative language depending entirely on Indentation — not a programming language, just an orderly way to describe data. [ WATCH OUT · Most important rule ] Never use Tab — always two Spaces . Mixing them is the #1 cause of failed Y AML files, and the error appears far from its real line. ▸ TASK [The fir st rule] document start Files always start with three dashes --- — declaring the start of the YAML document: --- ▸ TASK [The thr ee data str uctures] everything builds from these ① Key-Value name: Ahmed Key and value — the simplest structure. ② Dictionar y employee: name: Mohamed age: 30 is_manager: true Multiple keys under a parent key. ③ List skills: - Linux - Ansible - Docker A dash per item. [ KEY IDEA ] The Playbook in the next chapter is nothing new — it's exactly a List of Dictionar ies : each Play is an item in a List, each T ask inside is a Dictionary. Understand these three structures and you understand all of Ansible.  EXAM The three golden rules: ① Start with --- · ② Spaces, nev er Tabs · ③ Three structures only: K ey-Value, Dictionar ies, Lists . ⏭ Language in hand — your first real full Playbook: → Chapter 1

CHAPTER 11 · PLAY  Playbooks — Write & Run  9 MIN A Playbook is a YAML file containing a set of Plays , and each Play contains a set of Tasks — executing a complete automation scenario against a specific server group. This is Ansible's beating heart. [ Hierarchy ] Playbook site.yml ◂ contains Plays hosts · become ◂ contain Tasks steps ◂ call Modules apt · service ▸ TASK [Example: Playbook t o install & r un Apache] create site.yml --- - name: Install and Start Apache Web Server hosts: web become: yes tasks: - name: Install Apache Package apt: name: apache2 state: present - name: Ensure Apache Service is Running and Enabled service: name: apache2 state: started enabled: yes ▸ TASK [Running the Playbook] execute it $ ansible-playbook -i hosts.ini site.yml PLAY [Install and Start Apache Web Server] TASK [Gathering Facts] ok: [192.168.1.101] TASK [Install Apache Package] changed: [192.168.1.101] TASK [Ensure Apache Service is Running and Enabled] changed: [192.168.1.101] PLAY RECAP 192.168.1.101 : ok=3 changed=2 failed=0 [ DEBUG · Line by line ] hosts: web → target the web group · become: yes → root privileges · every T ask = descriptive Name + Module + desired State . We don't say "

CHAPTER 11·B 粒 Playbooks — Removal & Results  7 MIN The same power that installs also removes — by flipping the State. Then we master the three result indicators. ▸ TASK [Playbook t o stop & remove Apache] reverse order --- - name: Stop and Remove Apache Web Server hosts: web become: yes tasks: - name: Stop Apache Service service: name: apache2 state: stopped - name: Remove Apache Package apt: name: apache2 state: absent [ KEY IDEA ] Reverse logical order: stop the Ser vice fir st , then remove the P ackage — deleting a package while its service runs = unpredictable behavior. The whole secret is in state : present / absent / started / stopped — four values that rule the world. ▸ TASK [R esult indicat ors] the three colors Indicator Color Meaning ok Green The server is already in the Desired S tate — no change required. changed Yellow The Change was applied successfully. failed Red An Error occurred — execution stopped on that server. [ RESCUED · If you see failed ] Read the red T ask name first — which st ep failed. Then the line under it — why (network? permissions? wrong package name?). 90% of failures are solved from these lines alone.  EXAM ok vs changed is the cor e of Ansib

CHAPTER 12 · PART 1 OF 3  Roles — The Concept & Anatomy  8 MIN As automation projects grow, keeping all tasks and instructions in one Playbook file becomes hard to maintain . Ansible Roles give you a standard folder structure to organize the project and split it into Modular & Reusable components. [ ASIDE · The analogy ] Think of a Playbook as one long recipe scrawled on a single page — works for cooking once. A Role is a recipe car d box : ingredients in one drawer, steps in another, serving notes in a third. Anyone can pick up the box and cook your dish, because everything lives where convention says it should.  12.1 Why Roles exist — the pr oblem they solv e Imagine a Playbook that installs a full web stack: packages, config files, templates, handlers to restart services, variables for different environments. At 300+ lines it becomes unreadable, untestable, and unshareable . Roles split this monolith by concern : "what runs" (tasks), "what gets copied" (files), "what gets rendered" (templates), "what varies" (vars). Each concern lives in its own folder — and Ansible knows where to find each one by convention, no wiring needed. ▸ TASK [The R ole's folder str ucture] role anato

CHAPTER 12·B · PART 2 OF 3  Templates & Handlers — Inside the Folders  10 MIN Two Role folders confuse every beginner: templates/ and handlers/ . Here's both, made concrete with one realistic example — an Apache Role deploying a custom page. 12.3 Templat es — files with holes for v ariables A template is a text file with Jinja2 placeholders — {{ variable }} — inside. CHAPTER 12·C · PART 3 OF 3  Ansible Galaxy — Use & Share Roles  8 MIN Ansible Galaxy is the official open-source repository where the community publishes ready-made Roles and Collections . EXECUTIVE SUMMARY  The Map — The Whole Task start here One Ansible Role, eight steps, one running MariaDB server. Here's the route — every line links to its section. The mission is defined in Section 1 — Objective & End State : automate a complete MariaDB setup so it's repeatable and version-controlled — ending with a custom config under /opt/mariadb , an application database, a dedicated user, and seeded schema. The cast of tools is listed in Section 2 : Ansible as the engine, the community.mysql collection for DB/user management, PyMySQL on the target, and Jinja2 templates for rendering config. The battlefield layout is in Section 3 — Project Structure : a playbook entry point, an inventory, requirements, group_vars for the secret, and the mariadb role holding everything. Then the build itself, in three pages: Steps 1–3 (install packages, enable & start the service, create the config folder), Steps 4–5 (deploy my.cnf + initdb.sql from templates, symlink into the OS config path, restart via handler with a flush), and Steps 6–8 (create the database, create the user with scoped grants, import the seed SQL). Operations: Section 5 — Running It (collection install + the playbook comma

SECTION 01  Objective & End State  4 MIN The mission: automate a complete MariaDB setup on a Linux server using Ansible — so the whole process is repeatable, version-controlled, and doesn't rely on manual steps . [ KEY IDEA ] This isn't "install a database." It's " encode a datab ase setup int o code " — so any server, any time, run once, ends up identical. The value isn't the first run; it's the hundredth run being free. ▸ TASK [The End S tate] what exists when the playbook finishes A running MariaDB server with all four of these: 1️⃣ Custom configuration Deployed from a known location — /opt/mariadb — charset, port, max connections, InnoDB buffer pool. Not hidden in OS default files. 2️⃣ An application datab ase A dedicated database (default: myapp_db ) created only if it doesn't already exist. 3️⃣ A dedicat ed application user (default: myapp_user @ localhost ) with full privileges on that database only — not the whole server. 4️⃣ Initialized schema & seed data The database starts with its tables and initial rows from a versioned SQL script. ▸ TASK [Why this matt ers] manual vs automated ❌ Manual setup SSH in, remember the package names, edit config by hand, restart, create DB

SECTION 02 藺 The Tools — What & Why  5 MIN Six tools carry this task. Knowing why each one exists matters more than knowing their names. Tool Purpose Ansible The automation engine — runs all the steps idempot ently (safe to re-run, changes only what needs changing). community .mysql collection Provides the mysql_db and mysql_user modules for database and user management. community .general collection Supporting modules used alongside the core set. MariaDB The database server itself — version 10.11.x, installed via the OS package manager. PyMySQL The Python library that Ansible's mysql modules need on the tar get host to connect and run SQL. Jinja2 t emplat es Used to render my.cnf and initdb.sql from variables — one template, many environments. mysql client / mysqldump Manual verification, querying, and backups — the human-side tools after automation finishes. ▸ TASK [The tw o most -misunder stood pieces] clarifications  Why PyMySQL on the tar get? Ansible is agentless — but its mysql_db / mysql_user modules execute on the managed node and speak to MariaDB through a Python driver. No PyMySQL → the DB tasks fail with a "python mysql module not found" error, even though MariaDB its

SECTION 03  Project Structure — The Tree  5 MIN Every file in the project, and what it's for. This tree is the architecture: mariadb_project/ ├── playbook.yml # Entry point — runs the mariadb role ├── inventory.ini # Target host(s) ├── requirements.yml # Ansible Galaxy collections needed ├── group_vars/ │ └── db_servers/ │ └── vault.yml.example # Template for storing the DB password securely └── roles/ └── mariadb/ ├── defaults/main.yml # All tunable variables (db name, user, password...) ├── vars/ │ ├── Debian.yml # apt-based package/service names │ └── RedHat.yml # dnf/yum-based package/service names ├── tasks/main.yml # The 8 provisioning steps ├── handlers/main.yml # Restart handler └── templates/ ├── my.cnf.j2 # Config file template └── initdb.sql.j2 # DB init/seed script template ▸ TASK [R eading the tr ee] four things to notice  vars/ split by family Debian.yml vs RedHat.yml — package and service names differ per distro . The role loads the right file per OS, so the same task code works everywhere.  vault.yml.example The .example suffix is deliberate: it's a template to copy into your own (Ansible-Vault-encrypted) file. The real password never enters Git.  Two Jinja2 t

SECTION 04 · PART 1 OF 3 隣 Steps 1–3 — Install · Service · Folder  7 MIN The foundation phase: get MariaDB on the machine, running, and a home ready for its custom config. 1 Install Mar iaDB + PyMySQL The role installs mariadb-server and mariadb-client (Debian) or mariadb-server / mariadb (RedHat) via the OS package manager — plus PyMySQL , so Ansible's mysql modules can connect later in Steps 6–8. The OS-specific package names come from the vars/ Debian.yml / RedHat.yml split. 2 Enable and star t the ser vice The mariadb systemd service is enabled (starts on boot) and started immediately. Both in one task — a fresh server goes from "no database" to "database accepting local connections" in a single step. 3 Create the configuration folder A directory is created at /opt/mariadb to hold the custom config and init script — kept separate from the OS's default config locations . Everything this deployment owns lives in one known place. [ After steps 1–3 — the server state ]  mariadb-server installed +  PyMySQL installed + ⚡ service: enabled + started +  /opt/mariadb/ ready [ KEY IDEA ] Step 1's quiet hero is PyMySQL — installing it now, alongside the packages, means S teps 6–8 won't

SECTION 04 · PART 2 OF 3  Steps 4–5 — Config Deploy + Restart  8 MIN The most interesting pair of steps: render the custom files from templates, make MariaDB actually read them, and restart at exactly the right moment. 4 Deploy the config file and init scr ipt  my.cnf is rendered from templates/my.cnf.j2 into /opt/mariadb/my.cnf — charset, port, max connections, InnoDB buffer pool size, etc.  initdb.sql is rendered from templates/initdb.sql.j2 into /opt/mariadb/initdb.sql .  Because MariaDB doesn't read /opt by default , the role symlinks the config into the distro's real include directory — so the settings actually take effect. [ The symlink bridge — where the config goes per distro ] /opt/mariadb/my.cnf the real file ── symlink ── ► Debian: /etc/mysql/mariadb.conf.d/99-custom.cnf /opt/mariadb/my.cnf ── symlink ── ► RedHat: /etc/my.cn.d/ Same source file, different landing spot per OS family — the vars/ split from Section 3 decides which. 5 Restart MariaDB — via handler , flushed immediat ely The config deployment notifies a handler that restarts the mariadb service — and the playbook flushes handlers immediately so the new configuration is live before the next steps run . SECTION 04 · PART 3 OF 3  Steps 6–8 — DB · User · Seed  8 MIN With MariaDB installed, configured, and freshly restarted — the actual database assets get created. All three steps use the community.mysql collection modules, all three are idempotent. 6 Create the datab ase community.mysql.mysql_db creates the application database — default name myapp_db — if it doesn't already exist . Second run? The database is there → status ok , untouched. 7 Create the user and grant pr ivileges community.mysql.mysql_user creates the application user — default myapp_user @ localhost — and grants ALL PRIVILEGES on the new database only . [ KEY IDEA · Scope matters ] "On the new database only — not on the whole server." The app can fully own its own database but cannot touch mysql.* , other databases, or server settings. Least privilege, enforced at grant time. 8 Initialize the datab ase community.mysql.mysql_db with state: import runs /opt/mariadb/initdb.sql against the new database — creating the starting schema/tables and seeding the initial rows. The SQL itself came from the initdb.sql.j2 template rendered back in Step 4. [ Steps 6–8 — the chain ] 6️⃣ mysql_db create myapp_db ── ► 7️⃣ mysql_use

SECTION 05 ▶ Running It — The Commands  6 MIN Two commands from a fresh clone to a running database. First the terminal, then what every piece means: ▸ TASK [The exact commands] from the project root cd mariadb_project # Install required collections $ ansible-galaxy collection install -r requirements.yml # Run the playbook $ ansible-playbook -i inventory.ini playbook.yml \ --ask-become-pass \ -e mariadb_db_password= 'YourStrongPassword' ▸ TASK [The inv entory note] pointing at your target inventory.ini should point at the target host — two common shapes:  Local t esting localhost ansible_connection=local Runs against the same machine — no SSH involved.  Remote server myserver ansible_host=10.0.0.5 A real hostname/IP — uses standard SSH. ▸ TASK [Ev ery flag decoded] nothing is magic -i inventory.ini which hosts t o run against --ask-become-pass prompts for the sudo p assw ord (p ackage installs need r oot) -e var=value extra-v ar — injects the DB p assw ord int o the run [ DEBUG · The two commands, in order ] Command 1 stocks your control node with the community .mysql and community .general collections (Section 2). Command 2 does the actual work on the target. Skip command 1 → c

SECTION 06 ✅ Verifying the Result  6 MIN A finished playbook proves nothing — a green recap means the tasks ran, not that the outcome is correct. Five checks, each mapping to one end-state promise from Section 1: ▸ TASK [Check 1 — the ser vice is aliv e] end state: running server $ sudo systemctl status mariadb --no-pager ● mariadb.service — MariaDB 10.11.x database server Active: active (running) ▸ TASK [Check 2 — the cust om config actually applied] end state: /opt/mariadb config live $ sudo mysql -e "SHOW VARIABLES LIKE 'character_set_server';" +----------------------+---------+ character_set_server utf8mb4 ← proves the symlinked config loaded ▸ TASK [Checks 3 & 4 — datab ase and user exist] end states: DB + scoped user $ sudo mysql -e "SHOW DATABASES;" myapp_db ← the application database is there $ sudo mysql -e "SHOW GRANTS FOR 'myapp_user'@'localhost';" GRANT ALL PRIVILEGES ON `myapp_db`.* TO ... ← scoped, not server-wide ▸ TASK [Check 5 — seeded data is pr esent] end state: schema + rows $ sudo mysql myapp_db -e "SELECT * FROM app_info;" ...seeded rows appear... ← Step 8's import actually landed [ KEY IDEA ] Each check targets a specific st ep from Section 4: status → S tep

SECTION 07 ➕ Adding New Data — Two Paths  5 MIN There are two legitimate ways to put new data into this database — and they serve different purposes . Knowing which to reach for is the whole lesson. ▸ TASK [Path 1 — one-o ff, via the mysql client] quick, manual, not reproducible $ mysql -u myapp_user -p 'YourStrongPassword' -D myapp_db \ -e "INSERT INTO app_info (key_name, value) VALUES ('app_name', 'MyApp');" Fast for a quick test row or an ad-hoc fix. But: it lives only on this server, in this moment — a rebuilt machine won't have it. ▸ TASK [Path 2 — per manent / r epeatable, via the r ole] the Ansible way Add your CREATE TABLE / INSERT statements to roles/mariadb/templates/initdb.sql.j2 , then rerun the playbook — so the schema stays reproducible on any server it's deployed to : ✏ edit initdb.sql.j2 ── ► ▶ rerun playbook ── ► ✅ schema reproducible everywhere [ KEY IDEA · The decision rule ] Will this data need t o exist on the next ser ver too? Yes → it belongs in initdb.sql.j2 (version-controlled, part of the state). No → the mysql client is fine. Everything reproducible goes in code; everything throwaway stays in the client. SECTION 08  Viewing the Data — 4 Ways  5 MIN "Where is my data?" has four different honest answers — each useful in a different situation, and one of them is a trap. 1️⃣ The seed file — plain t ext $ cat /opt/mariadb/initdb.sql The source that seeded the DB — readable, versioned, rendered from the template. Read this to see wh at was s u ppo s e d t o be c r e at e d . 2️⃣ On-disk st orage — the trap ⚠ /var/lib/mysql/<db_name>/ Binary .ibd files — not human-readable; never edit these directly . This is where the data physically lives, but it belongs to MariaDB, not to you. 3️⃣ Readable full snapshot $ sudo mysqldump myapp_db > myapp_db_backup.sql Schema + data exported as readable SQL — the proper way to capture the complete current state (also your backup move). 4️⃣ Querying dir ectly $ sudo mysql myapp_db -e "SELECT * FROM <table>;" The everyday move — ask the live server a question, get the live answer. ▸ TASK [Choosing a view er] which one when? You want to... Reach for See what the automation intended to create 1️⃣ cat initdb.sql Back up or hand off the full current state 3️⃣ mysqldump Check rows right now 4️⃣ mysql -e "SELECT..." Satisfy curiosity about storage internals 2️

SECTION 09 ⚠ Gotchas — Lessons From the Trench  real errors Three things that actually went sideways while building this task. Each one costs minutes (or hours) the first time — reading them here costs you seconds. [ GOTCHA 1 · Two interpreters, one prompt ] The mysql client and the bash shell are two differ ent command interpreters . SQL pasted into bash — or shell commands pasted into an open mysql session — produces confusing, unrelated errors . Always check the prompt before typing:  $ means b ash Shell commands live here: sudo systemctl... , cat , mysql -e "..." . SQL typed here = syntax error nonsense.  MariaDB [db]> means mysql SQL lives here: SELECT... , SHOW... . Shell commands typed here = ERROR 1064 nonsense. [ GOTCHA 2 · Multi-line SQL ] Multi-line SQL is safest saved to a .sql file and piped in ( mysql ... < file.sql ) rather than pasted interactively. P asting long statements into the client invites partial-line errors, lost semicolons, and copy bugs — the file is repeatable, the paste is a gamble. [ GOTCHA 3 · bind-address = 127.0.0.1 ] The deployed config sets bind-address = 127.0.0.1 — the server only accepts local connections . This is intentional for a dev/loc
