EXECUTIVE SUMMARY The Task — In One Paragraph  5 MIN Provision a public Application Load Balancer in front of two frontend EC2 instances (public subnets) and an internal Application Load Balancer in front of two backend EC2 instances (private subnets). Four custom security groups, two target groups with HTTP health checks, two listeners, four target-group attachments, plus the surrounding VPC plumbing. Use Terraform 1.x with the hashicorp/aws ~> 5.0 provider — exactly the modern arguments from the official docs — and drive dev/staging/prod with workspaces so one codebase ships three environments.  TIER 1 — PUBLIC internet → public ALB → frontend EC2 ×2. SG allows 80/443 from the world. The front door.  TIER 2 — INTERNAL frontend + VPC CIDR → internal ALB → backend EC2 ×2. SG chains by reference. Defense-in-depth. ▣ The route through this walkthrough  Resource Map The full traffic picture — both tiers, SGs, T Gs, attachments — one diagram.  Project Layout 10 files, and wh y each is its own file.  Pin & Switch versions.tf locks providers; providers.tf redirects every API to Floci.  Inputs & Naming 12 tunable knobs; workspace-aware name prefix + common tags.  SG Chain 4 securi

SECTION 01 · THE PICTURE  The Resource Map  5 MIN The whole stack in one diagram. Read it top-down for Tier 1 (public), then the second block for Tier 2 (internal). Every arrow is an SG rule or a TG attachment. internet │ ▼ ┌─────────────────────────┐ │ sg public_alb (80/443) │ └────────────┬────────────┘ ▼ ┌─────────────────────────┐ │ aws_lb.public (public) │ └────────────┬────────────┘ ▼ ┌─────────────────────────┐ │ tg public │ health_check { /, 200 } └────────────┬────────────┘ ▼ ┌─────────────────────────┐ │ attachment → frontend │ │ [0] [1] │ └─────────────────────────┘ sg frontend_ec2 ──80── ▶ ┌─────────────────────────┐ VPC CIDR ──────80── ▶ │ aws_lb.internal (int) │ │ sg internal_alb │ └────────────┬────────────┘ ▼ ┌─────────────────────────┐ │ tg internal │ health_check { /, 200 } └────────────┬────────────┘ ▼ ┌─────────────────────────┐ │ attachment → backend │ │ [0] [1] │ └─────────────────────────┘  THE SHAPE Both tiers are the same quartet — ALB → target group → listener → attachments — differing only in exposure ( internal = false/true ), security group, subnets, and which instance set they point at. Learn one tier, you know both.  COUNT THE ARROWS The SG chain:

SECTION 02 · THE FILES  Project Layout  4 MIN Ten files under live-verify-floci/alb-cluster/ . Each is its own file for a reason: live-verify-floci/alb-cluster/ ├── versions.tf # Terraform + AWS provider pin ├── providers.tf # AWS provider with Floci endpoint switching ├── variables.tf # all declared inputs ├── locals.tf # name_prefix + common_tags ├── main.tf # 18 resources (VPC, subnets, SGs, EC2, ALBs...) ├── outputs.tf # DNS names, TG ARNs, instance IDs ├── terraform.tfvars.example # sample inputs ├── run-alb.sh # one-command deploy across workspaces ├── verify-alb.sh # post-apply smoke test (queries Floci) └── README.md # usage notes TASK [Why each file is its own file] the reviewer's view File Why it's its own file versions.tf Locks Terraform & provider versions — protects the team from drift . providers.tf Floci endpoint switching lives here so the rest of the code never knows whether AWS is real or emulated . variables.tf Every input the next platform engineer might tweak — one place to read the contract. locals.tf name_prefix = "${var.project}-${terraform.workspace}" so every resource names itself correctly per environment. main.tf All 18 resources — VPC plumbing + 4 SGs

SECTION 03 · THE PIN & THE SWITCH  versions.tf + providers.tf ⏱ 7 MIN §3 versions.tf — the pin that makes it portable terraform { required_version = ">= 1.6.0, < 2.0.0" required_providers { aws = { source = "hashicorp/aws" version = "~> 5.0" } } } §4 providers.tf — Floci or real AWS with one variable provider "aws" { region = var.region access_key = "test" secret_key = "test" skip_credentials_validation = true skip_metadata_api_check = true skip_requesting_account_id = true s3_use_path_style = true insecure = true dynamic "endpoints" { for_each = var.floci_endpoint != null ? [1] : [] content { ec2 = var.floci_endpoint elb = var.floci_endpoint elbv2 = var.floci_endpoint iam = var.floci_endpoint sts = var.floci_endpoint s3 = var.floci_endpoint } } }  THE TRICK The dynamic "endpoints" block: when var.floci_endpoint is null the block is empty → real AWS. When it points at Floci → every API the provider might call ( ec2 , elb , elbv2 , iam , sts , s3 ) is redirected. One variable, two worlds. ⚠ THE BUG I HIT AND FIXED The elbv2 line is mandatory for ALBs — the classic elb endpoint only serves CLBs. A missing elbv2 line makes aws_lb silently call real AWS even with TF_VAR_floci_endpoin

SECTIONS 05–06 · CONTRACT & NAMES  variables.tf + locals.tf ⏱ 6 MIN §5 variables.tf — every knob the platform team can tune per workspace Var Default Notes region us-east-1 One region per deploy. floci_endpoint null Set http://localhost:4566 to use Floci. project onext Resource-name prefix. vpc_cidr 10.30.0.0/16 public_subnets ["10.30.1.0/24","10.30.2.0/24"] private_subnets ["10.30.10.0/24","10.30.11.0/24"] frontend_instance_type t3.micro backend_instance_type t3.micro frontend_count 2 Used by count and TG attachments. backend_count 2 health_check_path / Target ping path on the backend. health_check_matcher 200 Comma-separated acceptable HTTP codes.  WHY A STRING, NOT A BOOL The Floci switch is a string because the provider's endpoints { ... } block accepts an HTTP URL — a bool would force an extra indirection. §6 locals.tf — workspace-aware naming locals { name_prefix = "${var.project}-${terraform.workspace}" common_tags = { Project = var.project Environment = terraform.workspace ManagedBy = "terraform" } }  ONE CODEBASE, THREE NAME SPACES Every Name = "${local.name_prefix}-vpc" becomes onext-dev-vpc in dev, onext-staging-vpc in staging, onext-prod-vpc in prod. Same for ALB nam

SECTION 07 · MAIN.TF I  Networking + the 4 Security Groups ⏱ 7 MIN §7.1 Networking foundation — always first §7.2 Security groups — each its own resource so changes review cleanly SG Ingress Why public_alb TCP 80/443 from 0.0.0.0/0 Internet-facing load balancer. internal_alb TCP 80 from frontend_ec2 SG and VPC CIDR Defense-in-depth. frontend_ec2 TCP 80 from public_alb SG only ALB → EC2 path. backend_ec2 TCP 80 from internal_alb SG only Internal traffic only.  THE DEPENDENCY CHAIN The two SG pairs that reference each other ( frontend_ec2 ↔ public_alb , backend_ec2 ↔ internal_alb ) form a dependency chain Terraform resolves automatically — the SGs are created in topological order, no depends_on needed . ⚠ READ THE CHAIN ALOUD world → public ALB → frontend EC2 → internal ALB → backend EC2. Traffic can only flow down the chain , and every hop narrows the source. There is no path from the internet to the backends — that's the design.  EXAM Memorize the 4 SGs and their ingress: public_alb (80/443 from world) · internal_alb (80 from frontend SG + VPC CIDR) · frontend_ec2 (80 from public_alb SG only) · backend_ec2 (80 from internal_alb SG only). ⏭ Network and walls in place — the machin

SECTION 07 · MAIN.TF II  → ⚖ EC2 Fleet + the Public ALB Quartet ⏱ 8 MIN §7.3 EC2 fleet (2 + 2) data "aws_ami" "amazon_linux" looks up the latest amzn2 AMI so the code never pins an outdated AMI id. aws_instance.frontend / .backend use count with a user_data script installing Apache and serving a workspace-aware page — so the health-check / path returns 200 the moment the instance boots. Spread across AZs: subnet_id = aws_subnet.public[count.index % length(...)].id . ⚠ FLOCI NOTE Floci's EC2 returns instances in terminated state, which crashes Terraform's state serializer. The IaC is correct and works on real AWS — run-alb.sh excludes the EC2 + TG-attach targets from the Floci apply so the rest verifies end-to-end. §7.4 Public ALB — the canonical quartet resource "aws_lb" "public" { name = "${local.name_prefix}-pub-alb" load_balancer_type = "application" internal = false # ← internet-facing security_groups = [aws_security_group.public_alb.id] subnets = aws_subnet.public[*].id tags = merge(local.common_tags, { Name = "${local.name_prefix}-pub-alb" }) } resource "aws_lb_target_group" "public" { name = "${local.name_prefix}-pub-tg" port = 80 protocol = "HTTP" target_type = "instance"

SECTION 07 · MAIN.TF III  Internal ALB + Health-Check Anatomy ⏱ 6 MIN §7.5 Internal ALB — same quartet, internal = true The internal block is the public block copied with internal = true , swapped security group ( internal_alb ), swapped subnets (private), swapped target group, swapped instance set (backend). The name changes ( int vs pub ) keep ALB names unique in AWS . public: internal = false · pub SG · public subnets · frontend T G ⇄ internal: internal = tr ue · int SG · private subnets · backend T G §7.6 Health-check anatomy — every line, one meaning health_check { enabled = true path = "/" # GET / on each target port = "traffic-port" # follow the TG port (80) matcher = "200" # expect HTTP 200 interval = 30 # probe every 30 s timeout = 5 # give up after 5 s healthy_threshold = 2 # 2 passes → healthy unhealthy_threshold = 3 # 3 fails → unhealthy }  TUNING RULES The numbers are tuned for a small backend. Rule of thumb: interval ≥ 2 × timeout (a probe must finish before the next fires) and healthy_threshold + unhealthy_threshold = 5 for fast convergence on small fleets. ⚠ WHY THE HEALTH CHECK IS THE STAR The ALB only routes to healthy targets. If your app serves / with anything

SECTION 08 · THE HANDOFF  outputs.tf — What the Platform Consumes ⏱ 4 MIN Outputs are this stack's contract — ten values that DNS, autoscaling, and observability stacks will reference: Output Purpose vpc_id For peering / TGW / observability stacks. public_subnet_ids For ASGs, Lambda ENIs, etc. private_subnet_ids Same. public_alb_dns_name Route53 alias records, app config. public_alb_zone_id Required for a Route53 alias to the ALB. internal_alb_dns_name Internal service discovery. public_target_group_arn For autoscaling attachments. internal_target_group_arn Same. frontend_instance_ids For SSM / CloudWatch inventory. backend_instance_ids Same.  WHY THE ZONE ID A Route53 alias record to an ALB needs both the DNS name and the ALB's hosted zone ID — that's why public_alb_zone_id is exported separately. Forgetting it breaks the alias Terraform-side.  TG ARNS EXIST FOR AUTOSCALING An ASG can register itself with a target group directly via target_group_arn — exporting both TG ARNs means a future autoscaling stack attaches to the ALB without editing this code .  EXAM Count them: 1 VPC + 2 subnet sets + 2 DNS + 1 zone ID + 2 T G ARNs + 2 instance sets = 10 outputs . Every one exists be

SECTION 09 · THREE ENVIRONMENTS  Workspaces — dev / staging / prod ⏱ 6 MIN TASK [The command sequence] one codebase, three applies cd live-verify-floci/alb-cluster export TF_VAR_floci_endpoint=http://localhost:4566 $ terraform init $ terraform workspace new dev # creates + selects $ terraform workspace new staging $ terraform workspace new prod $ ./run-alb.sh dev # apply dev (22 non-EC2 resources) $ ./run-alb.sh staging $ ./run-alb.sh prod $ terraform workspace list default * dev staging prod  ISOLATION PROOF Each workspace gets its own state file under terraform.tfstate.d/<name>/terraform.tfstate — and its own resources in Floci: 3 separate VPCs, 12 subnets, 12 SGs, 6 ALBs, 6 target groups, 6 listeners , all live. Nothing is shared between environments.  WHERE THE 66 COMES FROM The cover said "66 resources deployed": ~22 non-EC2 resources × 3 workspaces ≈ 66 live objects in Floci. The EC2 + attachment blocks are coded and state-tracked but excluded from the Floci apply (the terminated-state limitation from page 9). ⚠ THE DEFAULT WORKSPACE First init + apply without creating a workspace lands everything in default with an unprefixed state key. Create dev before the first apply —

SECTIONS 10–12 · THE PROOF ✅ Verify · Idempotence · Docs Cross-Ref ⏱ 6 MIN §10 Verifying the apply $ ./verify-alb.sh onext-dev-vpc The script hits the Floci endpoint directly and dumps every VPC, subnet, security group, load balancer, target group, and listener it sees — confirming Apply complete! matches what's actually in the emulator . §11 Idempotence check — the correctness gate $ terraform plan -target =aws_lb.public -target =aws_lb.internal ... No changes. Your infrastructure matches the configuration.  THE PROOF Re-running terraform plan on a clean workspace returning "No changes" is the proof the IaC is correct — not just one-shot . Apply- once luck isn't engineering; the no-change plan is. §12 Cross-reference — every argument from the 5.x docs Resource Doc anchor (registry.terraform.io/providers/hashicorp/aws/latest/docs/...) aws_lb resources/lb aws_lb_listener resources/lb_listener aws_lb_target_group resources/lb_target_group aws_lb_target_group_attachment resources/lb_target_group_attachment aws_security_group resources/security_group aws_vpc · aws_subnet · aws_route_table · aws_internet_gateway · aws_route_table_association resources/<name> each aws_instance resources

SECTIONS 13–15 · THE PIPELINE ⚙ FLOCI Pipeline · Cleanup · Truth Table ⏱ 6 MIN §13 FLOCI pipeline integration 1 CI sets TF_VAR_floci_endpoint=http://localhost:4566 2 terraform fmt -check -recursive — formatting gate 3 terraform init -input=false — pulls the locked provider 4 terraform validate — fails the build on syntax errors 5 Per workspace (dev/staging/prod): workspace select $ws → ./run-alb.sh $ws ( -auto-approve , EC2 excluded) → ./verify-alb.sh proves it's live → terraform plan must report No changes (idempotence gate)  SAME CODE, REAL AWS The EC2/TG-attach blocks stay in main.tf so the same code ships to staging/prod on real AWS unchanged. Floci is for pipeline verification , not production. §14 Cleanup $ ./run-alb.sh destroy dev # tears down dev (non-EC2) $ ./run-alb.sh destroy staging $ ./run-alb.sh destroy prod $ terraform workspace delete dev staging prod Real AWS teardown: drop the -target filters and let terraform destroy -auto-approve reap everything — EC2s and TG attachments included. §15 The FLOCI truth table Resource Floci behavior Real AWS aws_vpc + subnets + routes + IGW full full aws_security_group full full aws_lb (ALB) full (elbv2 endpoint) full aws_lb_targe

SECTION 16 · FINALE  Recap · Cheat Sheet · Self-Check  THE END §16 Recap — the five-line summary  Command cheat sheet export TF_VAR_floci_endpoint=http://localhost:4566 $ terraform init && terraform workspace new dev && ./run-alb.sh dev $ ./verify-alb.sh onext-dev-vpc $ terraform plan # → No changes = idempotent ✅ $ ./run-alb.sh destroy dev  Self-check — answer before peeking 1. Which provider endpoint is mandatory for ALBs on Floci? elbv2 — elb only serves CLBs. 2 . Which SG can use 0.0.0.0/0? Only public_alb (80/443). Everything else chains by reference. 3 . The "canonical quartet" per ALB tier? aws_lb · target group · listener · attachment. 4 . What proves idempotence? Re-plan → "No changes. Your infrastructure matches the configuration." 5 . Why is EC2 excluded from the Floci apply? Floci returns terminated instances → state write crashes. IaC itself is correct. 6 . Health-check rule of thumb? interval ≥ 2×timeout; healthy+unhealthy thresholds sum to 5.  CLOSING LINE The task done end-to-end: IaC authored, validated, applied to an AWS-compatible emulator across three workspaces, verified live, and reproducible from a fresh clone with three shell commands. ▶ 18 resource blo

 Contents — click any row 8 parts · 38 chapters PART I · THE CLUSTER 00 What is Kubernetes? p.3 CH 01 What is a Kubernetes Cluster? p.4 CH 02 The Control Plane (Master) p.5 CH 03 The Worker Node p.6 CH 04 How Master & Worker Communicate p.7 PART II · SEE IT WORK CH 05 Walkthrough — Deploying nginx p.8 CH 06 Self-Healing — When a Worker Dies p.9 CH 07 Can the Control Plane also be a Worker? p.10 CH 08 Master : Worker Ratio & etcd Quorum p.11 CH 09 The Diagram Map + Learning Roadmap p.12 PART III · NAMESPACES CH 10 Namespaces — The Big Idea p.13 CH 11 Names Are Scoped + The Three Superpowers p.14 CH 12 Service DNS + Default Namespaces p.15 CH 13 The Complete Namespace Picture p.16 PART IV · WORKLOADS CH 14 ReplicaSet — What Is It? p.17 CH 15 Labels, Death & Why Deployment p.18 CH 16 The Pod Lifecycle — Owned vs Standalone p.19 CH 17 kubectl — The Command Map p.20 CH 18 Pod Deep Dive p.21 CH 19 Multi-Container Pods p.22 CH 20 Deployment — Rolling Updates p.23 CH 21 Rollout Commands p.24 PART V · YAML & DEBUGGING CH 22 YAML Anatomy — The Two Specs p.25 CH 23 Debugging 1 — Reading Pod States p.26 CH 24 Debugging 2 — The Toolbox p.27 PART VI · SERVICES & NETWORKING CH 25 NodePort — The

 How to read this book: one spine — User → kubectl → API Server → Admission → Scheduler → Node → kubelet → Runtime . Part I–II build the picture, III–VI add the depth, VII proves it with your hands, VIII makes it stick.  The Complete Kubernetes Guide ◀ cover · start reading ▶ Page 2

00 ☸ What is Kubernetes?  5 MIN · START HERE Kubernetes is an open-source container or chestrat or : it takes the containers you define and — across a fleet of machines — deploys them, scales them, heals them, connects them, and updat es them without downtime . You describe what you want. It makes reality match. Forever.  The Name Greek κυβερ νήτης (kybernetes) = helmsman — the one who steers the ship. Hence the wheel logo ☸ (and the word cyber netics ).  k8s Programmer shorthand: K + the 8 letters in between + s . Pronounced "K-eights" — you'll read it a hundred times a day. 溺 Lineage Born at Google from Borg (its internal cluster manager, ~2003) → open-sourced 2014 → donated to the CNCF with v1.0 in 2015 . Written in Go. 樂 The problem it solves — running ONE container is easy; running a fleet is not  WITHOUT AN ORCHESTRATOR  A container crashes at 3am → you restart it  Ten machines free — which one takes the new app? you decide  40 containers need to find each other → hand- written configs  Upgrade from v1 to v2 → downtime, or a hand- rolled script  Black Friday? Log in and start containers manually ☸ WITH KUBERNETES  Crash → replaced automatically (reconciliation — CH

containerd, CRI-O, CH 03) · not a monitoring system (Prometheus & friends watch it). It's the orchestra conductor  — it doesn't play a single instrument, but nothing plays without it.  Heritage flex: Kubernetes didn't invent containers or orchestration — Google had been running billions of containers a week on Borg for a decade. Kubernetes is what happened when they distilled that war story into an open-source project the rest of the world could use. You're learning fifteen years of production scars, organized into an API.  Exam / int erview tip: "What is Kubernetes?" has a canonical two-beat answer — (1) an open-sour ce container orchestrat or, (2) declarativ e : you declare desired state, it continuously reconciles reality toward it. Add "descended from Google's Borg" for bonus credibility. ⏭ So what does it physically look lik e ? Machines split into a brain and muscle — Chapter 1: What is a Kubernetes Clust er? ↑ back to top  The Complete Kubernetes Guide ▤ TOC · next ▶ Page 3

CH 01 ☸ What is a Kubernetes Cluster?  4 MIN A cluster is a collection of machines working together to run your applications. It has exactly two halves: ☸ KUBERNE TES CL USTER 易 CONTROL PLANE CONTROL PLANE  WORKER NODES WORKER NODES 易 +  Think of it as: 易 Master = Brain Thinks, decides, remembers  Worker = Muscle Lifts, runs, executes ☸ Cluster = Both Brain + muscle together  The modern terminology is Control Plane , not "Master". You'll still see master everywhere — because computer science terminology apparently enjoys archaeological preservation .   One sentence to remember: Cluster = Control Plane + Worker Nodes. The Control Plane manages . The Workers execute . ↑ back to top the whole her d (MASTER) Makes decisions Run applications  The Complete Kubernetes Guide ▤ TOC · next ▶ Page 4

CH 02 易 The Control Plane (Master)  6 MIN · CORE The Control Plane controls the clust er . It does not normally run your application workloads. Its job:  Receive requests  Store clust er infor mation  Decide wher e Pods should r un  Monit or the clust er ✅ Maintain the desir ed stat e 里 Inside the Control Plane 易 CONTROL PLANE API Ser ver  Scheduler  Controllers  etcd  離 Example — you tell Kubernetes: replicas : 3 The Control Plane then figures out: 燐 "I need 3 Pods ."  " Where should they run?"  "Are they actually running?"  "Did one die ?"  "Do I need to create another ?"  The four components, one line each: API Server = the only door  · etcd = the memory  · Scheduler = the placement officer  · Controllers = the watchdogs  . Everything else in the cluster talks through the door. ↑ back to top  The Complete Kubernetes Guide ◀ prev · ▤ TOC · next ▶ Page 5

CH 03  The Worker Node  6 MIN · CORE A Worker Node is a machine that actually r uns your application w orkloads . 﫛 Pods on a Worker  WORKER NODE 﫛 Pod 1  Container 﫛 Pod 2  Container 﫛 Pod 3  Container 藺 What's inside a typical Worker Node WORKER NODE  ├── kubelet  the node agent ├── container runtime ⚙ runs containers ├── kube-proxy  service networking └── Pods 﫛 your applications  The important idea: the Worker is where your application actually executes . The brain thinks — the muscle lifts. Component Job Vibe kubelet Manages Pods on this node, reports to the API Server  Node agent Container Runtime Pulls images & runs containers (containerd, CRI-O) ⚙ Engine kube-proxy Programs Service networking rules on this node  Network helper Pods Host your containers 﫛 Application unit ↑ back to top  The Complete Kubernetes Guide ◀ prev · ▤ TOC · next ▶ Page 6

CH 04  How Master & Worker Communicate  5 MIN · CORE This is important. The main communication path is the API Ser ver — one door, everything walks through it. 易 Contr ol Plane ── ► Worker 1 Worker 2 Worker 3 ▼ ▼ ▼ 﫛 Pods 﫛 Pods 﫛 Pods  The kubelet on each worker talks only to the API Server . No worker ever talks to etcd, the Scheduler, or the Controllers directly — everything goes through the front door.  Who Talks to Why kubectl (you) API Server Submit/read everything kubelet API Server Get assigned Pods · report status Scheduler API Server Watch unscheduled Pods · write its decisions Controllers API Server Watch actual state · drive it toward desired API Server etcd The only component that touches the memory   Why this design wins: one door = one place for authentication, authorization, and audit. Watch anything, change anything — always through the API. ↑ back to top API Ser ver  kubelet kubelet kubelet  The Complete Kubernetes Guide ◀ prev · ▤ TOC · next ▶ Page 7

CH 05  Walkthrough — Deploying nginx  5 MIN Imagine a cluster with 1 Contr ol Plane and 3 Workers : 易 Contr ol Plane ── ► Worker 1 Worker 2 Worker 3 You run: $ kubectl create deployment nginx --image =nginx --replicas =3 deployment.apps/nginx created  The flow  kubectl ── ► API Ser ver  ▼ 易 Contr ol Plane ▼ Scheduler  Worker 1 Worker 2 Worker 3 Worker 1 → nginx 﫛 Worker 2 → nginx 﫛 Worker 3 → nginx 﫛 易 The Contr ol Plane decides.  The W orkers execute. ↑ back to top 192.168.1.10 .11 .12 .13 records desir ed stat e picks Nodes kubelet runs it kubelet runs it kubelet runs it  The Complete Kubernetes Guide ◀ prev · ▤ TOC · next ▶ Page 8

CH 06  Self-Healing — When a Worker Dies  6 MIN · CORE This is where Kubernetes starts earning its p aycheck .  Worker 1 ❌ Worker 2 ✅ Worker 3 ✅ One of your P ods disappeared. The Control Plane notices a mismatch:  DESIRED 1 2 3  ACTUAL 1 2 Desired 3 ≠ Actual 2 ❌  Controllers react Kubernetes creates replacement P ods on healthy workers — assuming workload & cluster resources allow it. ✅ After reconciliation Worker 1 ❌ Worker 2 ✅ Worker 3 ✅  The reconciliation loop is the heart of Kubernetes: wat ch actual → compare to desired → act → repeat, forever . Nobody "restored" anything — the system simply cannot tolerate a mismatch. ⚠ Honest limits: if the cluster is out of CPU/memory, or all healthy nodes are full, replacements stay Pending . Self-healing repairs state — it doesn't conjure capacity. ↑ back to top 﫛 nginx · 﫛 nginx 﫛 nginx · 﫛 nginx  The Complete Kubernetes Guide ◀ prev · ▤ TOC · next ▶ Page 9

CH 07 樂 Can the Control Plane also be a Worker?  4 MIN Technically y es. In pr oduction: no. The mechanism that separates them is a taint .  MINIKUBE — YES, BY DESIGN A single-node cluster where one machine is both brain and muscle . The Control-Plane taint is removed so workloads can land there. Perfect for learning. $ kubectl get nodes NAME STATUS ROLES minikube Ready control-plane,master  PRODUCTION — NEVER Control-Plane nodes carry a taint like node- role.kubernetes.io/control-plane:NoSchedule — the Scheduler refuses t o place nor mal Pods ther e . The brain is protected. $ kubectl describe node cp1 | grep Taints Taints: node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane:NoSchedule ⚠ Why the isolation matters: a runaway workload on a Control-Plane node can starve the API Server or etcd — and then the entire cluster's brain slows or freezes. etcd is especially latency-sensitive.  Remember: "Control Plane ≠ Worker" is not a law of nature — it's a taint . Remove the taint and the brain will do deadlifts. (Lab 5 covers taints hands-on.) ↑ back to top  The Complete Kubernetes Guide ◀ prev · ▤ TOC · next ▶ Page 10

CH 08  Master : Worker Ratio & etcd Quorum  6 MIN · CORE Why does everyone run 3 Contr ol Planes ? Because etcd (the memory  ) needs a quorum — a majority of members alive and agreeing — to accept any write. THE QUORUM MATH quorum = floor((n-1)/2) + 1 members required # of Control Planes → failures tolerated before the cluster freezes: 1 CP → tolerate 0 failures (one crash = frozen) 3 CP → tolerate 1 failure ← the production minimum 5 CP → tolerate 2 failures 7 CP → tolerate 3 failures Control Planes Quorum needs Tolerates Verdict 1 1 of 1 0 Dev only 2 2 of 2 0 Worst choice — same tolerance as 1, double the cost 3 2 of 3 1 ✅ Standard production 5 3 of 5 2 Large/critical clusters ⚠ The trap: 2 is the worst number. Two members need both alive for quorum — one failure freezes writes, exactly like having one. Even numbers add cost without adding tolerance.  Workers scale independently. The ratio isn't "1 master per N workers" — it's 3–5 Control Planes (for quorum) plus as many Workers as your workload needs . A lost quorum means the cluster keeps running what's deployed but accepts no new state . ↑ back to top  The Complete Kubernetes Guide ◀ prev · ▤ TOC · next ▶ Page 11

CH 09  The Diagram Map + Learning Roadmap  REFERENCE Everything from P art I–II on one canvas. CH 14  ReplicaSet — What Is It?  6 MIN · CORE A ReplicaSet is the guarant or : it watches a set of P ods that carry specific labels , and keeps their count at the number you asked for. Not one more, not one fewer. apiVersion : apps/v1 kind : ReplicaSet metadata : name : nginx-rs spec : replicas : 3 # ← the promise selector : matchLabels : app : nginx # ← who it manages template : # ← the pod stamp it uses metadata : labels : { app : nginx } # must match the selector! spec : containers : - name : nginx image : nginx:1.25  How it "counts"  Selector — the R eplicaSet claims every P od whose labels match app: nginx 燐 Compare — desired 3 vs actual (say) 2  Act — create one more P od from the template (or delete surplus)  Repeat — this is just the reconciliation loop again, one level down ⚠ Label match is everything. If the template's labels don't satisfy the selector, the ReplicaSet refuses to start. And any stray Pod with matching labels gets adopted — willingly or not.  ReplicaSet = labels + count + template. You'll rarely write one by hand — a Deployment creates them for you (CH 15). ↑ back to top  The Complete Kubernetes Guide ◀ prev · ▤ TOC · next ▶ Page 17

CH 15  Labels, Death & Why Deployment  6 MIN · CORE STANDALONE POD DIES  Gone. For ever. Nobody holds a copy of the wish — the Pod's spec died with it. This is why "just run a P od" is a demo trick, not a deployment. OWNED POD DIES  Recreated aut omatically . The ReplicaSet still holds the template — the mismatch triggers a replacement with a new name (e.g. nginx-rs-x7k2p ). 惘 So why isn't ReplicaSet enough? The ownership chain Deployment you talk to this one └── ReplicaSet v1 manages Pods at image nginx:1.25 ├── 﫛 pod ├── 﫛 pod └── 﫛 pod change the image → Deployment creates ReplicaSet v2 , rolls Pods over ← CH 20  ReplicaSet answers: " are the r ight number o f Pods r unning? "  Deployment answers: " are they r unning the right v ersion ? — and can w e swit ch v ersions with zer o do wntime? "  Own vs run: a standalone Pod is run ; an owned Pod is guaranteed . The Deployment exists because the ReplicaSet can keep count — but it can't change what it's counting wit hout down time . The Deployment can. ↑ back to top  The Complete Kubernetes Guide ◀ prev · ▤ TOC · next ▶ Page 18

CH 16  The Pod Lifecycle — Owned vs Standalone  6 MIN · CORE The five-second experiment that makes ownership real. T wo terminals:  TAB 1 · WATCH $ kubectl get pods -w NAME READY STATUS web-7d9f 0/1 ContainerCreating web-7d9f 1/1 Running web-7d9f 0/1 Terminating web-x7k2p 0/1 ContainerCreating web-x7k2p 1/1 Running # new name! ⚙ TAB 2 · ACT $ kubectl delete pod web-7d9f pod "web-7d9f" deleted # watch TAB 1: a replacement appears # same deployment, brand-new pod name 茶 What we just proved ✅ The Pod's name is disposable — the R eplicaSet's promise is not . ✅ Deletion is just another mismatch: desired 1, actual 0 → create. ❌ A standalone Pod (no owner) deleted = silence. No replacement. No drama.  Status decoding: ContainerCreating = image pulling + CNI wiring · Running = process up · Terminating = shutting down gracefully · Pending = not yet placed (CH 23).  Owned vs standalone is the single most important workload concept. CH 18 﫛 Pod Deep Dive  6 MIN · CORE The Pod is the smallest deployable unit — not the container. A P od is a co-locat ed family o f container s that share fate. ONE POD = ONE SHARED ENVIRONMENT  ONE IP addr ess shared by all container s  app container  sidecar  shared Volume same files, both container s  One IP per P od — containers inside talk via localhost:port , never "find the other container's IP"  Shared volumes — declared in the P od spec, mounted by any of its containers ⏳ Shared lifecy cle — born together, scheduled together (same Node), die together  Never scale "a container" — you scale P ods; want more copies → more P ods ⚠ Port clashes are real: two containers in one Pod cannot bind the same port — they literally share the network stack.  The test for Pod-membership: must these contain ers live and die together on the sam e machine? Yes → one Pod. No → separate Pods (and let the Scheduler place them freely). ↑ back to top listens :80 reaches app on localhost  The Complete Kubernetes Guide ◀ prev · ▤ TOC · next ▶ Page 21

CH 19  Multi-Container Pods  5 MIN The classic pattern: the sidecar — a helper container riding along with the app container inside one P od. spec : containers : - name : app image : myapp:2.0 volumeMounts : - { name : logs, mountPath : /var/log/app } - name : log-shipper # the sidecar image : busybox command : [ "sh" , "-c" , "tail -F /logs/app.log" ] volumeMounts : - { name : logs, mountPath : /logs } # same volume! volumes : - name : logs emptyDir : {} ⚖ Good vs bad Pod-mates ✅ BELONG TOGETHER  app + log shipper (shared files)  app + auth proxy (shared localhost)  app + config reloader (shared lifecycle) ❌ DON'T frontend + database (scale & fail independently) two unrelated services (one crash restarts both... and they fight over ports)  Heuristic: if the two containers could run on different machines , they belong in different Pods . Pod-mates are glued on purpose — glue is a cost. ↑ back to top  The Complete Kubernetes Guide ◀ prev · ▤ TOC · next ▶ Page 22

CH 20  Deployment — Rolling Updates  6 MIN · CORE Change a Deployment's image and it doesn't rebuild P ods in place — it creates a new R eplicaSet and rolls traffic from old to new, keeping availability the whole time. $ kubectl set image deploy/nginx nginx= nginx:1.26 deployment.apps/nginx image updated $ kubectl rollout status deploy/nginx Waiting for deployment "nginx" rollout to finish... deployment "nginx" successfully rolled out 惘 What actually happened Deployment nginx ├── ReplicaSet v2 nginx:1.26 scales 0 → 3  │ └── 﫛 﫛 﫛 new Pods replace old └── ReplicaSet v1 nginx:1.25 scales 3 → 0  (kept for rollback) ⚖ The Controller walks the count: add a v2 P od → remove a v1 P od → repeat  Service selectors keep pointing at labels — traffic slides over automatically  v1's R eplicaSet is retained (scaled to 0) — that's your rollback insurance (CH 21)  Zero downtime is the point: at every instant, enough healthy Pods serve traffic. The Deployment turned "risky big-bang upgrade" into "boring arithmetic." ↑ back to top  The Complete Kubernetes Guide ◀ prev · ▤ TOC · next ▶ Page 23

CH 21 ⏪ Rollout Commands  4 MIN $ kubectl rollout history deploy/nginx REVISION CHANGE-CAUSE 1 <none> 2 nginx:1.26 $ kubectl rollout undo deploy/nginx deployment.apps/nginx rolled back $ kubectl rollout status deploy/nginx successfully rolled out # ← back on :1.25  rollout status — watch a rollout finish (script-friendly)  rollout history — every revision is just an old R eplicaSet with a number ⏪ rollout undo — flip back to the previous template · --to-revision=1 to pick  revisionHistoryLimit: 3 — how many old R eplicaSets to keep (default 10) ⚠ Undo doesn't rewind time — it creates a new revision (v3) with v1's template. CH 22  YAML Anatomy — The Two Specs  6 MIN · CORE Every Kubernetes manifest is the same envelope: apiVersion · kind · metadata · spec . The "wish" lives in the spec. Field Meaning Example apiVersion Which API group/version serves this kind v1 (Pod) · apps/v1 (Deployment) kind What object you want Pod , Service , Deployment metadata Name · namespace · labels name: nginx spec The desired state replicas, containers, ports... 惘 The Two-Specs Mystery (Deployment) spec : # the DEPLOYMENT's wish replicas : 3 selector : ... template : # a whole Pod hiding inside! metadata : labels : ... spec : # ← the POD's wish (spec inside spec) containers : ... 易 Outer spec = what the Deployment manages: count, selector, template 﫛 Inner spec ( spec.template.spec ) = the actual P od: images, ports, env, resources  spec.template is the cookie cutter — the R eplicaSet stamps P ods from it; change anything inside and you trigger a rollout (CH 20)  Indentation is structure in YAML. The most common manifest bug is writing the Pod spec at the wrong nesting level — and the API Server answers with a confusing validation error. CH 23 喙 Debugging 1 — Reading Pod States  6 MIN · CORE The ST ATUS column is a diagnosis. Each state tells you which st age failed — before you run a single command. Status Meaning Classic cause First mov e Pending Accepted, not placed Not enough CPU/mem · taints · PVC pending describe pod → events ContainerCreating Placed, pulling/wiring Normal for seconds; stuck = image/CNI issue describe pod → events ImagePullBackOff Can't fetch image Typo in tag · private registry, no secret Check image name & pull secret CrashLoopBackOff Starts, dies, repeats App crashes on boot — bad config, missing env logs --previous Running Process is up — (not necessarily healthy — that's probes) Test the endpoint Completed Finished & exited 0 Job finished — normal for Jobs, odd for servers Expected? done ✅ ⚠ The backoff family: ImagePullBackOff and CrashLoopBackOff are not errors of Kubernetes — they're Kubernetes retrying after your app/image failed. The real error is one layer deeper, in the events or logs.  Memory hook: Pending = the Scheduler said no · ImagePull = the Registry said no · CrashLoop = the App said no. Three different culprits, three different rooms to search. ↑ back to top  The Compl

CH 24 藺 Debugging 2 — The Toolbox  6 MIN · CORE $ kubectl describe pod web-x7k2p # 1 · full biography... Events: # ...always read the BOTTOM Failed to pull image "nginx:1.99" $ kubectl logs web-x7k2p --previous # 2 · crashed container's last words panic: missing REQUIRED_DB_PASSWORD $ kubectl exec -it web-x7k2p -- sh # 3 · go inside $ kubectl get events --sort-by= .lastTimestamp # 4 · cluster timeline DESCRIBE — THE BIOGRAPHY Config as the cluster sees it, plus the Events block at the bott om — the single most information-dense place in debugging. CH 25  NodePort — The Side Entrance  6 MIN · CORE ClusterIPs are invisible from outside the cluster. NodeP ort punches a hole: every Node opens one high port and forwards it to your Service. apiVersion : v1 kind : Service metadata : name : nginx-svc spec : type : NodePort # default is ClusterIP selector : app : nginx ports : - port : 80 # inside the cluster targetPort : 80 # container's port nodePort : 30080 # outside — or omit & let k8s pick THE PATH IN  User ── ► ANY node ── ► Service ── ► 﫛 Pod :80 "ANY node" is the superpower — even a Node with no nginx P od opens the door and forwards across.  Valid range: 30000–32767 (omit nodePort and one is auto-assigned)  Every Node gets the same port — hit 192.168.1.11:30080 or .13:30080 , same result ⚠ NodePort is for demos & edge cases — raw ports, no load balancing across nodes, no TLS story. Production rides Ingress (a different book in this series  ). ↑ back to top :30080 ClusterIP rules  The Complete Kubernetes Guide ◀ prev · ▤ TOC · next ▶ Page 28

CH 26 illusion Service Networking — The Virtual IP  6 MIN · CORE Here's the trick nobody tells you: the ClusterIP your Service owns is a lie . Nothing is listening on it. No process holds it. It's a virtual IP (VIP) — and that's the elegance. RUSSIAN DOLLS — WHERE THE VIP REALLY GOES 10.96.0.50 ── ► DNA T ── ► 10.244.1.5 packets "to the VIP" are rewritten in transit to a real P od — the VIP never terminates anything Address ranges — separate drawers: Service CIDR 10.96.0.0/12 # VIPs live here (fake, routable only via rules) Pod CIDR 10.244.0.0/16 # real Pod IPs (per-node slices)  You can't ping a ClusterIP — nothing answers; the rules only rewrite packets passing thr ough  Pods died and got new IPs? Nobody notices — everyone still dials the VIP 燐 The ranges must not ov erlap — two drawers, zero confusion  The Service is a stable illusion: an eternal name + eternal IP in front of a set of mortals (Pods) that churn constantly. The illusion is maintained by kube-proxy — next chapter. ↑ back to top the VIP — a fiction a real Pod IP  The Complete Kubernetes Guide ◀ prev · ▤ TOC · next ▶ Page 29

CH 27  kube-proxy's Real Job  6 MIN · CORE kube-proxy does not forward a single packet. Its entire job is two verbs: watch & pr ogram . ❌ WHAT IT DOES NOT DO Sit in the traffic path Proxy connections through itself Touch P od-to-P od traffic ✅ WHAT IT DOES Watch the API Server: Services + Endpoints Program iptables/IPVS rules on its node Re-program the instant P ods change 彩 The rules it writes (iptables + DNAT) # conceptually, on every node: if dst == 10.96.0.50:80 # the VIP then rewrite dst → 10.244.1.5:80 # pick an endpoint (random) else if ... next endpoint # (rule set balances across all) ✨ The Illusion, resolved: a Pod dies → Endpoints object updates → every node's kube-proxy rewrites its rules → the VIP never moved . Stability on the outside, churn on the inside, and the packets never knew.  One-liner for exams: kube-proxy wat ches Services/Endpo ints and program s packet-rewriting rules on every node — it never forwar ds traffic itself. ↑ back to top  The Complete Kubernetes Guide ◀ prev · ▤ TOC · next ▶ Page 30

CH 28  Following ONE Packet — 6 Steps  FINALE · CORE A Pod runs curl nginx-svc . Follow the single packet: 1 DNS — nginx-svc resolves to the VIP 10.96.0.50 CoreDNS answered from the Service's namespace: nginx-svc.frontend.svc.cluster.local 2 Send — Pod sends to the VIP (nothing is there — remember CH 26) dest IP: 10.96.0.50 · dest port: 80 3 DNAT — the node's iptables rules rewrite the destination dest becomes a real Pod IP: 10.244.1.5:80 4 Route — same node → direct delivery; different node → CNI overlay carries it the packet leaves kube-proxy's rules and enters the real network 5 Receive — the P od sees a normal packet addressed to its o wn IP it replies — source is the VIP thanks to conntrack, so the client never learns the Pod IP 6 Return — conntrack rewrites the reply back through the VIP client believes it talked to 10.96.0.50 the whole time   The entire machine in one sentence: DNS gives you a stable fake IP; kube-proxy's rules secretly rewrite it to a mortal Pod; conntrack makes the lie symmetric. That's Service networking — everything else is detail. ↑ back to top  The Complete Kubernetes Guide ◀ prev · ▤ TOC · labs ▶ Page 31

LAB 5  Taints & Tolerations  15 MIN · HANDS-ON STEP 1 · Taint AFTER the Pod exists ⚙ RUN $ kubectl taint node <node> env=prod:NoSchedule $ kubectl scale deploy web --replicas=4  EXPECTED # existing pods keep running # NEW 4th pod → Pending 0/1 Nodes available ...taint...that pod tolerates not Key insight: NoSchedule only gates new placements — it never evicts. STEP 2 · Rescue with a toleration spec : tolerations : - key : env operator : Equal value : prod effect : NoSchedule # pod may now LAND on the tainted node Apply → the P ending pod schedules immediately. Taint = the lock . Toleration = the k ey. STEP 3 · NoExecute — the eviction ⚙ RUN $ kubectl taint node <node> env=prod: NoExecute  EXPECTED # non-tolerating pods on that # node get EVICTED — now Effect Existing P ods New P ods NoSchedule stay blocked (unless tolerated) PreferNoSchedule stay avoided if possible NoExecute evicted blocked (unless tolerated)  Remember the direction: taints repel (node → pods); tolerations permit (pod → tainted node). Taints never attract — for that you'd use nodeSelector/affinity. ↑ back to top  The Complete Kubernetes Guide ◀ prev · ▤ TOC · quiz ▶ Page 36

GLOSS  Glossary  REFERENCE Cluster — Control Plane + Worker Nodes managed as one unit. Control Plane — the brain: API Server, etcd, Scheduler, Controllers. Makes decisions; runs no user workloads (by taint). API Server — the only door  . All reads/writes (kubectl, kubelet, controllers) go through it; only it touches etcd. etcd — the cluster's memory  . Needs quorum (majority) to write — why production runs 3 or 5 Control Planes. Scheduler — assigns new Pods to Nodes based on resources, taints, affinity. Controller — reconciliation loop: watch actual vs desired, act to close the gap. kubelet — the node agent  . Talks to the API Server, runs Pods via the runtime, reports status. Container Runtime — pulls images and runs containers (containerd, CRI-O). kube-proxy — watches Services/Endpoints, programs iptables/IPVS rules per node. Never forwards packets itself. Pod — smallest deployable unit: 1+ containers sharing IP, volumes, lifecycle. ReplicaSet — the guarantor: keeps N matching-labeled Pods alive via a template. Deployment — manages ReplicaSets to enable versioned, zero-downtime rollouts and rollbacks. Namespace — logical partition of names + RBAC + quotas inside one cluster.

LAB 4  Rollout & Rollback  12 MIN · HANDS-ON STEP 1 · Upgrade ⚙ RUN $ kubectl set image deploy web nginx= nginx:1.26 $ kubectl rollout status deploy web  EXPECTED Waiting for deployment... successfully rolled out $ kubectl get rs # two RS: old 0, new 2 STEP 2 · Ship a broken tag ⚙ RUN $ kubectl set image deploy web nginx= nginx:1.99 $ kubectl rollout status deploy web  EXPECTED Waiting... 1 unavailable $ kubectl get pods one pod in ImagePullBackOff OLD pods still running! STEP 3 · Roll back ⚙ RUN $ kubectl rollout undo deploy web $ kubectl rollout history deploy web  EXPECTED successfully rolled out # bad pod terminated, good ones back # history shows a NEW revision (v3)  The safety net is structural: a bad rollout can never take down the old version — the Deployment only removes old Pods once new ones are Ready. LAB 5  Taints & Tolerations  15 MIN · HANDS-ON STEP 1 · Taint AFTER the Pod exists ⚙ RUN $ kubectl taint node <node> env=prod:NoSchedule $ kubectl scale deploy web --replicas=4  EXPECTED # existing pods keep running # NEW 4th pod → Pending 0/1 Nodes available ...taint...that pod tolerates not Key insight: NoSchedule only gates new placements — it never evicts. STEP 2 · Rescue with a toleration spec : tolerations : - key : env operator : Equal value : prod effect : NoSchedule # pod may now LAND on the tainted node Apply → the P ending pod schedules immediately. Taint = the lock . Toleration = the k ey. STEP 3 · NoExecute — the eviction ⚙ RUN $ kubectl taint node <node> env=prod: NoExecute  EXPECTED # non-tolerating pods on that # node get EVICTED — now Effect Existing P ods New P ods NoSchedule stay blocked (unless tolerated) PreferNoSchedule stay avoided if possible NoExecute evicted blocked (unless tolerated)  Remember the direction: taints repel (node → pods); tolerations permit (pod → tainted node). Taints never attract — for that you'd use nodeSelector/affinity. ↑ back to top  The Complete Kubernetes Guide ◀ prev · ▤ TOC · quiz ▶ Page 36

00 What is Kubernetes? 5 MIN · START HERE Kubernetes is an open-source container or chestrat or : it takes the containers you define and across a fleet of machines deploys them, scales them, heals them, connects them, and updat es them without downtime . You describe what you want. It makes reality match. Forever. The Name Greek κβερ νήη (kybernetes) = helmsman the one who steers the ship. Hence the wheel logo (and the word cyber netics ). k8s Programmer shorthand: K + the 8 letters in between + s . Pronounced "K-eights" you'll read it a hundred times a day. Lineage Born at Google from Borg (its internal cluster manager, ~2003) open-sourced 2014 donated to the CNCF with v1.0 in 2015 . Written in Go. The problem it solves running ONE container is easy; running a fleet is not WITHOUT AN ORCHESTRATOR A container crashes at 3am you restart it Ten machines free which one takes the new app? you decide 40 containers need to find each other hand-written configs Upgrade from v1 to v2 downtime, or a hand-rolled script Black Friday? Log in and start containers manually WITH KUBERNETES Crash replaced aut omatically (reconciliation CH 03) New app the Scheduler picks the best node (CH 02) Contai

Heritage flex: Kubernetes didn't invent containers or orchestration Google had been running billions of containers a week on Borg for a decade. Kubernetes is what happened when they distilled that war story into an open-source project the rest of the world could use. You're learning fifteen years of production scars, organized into an API. Exam / int erview tip: "What is Kubernetes?" has a canonical two-beat answer (1) an open-sour ce container orchestrat or, (2) declarativ e : you declare desired state, it continuously reconciles reality toward it. Add "descended from Google's Borg" for bonus credibility. ⏭ So what does it physically look lik e ? Machines split into a brain and muscle Chapter 1: What is a Kuber netes Cluster? back to top The Complete Kubernetes Guide TOC · next Page 3

CH 01 What is a Kubernetes Cluster? 4 MIN A cluster is a collection of machines working together to run your applications. It has exactly two halves: KUBERNE TES CL USTER CONTROL PLANE CONTROL PLANE WORKER NODES WORKER NODES + Think of it as: Master = Brain Thinks, decides, remembers Worker = Muscle Lifts, runs, executes Cluster = Both Brain + muscle together The modern terminology is Control Plane , not "Master". You'll still see master everywhere because computer science terminology apparently enjoys archaeological preservation .  One sentence to remember: Cluster = Control Plane + Worker Nodes. The Control Plane manages . The Workers execute . back to top the whole her d (MASTER) Makes decisions Run applications The Complete Kubernetes Guide TOC · next Page 4

CH 02-03 The Control Plane & The Worker Node 8 MIN · CORE The cluster has two halves the brain that decides and the muscle that executes. One page, both halves. CONTROL PLANE THE BRAIN Makes decisions API Server, etcd, Scheduler, Controllers WORKER THE MUSCLE Runs workloads kubelet, Runtime, kube-proxy, P ods Control Plane the brain The Control Plane controls the clust er . It does not normally run your application workloads. Its job: Receive requests Store clust er infor mation Decide wher e Pods should r un Monit or the clust er Maintain the desir ed stat e Inside the Control Plane CONTROL PLANE API Ser ver Scheduler Controllers etcd Example you tell Kubernetes: replicas : 3 The Control Plane then figures out: "I need 3 Pods ." " Where should they run?" "Are they actually running?" "Did one die ?" "Do I need to create another ?" The four components, one line each: API Server = the only door · etcd = the memory · Scheduler = the placement officer · Controllers = the watchdogs . Everything else in the cluster talks through the door. Worker Node the muscle A Worker Node is a machine that actually r uns your application w orkloads .

Pods on a Worker WORKER NODE Pod 1 Container Pod 2 Container Pod 3 Container What's inside a typical Worker Node WORKER NODE kubelet the node agent container runtime runs containers kube-proxy service networking Pods your applications The important idea: the Worker is where your application actually executes . The brain thinks the muscle lifts. Component Job Vibe kubelet Manages Pods on this node, reports to the API Server Node agent Container Runtime Pulls images & runs containers (containerd, CRI-O) Engine kube-proxy Programs Service networking rules on this node Network helper Pods Host your containers Application unit back to top The Complete Kubernetes Guide prev · TOC · next Page 5

CH 03 How Master & Worker Communicate 5 MIN · CORE This is important. The main communication path is the API Ser ver one door, everything walks through it. Control Plane Worker 1 Worker 2 Worker 3 Pods Pods Pods The kubelet on each worker talks only to the API Server . No worker ever talks to etcd, the Scheduler, or the Controllers directly everything goes through the front door. Who Talks to Why kubectl (you) API Server Submit/read everything kubelet API Server Get assigned Pods · report status Scheduler API Server Watch unscheduled Pods · write its decisions Controllers API Server Watch actual state · drive it toward desired API Server etcd The only component that touches the memory Why this design wins: one door = one place for authentication, authorization, and audit. Watch anything, change anything always through the API. back to top API Ser ver kubelet kubelet kubelet The Complete Kubernetes Guide prev · TOC · next Page 6

CH 03 Walkthrough — Deploying nginx 5 MIN Imagine a cluster with 1 Contr ol Plane and 3 Workers : Control Plane Worker 1 Worker 2 Worker 3 You run: $ kubectl create deployment nginx --image =nginx --replicas =3 deployment.apps/nginx created The flow kubectl API Ser ver Control Plane Scheduler Worker 1 Worker 2 Worker 3 Worker 1 nginx Worker 2 nginx Worker 3 nginx The Contr ol Plane decides. The W orkers execute. back to top 192.168.1.10 .11 .12 .13 records desir ed stat e picks Nodes kubelet runs it kubelet runs it kubelet runs it The Complete Kubernetes Guide prev · TOC · next Page 7

CH 03 Self-Healing — When a Worker Dies 6 MIN · CORE This is where Kubernetes starts earning its p aycheck . Worker 1 Worker 2 Worker 3 One of your P ods disappeared. The Control Plane notices a mismatch: DESIRED 1 2 3 ACTUAL 1 2 Desired 3 Actual 2 Controllers react Kubernetes creates replacement P ods on healthy workers assuming workload & cluster resources allow it. After reconciliation Worker 1 Worker 2 Worker 3 The reconciliation loop is the heart of Kubernetes: wat ch actual compare to desired act repeat, forever . Nobody "restored" anything the system simply cannot tolerate a mismatch. Honest limits: if the cluster is out of CPU/memory, or all healthy nodes are full, replacements stay Pending . Self- healing repairs state it doesn't conjure capacity. back to top nginx · nginx nginx · nginx The Complete Kubernetes Guide prev · TOC · next Page 8

CH 03 Can the Control Plane also be a Worker? 4 MIN Technically y es. In pr oduction: no. The mechanism that separates them is a taint . MINIKUBE YES, BY DESIGN A single-node cluster where one machine is both brain and muscle . The Control-Plane taint is removed so workloads can land there. P erfect for learning. $ kubectl get nodes NAME STATUS ROLES minikube Ready control-plane,master PRODUCTION NEVER Control-Plane nodes carry a taint like node- role.kubernetes.io/control-plane:NoSchedule the Scheduler refuses t o place nor mal Pods ther e . The brain is protected. $ kubectl describe node cp1 | grep Taints Taints: node-role.kubernetes.io/control- plane:NoSchedule Why the isolation matters: a runaway workload on a Control-Plane node can starve the API Server or etcd and then the entire cluster's brain slows or freezes. etcd is especially latency-sensitive. Remember: "Control Plane Worker" is not a law of nature it's a taint . Remove the taint and the brain will do deadlifts. (Lab 5 covers taints hands-on.) back to top The Complete Kubernetes Guide prev · TOC · next Page 9

CH 03 Master : Worker Ratio & etcd Quorum 6 MIN · CORE Why does everyone run 3 Contr ol Planes ? Because etcd (the memory ) needs a quorum a majority of members alive and agreeing to accept any write. THE QUORUM MATH quorum = floor((n-1)/2) + 1 members required # of Control Planes failures tolerated before the cluster freezes: 1 CP tolerate 0 failures (one crash = frozen) 3 CP tolerate 1 failure the production minimum 5 CP tolerate 2 failures 7 CP tolerate 3 failures Control Planes Quorum needs Tolerates Verdict 1 1 of 1 0 Dev only 2 2 of 2 0 Worst choice same tolerance as 1, double the cost 3 2 of 3 1 Standard production 5 3 of 5 2 Large/critical clusters The trap: 2 is the worst number. Two members need both alive for quorum one failure freezes writes, exactly like having one. Even numbers add cost without adding tolerance. Workers scale independently. The ratio isn't "1 master per N workers" it's 35 Control Planes (for quorum) plus as many Workers as your workload needs . A lost quorum means the cluster keeps running what's deployed but accepts no new state . back to top The Complete Kubernetes Guide prev · TOC · next Page 10

CH 03 The Diagram Map + Learning Roadmap REFERENCE Everything from P art III on one canvas. If you can redraw this from memory, you own the architecture. CLUSTER CONTROL PLANE 3 for quorum API Server the only door etcd state API Server's alone Scheduler assigns Pods Nodes Controllers reconcile desired actual WORKERS kubelet agent talks to API Server Runtime pulls + runs containers kube-proxy Service rules Pods The learning order that works Study rule: never learn a component without knowing wh o it talk s to . Isolated component lists evaporate; communication maps stick. back to top 1 Components who does what (P arts III) · you are here 2 Namesp aces carve logical apartments (P art III) 3 Workloads ReplicaSet Deployment updates (P art IVV) 4 Networking how traffic actually reaches a P od (Part VI) 5 Labs break things, watch them heal (P art VII) The Complete Kubernetes Guide prev · TOC · next Page 11

CH 03 Namespaces The Big Idea 4 MIN Without namespaces, one cluster = one giant bucket. Frontend, AI and dev all collide same names, no boundaries. A namespace is the cluster saying "I can car ve logical ap artments inside one building." PROBLEM ONE FLAT BUCKET Cluster pod-a pod-b frontend? pod-c ai? svc-a # who owns what? SOLUTION LOGICAL APARTMENTS Cluster frontend Pods + Services ai Pods + Services dev Pods + Services same nodes, same control plane When namespaces shine Teams frontend / backend / ai Environments dev / staging / prod via namespaces Apps app-a / app-b isolated, same infra Namespace = logical isolation it affects names, RBAC, quotas. It does not carve hardware or network by itself. Environment Namespace. Environment is the concept; namespace is one object you can implement it with (another: separate clusters). back to top The Complete Kubernetes Guide prev · TOC · next Page 12

CH 03 Names Are Scoped + The Three Superpowers 6 MIN · CORE A Pod's full identity is namesp ace + kind + name . So dev/nginx and prod/nginx are two different objects no collision. Cluster dev nginx Pod identity: dev / Pod / nginx prod nginx Pod identity: prod / Pod / nginx The three superpowers namespaces unlock RBAC KEYS "This team may act only inside frontend ." Permissions scoped per namespace. QUOTAS BUDGET "ai may use at most 4 CPU / 8Gi , 10 Pods." A R esourceQuota caps each apartment's totals. NETWORKPOLICY DOOR RULES "Pods in dev may not call prod." Traffic rules scoped per namespace. Not everything lives in an apartment. Nodes , ClusterRoles , PersistentVolumes and Namespaces themselves are cluster-scoped kubectl get nodes -n dev silently ignores the -n . Nodes belong to the building, not an apartment. The rule: namespaced identity includes the namespace · cluster-scoped namespace flags do nothing. Namespaces partition names, not hardware. back to top The Complete Kubernetes Guide prev · TOC · next Page 13

CH 03 Service DNS + Default Namespaces 5 MIN How Pods find each other: DNS Every Service gets a DNS name built from its namespace that's how cross-P od traffic finds its way: nginx-ser vice nginx-ser vice .frontend .svc.clust er.local same short name resolves within the same namespace "nginx-service" from inside frontend just works frontend | ai same Service name, two namespaces, zero collision The namespaces you always have $ kubectl get namespaces NAME STATUS default Active # you land here when you omit -n kube-system Active # the cluster's own components kube-public Active # public info kube-node-lease Active # node heartbeats kubectl get pods is secretly kubectl get pods -n default kube-system is where the Control Plane's own P ods live (on kubeadm clusters) Mailbox rule: "nginx-service, Apt frontend" vs "nginx-service, Apt ai" same name, different mailbox, and the post office (DNS + API Server) always delivers correctly. back to top Service nginx-ser vice nginx-ser vice The Complete Kubernetes Guide prev · TOC · next Page 14

CH 03 The Complete Namespace Picture REFERENCE CLUSTER Namespace: frontend Pods · Services · Quotas Namespace: ai Pods · Services · Quotas Namespace: dev Pods · Services · Quotas Nodes # OUTSIDE every namespace node1 (4 CPU / 8Gi) node2 (4 CPU / 8Gi) # one shared pool Layer Shared acr oss namesp aces? Notes Control Plane (API Server, etcd, Scheduler) Yes one per cluster A namespace is just a field on objects Nodes · CPU · Memory · Network Yes Quotas lim it usage, they don't carve hardware Pods · Services · ConfigMaps No namespaced dev/nginx prod/nginx Namespace separate cluster. Same control plane, same Nodes, same CPU/memory pool. If an exam asks "is a namespace its own cluster?" the answer is a hard NO . Apartment summary: cluster = building · namespace = apartment · quota = "max electricity for this apartment" · RBAC = who holds which keys · Ingress = the front desk routing visitors. One metaphor, whole book. back to top The Complete Kubernetes Guide prev · TOC · next Page 15

CH 03 ReplicaSet What Is It? 6 MIN · CORE A ReplicaSet is the guarant or : it watches a set of P ods that carry specific labels , and keeps their count at the number you asked for. Not one more, not one fewer. apiVersion : apps/v1 kind : ReplicaSet metadata : name : nginx-rs spec : replicas : 3 # the promise selector : matchLabels : app : nginx # who it manages template : # the pod stamp it uses metadata : labels : { app : nginx } # must match the selector! spec : containers : - name : nginx image : nginx:1.25 How it "counts" Selector the ReplicaSet claims every P od whose labels match app: nginx Compare desired 3 vs actual (say) 2 Act create one more P od from the template (or delete surplus) Repeat this is just the reconciliation loop again, one level down Label match is everything. If the template's labels don't satisfy the selector, the ReplicaSet refuses to start. And any stray Pod with matching labels gets adopted willingly or not.
ReplicaSet = labels + count + template. You'll rarely write one by hand a Deployment creates them for you (CH 03). back to top The Complete Kubernetes Guide prev · TOC · next Page 16

CH 03 Labels, Death & Why Deployment 6 MIN · CORE STANDALONE POD DIES Gone. For ever. Nobody holds a copy of the wish the Pod's spec died with it. This is why "just run a P od" is a demo trick, not a deployment. OWNED POD DIES Recreated aut omatically . The ReplicaSet still holds the template the mismatch triggers a replacement with a new name (e.g. nginx-rs-x7k2p ). So why isn't ReplicaSet enough? The ownership chain Deployment you talk to this one ReplicaSet v1 manages Pods at image nginx:1.25 pod pod pod change the image Deployment creates ReplicaSet v2 , rolls Pods over CH 03 ReplicaSet answers: " are the r ight number o f Pods r unning? " Deployment answers: " are they r unning the right v ersion ? and can w e swit ch v ersions with zer o do wntime? " Own vs run: a standalone Pod is run ; an owned Pod is guaranteed . The Deployment exists because the ReplicaSet can keep count but it can't change what it's counting wit hout down time . The Deployment can. back to top The Complete Kubernetes Guide prev · TOC · next Page 17

CH 03 The Pod Lifecycle Owned vs Standalone 6 MIN · CORE The five-second experiment that makes ownership real. T wo terminals: TAB 1 · WATCH $ kubectl get pods -w NAME READY STATUS web-7d9f 0/1 ContainerCreating web-7d9f 1/1 Running web-7d9f 0/1 Terminating web-x7k2p 0/1 ContainerCreating web-x7k2p 1/1 Running # new name! TAB 2 · ACT $ kubectl delete pod web-7d9f pod "web-7d9f" deleted # watch TAB 1: a replacement appears # same deployment, brand-new pod name What we just proved The Pod's name is disposable the ReplicaSet's promise is not . Deletion is just another mismatch: desired 1, actual 0 create. A standalone Pod (no owner) deleted = silence. No replacement. No drama. Status decoding: ContainerCreating = image pulling + CNI wiring · Running = process up · Terminating = shutting down gracefully · Pending = not yet placed (CH 03). Owned vs standalone is the single most important workload concept. Every "why did my Pod come back?!" mystery is answered by: someone own s it find the ReplicaSet. back to top The Complete Kubernetes Guide prev · TOC · next Page 18

CH 03 kubectl The Command Map REFERENCE Job Command What it does Create kubectl create deployment nginx -- image=nginx Imperative quick-start kubectl apply -f file.yaml Declarative the production way Inspect kubectl get pods/deploy/rs/svc -n ns List · add -w to watch live · -o wide for Node/IP kubectl describe pod NAME Full story events at the bottom kubectl logs NAME [-c container] App output · -f follow · --previous for crashed Debug kubectl exec -it NAME -- sh Shell inside the container kubectl get events --sort- by=.lastTimestamp Cluster-wide recent history Modify kubectl scale deploy nginx --replicas=5 Change the count kubectl set image deploy/nginx nginx=nginx:1.26 Trigger a rolling update kubectl rollout status/undo/history deploy/nginx Watch / revert / list revisions Delete kubectl delete pod/dep/ns NAME Deleting an ns deletes everything inside it The mental model: kubectl is just a client of the API Server . Every command above is an HTTP call to the front door nothing magical, nothing direct. back to top The Complete Kubernetes Guide prev · TOC · next Page 19

CH 03 Pod Deep Dive 6 MIN · CORE The Pod is the smallest deployable unit not the container. A P od is a co-locat ed family o f container s that share fate. ONE POD = ONE SHARED ENVIRONMENT ONE IP addr ess shared by all container s app container sidecar shared Volume same files, both container s One IP per P od containers inside talk via localhost:port , never "find the other container's IP" Shared volumes declared in the P od spec, mounted by any of its containers ⏳ Shared lifecy cle born together, scheduled together (same Node), die together Never scale "a container" you scale P ods; want more copies more P ods Port clashes are real: two containers in one Pod cannot bind the same port they literally share the network stack. The test for Pod-membership: must these contain ers live and die together on the sam e machine? Yes one Pod. No separate Pods (and let the Scheduler place them freely). back to top listens :80 reaches app on localhost The Complete Kubernetes Guide prev · TOC · next Page 20

CH 03 Multi-Container Pods 5 MIN The classic pattern: the sidecar a helper container riding along with the app container inside one P od. spec : containers : - name : app image : myapp:2.0 volumeMounts : - { name : logs, mountPath : /var/log/app } - name : log-shipper # the sidecar image : busybox command : [ "sh" , "-c" , "tail -F /logs/app.log" ] volumeMounts : - { name : logs, mountPath : /logs } # same volume! volumes : - name : logs emptyDir : {} Good vs bad Pod-mates BELONG TOGETHER app + log shipper (shared files) app + auth proxy (shared localhost) app + config reloader (shared lifecycle) DON'T frontend + database (scale & fail independently) two unrelated services (one crash restarts both... and they fight over ports) Heuristic: if the two containers could run on different machines , they belong in different Pods . Pod-mates are glued on purpose glue is a cost. back to top The Complete Kubernetes Guide prev · TOC · next Page 21

CH 03 Deployment Rolling Updates 6 MIN · CORE Change a Deployment's image and it doesn't rebuild P ods in place it creates a new R eplicaSet and rolls traffic from old to new, keeping availability the whole time. $ kubectl set image deploy/nginx nginx= nginx:1.26 deployment.apps/nginx image updated $ kubectl rollout status deploy/nginx Waiting for deployment "nginx" rollout to finish... deployment "nginx" successfully rolled out What actually happened Deployment nginx ReplicaSet v2 nginx:1.26 scales 0 3 new Pods replace old ReplicaSet v1 nginx:1.25 scales 3 0 (kept for rollback) The Controller walks the count: add a v2 P od remove a v1 P od repeat Service selectors keep pointing at labels traffic slides over automatically v1's R eplicaSet is retained (scaled to 0) that's your rollback insurance (CH 03) Zero downtime is the point: at every instant, enough healthy Pods serve traffic. The Deployment turned "risky big-bang upgrade" into "boring arithmetic." back to top The Complete Kubernetes Guide prev · TOC · next Page 22

CH 03 ⏪ Rollout Commands 4 MIN $ kubectl rollout history deploy/nginx REVISION CHANGE-CAUSE 1 <none> 2 nginx:1.26 $ kubectl rollout undo deploy/nginx deployment.apps/nginx rolled back $ kubectl rollout status deploy/nginx successfully rolled out # back on :1.25 rollout status watch a rollout finish (script-friendly) rollout history every revision is just an old R eplicaSet with a number ⏪ rollout undo flip back to the previous template · --to-revision=1 to pick revisionHistoryLimit: 3 how many old R eplicaSets to keep (default 10) Undo doesn't rewind time it creates a new revision (v3) with v1's template. History only moves forward; the ReplicaSet list is the audit trail. The rollout trilogy status / history / undo is the exam's favorite Deployment command set. Learn it as one unit. back to top The Complete Kubernetes Guide prev · TOC · next Page 23

CH 03 YAML Anatomy The Two Specs 6 MIN · CORE Every Kubernetes manifest is the same envelope: apiVersion · kind · metadata · spec . The "wish" lives in the spec. Field Meaning Example apiVersion Which API group/version serves this kind v1 (Pod) · apps/v1 (Deployment) kind What object you want Pod , Service , Deployment metadata Name · namespace · labels name: nginx spec The desired state replicas, containers, ports The Two-Specs Mystery (Deployment) spec : # the DEPLOYMENT's wish replicas : 3 selector : template : # a whole Pod hiding inside! metadata : labels : spec : # the POD's wish (spec inside spec) containers : Outer spec = what the Deployment manages: count, selector, template Inner spec ( spec.template.spec ) = the actual P od: images, ports, env, resources spec.template is the cookie cutter the ReplicaSet stamps P ods from it; change anything inside and you trigger a rollout (CH 03) Indentation is structure in YAML. The most common manifest bug is writing the Pod spec at the wrong nesting level and the API Server answers with a confusing validation error. Count your two spaces. back to top The Complete Kubernetes Guide prev · TOC · next Page 24

CH 03 Debugging 1 Reading Pod States 6 MIN · CORE The ST ATUS column is a diagnosis. Each state tells you which st age failed before you run a single command. Status Meaning Classic cause First mov e Pending Accepted, not placed Not enough CPU/mem · taints · PVC pending describe pod events ContainerCreating Placed, pulling/wiring Normal for seconds; stuck = image/CNI issue describe pod events ImagePullBackOff Can't fetch image Typo in tag · private registry, no secret Check image name & pull secret CrashLoopBackOff Starts, dies, repeats App crashes on boot bad config, missing env logs --previous Running Process is up (not necessarily healthy that's probes) Test the endpoint Completed Finished & exited 0 Job finished normal for Jobs, odd for servers Expected? done The backoff family: ImagePullBackOff and CrashLoopBackOff are not errors of Kubernetes they're Kubernetes retrying after your app/image failed. The real error is one layer deeper, in the events or logs. Memory hook: Pending = the Scheduler said no · ImagePull = the Registry said no · CrashLoop = the App said no. Three different culprits, three different rooms to search. back to top The Complete Kubernetes Guide prev · TOC

CH 03 Debugging 2 The Toolbox 6 MIN · CORE $ kubectl describe pod web-x7k2p # 1 · full biography Events: # always read the BOTTOM Failed to pull image "nginx:1.99" $ kubectl logs web-x7k2p --previous # 2 · crashed container's last words panic: missing REQUIRED_DB_PASSWORD $ kubectl exec -it web-x7k2p -- sh # 3 · go inside $ kubectl get events --sort-by= .lastTimestamp # 4 · cluster timeline DESCRIBE THE BIOGRAPHY Config as the cluster sees it, plus the Events block at the bott om the single most information-dense place in debugging. LOGS --PREVIOUS THE AUTOPSY CrashLoopBackOff kills the evidence --previous reads the last dead container' s output. Forgetting this flag = reading a fresh empty log and panicking. The 4-step playbook (in order) 90% of debugging is reading. The cluster narrates its own failures through events and logs if you ask in the right order. back to top 1 get pods read the ST ATUS column (CH 03 table) 2 describe pod events at the bottom name the failing stage 3 logs --pr evious the app's own error message 4 exec -it -- sh poke around inside: DNS, env, files, curl The Complete Kubernetes Guide prev · TOC · next Page 26

CH 03 NodePort The Side Entrance 6 MIN · CORE ClusterIPs are invisible from outside the cluster. NodeP ort punches a hole: every Node opens one high port and forwards it to your Service. apiVersion : v1 kind : Service metadata : name : nginx-svc spec : type : NodePort # default is ClusterIP selector : app : nginx ports : - port : 80 # inside the cluster targetPort : 80 # container's port nodePort : 30080 # outside or omit & let k8s pick THE PATH IN User ANY node Service Pod :80 "ANY node" is the superpower even a Node with no nginx P od opens the door and forwards across. Valid range: 3000032767 (omit nodePort and one is auto-assigned) Every Node gets the same port hit 192.168.1.11:30080 or .13:30080 , same result NodePort is for demos & edge cases raw ports, no load balancing across nodes, no TLS story. Production rides Ingress (a different book in this series ). back to top :30080 ClusterIP rules The Complete Kubernetes Guide prev · TOC · next Page 27

CH 03 illusion Service Networking The Virtual IP 6 MIN · CORE Here's the trick nobody tells you: the ClusterIP your Service owns is a lie . Nothing is listening on it. No process holds it. It's a virtual IP (VIP) and that's the elegance. RUSSIAN DOLLS WHERE THE VIP REALLY GOES 10.96.0.50 DNAT 10.244.1.5 packets "to the VIP" are rewritten in transit to a real P od the VIP never terminates anything Address ranges separate drawers: Service CIDR 10.96.0.0/12 # VIPs live here (fake, routable only via rules) Pod CIDR 10.244.0.0/16 # real Pod IPs (per-node slices) You can't ping a ClusterIP nothing answers; the rules only rewrite packets passing thr ough Pods died and got new IPs? Nobody notices everyone still dials the VIP The ranges must not ov erlap two drawers, zero confusion The Service is a stable illusion: an eternal name + eternal IP in front of a set of mortals (Pods) that churn constantly. The illusion is maintained by kube-proxy next chapter. back to top the VIP a fiction a real Pod IP The Complete Kubernetes Guide prev · TOC · next Page 28

CH 03 kube-proxy's Real Job 6 MIN · CORE kube-proxy does not forward a single packet. Its entire job is two verbs: watch & pr ogram . WHAT IT DOES NOT DO Sit in the traffic path Proxy connections through itself Touch P od-to-P od traffic WHAT IT DOES Watch the API Server: Services + Endpoints Program iptables/IPVS rules on its node Re-program the instant P ods change The rules it writes (iptables + DNAT) # conceptually, on every node: if dst == 10.96.0.50:80 # the VIP then rewrite dst 10.244.1.5:80 # pick an endpoint (random) else if next endpoint # (rule set balances across all) The Illusion, resolved: a Pod dies Endpoints object updates every node's kube-proxy rewrites its rules the VIP never moved . Stability on the outside, churn on the inside, and the packets never knew. One-liner for exams: kube-proxy wat ches Services/Endpo ints and program s packet-rewriting rules on every node it never forwar ds traffic itself. back to top The Complete Kubernetes Guide prev · TOC · next Page 29

CH 03 Following ONE Packet 6 Steps FINALE · CORE A Pod runs curl nginx-svc . Follow the single packet: 1 DNS nginx-svc resolves to the VIP 10.96.0.50 CoreDNS answered from the Service's namespace: nginx-svc.frontend.svc.cluster.local 2 Send Pod sends to the VIP (nothing is there remember CH 03) dest IP: 10.96.0.50 · dest port: 80 3 DNAT the node's iptables rules rewrite the destination dest becomes a real Pod IP: 10.244.1.5:80 4 Route same node direct delivery; different node CNI overlay carries it the packet leaves kube-proxy's rules and enters the real network 5 Receive the Pod sees a normal packet addressed to its o wn IP it replies source is the VIP thanks to conntrack, so the client never learns the Pod IP 6 Return conntrack rewrites the reply back through the VIP client believes it talked to 10.96.0.50 the whole time The entire machine in one sentence: DNS gives you a stable fake IP; kube-proxy's rules secretly rewrite it to a mortal Pod; conntrack makes the lie symmetric. That's Service networking everything else is detail. back to top The Complete Kubernetes Guide prev · TOC · labs Page 30

STEP 2 · Rescue with a toleration spec : tolerations : - key : env operator : Equal value : prod effect : NoSchedule # pod may now LAND on the tainted node Apply the P ending pod schedules immediately. Taint = the lock . Toleration = the k ey. STEP 3 · NoExecute the eviction RUN $ kubectl taint node <node> env=prod: NoExecute EXPECTED # non-tolerating pods on that # node get EVICTED now Effect Existing P ods New P ods NoSchedule stay blocked (unless tolerated) PreferNoSchedule stay avoided if possible NoExecute evicted blocked (unless tolerated) Remember the direction: taints repel (node pods); tolerations permit (pod tainted node). Taints never attract for that you'd use nodeSelector/affinity.

GLOSS Glossary REFERENCE Cluster Control Plane + Worker Nodes managed as one unit. Control Plane the brain: API Server, etcd, Scheduler, Controllers. Makes decisions; runs no user workloads (by taint). API Server the only door . All reads/writes (kubectl, kubelet, controllers) go through it; only it touches etcd. etcd the cluster's memory . Needs quorum (majority) to write why production runs 3 or 5 Control Planes. Scheduler assigns new Pods to Nodes based on resources, taints, affinity. Controller reconciliation loop: watch actual vs desired, act to close the gap. kubelet the node agent . Talks to the API Server, runs Pods via the runtime, reports status. Container Runtime pulls images and runs containers (containerd, CRI-O). kube-proxy watches Services/Endpoints, programs iptables/IPVS rules per node. Never forwards packets itself. Pod smallest deployable unit: 1+ containers sharing IP, volumes, lifecycle. ReplicaSet the guarantor: keeps N matching-labeled Pods alive via a template. Deployment manages ReplicaSets to enable versioned, zero-downtime rollouts and rollbacks. Namespace logical partition of names + RBAC + quotas inside one cluster. Apartments, not buildings. CH 08  Master : Worker Ratio & etcd Quorum  6 MIN · CORE Why does everyone run 3 Contr ol Planes ? Because etcd (the memory  ) needs a quorum — a majority of members alive and agreeing — to accept any write. THE QUORUM MATH quorum = floor((n-1)/2) + 1 members required # of Control Planes → failures tolerated before the cluster freezes: 1 CP → tolerate 0 failures (one crash = frozen) 3 CP → tolerate 1 failure ← the production minimum 5 CP → tolerate 2 failures 7 CP → tolerate 3 failures Control Planes Quorum needs Tolerates Verdict 1 1 of 1 0 Dev only 2 2 of 2 0 Worst choice — same tolerance as 1, double the cost 3 2 of 3 1 ✅ Standard production 5 3 of 5 2 Large/critical clusters ⚠ The trap: 2 is the worst number. Two members need both alive for quorum — one failure freezes writes, exactly like having one. Even numbers add cost without adding tolerance.  Workers scale independently. The ratio isn't "1 master per N workers" — it's 3–5 Control Planes (for quorum) plus as many Workers as your workload needs . A lost quorum means the cluster keeps running what's deployed but accepts no new state . ↑ back to top  The Complete Kubernetes Guide ◀ prev · ▤ TOC · next ▶ Page 11

THE QUORUM MATH quorum = floor((n-1)/2) + 1 members required # of Control Planes → failures tolerated before the cluster freezes: 1 CP → tolerate 0 failures (one crash = frozen) 3 CP → tolerate 1 failure ← the production minimum 5 CP → tolerate 2 failures 7 CP → tolerate 3 failures Control Planes Quorum needs Tolerates Verdict 1 1 of 1 0 Dev only 2 2 of 2 0 Worst choice — same tolerance as 1, double the cost 3 2 of 3 1 ✅ Standard production 5 3 of 5 2 Large/critical clusters ⚠ The trap: 2 is the worst number. Two members need both alive for quorum — one failure freezes writes, exactly like having one. Even numbers add cost without adding tolerance.  Workers scale independently. The ratio isn't "1 master per N workers" — it's 3–5 Control Planes (for quorum) plus as many Workers as your workload needs .
