CH 00 ☸ What is Kubernetes?  5 MIN · START HERE Kubernetes is an open-source container or chestrat or : it takes the containers you define and — across a fleet of machines — deploys them, scales them, heals them, connects them, and updat es them without downtime . You describe what you want. It makes reality match. Forever.  The Name Greek κυβερνήτης (kybernetes) = helmsman — the one who steers the ship. Hence the wheel logo ☸ (and the word cybernetics ).  k8s Programmer shorthand: K + the 8 letters in between + s . Pronounced "K-eights" — you'll read it a hundred times a day. 溺 Lineage Born at Google from Borg (its internal cluster manager, ~2003) → open-sourced 2014 → donated to the CNCF with v1.0 in 2015 . Written in Go. 樂 The problem it solves — running ONE container is easy; running a fleet is not  WITHOUT AN ORCHESTRATOR  A container crashes at 3am → you restart it  Ten machines free — which one takes the new app? you decide  40 containers need to find each other → hand-written configs  Upgrade from v1 to v2 → downtime, or a hand-rolled script  Black Friday? Log in and start containers manually ☸ WITH KUBERNETES  Crash → replaced automatically (reconciliation — CH 0

CH 00 ☸ What is Kubernetes? — continued  5 MIN · START HERE ⚠ What Kubernetes is NOT: not a programming language · not a PaaS (it ships buildin g blo cks , not opinions) · not a container builder (Docker/CI build images — k8s runs them) · not a runtime itself (it drives one — containerd, CRI-O, CH 03) · not a monitoring system (Prometheus & friends watch it). It's the orchestra conductor  — it doesn't play a single instrument, but nothing plays without it.  Heritage flex: Kubernetes didn't invent containers or orchestration — Google had been running billions of containers a week on Borg for a decade. Kubernetes is what happened when they distilled that war story into an open-source project the rest of the world could use. You're learning fifteen years of production scars, organized into an API.  Exam / int erview tip: "What is Kubernetes?" has a canonical two-beat answer — (1) an open-sour ce container orchestrat or, (2) declarativ e : you declare desired state, it continuously reconciles reality toward it. Add "descended from Google's Borg" for bonus credibility. ⏭ So what does it physically look lik e ? Machines split into a brain and muscle — Chapter 1: What is a Kubernetes

CH 01 ☸ What is a Kubernetes Cluster?  4 MIN A cluster is a collection of machines working together to run your applications. It has exactly two halves: ☸ KUBERNE TES CL USTER 易 CONTROL PLANE CONTROL PLANE  WORKER NODES WORKER NODES 易 +  Think of it as: 易 Master = Brain Thinks, decides, remembers  Worker = Muscle Lifts, runs, executes ☸ Cluster = Both Brain + muscle together  The modern terminology is Control Plane , not "Master". You'll still see master everywhere — because computer science terminology apparently enjoys archaeological preservation .   One sentence to remember: Cluster = Control Plane + Worker Nodes. The Control Plane manages . The Workers execute . ↑ back to top the whole her d (MASTER) Makes decisions Run applications  The Complete Kubernetes Guide ▤ TOC · next ▶ Page 6

CH 02 易 The Control Plane (Master)  6 MIN · CORE The Control Plane controls the clust er . It does not normally run your application workloads. Its job:  Receive requests  Store clust er infor mation  Decide wher e Pods should r un  Monit or the clust er ✅ Maintain the desir ed stat e 里 Inside the Control Plane 易 CONTROL PLANE API Ser ver  Scheduler  Controllers  etcd  離 Example — you tell Kubernetes: replicas : 3 The Control Plane then figures out: 燐 "I need 3 Pods ."  " Where should they run?"  "Are they actually running?"  "Did one die ?"  "Do I need to create another ?"  The four components, one line each: API Server = the only door  · etcd = the memory  · Scheduler = the placement officer  · Controllers = the watchdogs  . Everything else in the cluster talks through the door. ↑ back to top  The Complete Kubernetes Guide ◀ prev · ▤ TOC · next ▶ Page 7

CH 03  The Worker Node  6 MIN · CORE A Worker Node is a machine that actually r uns your application w orkloads . 﫛 Pods on a Worker  WORKER NODE 﫛 Pod 1  Container 﫛 Pod 2  Container 﫛 Pod 3  Container 藺 What's inside a typical Worker Node WORKER NODE  ├── kubelet  the node agent ├── container runtime ⚙ runs containers ├── kube-proxy  service networking └── Pods 﫛 your applications  The important idea: the Worker is where your application actually executes . The brain thinks — the muscle lifts. Component Job Vibe kubelet Manages Pods on this node, reports to the API Server  Node agent Container Runtime Pulls images & runs containers (containerd, CRI-O) ⚙ Engine kube-proxy Programs Service networking rules on this node  Network helper Pods Host your containers 﫛 Application unit ↑ back to top  The Complete Kubernetes Guide ◀ prev · ▤ TOC · next ▶ Page 8

CH 04  How Master & Worker Communicate  5 MIN · CORE This is important. The main communication path is the API Ser ver — one door, everything walks through it. 易 Contr ol Plane ── ► Worker 1 Worker 2 Worker 3 ▼ ▼ ▼ 﫛 Pods 﫛 Pods 﫛 Pods  The kubelet on each worker talks only to the API Server . No worker ever talks to etcd, the Scheduler, or the Controllers directly — everything goes through the front door.  Who Talks to Why kubectl (you) API Server Submit/read everything kubelet API Server Get assigned Pods · report status Scheduler API Server Watch unscheduled Pods · write its decisions Controllers API Server Watch actual state · drive it toward desired API Server etcd The only component that touches the memory   Why this design wins: one door = one place for authentication, authorization, and audit. Watch anything, change anything — always through the API. ↑ back to top API Ser ver  kubelet kubelet kubelet  The Complete Kubernetes Guide ◀ prev · ▤ TOC · next ▶ Page 9

CH 05  Walkthrough — Deploying nginx  5 MIN Imagine a cluster with 1 Contr ol Plane and 3 Workers : 易 Contr ol Plane ── ► Worker 1 Worker 2 Worker 3 You run: $ kubectl create deployment nginx --image =nginx --replicas =3 deployment.apps/nginx created  The flow  kubectl ── ► API Ser ver  ▼ 易 Contr ol Plane ▼ Scheduler  Worker 1 Worker 2 Worker 3 Worker 1 → nginx 﫛 Worker 2 → nginx 﫛 Worker 3 → nginx 﫛 易 The Contr ol Plane decides.  The W orkers execute. ↑ back to top 192.168.1.10 .11 .12 .13 records desir ed stat e picks Nodes kubelet runs it kubelet runs it kubelet runs it  The Complete Kubernetes Guide ◀ prev · ▤ TOC · next ▶ Page 10

CH 06  Self-Healing — When a Worker Dies  6 MIN · CORE This is where Kubernetes starts earning its p aycheck .  Worker 1 ❌ Worker 2 ✅ Worker 3 ✅ One of your P ods disappeared. The Control Plane notices a mismatch:  DESIRED 1 2 3  ACTUAL 1 2 Desired 3 ≠ Actual 2 ❌  Controllers react Kubernetes creates replacement P ods on healthy workers — assuming workload & cluster resources allow it. ✅ After reconciliation Worker 1 ❌ Worker 2 ✅ Worker 3 ✅  The reconciliation loop is the heart of Kubernetes: wat ch actual → compare to desired → act → repeat, forever . Nobody "restored" anything — the system simply cannot tolerate a mismatch. ⚠ Honest limits: if the cluster is out of CPU/memory, or all healthy nodes are full, replacements stay Pending . Self-healing repairs state — it doesn't conjure capacity. ↑ back to top 﫛 nginx · 﫛 nginx 﫛 nginx · 﫛 nginx  The Complete Kubernetes Guide ◀ prev · ▤ TOC · next ▶ Page 11

CH 07 樂 Can the Control Plane also be a Worker?  4 MIN Technically y es. In pr oduction: no. The mechanism that separates them is a taint .  MINIKUBE — YES, BY DESIGN A single-node cluster where one machine is both brain and muscle . The Control-Plane taint is removed so workloads can land there. Perfect for learning. $ kubectl get nodes NAME STATUS ROLES minikube Ready control-plane,master  PRODUCTION — NEVER Control-Plane nodes carry a taint like node- role.kubernetes.io/control-plane:NoSchedule — the Scheduler refuses t o place nor mal Pods ther e . The brain is protected. $ kubectl describe node cp1 | grep Taints Taints: node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane:NoSchedule ⚠ Why the isolation matters: a runaway workload on a Control-Plane node can starve the API Server or etcd — and then the entire cluster's brain slows or freezes. etcd is especially latency-sensitive.  Remember: "Control Plane ≠ Worker" is not a law of nature — it's a taint . Remove the taint and the brain will do deadlifts. (Lab 5 covers taints hands-on.) ↑ back to top  The Complete Kubernetes Guide ◀ prev · ▤ TOC · next ▶ Page 12

CH 08  Master : Worker Ratio & etcd Quorum  6 MIN · CORE Why does everyone run 3 Contr ol Planes ? Because etcd (the memory  ) needs a quorum — a majority of members alive and agreeing — to accept any write. THE QUORUM MATH quorum = floor((n-1)/2) + 1 members required # of Control Planes → failures tolerated before the cluster freezes: 1 CP → tolerate 0 failures (one crash = frozen) 3 CP → tolerate 1 failure ← the production minimum 5 CP → tolerate 2 failures 7 CP → tolerate 3 failures Control Planes Quorum needs Tolerates Verdict 1 1 of 1 0 Dev only 2 2 of 2 0 Worst choice — same tolerance as 1, double the cost 3 2 of 3 1 ✅ Standard production 5 3 of 5 2 Large/critical clusters ⚠ The trap: 2 is the worst number. Two members need both alive for quorum — one failure freezes writes, exactly like having one. Even numbers add cost without adding tolerance.  Workers scale independently. The ratio isn't "1 master per N workers" — it's 3–5 Control Planes (for quorum) plus as many Workers as your workload needs . A lost quorum means the cluster keeps running what's deployed but accepts no new state . ↑ back to top  The Complete Kubernetes Guide ◀ prev · ▤ TOC · next ▶ Page 13

CH 09  The Diagram Map + Learning Roadmap  REFERENCE Everything from P art I–II on one canvas. If you can redraw this from memory, you own the architecture. ☸ CLUSTER ├── 易 CONTROL PLANE ×3 for quorum │ ├── API Server  the only door │ ├── etcd  state — API Server's alone │ ├── Scheduler  assigns Pods → Nodes │ └── Controllers  reconcile desired ↔ actual └──  WORKERS ├── kubelet  agent — talks to API Server ├── Runtime ⚙ pulls + runs containers ├── kube-proxy  Service rules └── Pods 﫛  The learning order that works  Study rule: never learn a component without knowing wh o it talk s to . Isolated component lists evaporate; communication maps stick. ↑ back to top 1 Components — who does what (P arts I–II) · you are here ✅ 2 Namesp aces — carve logical apartments (P art III) 3 Workloads — ReplicaSet → Deployment → updates (P art IV–V) 4 Networking — how traffic actually reaches a P od (Part VI) 5 Labs — break things, watch them heal (P art VII)  The Complete Kubernetes Guide ◀ prev · ▤ TOC · next ▶ Page 14

CH 10  Namespaces — The Big Idea  4 MIN Without namespaces, one cluster = one giant bucket. Frontend, AI and dev all collide — same names, no boundaries. A namespace is the cluster saying "I can car ve logical ap artments inside one building." PROBLEM — ONE FLAT BUCKET Cluster ├── pod-a ├── pod-b frontend? ├── pod-c ai? └── svc-a # who owns what? SOLUTION — LOGICAL APARTMENTS Cluster ├── frontend Pods + Services ├── ai Pods + Services └── dev Pods + Services same nodes, same control plane When namespaces shine  Teams frontend / backend / ai  Environments dev / staging / prod via namespaces 里 Apps app-a / app-b isolated, same infra  Namespace = logical isolation — it affects names, RBAC, quotas. It does not carve hardware or network by itself.  Environment ≠ Namespace. Environment is the concept; namespace is one object you can implement it with (another: separate clusters). ↑ back to top  The Complete Kubernetes Guide ◀ prev · ▤ TOC · next ▶ Page 15

CH 11  Names Are Scoped + The Three Superpowers  6 MIN · CORE A Pod's full identity is namesp ace + kind + name . So dev/nginx and prod/nginx are two different objects — no collision. Cluster ├── dev │ └── nginx Pod ← identity: dev / Pod / nginx └── prod └── nginx Pod ← identity: prod / Pod / nginx ⚡ The three superpowers namespaces unlock 着 RBAC — KEYS "This team may act only inside frontend ." Permissions scoped per namespace.  QUOTAS — BUDGET "ai may use at most 4 CPU / 8Gi , 10 Pods." A R esourceQuota caps each apartment's totals.  NETWORKPOLICY — DOOR RULES "Pods in dev may not call prod." Traffic rules scoped per namespace. ⚠ Not everything lives in an apartment. Nodes , ClusterRoles , PersistentVolumes and Namespaces themselves are cluster-scoped — kubectl get nodes -n dev silently ignores the -n . Nodes belong to the building, not an apartment.  The rule: namespaced → identity includes the namespace · cluster-scoped → namespace flags do nothing. Namespaces partition names, not hardware. ↑ back to top  The Complete Kubernetes Guide ◀ prev · ▤ TOC · next ▶ Page 16

CH 12 吝 Service DNS + Default Namespaces  5 MIN  How Pods find each other: DNS Every Service gets a DNS name built from its namespace — that's how cross-P od traffic finds its way: nginx-ser vice ── ► nginx-ser vice .frontend .svc.clust er.local same short name resolves within the same namespace — "nginx-service" from inside frontend just works frontend | ai ← same Service name, two namespaces, zero collision  The namespaces you always have $ kubectl get namespaces NAME STATUS default Active # you land here when you omit -n kube-system Active # the cluster's own components kube-public Active # public info kube-node-lease Active # node heartbeats  kubectl get pods is secretly kubectl get pods -n default  kube-system is where the Control Plane's own P ods live (on kubeadm clusters)  Mailbox rule: "nginx-service, Apt frontend" vs "nginx-service, Apt ai" — same name, different mailbox, and the post office (DNS + API Server) always delivers correctly. ↑ back to top Service nginx-ser vice nginx-ser vice  The Complete Kubernetes Guide ◀ prev · ▤ TOC · next ▶ Page 17

CH 13  The Complete Namespace Picture  REFERENCE ☸ CLUSTER ├── Namespace: frontend Pods · Services · Quotas ├── Namespace: ai Pods · Services · Quotas ├── Namespace: dev Pods · Services · Quotas │ └── Nodes # OUTSIDE every namespace ├── node1 (4 CPU / 8Gi) └── node2 (4 CPU / 8Gi) # one shared pool Layer Shared across namespaces? Notes Control Plane (API Server, etcd, Scheduler) ✅ Yes — one per cluster A namespace is just a field on objects Nodes · CPU · Memory · Network ✅ Yes Quotas lim it usage, they don't carve hardware Pods · Services · ConfigMaps ❌ No — namespaced dev/nginx ≠ prod/nginx  Namespace ≠ separate cluster. Same control plane, same Nodes, same CPU/memory pool. If an exam asks "is a namespace its own cluster?" — the answer is a hard NO .  Apartment summary: cluster = building · namespace = apartment · quota = "max electricity for this apartment" · RBAC = who holds which keys · Ingress = the front desk routing visitors. One metaphor, whole book. ↑ back to top  The Complete Kubernetes Guide ◀ prev · ▤ TOC · next ▶ Page 18

CH 14  ReplicaSet — What Is It?  6 MIN · CORE A ReplicaSet is the guarant or : it watches a set of P ods that carry specific labels , and keeps their count at the number you asked for. Not one more, not one fewer. apiVersion : apps/v1 kind : ReplicaSet metadata : name : nginx-rs spec : replicas : 3 # ← the promise selector : matchLabels : app : nginx # ← who it manages template : # ← the pod stamp it uses metadata : labels : { app : nginx } # must match the selector! spec : containers : - name : nginx image : nginx:1.25  How it "counts"  Selector — the R eplicaSet claims every P od whose labels match app: nginx 燐 Compare — desired 3 vs actual (say) 2  Act — create one more P od from the template (or delete surplus)  Repeat — this is just the reconciliation loop again, one level down ⚠ Label match is everything. If the template's labels don't satisfy the selector, the ReplicaSet refuses to start. And any stray Pod with matching labels gets adopted — willingly or not.  ReplicaSet = labels + count + template. You'll rarely write one by hand — a Deployment creates them for you (CH 15). ↑ back to top  The Complete Kubernetes Guide ◀ prev · ▤ TOC · next ▶ Page 19

CH 15  Labels, Death & Why Deployment  6 MIN · CORE STANDALONE POD DIES  Gone. For ever. Nobody holds a copy of the wish — the Pod's spec died with it. This is why "just run a P od" is a demo trick, not a deployment. OWNED POD DIES  Recreated aut omatically . The ReplicaSet still holds the template — the mismatch triggers a replacement with a new name (e.g. nginx-rs-x7k2p ). 惘 So why isn't ReplicaSet enough? The ownership chain Deployment you talk to this one └── ReplicaSet v1 manages Pods at image nginx:1.25 ├── 﫛 pod ├── 﫛 pod └── 﫛 pod change the image → Deployment creates ReplicaSet v2 , rolls Pods over ← CH 20  ReplicaSet answers: " are the r ight number o f Pods r unning? "  Deployment answers: " are they r unning the right v ersion ? — and can w e swit ch v ersions with zer o do wntime? "  Own vs run: a standalone Pod is run ; an owned Pod is guaranteed . The Deployment exists because the ReplicaSet can keep count — but it can't change what it's counting wit hout down time . The Deployment can. ↑ back to top  The Complete Kubernetes Guide ◀ prev · ▤ TOC · next ▶ Page 20

CH 16  The Pod Lifecycle — Owned vs Standalone  6 MIN · CORE The five-second experiment that makes ownership real. T wo terminals:  TAB 1 · WATCH $ kubectl get pods -w NAME READY STATUS web-7d9f 0/1 ContainerCreating web-7d9f 1/1 Running web-7d9f 0/1 Terminating web-x7k2p 0/1 ContainerCreating web-x7k2p 1/1 Running # new name! ⚙ TAB 2 · ACT $ kubectl delete pod web-7d9f pod "web-7d9f" deleted # watch TAB 1: a replacement appears # same deployment, brand-new pod name 茶 What we just proved ✅ The Pod's name is disposable — the R eplicaSet's promise is not . ✅ Deletion is just another mismatch: desired 1, actual 0 → create. ❌ A standalone Pod (no owner) deleted = silence. No replacement. No drama.  Status decoding: ContainerCreating = image pulling + CNI wiring · Running = process up · Terminating = shutting down gracefully · Pending = not yet placed (CH 23).  Owned vs standalone is the single most important workload concept. Every "why did my Pod come back?!" mystery is answered by: someone own s it — find the ReplicaSet. ↑ back to top  The Complete Kubernetes Guide ◀ prev · ▤ TOC · next ▶ Page 21

CH 17 ⌨ kubectl — The Command Map  REFERENCE Job Command What it does Create kubectl create deployment nginx -- image=nginx Imperative quick-start kubectl apply -f file.yaml Declarative — the production way Inspect kubectl get pods/deploy/rs/svc -n ns List · add -w to watch live · -o wide for Node/IP kubectl describe pod NAME Full story — events at the bottom kubectl logs NAME [-c container] App output · -f follow · --previous for crashed Debug kubectl exec -it NAME -- sh Shell inside the container kubectl get events --sort- by=.lastTimestamp Cluster-wide recent history Modify kubectl scale deploy nginx --replicas=5 Change the count kubectl set image deploy/nginx nginx=nginx:1.26 Trigger a rolling update kubectl rollout status/undo/history deploy/nginx Watch / revert / list revisions Delete kubectl delete pod/dep/ns NAME Deleting an ns deletes everything inside it ⚠  The mental model: kubectl is just a client of the API Server . Every command above is an HTTP call to the front door — nothing magical, nothing direct. ↑ back to top  The Complete Kubernetes Guide ◀ prev · ▤ TOC · next ▶ Page 22

CH 18 﫛 Pod Deep Dive  6 MIN · CORE The Pod is the smallest deployable unit — not the container. A P od is a co-locat ed family o f container s that share fate. ONE POD = ONE SHARED ENVIRONMENT  ONE IP addr ess shared by all container s  app container  sidecar  shared Volume same files, both container s  One IP per P od — containers inside talk via localhost:port , never "find the other container's IP"  Shared volumes — declared in the P od spec, mounted by any of its containers ⏳ Shared lifecy cle — born together, scheduled together (same Node), die together  Never scale "a container" — you scale P ods; want more copies → more P ods ⚠ Port clashes are real: two containers in one Pod cannot bind the same port — they literally share the network stack.  The test for Pod-membership: must these contain ers live and die together on the sam e machine? Yes → one Pod. No → separate Pods (and let the Scheduler place them freely). ↑ back to top listens :80 reaches app on localhost  The Complete Kubernetes Guide ◀ prev · ▤ TOC · next ▶ Page 23

CH 19  Multi-Container Pods  5 MIN The classic pattern: the sidecar — a helper container riding along with the app container inside one P od. spec : containers : - name : app image : myapp:2.0 volumeMounts : - { name : logs, mountPath : /var/log/app } - name : log-shipper # the sidecar image : busybox command : [ "sh" , "-c" , "tail -F /logs/app.log" ] volumeMounts : - { name : logs, mountPath : /logs } # same volume! volumes : - name : logs emptyDir : {} ⚖ Good vs bad Pod-mates ✅ BELONG TOGETHER  app + log shipper (shared files)  app + auth proxy (shared localhost)  app + config reloader (shared lifecycle) ❌ DON'T frontend + database (scale & fail independently) two unrelated services (one crash restarts both... and they fight over ports)  Heuristic: if the two containers could run on different machines , they belong in different Pods . Pod-mates are glued on purpose — glue is a cost. ↑ back to top  The Complete Kubernetes Guide ◀ prev · ▤ TOC · next ▶ Page 24

CH 20  Deployment — Rolling Updates  6 MIN · CORE Change a Deployment's image and it doesn't rebuild P ods in place — it creates a new R eplicaSet and rolls traffic from old to new, keeping availability the whole time. $ kubectl set image deploy/nginx nginx= nginx:1.26 deployment.apps/nginx image updated $ kubectl rollout status deploy/nginx Waiting for deployment "nginx" rollout to finish... deployment "nginx" successfully rolled out 惘 What actually happened Deployment nginx ├── ReplicaSet v2 nginx:1.26 scales 0 → 3  │ └── 﫛 﫛 﫛 new Pods replace old └── ReplicaSet v1 nginx:1.25 scales 3 → 0  (kept for rollback) ⚖ The Controller walks the count: add a v2 P od → remove a v1 P od → repeat  Service selectors keep pointing at labels — traffic slides over automatically  v1's R eplicaSet is retained (scaled to 0) — that's your rollback insurance (CH 21)  Zero downtime is the point: at every instant, enough healthy Pods serve traffic. The Deployment turned "risky big-bang upgrade" into "boring arithmetic." ↑ back to top  The Complete Kubernetes Guide ◀ prev · ▤ TOC · next ▶ Page 25

CH 21 ⏪ Rollout Commands  4 MIN $ kubectl rollout history deploy/nginx REVISION CHANGE-CAUSE 1 <none> 2 nginx:1.26 $ kubectl rollout undo deploy/nginx deployment.apps/nginx rolled back $ kubectl rollout status deploy/nginx successfully rolled out # ← back on :1.25  rollout status — watch a rollout finish (script-friendly)  rollout history — every revision is just an old R eplicaSet with a number ⏪ rollout undo — flip back to the previous template · --to-revision=1 to pick  revisionHistoryLimit: 3 — how many old R eplicaSets to keep (default 10) ⚠ Undo doesn't rewind time — it creates a new revision (v3) with v1's template. CH 22  YAML Anatomy — The Two Specs  6 MIN · CORE Every Kubernetes manifest is the same envelope: apiVersion · kind · metadata · spec . The "wish" lives in the spec. Field Meaning Example apiVersion Which API group/version serves this kind v1 (Pod) · apps/v1 (Deployment) kind What object you want Pod , Service , Deployment metadata Name · namespace · labels name: nginx spec The desired state replicas, containers, ports... 惘 The Two-Specs Mystery (Deployment) spec : # the DEPLOYMENT's wish replicas : 3 selector : ... template : # a whole Pod hiding inside! metadata : labels : ... spec : # ← the POD's wish (spec inside spec) containers : ... 易 Outer spec = what the Deployment manages: count, selector, template 﫛 Inner spec ( spec.template.spec ) = the actual P od: images, ports, env, resources  spec.template is the cookie cutter — the R eplicaSet stamps P ods from it; change anything inside and you trigger a rollout (CH 20)  Indentation is structure in YAML. CH 23 喙 Debugging 1 — Reading Pod States  6 MIN · CORE The ST ATUS column is a diagnosis. Each state tells you which st age failed — before you run a single command. Status Meaning Classic cause First move Pending Accepted, not placed Not enough CPU/mem · taints · PVC pending describe pod → events ContainerCreating Placed, pulling/wiring Normal for seconds; stuck = image/CNI issue describe pod → events ImagePullBackOff Can't fetch image Typo in tag · private registry, no secret Check image name & pull secret CrashLoopBackOff Starts, dies, repeats App crashes on boot — bad config, missing env logs --previous Running Process is up — (not necessarily healthy — that's probes) Test the endpoint Completed Finished & exited 0 Job finished — normal for Jobs, odd for servers Expected? done ✅ ⚠ The backoff family: ImagePullBackOff and CrashLoopBackOff are not errors of Kubernetes — they're Kubernetes retrying after your app/image failed. The real error is one layer deeper, in the events or logs.  Memory hook: Pending = the Scheduler said no · ImagePull = the Registry said no · CrashLoop = the App said no. Three different culprits, three different rooms to search. ↑ back to top  The Comple

Events: # ...always read the BOTTOM Failed to pull image "nginx:1.99" $ kubectl logs web-x7k2p --previous # 2 · crashed container's last words panic: missing REQUIRED_DB_PASSWORD $ kubectl exec -it web-x7k2p -- sh # 3 · go inside $ kubectl get events --sort-by= .lastTimestamp # 4 · cluster timeline DESCRIBE — THE BIOGRAPHY Config as the cluster sees it, plus the Events block at the bott om — the single most information-dense place in debugging. CH 25  NodePort — The Side Entrance  6 MIN · CORE ClusterIPs are invisible from outside the cluster. NodeP ort punches a hole: every Node opens one high port and forwards it to your Service. apiVersion : v1 kind : Service metadata : name : nginx-svc spec : type : NodePort # default is ClusterIP selector : app : nginx ports : - port : 80 # inside the cluster targetPort : 80 # container's port nodePort : 30080 # outside — or omit & let k8s pick THE PATH IN  User ── ► ANY node ── ► Service ── ► 﫛 Pod :80 "ANY node" is the superpower — even a Node with no nginx P od opens the door and forwards across.  Valid range: 30000–32767 (omit nodePort and one is auto-assigned)  Every Node gets the same port — hit 192.168.1.11:30080 or .13:30080 , same result ⚠ NodePort is for demos & edge cases — raw ports, no load balancing across nodes, no TLS story. CH 26  Service Networking — The Virtual IP  6 MIN · CORE Here's the trick nobody tells you: the ClusterIP your Service owns is a lie . Nothing is listening on it. No process holds it. It's a virtual IP (VIP) — and that's the elegance. RUSSIAN DOLLS — WHERE THE VIP REALLY GOES 10.96.0.50 ── ► DNA T ── ► 10.244.1.5 packets "to the VIP" are rewritten in transit to a real P od — the VIP never terminates anything Address ranges — separate drawers: Service CIDR 10.96.0.0/12 # VIPs live here (fake, routable only via rules) Pod CIDR 10.244.0.0/16 # real Pod IPs (per-node slices)  You can't ping a ClusterIP — nothing answers; the rules only rewrite packets passing thr ough  Pods died and got new IPs? Nobody notices — everyone still dials the VIP 燐 The ranges must not ov erlap — two drawers, zero confusion  The Service is a stable illusion: an eternal name + eternal IP in front of a set of mortals (Pods) that churn constantly. The illusion is maintained by kube-proxy — next chapter. ↑ back to top the VIP — a fiction a real Pod IP  The Complete Kubernetes Guide ◀ prev · ▤ TOC · next ▶ Page 31

CH 27  kube-proxy's Real Job  6 MIN · CORE kube-proxy does not forward a single packet. Its entire job is two verbs: watch & pr ogram . ❌ WHAT IT DOES NOT DO Sit in the traffic path Proxy connections through itself Touch P od-to-P od traffic ✅ WHAT IT DOES Watch the API Server: Services + Endpoints Program iptables/IPVS rules on its node Re-program the instant P ods change 彩 The rules it writes (iptables + DNAT) # conceptually, on every node: if dst == 10.96.0.50:80 # the VIP then rewrite dst → 10.244.1.5:80 # pick an endpoint (random) else if ... next endpoint # (rule set balances across all) ✨ The Illusion, resolved: a Pod dies → Endpoints object updates → every node's kube-proxy rewrites its rules → the VIP never moved . Stability on the outside, churn on the inside, and the packets never knew.  One-liner for exams: kube-proxy wat ches Services/Endpo ints and programs packet-rewriting rules on every node — it never forwar ds traffic itself. ↑ back to top  The Complete Kubernetes Guide ◀ prev · ▤ TOC · next ▶ Page 32

CH 28  Following ONE Packet — 6 Steps  FINALE · CORE A Pod runs curl nginx-svc . Follow the single packet:  The entire machine in one sentence: DNS gives you a stable fake IP; kube-proxy's rules secretly rewrite it to a mortal Pod; conntrack makes the lie symmetric. That's Service networking — everything else is detail. ↑ back to top 1 DNS — nginx-svc resolves to the VIP 10.96.0.50 · CoreDNS answered from the Service's namespace 2 Send — Pod sends to the VIP (nothing is there — remember CH 26) · dest: 10.96.0.50:80 3 DNAT — the node's iptables rules rewrite the destination → a real P od IP: 10.244.1.5:80 4 Route — same node → direct delivery; different node → CNI overlay carries it 5 Receive — the P od sees a normal packet addressed to its o wn IP · it replies 6 Return — conntrack rewrites the reply back through the VIP — the client believes it talked to 10.96.0.50 the whole time   The Complete Kubernetes Guide ◀ prev · ▤ TOC · labs ▶ Page 33

LAB 5  Taints & Tolerations  15 MIN · HANDS-ON STEP 1 · Taint AFTER the Pod exists ⚙ RUN $ kubectl taint node <node> env=prod:NoSchedule $ kubectl scale deploy web --replicas=4  EXPECTED # existing pods keep running # NEW 4th pod → Pending 0/1 Nodes available ...taint...that pod tolerates not Key insight: NoSchedule only gates new placements — it never evicts. STEP 2 · Rescue with a toleration spec : tolerations : - key : env operator : Equal value : prod effect : NoSchedule # pod may now LAND on the tainted node Apply → the P ending pod schedules immediately. Taint = the lock . Toleration = the k ey. STEP 3 · NoExecute — the eviction ⚙ RUN $ kubectl taint node <node> env=prod: NoExecute  EXPECTED # non-tolerating pods on that # node get EVICTED — now Effect Existing Pods New Pods NoSchedule stay blocked (unless tolerated) PreferNoSchedule stay avoided if possible NoExecute evicted blocked (unless tolerated)  Remember the direction: taints repel (node → pods); tolerations permit (pod → tainted node). Taints never attract — for that you'd use nodeSelector/affinity (Book 04 in depth). ↑ back to top  The Complete Kubernetes Guide ◀ prev · ▤ TOC · quiz ▶ Page 38

GLOSS  Glossary  REFERENCE Cluster — Control Plane + Worker Nodes managed as one unit. Control Plane — the brain: API Server, etcd, Scheduler, Controllers. Makes decisions; runs no user workloads (by taint). API Server — the only door  . All reads/writes (kubectl, kubelet, controllers) go through it; only it touches etcd. etcd — the cluster's memory  . Needs quorum (majority) to write — why production runs 3 or 5 Control Planes. Scheduler — assigns new Pods to Nodes based on resources, taints, affinity. Controller — reconciliation loop: watch actual vs desired, act to close the gap. kubelet — the node agent  . Talks to the API Server, runs Pods via the runtime, reports status. Container Runtime — pulls images and runs containers (containerd, CRI-O). kube-proxy — watches Services/Endpoints, programs iptables/IPVS rules per node. Never forwards packets itself. Pod — smallest deployable unit: 1+ containers sharing IP, volumes, lifecycle. ReplicaSet — the guarantor: keeps N matching-labeled Pods alive via a template. Deployment — manages ReplicaSets to enable versioned, zero-downtime rollouts and rollbacks. Namespace — logical partition of names + RBAC + quotas inside one cluster.

CH 14  ReplicaSet — What Is It?  6 MIN · CORE A ReplicaSet is the guarant or : it watches a set of P ods that carry specific labels , and keeps their count at the number you asked for. Not one more, not one fewer. apiVersion : apps/v1 kind : ReplicaSet metadata : name : nginx-rs spec : replicas : 3 # ← the promise selector : matchLabels : app : nginx # ← who it manages template : # ← the pod stamp it uses metadata : labels : { app : nginx } # must match the selector! spec : containers : - name : nginx image : nginx:1.25  How it "counts"  Selector — the R eplicaSet claims every P od whose labels match app: nginx 燐 Compare — desired 3 vs actual (say) 2  Act — create one more P od from the template (or delete surplus)  Repeat — this is just the reconciliation loop again, one level down ⚠ Label match is everything. If the template's labels don't satisfy the selector, the ReplicaSet refuses to start. And any stray Pod with matching labels gets adopted — willingly or not.  ReplicaSet = labels + count + template. You'll rarely write one by hand — a Deployment creates them for you (CH 15). ↑ back to top  The Complete Kubernetes Guide ◀ prev · ▤ TOC · next ▶ Page 17

CH 15  Labels, Death & Why Deployment  6 MIN · CORE STANDALONE POD DIES  Gone. For ever. Nobody holds a copy of the wish — the Pod's spec died with it. This is why "just run a P od" is a demo trick, not a deployment. OWNED POD DIES  Recreated aut omatically . The ReplicaSet still holds the template — the mismatch triggers a replacement with a new name (e.g. nginx-rs-x7k2p ). 惘 So why isn't ReplicaSet enough? The ownership chain Deployment you talk to this one └── ReplicaSet v1 manages Pods at image nginx:1.25 ├── 﫛 pod ├── 﫛 pod └── 﫛 pod change the image → Deployment creates ReplicaSet v2 , rolls Pods over ← CH 20  ReplicaSet answers: " are the r ight number o f Pods r unning? "  Deployment answers: " are they r unning the right v ersion ? — and can w e swit ch v ersions with zer o do wntime? "  Own vs run: a standalone Pod is run ; an owned Pod is guaranteed . The Deployment exists because the ReplicaSet can keep count — but it can't change what it's counting wit hout down time . The Deployment can. ↑ back to top  The Complete Kubernetes Guide ◀ prev · ▤ TOC · next ▶ Page 18

CH 16  The Pod Lifecycle — Owned vs Standalone  6 MIN · CORE The five-second experiment that makes ownership real. T wo terminals:  TAB 1 · WATCH $ kubectl get pods -w NAME READY STATUS web-7d9f 0/1 ContainerCreating web-7d9f 1/1 Running web-7d9f 0/1 Terminating web-x7k2p 0/1 ContainerCreating web-x7k2p 1/1 Running # new name! ⚙ TAB 2 · ACT $ kubectl delete pod web-7d9f pod "web-7d9f" deleted # watch TAB 1: a replacement appears # same deployment, brand-new pod name 茶 What we just proved ✅ The Pod's name is disposable — the R eplicaSet's promise is not . ✅ Deletion is just another mismatch: desired 1, actual 0 → create. ❌ A standalone Pod (no owner) deleted = silence. No replacement. No drama.  Status decoding: ContainerCreating = image pulling + CNI wiring · Running = process up · Terminating = shutting down gracefully · Pending = not yet placed (CH 23).  Owned vs standalone is the single most important workload concept. Every "why did my Pod come back?!" mystery is answered by: someone own s it — find the ReplicaSet. ↑ back to top  The Complete Kubernetes Guide ◀ prev · ▤ TOC · next ▶ Page 19

CH 17 ⌨ kubectl — The Command Map  REFERENCE Job Command What it does Create kubectl create deployment nginx -- image=nginx Imperative quick-start kubectl apply -f file.yaml Declarative — the production way Inspect kubectl get pods/deploy/rs/svc -n ns List · add -w to watch live · -o wide for Node/IP kubectl describe pod NAME Full story — events at the bottom kubectl logs NAME [-c container] App output · -f follow · --previous for crashed Debug kubectl exec -it NAME -- sh Shell inside the container kubectl get events --sort- by=.lastTimestamp Cluster-wide recent history Modify kubectl scale deploy nginx --replicas=5 Change the count kubectl set image deploy/nginx nginx=nginx:1.26 Trigger a rolling update kubectl rollout status/undo/history deploy/nginx Watch / revert / list revisions Delete kubectl delete pod/dep/ns NAME Deleting an ns deletes everything inside it ⚠  The mental model: kubectl is just a client of the API Server . CH 18 﫛 Pod Deep Dive  6 MIN · CORE The Pod is the smallest deployable unit — not the container. A P od is a co-locat ed family o f container s that share fate. ONE POD = ONE SHARED ENVIRONMENT  ONE IP addr ess shared by all container s  app container  sidecar  shared Volume same files, both container s  One IP per P od — containers inside talk via localhost:port , never "find the other container's IP"  Shared volumes — declared in the P od spec, mounted by any of its containers ⏳ Shared lifecy cle — born together, scheduled together (same Node), die together  Never scale "a container" — you scale P ods; want more copies → more P ods ⚠ Port clashes are real: two containers in one Pod cannot bind the same port — they literally share the network stack.  The test for Pod-membership: must these contain ers live and die together on the sam e machine? Yes → one Pod. No → separate Pods (and let the Scheduler place them freely). ↑ back to top listens :80 reaches app on localhost  The Complete Kubernetes Guide ◀ prev · ▤ TOC · next ▶ Page 21

CH 19  Multi-Container Pods  5 MIN The classic pattern: the sidecar — a helper container riding along with the app container inside one P od. spec : containers : - name : app image : myapp:2.0 volumeMounts : - { name : logs, mountPath : /var/log/app } - name : log-shipper # the sidecar image : busybox command : [ "sh" , "-c" , "tail -F /logs/app.log" ] volumeMounts : - { name : logs, mountPath : /logs } # same volume! volumes : - name : logs emptyDir : {} ⚖ Good vs bad Pod-mates ✅ BELONG TOGETHER  app + log shipper (shared files)  app + auth proxy (shared localhost)  app + config reloader (shared lifecycle) ❌ DON'T frontend + database (scale & fail independently) two unrelated services (one crash restarts both... and they fight over ports)  Heuristic: if the two containers could run on different machines , they belong in different Pods . Pod-mates are glued on purpose — glue is a cost. ↑ back to top  The Complete Kubernetes Guide ◀ prev · ▤ TOC · next ▶ Page 22

CH 20  Deployment — Rolling Updates  6 MIN · CORE Change a Deployment's image and it doesn't rebuild P ods in place — it creates a new R eplicaSet and rolls traffic from old to new, keeping availability the whole time. $ kubectl set image deploy/nginx nginx= nginx:1.26 deployment.apps/nginx image updated $ kubectl rollout status deploy/nginx Waiting for deployment "nginx" rollout to finish... deployment "nginx" successfully rolled out 惘 What actually happened Deployment nginx ├── ReplicaSet v2 nginx:1.26 scales 0 → 3  │ └── 﫛 﫛 﫛 new Pods replace old └── ReplicaSet v1 nginx:1.25 scales 3 → 0  (kept for rollback) ⚖ The Controller walks the count: add a v2 P od → remove a v1 P od → repeat  Service selectors keep pointing at labels — traffic slides over automatically  v1's R eplicaSet is retained (scaled to 0) — that's your rollback insurance (CH 21)  Zero downtime is the point: at every instant, enough healthy Pods serve traffic. The Deployment turned "risky big-bang upgrade" into "boring arithmetic." ↑ back to top  The Complete Kubernetes Guide ◀ prev · ▤ TOC · next ▶ Page 23

The Deployment turned "risky big-bang upgrade" into "boring arithmetic." ↑ back to top  The Complete Kubernetes Guide ◀ prev · ▤ TOC · next ▶ Page 23

CH 21 ⏪ Rollout Commands  4 MIN $ kubectl rollout history deploy/nginx REVISION CHANGE-CAUSE 1 <none> 2 nginx:1.26 $ kubectl rollout undo deploy/nginx deployment.apps/nginx rolled back $ kubectl rollout status deploy/nginx successfully rolled out # ← back on :1.25  rollout status — watch a rollout finish (script-friendly)  rollout history — every revision is just an old R eplicaSet with a number ⏪ rollout undo — flip back to the previous template · --to-revision=1 to pick  revisionHistoryLimit: 3 — how many old R eplicaSets to keep (default 10) ⚠ Undo doesn't rewind time — it creates a new revision (v3) with v1's template. History only moves forward; the ReplicaSet list is the audit trail.  The rollout trilogy — status / history / undo — is the exam's favorite Deployment command set. Learn it as one unit. ↑ back to top  The Complete Kubernetes Guide ◀ prev · ▤ TOC · next ▶ Page 24

You've already met everything here in passing: daemon-like agents skipped your drains (Book 04 · CH 10), Promtail/node-exporter ride DaemonSets (your observability stack!), and Book 05 built the StatefulSet storage half. This book finishes ea

CH 01  DaemonSet — One Pod Per Node  6 MIN · CORE A Deployment says "run N replicas, I don 't care where." A DaemonSet says "run exactly ONE P od on E VERY node — new node joins, P od spawns; node leav es, Pod vanishes." Infrastructure agents live here. DEPLOYMENT VS DAEMONSET — THE PLACEMENT QUESTION Deployment "3 total, anywher e" ⇄ DaemonSet "1 per node, ev erywhere" 﫛 node1 﫛 node2 﫛 node3 ←  DaemonSet apiVersion : apps/v1 kind : DaemonSet metadata : { name : log-agent } spec : selector : { matchLabels : { app : log-agent } } template : # no `replicas:` field — the NODE LIST decides metadata : { labels : { app : log-agent } } spec : containers : - name : agent image : fluent/fluent-bit:2.2 volumeMounts : - { name : logs, mountPath : /var/log/pods , readOnly : true } volumes : - name : logs hostPath : { path : /var/log/pods } # node-local files (Book 05 · CH 02!) The four classic t enants Why per -node is mandat ory  Log collectors — Fluent Bit, Promtail container logs are files on each node's disk — only a local Pod can tail them (Book 01 · CH 03c logic)  Metric agents — node-exporter, Datadog agent host metrics only exist at the node  Networking — CNI plugins, kube-proxy

CH 02  DaemonSet — Updates & Node Lifecycle  5 MIN  Node churn — the automatic part node4 joins → kubelet registers → DaemonSet controller notices → Pod spawns within seconds node4 dies → node object removed (or heartbeat lost) → Pod garbage-collected node tainted? → DaemonSets auto-tolerate the infrastructure taints: not-ready · unreachable · disk-pressure · memory-pressure ✓ auto control-plane:NoSchedule ✗ NOT auto — add the toleration yourself # run your DS on control-plane nodes too (Book 04 · CH 05 taints, in action): tolerations : - { key : node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane, operator : Exists , effect : NoSchedule }  updateStrategy — rolling your agents Strategy Behavior Notes RollingUpdate default node by node, controlled by maxUnavailable no maxSurge for DaemonSets — agents replace in place, brief per-node gap is fine for infra OnDelete updated only when you delete each Pod manual control for scary infrastructure (CNI!) $ kubectl set image ds/log-agent agent=fluent/fluent-bit:2.3 daemonset.apps/log-agent image updated $ kubectl rollout status ds/log-agent daemon set "log-agent" successfully rolled out  nodeSelect or / affinity r espected: add nodeSelector: {gpu: "t

CH 03 ⏳ Jobs — Run to Completion  6 MIN · CORE Everything so far runs forever — servers don't exit. A Job runs P ods to completion : migrate a schema, render a video, process yesterday's files. Success = exit 0. Then it stops. apiVersion : batch/v1 kind : Job metadata : { name : nightly-etl } spec : completions : 5 # run 5 SUCCESSFUL pods total parallelism : 2 # ...but only 2 at a time backoffLimit : 4 # allow 4 failures before the JOB fails activeDeadlineSeconds : 3600 # hard wall-clock kill-switch ttlSecondsAfterFinished : 86400 # auto-cleanup 24h after done template : spec : restartPolicy : Never # OnFailure or Never — NEVER Always! containers : - name : etl image : myorg/etl:3.1 Field Question it answ ers completions / parallelism how many successes total / how many concurrent — omitted → 1 and 1 backoffLimit how many failed Pods before declaring the whole Job failed activeDeadlineSeconds when to give up regardless of retries ttlSecondsAfterFinished when the Job and its Pods clean themselves up completionMode: Indexed each Pod gets index JOB_COMPLETION_INDEX — sharding a work queue $ kubectl get job,pods -w NAME COMPLETIONS DURATION AGE nightly-etl 2/5 45s 45s NAME STATUS REST

CH 04  CronJobs — Schedules & Concurrency  6 MIN · CORE A CronJob creates a Job on a schedule — cron syntax you already know, wrapped around everything CH 03 taught. apiVersion : batch/v1 kind : CronJob metadata : { name : db-backup } spec : schedule : "30 2 * * *" # 02:30 daily (min hour dom month dow) timeZone : "Europe/Berlin" # stable zone — don't trust node clocks concurrencyPolicy : Forbid # ★ the policy that saves databases startingDeadlineSeconds : 300 # missed > 5 min ago → skip, don't stampede suspend : false # true = pause the schedule, keep the object successfulJobsHistoryLimit : 3 failedJobsHistoryLimit : 1 jobTemplate : # ← everything from CH 03 lives in here spec : backoffLimit : 2 template : spec : restartPolicy : Never containers : - name : dump image : postgres:16 command : [ pg_dump , -f , /backup/dump.sql , $DATABASE_URL ] concurr encyPolicy If the pr evious r un is still going... Use for Allow default start another anyway — runs overlap idempotent jobs (cache warmers) Forbid skip this tick backups, billing — two overlapping runs = disaster Replace kill the old run, start new "latest state wins" jobs ⚠ The overlap trap: a backup that takes 25 min on a 15-min s

This page completes the other half: ordered lifecy cle and stable identity — the two things a replica set of a database can't live without. StatefulSet db · replicas: 3 SCALE UP (ordered): db- 0 created → waits for Running & Ready → db- 1 → ... → db- 2 SCALE DOWN (reverse): db- 2 deleted first → then db- 1 → db- 0 last (primary dies last!) DELETION of the STS: same reverse order — and claims SURVIVE (Book 05 · CH 10) STABLE NETWORK IDENTITY # via the HEADLESS svc (Book 05 · CH 09): db- 0 .db.shop.svc.cluster.local db- 1 .db.shop.svc.cluster.local db- 2 .db.shop.svc.cluster.local # names survive rescheduling — # "follow db-0" is a TRUE forever PODMANAGEMENTPOLICY OrderedReady (default) strict sequence, wait-for-Ready — correct for most databases Parallel spawn/kill all at once — for peers that self-coordinate (e.g. some distributed DBs)  Why or dered matters: a primary must be Ready before followers attach to it — P arallel would race followers against a half- booted primary  Re-created in place: kill db-1 → the same name returns

CH 06  StatefulSet Updates — Partition Canaries  6 MIN · CORE Rolling a database's image is scarier than rolling nginx. S tatefulSets answer with partitioned r ollouts : update a controlled slice first, verify, then let it finish. spec : updateStrategy : type : RollingUpdate # or: OnDelete (manual, like DaemonSets) rollingUpdate : partition : 2 # ONLY pods with ordinal ≥ 2 update PARTITION: 2 ON A 3-REPLICA STATEFULSET — AFTER SET IMAGE db-0 db-1 db-2 the canary flies solo — verify it, then lower the partition to release the rest # the canary release, step by step: $ kubectl patch sts db --type =merge -p \ '{"spec":{"updateStrategy":{"rollingUpdate":{"partition":2}}}}' $ kubectl set image sts/db db=postgres: 17 $ kubectl get pod db-2 -o jsonpath= '{.spec.containers[0].image}' postgres: 17 # db-0/db-1 untouched ✓ $ # ...run your checks against db-2... then release: $ kubectl patch sts db --type =merge -p \ '{"spec":{"updateStrategy":{"rollingUpdate":{"partition":0}}}}' $ kubectl get pods -w db-2 1/1 Running (already new) db-1 0/1 Terminating → 1/1 on :17 # highest ordinal first! db-0 0/1 Terminating → 1/1 on :17  Roll direction is highest-ordinal-first — replicas (followers) upda

CH 07  HPA — Horizontal Pod Autoscaler  6 MIN · CORE The HP A watches a metric and edits spec.replicas for you — more copies under lo ad, few er when quiet . One controller, one loop (Book 01's reconciliation, aimed at sizing). apiVersion : autoscaling/v2 kind : HorizontalPodAutoscaler metadata : { name : web-hpa } spec : scaleTargetRef : { apiVersion : apps/v1, kind : Deployment, name : web } minReplicas : 2 # floor — never below (HA!) maxReplicas : 10 # ceiling — your wallet's guard rail metrics : - type : Resource resource : name : cpu target : { type : Utilization , averageUtilization : 60 } # "keep average CPU at 60% OF EACH POD'S REQUEST" ⚠ HPA needs requests set (Book 02 · CH 14). Utilization = actual usage ÷ request — no request means no denominator, and the HPA sits unknown . It also needs the metrics-server installed ( minikube addons enable metrics-server ) — the component that aggregates real usage. 燐 The math (it's one formula) desiredReplicas = ceil[ currentReplicas × (currentMetric ÷ targetMetric) ] 4 pods at 90% CPU, target 60%: ceil(4 × 90/60) = 6 pods 2 pods at 15%, target 60%: ceil(2 × 15/60) = 1 pod ...but within a ±10% tolerance band — no flapping on noise. .

The VP A answers "wrong SIZE o f copy" — it watches actual usage and adjusts each P od's requests/limits (Book 02 · CH 14). HORIZONTAL (HPA) 﫛 﫛 﫛 → load → 﫛 﫛 﫛 﫛 﫛 﫛 same size, more of them VERTICAL (VPA) 﫛 (200m) → load → 﫛 (500m) same count, bigger each # the VPA object — installed separately (CRDs + recommender component): apiVersion : autoscaling.k8s.io/v1 kind : VerticalPodAutoscaler metadata : { name : web-vpa } spec : targetRef : { apiVersion : apps/v1, kind : Deployment, name : web } updatePolicy : updateMode : Auto # Off | Initial | Recreate (Auto) Mode Behavior Off recommendations only — the right starting point: read kubectl describe vpa , tune your YAML yourself Initial apply recommended requests only to newly created Pods — no disruption Auto / Recreate evicts Pods to apply new sizes (Book 01's eviction, by an autoscaler this time) ⚠ The classic conflict: HPA on cpu + VPA on cpu = a feedback fight (VPA raises requests → utilization % falls → HPA scales down...). CH 09  Cluster Autoscaler — Nodes on Demand  OVERVIEW HPA and VP A resize within the cluster's capacity. The Cluster Autoscaler (CA) resizes the capacity itself — adding and removing nodes , driven by two signals: SCALE UP trigger: Pods stuck Pending — Book 04's funnel found NO feasible node — (requests don't fit / taints / affinity) CA asks the cloud provider (node group / ASG / MIG) for one more node → node joins → those Pending pods schedule ✓ SCALE DOWN trigger: a node is underutilized ~10+ min AND every Pod on it can be safely rescheduled onto other nodes → drain-style eviction → node removed → bill shrinks ✓ Pods CA will NO T evict (block scale-down) Why Pods under a restrictive PDB (Book 04 · CH 10) voluntary-disruption protection is honored Pods with local storage (emptyDir/hostPath) — unless cluster- autoscaler.kubernetes.io/safe-to-evict: "true" eviction = data loss (Book 05 · CH 02!) High-priority / system Pods (Book 04 · CH 09) pecking order respected Pods the controller wouldn't recreate elsewhere (anti-affinity pinned, standalone) they'd strand  Configuration is per cloud, per node group: you annotate/label node groups with min / max sizes and deploy the CA with yo

CH 10 里 The Trio Together — When to Use Which  REFERENCE Three autoscalers, three different questions . Confusing them is how clusters get expensive or fall over.  HPA  VPA  Cluster Autoscaler Question how many copies? how big is a copy? how many nodes? Adjusts spec.replicas requests/limits (via eviction) node-group size (cloud) Signal cpu/mem utilization, custom metrics observed usage history Pending Pods / idle nodes Layer Pods Pods Nodes Latency ~15 s checks recommend + evict (minutes) minutes (cloud API)  How they stack (the beautiful part)  HPA ── ► no node fits the new P ods → Pending ── ►  CA HPA creates the demand · CA creates the room — they compose by design; VP A right-sizes underneath (on different metrics!) Traffic-shaped lo ad? → HPA (resource or custom metric) Steady lo ad, badly sized pods? → VPA in Off → fix Y AML, maybe Initial Batch bursts, cost contr ol? → CA with sane group min/max ⚠ The two classic misconfigurations: (1) HPA + VPA on the same resource metric — feedback war (CH 08). (2) HPA minReplicas higher than the cluster can host, with no CA — permanent Pending (Book 04 · CH 01's funnel, now self-inflicted by an autoscaler).  Remember the ladder: H

GLOSS  Glossary  REFERENCE DaemonSet — one Pod per matching node; node joins spawn, node leaves collect; agent workloads (logs, metrics, CNI, CSI node plugins). updateStrategy (DS) — RollingUpdate (maxUnavailable; no maxSurge) or OnDelete. Job — run-to-completion workload: completions, parallelism, backoffLimit, activeDeadlineSeconds, ttlSecondsAfterFinished, completionMode Indexed. CronJob — schedule + Job template; concurrencyPolicy (Allow/Forbid/Replace), startingDeadlineSeconds, suspend, timeZone. StatefulSet — ordered lifecycle, stable names/DNS, per-replica storage (Book 05); podManagementPolicy OrderedReady/Parallel. partition — StatefulSet canary gate: only ordinals ≥ partition update; roll direction highest-first. OnDelete — update strategy: template applies only when you delete each Pod manually. HorizontalPodAutoscaler — scales replicas from metrics; v2 API; needs metrics-server + Pod requests; min/max rails; fast up, slow down (stabilization window). Utilization — actual usage ÷ resource request; the default HPA metric basis. VerticalPodAutoscaler — recommends/applies requests+limits; modes Off / Initial / Auto(Recreate); conflicts with HPA on the same metric. Cluster

CH 26 illusion Service Networking — The Virtual IP  6 MIN · CORE Here's the trick nobody tells you: the ClusterIP your Service owns is a lie . Nothing is listening on it. No process holds it. It's a virtual IP (VIP) — and that's the elegance. RUSSIAN DOLLS — WHERE THE VIP REALLY GOES 10.96.0.50 ── ► DNA T ── ► 10.244.1.5 packets "to the VIP" are rewritten in transit to a real P od — the VIP never terminates anything Address ranges — separate drawers: Service CIDR 10.96.0.0/12 # VIPs live here (fake, routable only via rules) Pod CIDR 10.244.0.0/16 # real Pod IPs (per-node slices)  You can't ping a ClusterIP — nothing answers; the rules only rewrite packets passing thr ough  Pods died and got new IPs? Nobody notices — everyone still dials the VIP 燐 The ranges must not ov erlap — two drawers, zero confusion  The Service is a stable illusion: an eternal name + eternal IP in front of a set of mortals (Pods) that churn constantly. The illusion is maintained by kube-proxy — next chapter. ↑ back to top the VIP — a fiction a real Pod IP  The Complete Kubernetes Guide ◀ prev · ▤ TOC · next ▶ Page 29

CH 26 illusion Service Networking — The Virtual IP  6 MIN · CORE Here's the trick nobody tells you: the ClusterIP your Service owns is a lie . Nothing is listening on it. No process holds it. It's a virtual IP (VIP) — and that's the elegance. RUSSIAN DOLLS — WHERE THE VIP REALLY GOES 10.96.0.50 ── ► DNA T ── ► 10.244.1.5 packets "to the VIP" are rewritten in transit to a real P od — the VIP never terminates anything Address ranges — separate drawers: Service CIDR 10.96.0.0/12 # VIPs live here (fake, routable only via rules) Pod CIDR 10.244.0.0/16 # real Pod IPs (per-node slices)  You can't ping a ClusterIP — nothing answers; the rules only rewrite packets passing thr ough  Pods died and got new IPs? Nobody notices — everyone still dials the VIP 燐 The ranges must not ov erlap — two drawers, zero confusion  The Service is a stable illusion: an eternal name + eternal IP in front of a set of mortals (Pods) that churn constantly. The illusion is maintained by kube-proxy — next chapter. ↑ back to top the VIP — a fiction a real Pod IP  The Complete Kubernetes Guide ◀ prev · ▤ TOC · next ▶ Page 29

CH 27  kube-proxy's Real Job  6 MIN · CORE kube-proxy does not forward a single packet. Its entire job is two verbs: watch & pr ogram . ❌ WHAT IT DOES NOT DO Sit in the traffic path Proxy connections through itself Touch P od-to-P od traffic ✅ WHAT IT DOES Watch the API Server: Services + Endpoints Program iptables/IPVS rules on its node Re-program the instant P ods change 彩 The rules it writes (iptables + DNAT) # conceptually, on every node: if dst == 10.96.0.50:80 # the VIP then rewrite dst → 10.244.1.5:80 # pick an endpoint (random) else if ... next endpoint # (rule set balances across all) ✨ The Illusion, resolved: a Pod dies → Endpoints object updates → every node's kube-proxy rewrites its rules → the VIP never moved . Stability on the outside, churn on the inside, and the packets never knew.  One-liner for exams: kube-proxy wat ches Services/Endpo ints and program s packet-rewriting rules on every node — it never forwar ds traffic itself. ↑ back to top  The Complete Kubernetes Guide ◀ prev · ▤ TOC · next ▶ Page 30

CH 27  kube-proxy's Real Job  6 MIN · CORE kube-proxy does not forward a single packet. Its entire job is two verbs: watch & pr ogram . ❌ WHAT IT DOES NOT DO Sit in the traffic path Proxy connections through itself Touch P od-to-P od traffic ✅ WHAT IT DOES Watch the API Server: Services + Endpoints Program iptables/IPVS rules on its node Re-program the instant P ods change 彩 The rules it writes (iptables + DNAT) # conceptually, on every node: if dst == 10.96.0.50:80 # the VIP then rewrite dst → 10.244.1.5:80 # pick an endpoint (random) else if ... next endpoint # (rule set balances across all) ✨ The Illusion, resolved: a Pod dies → Endpoints object updates → every node's kube-proxy rewrites its rules → the VIP never moved . Stability on the outside, churn on the inside, and the packets never knew.  One-liner for exams: kube-proxy wat ches Services/Endpo ints and program s packet-rewriting rules on every node — it never forwar ds traffic itself. ↑ back to top  The Complete Kubernetes Guide ◀ prev · ▤ TOC · next ▶ Page 30

CH 28  Following ONE Packet — 6 Steps  FINALE · CORE A Pod runs curl nginx-svc . Follow the single packet: 1 DNS — nginx-svc resolves to the VIP 10.96.0.50 CoreDNS answered from the Service's namespace: nginx-svc.frontend.svc.cluster.local 2 Send — Pod sends to the VIP (nothing is there — remember CH 26) dest IP: 10.96.0.50 · dest port: 80 3 DNAT — the node's iptables rules rewrite the destination dest becomes a real Pod IP: 10.244.1.5:80 4 Route — same node → direct delivery; different node → CNI overlay carries it the packet leaves kube-proxy's rules and enters the real network 5 Receive — the P od sees a normal packet addressed to its o wn IP it replies — source is the VIP thanks to conntrack, so the client never learns the Pod IP 6 Return — conntrack rewrites the reply back through the VIP client believes it talked to 10.96.0.50 the whole time   The entire machine in one sentence: DNS gives you a stable fake IP; kube-proxy's rules secretly rewrite it to a mortal Pod; conntrack makes the lie symmetric. That's Service networking — everything else is detail. ↑ back to top  The Complete Kubernetes Guide ◀ prev · ▤ TOC · labs ▶ Page 31

That's Service networking — everything else is detail. ↑ back to top  The Complete Kubernetes Guide ◀ prev · ▤ TOC · labs ▶ Page 31

LAB 1  Observe vs Control  15 MIN · HANDS-ON  TAB 1 · OBSERVE $ kubectl get deployments -w $ kubectl get pods -w $ kubectl get rs -w ⚙ TAB 2 · CONTROL $ kubectl create deploy web --image=nginx --replica $ kubectl delete pod <pod-name> $ kubectl scale deploy web --replicas=4 STEP 1 · Create ⚙ RUN $ kubectl create deployment web --image=nginx -- replicas=2 deployment.apps/web created  EXPECTED in TAB 1 web 2/2 READY web- aaaaa 1/1 Running web- bbbbb 1/1 Running STEP 2 · Kill a Pod ⚙ RUN $ kubectl delete pod web-aaaaa pod "web-aaaaa" deleted  EXPECTED web-aaaaa Terminating web- ccccc ContainerCreating web-ccccc Running # replacement! STEP 3 · What we proved A ReplicaSet owns the P ods → deletion is a mismatch, not a tragedy. The name died; the promise didn't. (S tandalone pods: kubectl run p1 --image=nginx then delete it — silence. T ry it.) ↑ back to top  The Complete Kubernetes Guide ◀ prev · ▤ TOC · next ▶ Page 32
