 Contents — click any row 7 parts · 22 chapters PART I · BEYOND NODEPORT CH 01 The Exposition Ladder p.3 CH 02 LoadBalancer — The Cloud Type p.4 CH 03 The Problem Ingress Solves p.5 PART II · INGRESS CH 04 Ingress & IngressClass p.6 CH 05 Host & Path Routing p.7 CH 06 TLS Termination p.8 CH 07 Ingress Controllers p.9 PART III · NETWORKPOLICY CH 08 The Default-Allow World p.10 CH 09 NetworkPolicy — Ingress Rules p.11 CH 10 Egress + The Default-Deny Playbook p.12 PART IV · DNS CH 11 CoreDNS — Discovery Internals p.13 CH 12 dnsPolicy & DNS Debugging p.14 PART V · WHAT'S NEXT CH 13 Gateway API — The Successor p.15 PART VI · LABS LAB 1 Path Routing via Ingress p.16 LAB 2 TLS on an Ingress p.17 LAB 3 Default-Deny → Selective Allow p.18 LAB 4 DNS Debugging from Inside a Pod p.19 PART VII · PROVE IT QUIZ Self-Check Quiz p.20 KEY Answer Key + Scoring p.21 GLOSS Glossary p.22 CHEAT One-Page Cheat Sheet p.23 FINALE Where to Next → Book 04 p.24  Assumes Books 01–02. You know ClusterIP/NodePort and the virtual-IP trick (Book 01 · CH 25–28), service DNS basics (Book 01 · CH 12), and Secrets — including the tls type (Book 02 · CH 05–07). This book takes traffic from "port 30080 and pray" to pro

CH 01 煮 The Exposition Ladder  4 MIN Three ways to reach a Service, each one delegating to the one below it. Book 01 showed the first two — this chapter frames them as a ladder , because every rung exists to fix the rung beneath. THE LADDER — TOP IS FOR HUMANS, BOTTOM IS MACHINERY ⚖ LoadBalancer  NodeP ort  ClusterIP LB forwards to NodeP orts · NodeP orts forward through kube-proxy DNA T to Pods — each rung hides the one below Rung Reach Kills it ClusterIP inside the cluster only literally unreachable from outside NodePort any node's IP + a high port raw ports, users hate :30080 , no LB across nodes, no TLS story LoadBalancer one cloud IP per Service $$$ per Service — 10 services = 10 LB bills, and still no path routing  One sentence: the ladder is a delegation chain — LoadBalancer → NodePort → ClusterIP → Pods . NodePort solved reachability but not usability; LoadBalancer solved usability but not your cloud invoice. The next rung up — Ingress — fixes the invoice. ⏭ First, the cloud rung in detail — CH 02: Lo adBalancer ↑ back to top cloud LB · one public IP 30000–32767 on ev ery node internal vir tual IP only  Book 03 · Services & Networking ▤ TOC · next ▶ Page 3

CH 02 ⚖ LoadBalancer — The Cloud Type  5 MIN apiVersion : v1 kind : Service metadata : name : web spec : type : LoadBalancer # on a supported platform selector : { app : web } ports : - port : 80 targetPort : 8080  What actually happens on apply API Ser ver ── ► Cloud Lo adBalancer Contr oller ▼ ☁ provisions ELB / Azur e LB / GCLB public IP assigned ── ► LB → NodeP orts ── ► 﫛 Pods $ kubectl get svc web NAME TYPE EXTERNAL-IP PORT(S) web LoadBalancer <pending> 80:31234/TCP # provisioning... web LoadBalancer 203.0.113.7 80:31234/TCP # ready ✓  The NodeP ort in the port column is the tell: LoadBalancer is NodeP ort under neath — the LB just fronts it  No cloud? On minikube run minikube tunnel and the <pending> becomes a real local IP; bare metal can run MetalLB to play the cloud controller's role  Cost model: one cloud LB per Ser vice that asks — this is exactly the tax CH 03 abolishes ⚠ <pending> forever? Either your platform has no LB controller (plain kubeadm, kind, Docker Desktop) or the cloud quota/IAM is blocking. The Service is never "broken" — the environment just can't fulfill the request.  One sentence: LoadBalancer = NodePort + a cloud wallet . Great for the one true

CH 03  The Problem Ingress Solves  4 MIN ❌ NAIVE: ONE LB PER SERVICE cloud LB #1 → web-svc cloud LB #2 → api-svc cloud LB #3 → admin-svc cloud LB #4 → docs-svc $ × 4 · TLS certs × 4 · WAF × 4 · no shared path rules · bill pain ✅ INGRESS: ONE EDGE, MANY ROUTES cloud LB (just 1) └── Ingress controller ├── shop.example.com → web-svc ├── example.com/api → api-svc ├── example.com/admin → admin-svc └── docs.example.com → docs-svc 1 bill · 1 TLS cert · L7 rules as YAML Ingress is Layer-7 awareness at the edge: it reads the HT TP hostname and path and routes accordingly — something NodeP ort/LoadBalancer (dumb T CP forwards) fundamentally cannot do.  https://shop.example.com ┐  https://example.com/api ┤ ── ►  Ingress ── ► web api docs  Apartment update: LoadBalancer built every visitor their own private bridge to one apartment. Ingress hired a front desk : one entrance, a directory, and it reads the address on your letter to send you to the right apartment.  One sentence: Ingress consolidates N cloud load balancers into one, and upgrades dumb port-forwarding into hostname/path-aware HTTP routing — declared as plain YAML, versioned with your app. ↑ back to top 1 LB · 1 TLS  Book 03

CH 04  Ingress & IngressClass  6 MIN · CORE Two facts before any Y AML: (1) an Ingress is just a rulebook — nothing for wards traffic until a contr oller reads it ; (2) ingressClassName declares which controller owns it. apiVersion : networking.k8s.io/v1 kind : Ingress metadata : name : main spec : ingressClassName : nginx # which referee handles this rulebook rules : - host : demo.local http : paths : - path : / pathType : Prefix backend : service : { name : web, port : { number : 80 } } Piece Role Apartment translation Ingress the routing rulebook ( declarative YAML) the front-desk directory IngressClass named type of controller; routes rulebooks to referees which security firm staffs the desk Ingress Controller actual reverse proxy watching Ingress objects the desk itself ⚠ The silent trap: kubectl apply an Ingress with no controller installed and you get zero errors — the object is stored, accepted, and does nothing. The classic symptom: Ingress exists, get ingress shows no ADDRESS, curl hangs. Check kubectl get ingressclass first. # minikube — one command installs ingress-nginx + the "nginx" IngressClass: $ minikube addons enable ingress $ kubectl get pods -n ingress-nginx i

CH 05  Host & Path Routing  6 MIN · CORE The full routing surface: multiple hosts , each with multiple paths , each pointing at its own Service. spec : ingressClassName : nginx rules : - host : shop.example.com # name-based virtual host http : paths : - path : /api pathType : Prefix backend : { service : { name : api-svc, port : { number : 80 } } } - path : / pathType : Prefix backend : { service : { name : web-svc, port : { number : 80 } } } - host : docs.example.com # second host, same edge http : paths : - path : / pathType : Prefix backend : { service : { name : docs-svc, port : { number : 80 } } } pathType Matches /api/v1 ? Prefix path and everything under it , by segments ✅ yes (for /api ) Exact only the literal path ❌ no — only /api itself ImplementationSpecific controller decides (nginx treats it like Prefix + regex support) controller-defined 燐 Order doesn 't matt er — nginx sorts by longest-prefix, so /api wins over / no matter where it's listed  No host field at all = catch-all for every hostname hitting the edge (handy, but easy to shadow specific rules — be deliberate)  Testing locally: map the hostname in /etc/hosts → <minikube-ip> demo.local shop.example.com , th

CH 06  TLS Termination  5 MIN "Termination" = the TLS handshake ends at the ingr ess . Users get HT TPS; your P ods receive plain HT TP on the internal network. One cert, managed once, at the edge. spec : tls : - hosts : [ shop.example.com ] secretName : shop-tls # type kubernetes.io/tls (Book 02 · CH 05) rules : - host : shop.example.com http : paths : - path : / pathType : Prefix backend : { service : { name : web-svc, port : { number : 80 } } } # plain HTTP here! # the secret the edge serves (self-signed for labs — Lab 2 does it live): $ openssl req -x509 -nodes -newkey rsa:2048 -days 365 \ -keyout tls.key -out tls.crt -subj "/CN=shop.example.com" $ kubectl create secret tls shop-tls --cert =tls.crt --key =tls.key TERMINATION POINT  HTTPS  ── ► Ingress ── ► HTTP (plain) ── ► 﫛 Pod :80  Re-encryption (HT TPS all the way to P ods) is possible but controller-specific — check before promising "end-to-end encrypted" in a security review  Production certs come from cert-manager (Let's Encrypt automation) — same secretName mechanism, the cert just appears ⚠ Missing/expired secret named in tls → nginx serves a fake default cert ; browsers scream. Diagnose: check the cert issuer, n

CH 07 吝 Ingress Controllers  6 MIN · CORE A controller is a reverse proxy in a P od + a reconciliation loop: watch Ingress objects → render proxy config → hot-reload. The ingress-nginx controller literally writes an nginx.conf for your rulebook. Ingress objects (the rulebooks) │ watch ▼ Controller Pod render config → reload proxy │ ▼ nginx/traefik/haproxy the process actually serving :80/:443 Controller Underlying pr oxy Know it for ingress-nginx nginx the de-facto standard; huge annotation ecosystem; minikube addon Traefik traefik (Go) CERT-by-default ACME, CRD-native, popular in homelab/k3s HAProxy haproxy raw TCP performance pedigree AWS ALB / GCE managed cloud LB Ingress provisions real ALB/GLB instead of in-cluster proxy ⚠ Annotation culture — power and trap: behavior beyond core routing (rewrites, CORS, IP allowlists, timeouts) arrives via per-controller annotations , e.g. nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/rewrite-target: / . Powerful — but non-portable : swap controllers and those annotations are silently meaningless. K8s-native versions of some of this live in the Gateway API (CH 13).  Which nginx is which? ingress-nginx = community/kubernetes project. nginx-ingress = F5/NGINX

CH 08  The Default-Allow World  5 MIN Book 01 built the flat network: every P od gets a routable IP and — by default — may talk t o every other P od . Frontend to database, and your-laptop-sidecar t o database , all equally welcome. NO NETWORKPOLICY = ZERO SEGMENTATION 﫛 frontend ── ► 﫛 payment -api ── ►  postgres  any compr omised pod same r ights! ── ►  postgres Assumption Reality "Only my Services can reach my Pods" ❌ Services are for discovery — Pod-to-Pod by raw IP works regardless "Namespaces isolate the network" ❌ Book 01 · CH 11: namespaces partition names , not traffic — cross-namespace Pod calls flow freely by default "We'd notice lateral movement" ❌ nothing logs what was never segmented  Why flat-by-default? The IP-per-Pod model promises "Pods are like hosts on one big network" — zero- config apps. The price is that security becomes opt-in , via the object the next chapter teaches.  One sentence: the Kubernetes network starts as a single open room — any pod, any pod, forever — until a NetworkPolicy walls off a table. Zero-trust here is a YAML you have to write. ↑ back to top :5432 direct line   Book 03 · Services & Networking ◀ prev · ▤ TOC · next ▶ Page 10

CH 09  NetworkPolicy — Ingress Rules  6 MIN · CORE The grammar in one sentence: "Pods select ed by podSelector may receive connections only fr om allow ed sources, only on allow ed ports." The instant one policy selects a P od, default-allow flips to default-deny for that Pod . apiVersion : networking.k8s.io/v1 kind : NetworkPolicy metadata : name : allow-frontend-to-api namespace : shop spec : podSelector : # THE TARGET — who is being protected matchLabels : { app : api } policyTypes : [ Ingress ] ingress : - from : # allowed SOURCES (any of these) - podSelector : # same-namespace pods with... matchLabels : { app : frontend } - namespaceSelector : # ...OR all pods from matching namespaces matchLabels : { kubernetes.io/metadata.name : monitoring } ports : - { protocol : TCP , port : 8080 } # ...only this port ⚠ The AND/OR trap (interview favorite): inside one from list item, podSelector + namespaceSelector = AND (pods matching this label in those namespaces). Across separate items = OR (either source). One character of YAML indentation changes the security meaning. ➕ Policies ar e additiv e: if two policies select the same P od, the allowed set is the union — policies can only ev

CH 10  Egress + The Default-Deny Playbook  6 MIN · CORE Same grammar, opposite direction. And the industry-standard starting posture: deny ev erything, then allow named f lows. kind : NetworkPolicy metadata : { name : default-deny-all, namespace : shop } spec : podSelector : {} # every pod in shop policyTypes : [ Ingress , Egress ] ingress : [] # empty = deny ALL inbound egress : [] # empty = deny ALL outbound ⚠ The classic default-deny self-own: deny-all egress instantly kills DNS — no pod can resolve anything . The very first egress allow in any cluster is DNS: kind : NetworkPolicy metadata : { name : allow-dns } spec : podSelector : {} policyTypes : [ Egress ] egress : - to : - namespaceSelector : matchLabels : { kubernetes.io/metadata.name : kube-system } ports : - { protocol : UDP , port : 53 } - { protocol : TCP , port : 53 }  The production playbook 1 · default -deny all → 2 · allow DNS :53 → 3 · allow app f lows frontend→api, api→db → 4 · allow ingr ess-ctrl → apps ⚠ CNI reality check: NetworkPolicy is just an API — the CNI plugin must enforce it . Calico, Cilium, Weave enforce; flannel does not (policies apply silently, block nothing). If policies "don't work", check yo

CH 11  CoreDNS — Discovery Internals  6 MIN · CORE Book 01 asserted "every Service gets a DNS name." Here's the machinery: a CoreDNS Deployment in kube- system , fronted by the kube-dns Service — the cluster's phone book. Pod resolv.conf → nameserver 10.96.0.10 │ query: "v1.default..." ▼ kube-dns Service (ClusterIP, stable — dogfooding!) ▼ CoreDNS Pods watch API Server → build zone in memory ▼ svc.cluster.local zone every Service & Pod IP, auto # the cluster zone lives in a ConfigMap — the "Corefile": $ kubectl -n kube-system get cm coredns -o yaml Corefile : | .:53 { kubernetes cluster.local # ← serves the cluster zone from the API forward . /etc/resolv.conf # everything else → upstream DNS } Query form Resolves Works from v1 same namespace pods in default (search list fills the rest) v1.dev Service v1 in ns dev anywhere v1.dev.svc.cluster.local full FQDN anywhere (always works) 彩 Zero registration: "create a Service" is the DNS record — CoreDNS watches the API, no sidecar config  It also serves Pod records ( ip-10-244-1- 5.default.pod.cluster.local ) and SVC/AAAA types — headless Services return P od IPs directly  One sentence: CoreDNS is a small API-watching DNS server — the

CH 12  dnsPolicy & DNS Debugging  6 MIN · CORE dnsPolicy Pod uses... When ClusterFirst default CoreDNS (cluster names + forwarded externals) 99% of Pods Default the node's resolv.conf — no cluster names! rare; e.g. heavy external-DNS workloads ClusterFirstWithHostNet CoreDNS even for hostNetwork Pods hostNetwork daemons that still need Service names None whatever dnsConfig supplies full manual control (custom nameservers/search) 瘝 ndots:5 — the sneaky perf tax # a default pod's resolv.conf: search default.svc.cluster.local svc.cluster.local cluster.local options ndots:5 # any name with <5 dots is tried AS-IS *and* against every search # suffix → "google.com" = 1 + 3 = 4 queries. measure, don't guess. 喙 The debug ladder (Lab 4 runs it live) $ kubectl exec dns -- nslookup v1 # 1 · short name (same ns) $ kubectl exec dns -- nslookup v1.dev # 2 · cross-namespace $ kubectl exec dns -- nslookup kubernetes.default # 3 · the built-in canary $ kubectl exec dns -- cat /etc/resolv.conf # 4 · who's my resolver? ✅ FQDN resolves but short name fails → search list/ ndots issue, not DNS death ✅ nothing resolves + timeouts → check CoreDNS P ods ( -n kube-system ) and the kube-dns Service endpoint

CH 13  Gateway API — The Successor  OVERVIEW Ingress won the world but shows its age: routing power locked behind vendor annotations , cross-namespace routing unsafe, one blob of Y AML mixing infra and app concerns. The Gateway API (SIG-Network, GA since v1.0 ) is the redesigned successor. INGRESS (2015 MODEL) behavior via per-controller annotations 啕 cross-namespace = footgun territory platform + app concerns in one object not going away — huge installed base GATEWAY API native fields — headers, weights, method routing cross-namespace via explicit ReferenceGrant role-split objects (see below) portable: any conforming implementation # role separation — the headline idea: GatewayClass # platform team: "we run nginx-gateway" Gateway # platform team: listener :443 + TLS cert HTTPRoute # APP team: my host/path → my svc ← attaches to the Gateway # (+ GRPCRoute, TLSRoute... — and app teams never touch LB config) kind : HTTPRoute metadata : { name : shop } spec : parentRefs : [{ name : edge-gateway }] # bind to the shared Gateway hostnames : [ shop.example.com ] rules : - matches : [{ path : { type : PathPrefix , value : /api }}] backendRefs : [{ name : api-svc, port : 80 , weight : 90

LAB 1  Path Routing via Ingress  15 MIN · HANDS-ON STEP 1 · Controller + two apps $ minikube addons enable ingress $ kubectl create deploy v1 --image=hashicorp/http-echo -- -text =hello-v1 $ kubectl create deploy v2 --image=hashicorp/http-echo -- -text =hello-v2 $ kubectl expose deploy v1 --port=5678 && kubectl expose deploy v2 --port=5678 # printf-style echo servers: perfect for proving WHO answered STEP 2 · The rulebook $ kubectl apply -f - <<EOF apiVersion : networking.k8s.io/v1 kind : Ingress metadata : { name : routes } spec : ingressClassName : nginx rules : - host : demo.local http : paths : - { path : /v1 , pathType : Prefix , backend : { service : { name : v1, port : { number : 5678 } } } } - { path : /v2 , pathType : Prefix , backend : { service : { name : v2, port : { number : 5678 } } } } EOF Add to /etc/hosts (admin): <minikube ip> demo.local  TEST $ curl demo.local/v1 hello-v1 $ curl demo.local/v2 hello-v2 # path → service, proven $ curl demo.local/v1/extra hello-v1 # Prefix catches subpaths  PROOF IT'S L7 # same port 80 for both — # only the PATH differed. # A NodePort could never do # this without 2 services # on 2 ports. Teardown: kubectl delete ingress routes

LAB 2  TLS on an Ingress  10 MIN · HANDS-ON STEP 1 · Cert + Secret (Book 02 · CH 05 in action) $ openssl req -x509 -nodes -newkey rsa:2048 -days 365 \ -keyout tls.key -out tls.crt -subj "/CN=demo.local" $ kubectl create secret tls demo-tls --cert =tls.crt --key =tls.key STEP 2 · Add the tls block to the Lab 1 Ingress $ kubectl patch ingress routes --type =merge -p \ '{"spec":{"tls":[{"hosts":["demo.local"],"secretName":"demo-tls"}]}}' $ kubectl get ingress routes HOSTS PORTS AGE demo.local 80, 443 # 443 appeared  TEST HTTPS $ curl - k https://demo.local/v1 hello-v1 # works! (-k: self-signed)  INSPECT THE CERT $ curl -kv https://demo.local 2>&1 | grep subject subject: CN=demo.local # the EDGE serves your secret — # pods never saw a cert Proved: termination happens at the Ingress (CH 06) — one self-signed secret, HT TPS at the edge, plain HT TP behind. Teardown: Lab 1 teardown + kubectl delete secret demo-tls . ↑ back to top  Book 03 · Services & Networking ◀ prev · ▤ TOC · next ▶ Page 17

LAB 3  Default-Deny → Selective Allow  12 MIN · HANDS-ON ⚠ CNI check first: minikube default (bridge/kindnet) does not enforce policies. Restart with Calico, or run this lab on a cluster whose CNI enforces: minikube delete && minikube start --cni=calico . STEP 1 · Players: a server, a labeled client, an unlabeled client $ kubectl create deploy v1 --image=hashicorp/http-echo -- -text =hello-v1 $ kubectl expose deploy v1 --port=5678 $ kubectl run client --image=busybox:1.36 --restart=Never -- sleep 9999 $ kubectl run stranger --image=busybox:1.36 --restart=Never -- sleep 9999 STEP 2 · Deny all ingress to v1 $ kubectl apply -f - <<EOF apiVersion : networking.k8s.io/v1 kind : NetworkPolicy metadata : { name : deny-v1 } spec : podSelector : { matchLabels : { app : v1 } } policyTypes : [ Ingress ] ingress : [] EOF $ kubectl exec client -- wget -qO- -T 3 http://v1:5678 wget: download timed out # ← BLOCKED. the room has a wall. STEP 3 · Allow only labeled callers $ kubectl apply -f - <<EOF apiVersion : networking.k8s.io/v1 kind : NetworkPolicy metadata : { name : allow-labeled } spec : podSelector : { matchLabels : { app : v1 } } ingress : - from : [{ podSelector : { matchLabels : { acce

LAB 4  DNS Debugging from Inside a Pod  8 MIN · HANDS-ON STEP 1 · The debug pod + the ladder $ kubectl run dns --image=busybox:1.36 --restart=Never -- sleep 9999 $ kubectl exec dns -- nslookup kubernetes.default Server: 10.96.0.10 # ← CoreDNS via kube-dns Service Name: kubernetes.default.svc.cluster.local Address: 10.96.0.1 # ← the API Server's ClusterIP  NAME FORMS $ kubectl exec dns -- nslookup kubernetes # ✅ short name (same ns) $ kubectl exec dns -- nslookup kube-dns.kube-system # ✅ ns-qualified $ kubectl exec dns -- nslookup \ kube-dns.kube-system.svc.cluster.local # ✅ full FQDN — always works  WHO CONFIGURED ME? $ kubectl exec dns -- cat /etc/resolv.conf nameserver 10.96.0.10 search default.svc.cluster.local svc.cluster.local cluster.local options ndots:5 # dnsPolicy ClusterFirst wrote # this file at pod start — CH 12 Proved: short names ride the search list; the resolver is the stable kube-dns VIP; ndots:5 is why "external domains feel slow" (CH 12's perf tax). Teardown: kubectl delete pod dns .  Interview habit unlocked: when someone says "DNS is broken in the cluster," you now open with kubectl exec ... nslookup kubernetes.default — the canary that separates cluster-D

QUIZ ✅ Self-Check Quiz ☑ 10 questions Q1. A LoadBalancer Service, examined closely, routes traffic to Pods via which underlying mechanism? A. NodePorts on every node B. Direct Pod IP registration C. Ingress rules D. HostNetwork daemons Q2. You apply an Ingress to a cluster with no controller installed. Result? A. Apply fails with a validation error B. Ingress is created and works over NodePort fallback C. Ingress is created but silently does nothing — no ADDRESS ever appears D. The API Server starts a default controller Q3. Which pathType matches /api and /api/v1/users ? A. Exact B. Prefix C. Whole D. Regex Q4. An Ingress tls entry's secretName must reference a Secret of which type? A. Opaque B. kubernetes.io/tls with tls.crt + tls.key C. dockerconfigjson D. basic-auth Q5. NetworkPolicies apply but block nothing. Most likely cause? A. Missing ingressClassName B. Policies need a namespace label C. The CNI (e.g. flannel) doesn't enforce NetworkPolicy D. policyTypes omitted Q6. A NetworkPolicy has podSelector: {} and empty ingress: [] . It affects... A. every Pod in that namespace B. only unlabeled Pods C. the whole cluster D. nothing — empty selector is invalid Q7. Two NetworkPolicie

KEY  Answer Key + Scoring grade yourself Q Ans Why — one line 1 A LB is NodePort + cloud wallet — the port column betrays it (CH 01–02) 2 C Ingress = rulebook; no referee, no game, no error (CH 04) 3 B Prefix matches the segment and everything under it (CH 05) 4 B tls type mandates tls.crt/tls.key keys — Book 02 · CH 05 (CH 06) 5 C Policy is an API; enforcement lives in the CNI — flannel won't (CH 10, Lab 3) 6 A Empty selector = all Pods in the namespace; empty rules = deny (CH 09–10) 7 D Additive union — policies grant, never revoke (CH 09) 8 D <svc>.<ns>.svc.cluster.local — CH 11 9 B Default = node's resolver; cluster names don't exist for that Pod (CH 12) 10 C Gateway = shared listener; HTTPRoute = app-owned rules (CH 13)  9–10 Ready for Book 04  6–8 Re-read missed chapters'  boxes  <6 Re-run Labs 1–4, then retake  Missed Q5 or Q7? Those are the two production incidents-in-waiting: unenforcing CNI (false security) and the additive-union rule (false restriction). Missed Q2? Remember: apply succeeds ≠ traffic flows . ↑ back to top  Book 03 · Services & Networking ◀ prev · ▤ TOC · next ▶ Page 21

GLOSS  Glossary  REFERENCE Exposition ladder — ClusterIP → NodePort → LoadBalancer; each rung delegates to the one below. LoadBalancer — Service type; a cloud controller provisions an external LB fronting NodePorts. One per Service = one bill per Service. MetalLB / minikube tunnel — ways to get LB behavior without a cloud (bare metal / local dev). Ingress — L7 routing rulebook (host/path → Service); inert without a controller. IngressClass — named controller type; spec.ingressClassName binds an Ingress to its referee. Ingress Controller — running reverse proxy (ingress-nginx, Traefik...) that watches Ingress objects and renders live proxy config. pathType — Prefix (segment + subtree) / Exact (literal) / ImplementationSpecific. TLS termination — HTTPS ends at the Ingress; Pod traffic is plain HTTP unless re-encrypted deliberately. Annotation — controller-specific behavior knob (rewrites, CORS...); powerful, non-portable. NetworkPolicy — namespaced firewall rules: podSelector (target) + ingress/egress (from/to/ports); additive union; CNI-enforced. Default-deny — posture where a selected Pod receives/sends nothing unless a policy allows it; empty rules array = deny all. ipBlock / na

CHEAT  One-Page Cheat Sheet  print me  TRAFFIC — COMMANDS $ minikube addons enable ingress $ kubectl get ingressclass $ kubectl get ingress # ADDRESS must appear! $ kubectl create secret tls t --cert=c --key=k $ curl -k https://demo.local/api # /etc/hosts: <minikube ip> demo.local  DNS — DEBUG LADDER $ kubectl run dns --image=busybox:1.36 -it --rm \ --restart=Never -- nslookup kubernetes.default $ ... nslookup svc.ns.svc.cluster.local $ kubectl exec dns -- cat /etc/resolv.conf # kube-dns VIP = 10.96.0.10 by default  DEFAULT-DENY SKELETON podSelector : {} policyTypes : [Ingress, Egress] ingress : [] # deny in egress : [] # deny out # FIRST allow: DNS udp+tcp 53 → kube-system # policies are ADDITIVE (union) # CNI must enforce (calico/cilium, NOT flannel) 煮 LADDER + RULES OF THUMB Need Reach for internal only ClusterIP quick demo, one app NodePort the one edge / TCP thing LoadBalancer HTTP host/path routing Ingress portable, canary, multi-team Gateway API 易 FACTS WORTH A JOB OFFER LB = NodeP ort underneath · Ingress without controller = silently dead (check ADDRESS + ingressclass) TLS terminates at the edge; P ods stay HT TP unless deliberately re-encrypted Annotations are vendor

FINALE  What You Can Do Now  Book 03 complete Book 01 built the machine, Book 02 dressed it — this book gave it a front door , a phone book , and locks between the r ooms .  TRAFFIC — fully mapped: ├── Ladder ClusterIP → NodePort → LB (each rung delegates) ├── Ingress host/path rules → Services · TLS at the edge ├── Controller the proxy that enforces the rulebook ├── NetworkPolicy default-deny → explicit allows (DNS first!) ├── CoreDNS svc.cluster.local · ndots · dnsPolicy └── Gateway API the portable future (Gateway + HTTPRoute) ✅ You can now... Choose the right rung per Service — and explain the cost of picking wrong Ship production Ingress: host/path rules, TLS secrets, controller triage (no ADDRESS? no controller) Write a default-deny NetworkP olicy set that doesn't strangle DNS — and prove enforcement on the real CNI Debug any "DNS broken" report with a four-command ladder instead of vibes Place Gateway API in the roadmap and say precisely what it fixes about Ingress  Where to next — Book 04 · Scheduling & Node Management: your traffic arrives at the right door now — Book 04 decides which machines run what : the full taints/tolerations system, node & pod affinity, topology

format.title: Config · Secrets & Access Control — Kubernetes Book 02

texts: CONFIG · SECRETS & ACCESS CONTROL Book 02 of the series — stop baking config into images. ConfigMaps for plain settings, Secrets for sensitive data (and the base64 truth), RBA C for who may do what, ServiceAccounts for workload identity, SecurityContext & P od Security S tandards for hardening, and R equests/Limits + QoS for the resource contract. ⚙ ConfigMap plain config  Secret sensitiv e data 着 RBAC who may do what  ServiceAccount worklo ad identity  Secur ityCont ext pod har dening  PSS three lev els  Requests/Limits the budget  QoS eviction or der K 8 S K N O W L E D G E B A S E · B O O K 0 2 · C O N T I N U E S B O O K 0 1 · 2 0 2 6

 Contents — click any row 6 parts · 24 chapters PART I · CONFIG INJECTION CH 01 ConfigMaps — What & Why p.3 CH 02 Creating & Mounting ConfigMaps p.4 CH 03 Hot-Reload — What Actually Updates p.5 PART II · SECRETS CH 04 Secrets — vs ConfigMaps p.6 CH 05 Secret Types & Creation p.7 CH 06 Mounting Secrets + imagePullSecrets p.8 CH 07 Base64 ≠ Encryption — The Truth p.9 PART III · ACCESS CONTROL (RBAC) CH 08 RBAC — The Big Idea p.10 CH 09 Roles & RoleBindings p.11 CH 10 ClusterRoles & When to Use Which p.12 CH 11 ServiceAccounts p.13 PART IV · HARDENING & RESOURCES CH 12 SecurityContext p.14 CH 13 Pod Security Standards p.15 CH 14 Requests & Limits p.16 CH 15 QoS Classes p.17 PART V · LABS LAB 1 ConfigMap: Prove Env ≠ Hot-Reload p.18 LAB 2 Secret: Encoded, Not Encrypted p.19 LAB 3 RBAC: Can-I as a ServiceAccount p.20 LAB 4 Trigger an OOMKill on Purpose p.21 PART VI · PROVE IT QUIZ Self-Check Quiz p.22 KEY Answer Key + Scoring p.23 GLOSS Glossary p.24 CHEAT One-Page Cheat Sheet p.25 FINALE Where to Next → Book 03 p.26  Assumes Book 01 complete. You already know Pods, ReplicaSets, Deployments, self-healing, and NodePort. This book adds the config layer (I–II), the permission layer (III)

CH 01 ⚙ ConfigMaps — What & Why  4 MIN The problem: bake LOG_LEVEL=debug into your image and every environment change = rebuild, r e-push, r e-pull . A ConfigMap decouples configuration from the image: one image, many configs. ❌ CONFIG BAKED INTO THE IMAGE app:v1 + debug → build → push app:v1 + info → build → push app:v1 + prod → build → push 3 images, 3 pipelines, 3 chances to drift ✅ CONFIG INJECTED AT RUNTIME app:v1 (built ONCE) + cfg-debug → dev cluster + cfg-staging → staging + cfg-prod → prod same image everywhere — only the map differs  Create one — three ways $ kubectl create configmap app-config --from-literal =LOG_LEVEL=debug $ kubectl create configmap app-conf --from-file =app.conf $ kubectl apply -f configmap.yaml # the declarative way (CH 02) configmap/app-config created  One sentence: a ConfigMap is a named bag of key/value pairs (or files) that lives inside a namespace — injected into Pods as env vars or files . It's the Kubernetes take on 12-factor config: config belongs to the environment, not the artifact . ⏭ How do P ods actually consume one? ← CH 02: Cr eating & Mounting ↑ back to top  Book 02 · Config, Secrets & RBA C ▤ TOC · next ▶ Page 3

CH 02  Creating & Mounting ConfigMaps  6 MIN · CORE apiVersion : v1 kind : ConfigMap metadata : { name : app-config } data : LOG_LEVEL : "debug" # simple key → env var app.conf : | # whole file as one key listen 8080 workers 4  Two consumption methods — they behave differently spec : containers : - name : app image : myapp:2.0 env : # METHOD 1 · single keys as env vars - name : LOG_LEVEL valueFrom : configMapKeyRef : { name : app-config, key : LOG_LEVEL } envFrom : # ...or import EVERY key as env - configMapRef : { name : app-config } volumeMounts : # METHOD 2 · keys as FILES - { name : cfg, mountPath : /etc/app } volumes : - name : cfg configMap : { name : app-config } # each key becomes a file  As env v ars  As volume files Shape flat KEY=value real files ( app.conf , nested keys ok) Update behavior never — snapshot at container start auto-updated by kubelet (~1 min, CH 03) Best for simple toggles, ports, feature flags config files, templates, anything the app re-reads  Rule of thumb: env vars are a snapshot , volume mounts are a live feed . Choose by asking: "does my app re- read its config file, or read the environment once at boot?" ↑ back to top  Book 02 · Config, Secr

CH 03  Hot-Reload — What Actually Updates  6 MIN · CORE The most-Googled ConfigMap question. The answer is a 2×2 matr ix — and one famous trap. Consumed as... ConfigMap changes → P od sees... Why Env var ❌ Never environment is fixed at container start (Linux process rules, not k8s') Volume file ✅ Yes — eventually (~1 min) kubelet syncs mounted files on its sync period Volume via subPath ❌ Never subPath mounts a copy ; the symlink chain is broken Env + app restart ✅ Yes (on next start) new container = fresh snapshot ⚠ "Eventually" means eventually: updates ride the kubelet sync period plus the API watch cache — up to ~1 minute of delay , in no guaranteed order. Apps that cache config at startup (Java, many frameworks) still see nothing until they re-read the file. The file changing ≠ your app noticing. volumes : - name : cfg configMap : { name : app-config, immutable : true } # freeze it entirely 流 immutable: true — rejects all updates (and can't be un-set without delete/recreate). T rade-off: zero hot- reload in exchange for protecting against accidental changes + better kubelet performance at scale.  Common production pattern: app watches its config file (or a sidecar triggers

CH 04  Secrets — vs ConfigMaps  6 MIN · CORE Same mechanism, different cargo. A Secret holds data you'd flinch to print in a git log : passwords, tokens, TLS keys, registry credentials. Aspect ⚙ ConfigMap  Secret Cargo plain config sensitive data (passwords, certs, tokens) Values on disk plain text base64-encoded ( data ) — CH 07 for what that does and doesn't mean Value size ~1 MiB ~1 MiB Consumed as env / volume env / volume — same two methods Default visibility anyone who can get it gated by RBAC — reading secrets is its own permission (Part III) Write convenience data data (pre-encoded) or stringData (plain — API encodes for you) ⚠ Do not skip this: base64 is encoding, not encryption — anyone can decode it with one command. By default, Secrets sit in etcd unencrypted. Real protection = etcd encryption-at-rest + tight RBAC (Part III). Full autopsy in CH 07. $ kubectl create secret generic db-pass --from-literal =PASSWORD= "s3cr3t" secret/db-pass created  Mental model: ConfigMap = the whiteboard in the apartment (anyone may read). Secret = the safe (base64 = the box it ships in; RBAC = who has the key). Same delivery mechanism, different trust level. ↑ back to top  Book 02 ·

CH 05  Secret Types & Creation  6 MIN · CORE type is a label that tells Kubernetes (and tooling) what shape the keys should take. The default is Opaque — "just key/values". Type Required keys Used by Opaque default anything you like app passwords, API keys, generic data kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson .dockerconfigjson imagePullSecrets — private registry auth (CH 06) kubernetes.io/tls tls.crt + tls.key Ingress TLS termination (Book 03) kubernetes.io/basic-auth username , password basic-auth integrations kubernetes.io/service-account- token — (API-managed) SA tokens — mostly automatic since v1.24 (CH 11)  Creation — imperative & declarative $ kubectl create secret generic db-pass --from-literal =PASSWORD= "s3cr3t" $ kubectl create secret docker-registry regcred \ --docker-server =registry.example.com --docker-username =ci \ --docker-password = $TOKEN $ kubectl create secret tls web-tls --cert =tls.crt --key =tls.key apiVersion : v1 kind : Secret metadata : { name : db-pass } type : Opaque stringData : # WRITE-only convenience — plain text in PASSWORD : "s3cr3t" # the API base64-encodes it into `data`  stringData never comes back out — kubectl get secret -o yaml always shows data

CH 06  Mounting Secrets + imagePullSecrets  6 MIN · CORE Same two doors as ConfigMaps — env vars (snapshot) and volumes (live feed) — plus a third, special-purpose door for the registry. spec : containers : - name : app image : myapp:2.0 env : - name : DB_PASSWORD valueFrom : secretKeyRef : { name : db-pass, key : PASSWORD } volumeMounts : - { name : sec, mountPath : /etc/secrets , readOnly : true } volumes : - name : sec secret : { secretName : db-pass } # keys → files, kubelet-synced  Prefer the volume door for sensitive data: env vars leak casually — they appear in kubectl describe , crash dumps, child processes ( /proc/<pid>/environ ), and some error reporters. A read-only file at a known path is easier to contain. (Hot-reload semantics from CH 03 apply identically to Secret volumes.)  imagePullSecrets — auth for pulling images # one-time: create the registry credential (CH 05) $ kubectl create secret docker-registry regcred ... # then attach it to the ServiceAccount — every Pod in that # namespace using this SA inherits it (recommended way) $ kubectl patch serviceaccount default -p \ '{"imagePullSecrets":[{"name":"regcred"}]}' # or per-Pod in the spec: spec : imagePullSecr

CH 07  Base64 ≠ Encryption — The Truth  6 MIN · MUST-KNOW The single most common Secrets misconception. W atch it die in one command: $ kubectl get secret db-pass -o jsonpath= '{.data.PASSWORD}' czNjcjN0 # looks safe... it is not $ echo czNjcjN0 | base64 -d s3cr3t # decoded by anyone, instantly ⚠ Base64 is a transport encoding — it makes binary-ish data YAML-safe. It's a locked box made of cardboard: the point is safe shipping, not safe keeping. Anyone with get secrets permission reads every "hidden" value. 暈 The four real layers of Secret protection Layer 1 · Encoding base64 NOT protection — just transport Layer 2 · Encryption at rest EncryptionConfiguration on kube-apiserver (aescbc / secretbox / KMS plugin) — encrypts in etcd Layer 3 · RBAC who may get/list secrets at all ← Part III Layer 4 · Externalization External Secrets / Vault — cluster never stores the real value long-term  Never commit raw manifests with real values to Git — use stringData + sealed/external secret tooling, or SOPS-style encryption ✅ Check your cluster: etcd encryption-at-rest is opt-in — many dev clusters run without it  Exam tip: "Are Secrets encrypted?" — the honest answer is "encoded by default; e

CH 08 着 RBAC — The Big Idea  6 MIN · CORE Authentication asks "who ar e you?" — authorization asks "may y ou do that ?" . RBAC is Kubernetes' answer to the second question, and it's one grammatical sentence:  WHO User · Gr oup · Ser viceAccount may  VERB get · list · wat ch · create · updat e · patch · delet e on  RESOUR CE pods · secr ets · deployments ... in  SCOPE namesp ace or clust er THE FOUR OBJECTS Role rules, namespaced RoleBinding attaches subjects → Role (ns) ClusterRole rules, cluster-wide ClusterRoleBinding subjects → ClusterRole (all) DEFAULT POSTURE Out of the box, RBA C grants regular users nothing — no R ole = no access. Even the default ServiceAccount in each namespace has zero API permissions (a hardening choice since v1.22). Every capability is granted explicitly . $ kubectl auth can-i delete pods -n dev no # ← your first authorization question  kubectl auth can-i <verb> <resource> [-n ns] is your constant companion — and with --as=... it answers for other identities (CH 09, Lab 3). Admins live in this command.  Carry the sentence: Role = the rules · Binding = who gets them · Scope = where they apply. Everything in the next three chapters is this sentence

CH 09  Roles & RoleBindings  6 MIN · CORE A Role is a namespaced rulebook; a RoleBinding hands that rulebook to people. W orked example — a CI bot that may read pods and manage config, nothing else: apiVersion : rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1 kind : Role metadata : name : ci-reader namespace : dev # Roles live IN a namespace rules : - apiGroups : [ "" ] # "" = core group (pods, secrets...) resources : [ pods , pods/log ] verbs : [ get , list , watch ] - apiGroups : [ "" ] resources : [ configmaps ] verbs : [ get , list , create , update , patch ] kind : RoleBinding metadata : { name : ci-reader-bind, namespace : dev } roleRef : apiGroup : rbac.authorization.k8s.io kind : Role name : ci-reader # the rulebook subjects : # WHO receives it - kind : ServiceAccount name : ci-bot namespace : dev # verify — answer FOR the bot without being the bot: $ kubectl auth can-i list pods -n dev \ --as =system:serviceaccount:dev:ci-bot yes $ kubectl auth can-i delete pods -n dev \ --as =system:serviceaccount:dev:ci-bot no # not in the rulebook → denied  Bindings are the only on-switch. Creating a Role changes nothing by itself; access exists only when a Binding names a subject. And verbs are litera

CH 10  ClusterRoles & When to Use Which  6 MIN · CORE A ClusterRole is a rulebook that isn't tied to a namespace. P airing it with the right binding type decides its reach: Pairing Effectiv e scope Use when... Role + RoleBinding one namespace team/app permissions (the 90% case) ClusterRole + RoleBinding one namespace per binding reuse one rulebook in many namespaces — bind the same ClusterRole to dev , qa , prod teams separately ClusterRole + ClusterRoleBinding entire cluster platform admins, controllers that watch everything Role + ClusterRoleBinding ❌ impossible — a cluster-wide binding can't reference a namespaced Role ⚠ The classic trap: some resources are cluster-scoped (Book 01 · CH 11): Nodes, PersistentVolumes, Namespaces, ClusterRoles . They cannot be governed by a namespaced Role — you must use a ClusterRole , even if you only want narrow access to, say, Nodes. # "let the monitoring bot READ nodes" — needs ClusterRole: kind : ClusterRole metadata : { name : node-reader } # note: no namespace field rules : - apiGroups : [ "" ] resources : [ nodes ] verbs : [ get , list , watch ]  Why ClusterRole + RoleBinding is the pro move: one canonical rulebook (audited once), names

CH 11  ServiceAccounts  6 MIN · CORE Users are for people ; a ServiceAccount (SA) is an identity for workloads — the "staff badge" your P od wears when it talks to the API Server.  Every namespace ships a default SA — P ods without an explicit serviceAccountName wear it  A Pod's SA gets a projected token mounted at /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount — that's the credential the app's k8s client uses (auto-discovered in-cluster)  Modern RBA C gives the default SA no per missions — a Pod that doesn't call the API should opt out: spec : serviceAccountName : ci-bot # wear THIS badge automountServiceAccountToken : false # ...or wear none  The full chain — badge → rulebook Pod wears ServiceAccount ci-bot │ └── RoleBinding grants ci-reader Role (CH 09) │ └── result: list pods ✓ · delete pods ✗ in ns dev only $ kubectl create serviceaccount ci-bot -n dev $ kubectl set serviceaccount deploy/web ci-bot -n dev $ kubectl auth can-i get secrets -n dev \ --as =system:serviceaccount:dev:ci-bot no # ← this is what a stolen Pod token can do. audit it. ⚠ The Pod-token threat model: anyone who can exec into your Pod can read its token and become that SA. Scope each SA's Role to the mi

CH 12  SecurityContext  6 MIN · CORE RBAC governs your P od's API permissions; the SecurityContext governs its Linux permissions. T wo levels apply: Level Fields Notes Pod-level spec.securityContext runAsUser · runAsGroup · runAsNonRoot · fsGroup defaults inherited by every container Container-level containers[].securityContext all of the above + readOnlyRootFilesystem · allowPrivilegeEscalation · capabilities · privileged overrides pod- level per container spec : securityContext : # POD level runAsNonRoot : true # refuse to start as uid 0 runAsUser : 1000 fsGroup : 2000 # group ownership for volumes containers : - name : app image : myapp:2.0 securityContext : # CONTAINER level readOnlyRootFilesystem : true # tamper-proof image FS allowPrivilegeEscalation : false capabilities : drop : [ "ALL" ] # shed Linux superpowers 隣 readOnlyRootFilesystem → writes must go to mounted emptyDir volumes — a common first hardening step  privileged: true ≈ root on the node — never for untrusted workloads (PSS · CH 13 forbids it outright at Baseline+)  Remember the pairing: RBAC = may it call the API? · SecurityContext = what can it do to the machine? Book 01's CH 07 taint story protected the no

CH 13  Pod Security Standards  5 MIN Checking every P od's SecurityContext by hand doesn't scale. Pod Secur ity Standar ds (PSS) define three ready- made security levels, enforced cluster-wide by namespace labels.  Privileged no restrictions — trusted, cluster- infrastructure workloads only  Baseline blocks the obviously dangerous (hostNetwork, privileged:true) while allowing common apps  Restricted current hardening best practice: runAsNonR oot, drop ALL capabilities, no privilege escalation # enforce on a namespace — three modes per level: $ kubectl label ns prod \ pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce =restricted \ pod-security.kubernetes.io/audit =restricted \ pod-security.kubernetes.io/warn =restricted  enforce — rejecting non-compliant P ods ·  audit — log violations · ⚠ warn — message the user 煮 Migration pattern: run warn+audit first, fix offenders, then switch on enforce ⚠ Version note: the old PodSecurityPolicy (PSP) was removed in Kubernetes v1.25 . If a tutorial teaches PSP, it's stale — the modern mechanism is PSS via Pod Security Admission (the labels above).  One line: PSS = cluster policy, three levels (Privileged → Baseline → Restricted), applied per-namespace

CH 14  Requests & Limits  6 MIN · CORE REQUESTS — the promise What the container is guarant eed . The Scheduler places P ods only on Nodes with enough request able capacity (Book 01 · CH 06's "P ending" mystery starts here). LIMITS — the ceiling The maximum the runtime enforces . What happens at the ceiling differs radically by r esource type — the table below is the exam's favorite nuance. containers : - name : app image : myapp:2.0 resources : requests : { cpu : "250m" , memory : "256Mi" } limits : { cpu : "500m" , memory : "512Mi" } Resource Exceeding the limit → Feels lik e CPU (compressible) Throttled — process slowed via CFS quota sluggish app, elevated latency, no restart Memory (incompressible) OOMKilled — SIGKILL, exit code 137 container dies; RestartPolicy kicks in → often CrashLoopBackOff $ kubectl describe pod oom-demo | grep -A3 Last State Last State: Terminated Reason: OOMKilled Exit Code: 137 # = 128 + 9 (SIGKILL) ⚠ The overcommit trap: total requests < node capacity < total limits is legal and common — the cluster borrows headroom. When a node runs out of real memory, the kube evicts by QoS class — which is exactly CH 15.  Memory hook: CPU over limit = tickets ge

CH 15  QoS Classes  5 MIN · CORE Every P od is silently stamped with a Quality-of-Security— sorry, Quality-of- Service class, derived purely from its requests/limits . It decides who gets evicted first when a node runs dry. Guaranteed every container: requests == limits for both cpu AND memory Burstable at least ONE requests/limits field set (anything else) BestEffort no requests, no limits — anything Class Derivation Eviction or der under node pr essure Guaranteed requests == limits (all containers) last — killed only after others Burstable some resources specified middle — those exceeding requests go first BestEffort nothing specified first — zero promises, zero protection $ kubectl get pod web -o jsonpath= '{.status.qosClass}' Burstable  Why this matters operationally: your database should be Guaranteed (it's the thing you least want killed); dev/experiment Pods can ride BestEffort as the cluster's shock absorber. QoS is how Kubernetes turns your YAML honesty into survival priority.  The chain, end to end: requests → where the Scheduler may place you · limits → what happens when you misbehave · QoS → who survives when the node itself starves. Part V now proves all of it hand

LAB 1  ConfigMap — Prove Env ≠ Hot- Reload  12 MIN · HANDS-ON STEP 1 · One ConfigMap, both consumption methods $ kubectl create configmap demo --from-literal =GREETING=hello $ kubectl run cfg-demo --image=busybox --restart=Never \ --overrides= '{"spec":{"containers":[{"name":"c","image":"busybox", "command":["sh","-c","sleep 9999"], "env":[{"name":"GREETING","valueFrom":{"configMapKeyRef":{"name":"demo","key":"GREETING"}}}], "volumeMounts":[{"name":"cfg","mountPath":"/etc/cfg"}]}], "volumes":[{"name":"cfg","configMap":{"name":"demo"}}]}}'  TAB 1 · OBSERVE $ kubectl exec cfg-demo -- printenv GREETING hello $ kubectl exec cfg-demo -- cat /etc/cfg/GREETING hello ⚙ TAB 2 · CHANGE IT $ kubectl patch cm demo -p \ '{"data":{"GREETING":"howdy"}}' configmap/demo patched STEP 2 · Wait ~1 min, re-check  ENV VAR — the snapshot $ kubectl exec cfg-demo -- printenv GREETING hello # ← UNCHANGED, forever  VOLUME FILE — the live feed $ kubectl exec cfg-demo -- cat /etc/cfg/GREETING howdy # ← updated by kubelet (~1 min) Proved: the matrix from CH 03 is real — env is a boot-time snapshot; volume mounts are kubelet-synced. Teardown: kubectl delete pod cfg-demo && kubectl delete cm demo . ↑ back to

LAB 2  Secret — Encoded, Not Encrypted  8 MIN · HANDS-ON STEP 1 · Create, mount, go inside $ kubectl create secret generic lab-sec --from-literal =PASSWORD= "hunter2" $ kubectl run sec-demo --image=busybox --restart=Never \ --overrides= '{"spec":{"containers":[{"name":"c","image":"busybox", "command":["sh","-c","sleep 9999"], "volumeMounts":[{"name":"s","mountPath":"/etc/sec","readOnly":true}]}], "volumes":[{"name":"s","secret":{"secretName":"lab-sec"}}]}}' STEP 2 · Read the "hidden" value — three levels of nakedness # inside the pod — the file is ALREADY DECODED for the app: $ kubectl exec sec-demo -- cat /etc/sec/PASSWORD hunter2 # from the API — only base64 stands in the way: $ kubectl get secret lab-sec -o jsonpath= '{.data.PASSWORD}' aHVudGVyMg== $ echo aHVudGVyMg== | base64 -d # → hunter2. instantly. Proved: CH 07's claim — base64 protects nothing; the kubelet even hands your app the decoded value. Protection lives in who may r un get secret (RBAC) and etcd encryption-at-rest. Teardown: kubectl delete pod sec-demo && kubectl delete secret lab-sec .  Interview one-liner born from this lab: "Secrets protect against casual exposure and unauthenticated reads — not against anyo

LAB 3 着 RBAC — Can-I as a ServiceAccount  12 MIN · HANDS-ON STEP 1 · Build the chain: SA → Role → Binding $ kubectl create ns rbac-lab $ kubectl create serviceaccount bot -n rbac-lab $ kubectl create role podlist --verb =get,list --resource =pods -n rbac-lab $ kubectl create rolebinding bot-bind --role =podlist \ --serviceaccount =rbac-lab:bot -n rbac-lab STEP 2 · Interrogate the bot's permissions $ K="--as=system:serviceaccount:rbac-lab:bot -n rbac-lab" $ kubectl auth can-i list pods $K # in the rulebook yes $ kubectl auth can-i delete pods $K # verbs are literal! no $ kubectl auth can-i list secrets $K # resources too no $ kubectl auth can-i list pods -n default $K # scope is namespaced! no STEP 3 · What we proved ✅ The bot may list pods — exactly one namespace, exactly the granted verbs ❌ Delete? Secrets? Other namespaces? All no — default posture is deny; the R ole's scope is absolute  --as lets you audit any identity without their cr edentials — the core of RBA C troubleshooting Teardown: kubectl delete ns rbac-lab — the cascade (Book 01 · Lab 3) removes the whole chain. ↑ back to top  Book 02 · Config, Secrets & RBA C ◀ prev · ▤ TOC · next ▶ Page 20

LAB 4  Trigger an OOMKill on Purpose  10 MIN · HANDS-ON STEP 1 · Deploy a Pod with a tiny memory limit and a big appetite $ kubectl set image deploy/oom-demo oom=polinux/stress \ -n default 2>/dev/null || kubectl create deploy oom-demo --image=polinux/stress \ -- stress --vm 1 --vm-bytes 200M --timeout 300s $ kubectl set resources deploy/oom-demo --limits =memory= 50Mi --requests =memory=30Mi $ kubectl get pods -w  TAB 1 · WATCH NAME STATUS RESTARTS oom-demo- aaaaa Running 0 oom-demo-aaaaa Error 1 # OOM! oom-demo-aaaaa Running 1 oom-demo-aaaaa Error 2 # again...  TAB 2 · AUTOPSY $ kubectl describe pod -l app=oom-demo Last State: Terminated Reason: OOMKilled Exit: 137 # 128+9 = SIGKILL by the # kernel's OOM killer STEP 2 · What we proved ✅ Memory limit exceeded → OOMKilled (137) , not throttled — CH 14's incompressible-resource rule ✅ The Deployment's reconciliation (Book 01 · CH 06) restarts it → it OOMs again → the classic CrashLoopBackOff signature 喙 Real-world translation: app that cr ash-loops r ight af ter startup + exit 137 = r aise the limit or f ix the leak Teardown: kubectl delete deploy oom-demo . (Then check its QoS: it had requests≠limits → Burstable — CH 15 in the

QUIZ ✅ Self-Check Quiz ☑ 10 questions Q1. A ConfigMap is consumed by a Pod both as an env var and as a volume file. You update the ConfigMap. What does the running Pod see? A. Both update within ~1 min B. Env unchanged; the volume file updates eventually C. Env updates; file unchanged D. Neither — a restart is always required Q2. A colleague says Secrets are "encrypted by Kubernetes". The accurate response? A. True — always encrypted in etcd B. True, but only for Opaque type C. False — values are base64- encoded ; encryption-at- rest must be explicitly enabled D. False — Secrets are stored in plain text in the API Server's memory Q3. Which Secret type must contain the key .dockerconfigjson ? A. Opaque B. kubernetes.io/tls C. kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson D. basic-auth Q4. By default, which identity may read Secrets in namespace dev ? A. Any authenticated user B. The default ServiceAccount C. Cluster admins only, forever D. Nobody beyond cluster-admin- tier until an RBAC Role/Binding grants it Q5. kubectl auth can-i get pods --as=system:serviceaccount:dev:bot answers... A. Can the bot authenticate? B. May bot perform get pods ? (authorization, impersonated) C. Do you have permissio

KEY  Answer Key + Scoring grade yourself Q Ans Why — one line 1 B Env = boot snapshot, never updates; volume files kubelet-synced ~1 min — CH 02/03 2 C Base64 is transport encoding; etcd encryption-at-rest is opt-in — CH 07 3 C dockerconfigjson type mandates the .dockerconfigjson key — CH 05/06 4 D Default posture is deny; even the default SA has zero permissions — CH 08/11 5 B can-i + --as = authorization check for an impersonated identity — CH 08/09 6 C RoleBinding may bind a ClusterRole, scoping it to its namespace — CH 10 7 C Guaranteed = requests==limits, cpu AND memory, every container — CH 15 8 D Memory is incompressible → OOMKill, 128+9=137 — CH 14, Lab 4 9 C readOnlyRootFilesystem is container-level SecurityContext — CH 12 10 B Restricted = hardening best practice; PSP is removed (v1.25) — CH 13  9–10 Ready for Book 03  6–8 Re-read the missed chapters'  boxes  <6 Re-run Labs 1–4, then retake  Missed Q2 or Q4? Those are the two real-world security gaps — "encoded ≠ encrypted" and "default deny". Missed Q6? The ClusterRole+RoleBinding combo is the most misremembered fact in RBAC. ↑ back to top  Book 02 · Config, Secrets & RBA C ◀ prev · ▤ TOC · next ▶ Page 23

GLOSS  Glossary  REFERENCE ConfigMap — namespaced key/value (or file) store for plain config; consumed as env vars or volume files. Hot-reload — volume-mounted ConfigMaps/Secrets update automatically (~1 min, eventual); env vars and subPath mounts never do. Secret — ConfigMap's sensitive sibling; base64-encoded values, RBAC-gated reads, same two consumption methods. Opaque — default Secret type: arbitrary key/value pairs. imagePullSecrets — registry credentials used by the kubelet to pull private images; best attached at ServiceAccount level. Base64 — transport encoding, not encryption. Decodable by anyone in one command. Encryption at rest — opt-in kube-apiserver EncryptionConfiguration that encrypts Secrets inside etcd. Authentication vs Authorization — who are you vs may you do that. RBAC answers the second. Role / ClusterRole — namespaced / cluster-level rulebooks: verbs on resources. RoleBinding / ClusterRoleBinding — attach subjects to rulebooks; a RoleBinding may bind a ClusterRole but scope it to its namespace. Subject — User, Group, or ServiceAccount named by a Binding. ServiceAccount — workload identity; its projected token (mounted in the Pod) is the credential Pods us

CHEAT  One-Page Cheat Sheet  print me ⚙ CONFIG & SECRETS — COMMANDS $ kubectl create configmap cm --from-literal=K=V --from-file=f.conf $ kubectl create secret generic s --from-literal=K=V $ kubectl create secret docker-registry reg --docker-server=... --docker-username=... $ kubectl create secret tls t --cert=crt --key=key $ kubectl get secret s -o jsonpath='{.data.K}' | base64 -d $ kubectl patch sa default -p '{"imagePullSecrets":[{"name":"reg"}]}' 着 RBAC — COMMANDS $ kubectl create role r --v $ kubectl create rolebindin $ kubectl create clusterrol $ kubectl auth can-i delete $ kubectl describe role/rol  HOT-RELOAD MATRIX Consumed as Updat es? env var never volume file yes (~1 min) subPath mount never  QOS + ENFORCEMENT Guaranteed: requests==limits (cpu+mem, all) Burstable: partial · BestEffort: none eviction: BestEffort → Burst>req → Guaranteed mem over limit → OOMKilled 137 cpu over limit → throttled $ kubectl get pod P -o jsonpath='{.status.qosClass}' 易 FACTS WORTH A JOB OFFER ConfigMap = whiteboard, Secret = safe — same delivery, different trust · both ~1 MiB, namespaced Base64 ≠ encryption — real layers: etcd encryption-at-rest + RBA C (+ external secret managers) Defaul

FINALE  What You Can Do Now  Book 02 complete Book 01 gave you the machine. This book gave it manner s — config, secrets, permissions, and a resource contract. ☸ POD — fully dressed now: ├── ⚙ ConfigMap plain config → env / files (hot-reload rules known) ├──  Secret sensitive data — encoded ≠ encrypted, RBAC-gated ├── 着 ServiceAccount + Role/RoleBinding = exactly what it may do ├──  SecurityContext runAsNonRoot · roFS · caps (PSS-enforced) └──  requests/limits → scheduler placement, throttle/OOM, QoS class ✅ You can now...
