CH 01  Why Storage Is Different  4 MIN Everything so far assumed P ods are expendable — and their filesyst em is t oo . A container's writable layer is built fresh from the image every time the container is replaced. Data written "inside the container" has a death wish. THE THREE LIVES OF DATA — HOW LONG DOES IT SURVIVE? 1 · Container writable layer dies with the CONTAINER crash → kubelet restarts → fresh layer → your writes GONE 2 · emptyDir volume dies with the POD survives container restarts — deleted when the Pod leaves the node 3 · PersistentVolumes outlives EVERYTHING pods, nodes, even the cluster's opinion — data remains ❌ FINE WITHOUT PERSISTENCE Stateless APIs (state lives in a DB elsewhere ) Static sites, proxies, workers Scratch space, temp files (emptyDir!)  DIES WITHOUT PERSISTENCE Databases (MySQL, P ostgres — Book 01's Y AML wrote nothing durable!) User uploads, sessions Message queues, ML models, indexes  Book 04 foreshadowed this: drain --delete-emptydir-data exists precisely because emptyDir data dies with the Pod — drain makes you admit it. And Book 01's MySQL lab ran on the container layer: that database was one crash away from amnesia.  One sentence: Kuber

CH 02  Volumes — The Pod's Attachments  6 MIN · CORE A Volume is a directory, declar ed at P od lev el, mount ed into container s . It outlives the containers in the P od — but its lifespan depends on its type . spec : containers : - name : app image : myapp:2.0 volumeMounts : - { name : scratch, mountPath : /tmp/cache } volumes : # declared at POD level — shared by containers - name : scratch emptyDir : {} Type Backing Lifespan Use for emptyDir node disk / RAM ( medium: Memory ) Pod's life scratch, multi-container share, checkpointing hostPath a path on the node survives the Pod — tied to the node ⚠ node agents, privileged daemons only configMap / secret API objects (Book 02 · CH 02/06) Pod's life, kubelet-synced config & credentials as files nfs an NFS share independent of Pod shared file storage persistentVolumeClaim a PV via binding independent — the star ⭐ real persistence (Part II) csi any CSI driver (CH 11) driver-defined ephemeral CSI volumes ⚠ hostPath is a loaded weapon: it hard-couples your Pod to a specific path on whatever node it lands on — rescheduling to another node = "where did my data go?" It can also read any path on the node (including / ) — a container-escap

CH 03 欄 PV & PVC — Supply Meets Demand  6 MIN · CORE The genius of Kubernetes storage is a divorce of concer ns : the people who provision storage (ops, storage admins) and the people who consume it (developers) never talk to each other. They meet through two objects.  PERSISTENTVOLUME — THE SUPPLY apiVersion : v1 kind : PersistentVolume metadata : { name : pv-warehouse-1 } spec : capacity : storage : 5Gi accessModes : [ ReadWriteOnce ] persistentVolumeReclaimPolicy : Retain hostPath : { path : /data/pv1 } Cluster-scoped (Book 01 · CH 11 promised!). Real storage: NFS, cloud disk, hostP ath. No namespace, owned by admins.  PERSISTENTVOLUMECLAIM — THE DEMAND apiVersion : v1 kind : PersistentVolumeClaim metadata : { name : db-data, namespace : shop } spec : resources : requests : storage : 3Gi accessModes : [ ReadWriteOnce ] storageClassName : "" # "" = manual binding only (CH 07) Namesp aced . Not storage — a wish : "I need 3Gi, RWO." The developer's entire vocabulary of storage. THE MEETING — BINDING TURNS TWO WISHES INTO A CONTRACT  Ops ── ►  PV ⇄  PVC ◄ ── ‍ Dev PVC bound → P ods mount the claim , never the volume: volumes: [{name: data, persistentVolumeClaim: {claimName:

CH 04  The Binding Process  6 MIN · CORE A controller (the PV contr oller , inside kube-controller-manager) continuously matches P ending claims to A vailable volumes. Four checks, all must pass: THE MATCHER'S FOUR QUESTIONS 1 · Cap acity PV ≥ r equest ? 2 · Access modes PV ⊇ request ed? 3 · storageClassName exact mat ch? 4 · select or labels mat ch? smallest PV that fits wins · binding is 1:1 — a bound PV is spoken for Check Rule Gotcha Capacity PV's storage ≥ PVC's request you get the whole PV, not a slice — a 3Gi claim on a 5Gi PV wastes 2Gi Access modes PV offers at least what the claim asks claim [RWO] can bind a PV offering [RWO, RWX] StorageClass exact string match — including "" claim with className: "" binds only PVs also stamped "" ; a claim with no field uses the default class (CH 07) Selector claim's selector.matchLabels ⊆ PV labels ops tags PVs ( tier: gold ), devs target the tag $ kubectl get pvc db-data NAME STATUS VOLUME CAPACITY ACCESS MODES db-data Pending # nobody fits — check the 4 questions db-data Bound pv-warehouse-1 5Gi RWO  Pre- binding: a PV can name its soulmate in spec.claimRef — skips the matchmaking entirely (migrations, DR drills)  Binding is excl

CH 05  Access Modes — RWO·ROX·RWX Decoded  6 MIN · CORE The names are honest about read/write but lying about the unit . The unit is NODES , not P ods — and that one fact explains half of all storage tickets. Mode Name says Really means Typical b acking ReadWriteOnce one writer read-write mounted by ONE NODE cloud block disks: EBS, PD, Azure Disk ReadOnlyMany many readers read-only on MANY nodes NFS, EFS (ro), pre-staged datasets ReadWriteMany shared write read-write on MANY nodes NFS, EFS, Azure Files, CephFS ReadWriteOncePod newer one writer read-write by ONE POD — truly exclusive (GA 1.29) block disks, with the strictest semantics ⚠ The interview trap: RWO ≠ one Pod. It's one node — so three Pods on the same node can all mount one RWO volume simultaneously , while the same three Pods spread across three nodes cannot. When your scaled Deployment mysteriously wedges, this is why: replicas scattered across nodes fight over one RWO claim. MULTI-ATTACH — THE CLASSIC FAILURE $ kubectl describe pod db-2 | tail -2 Events: Multi-Attach error for volume "pvc-abc": Volume is already exclusively attached to one node and can't be attached to another # Pod B (other node) wants the RWO volum

CH 06 ♻ Reclaim Policies & the PV Lifecycle  6 MIN · CORE A PV has a whole life after its claim dies. The reclaim policy decides what that afterlife looks like — and whether your data survives it. Available → Bound → PVC deleted → Released → policy decides → │ │ Retain: stays Released forever — data intact, ADMIN must intervene Delete: PV object + backing storage both destroyed ← dynamic default Recycle: scrub & re-offer — REMOVED from the API (dynamic provisioning replaced it) Policy PVC delet ed → Data Use when Retain PV → Released , never auto- reused kept — hostage until an admin acts databases, anything you'd cry over Delete PV + cloud disk annihilated gone truly ephemeral state, CI scratch # the Released hostage situation — and the escape: $ kubectl get pv NAME CAPACITY CLAIM RECLAIM STATUS pv-db 5Gi shop/db-data Retain Released # reuse it manually: clear the claimRef → back to Available # (data intact! next binding re-attaches the same disk) $ kubectl patch pv pv-db -p '{"spec":{"claimRef": null}}' ⚠ Two honest warnings: (1) the pvc-protection finalizer — a PVC in use by a Pod shows Terminating indefinitely; Kubernetes refuses to yank storage from a running Pod. (2) Default

CH 07  StorageClasses — Build on Demand  6 MIN · CORE Writing PV s by hand doesn't scale — it's the landlord hand-building a warehouse per lease. A StorageClass is the constr uction comp any : PVCs name it, and it builds the warehouse automatically. apiVersion : storage.k8s.io/v1 kind : StorageClass metadata : name : fast annotations : storageclass.kubernetes.io/is-default-class : "true" # THE default provisioner : ebs.csi.aws.com # WHO builds (CSI driver — CH 11) parameters : # the build spec, vendor-specific type : gp3 encrypted : "true" reclaimPolicy : Delete # default for dynamic volumes allowVolumeExpansion : true # grow later (CH 08) volumeBindingMode : WaitForFirstConsumer # smart timing (CH 08) DYNAMIC PROVISIONING — THE WHOLE DANCE, AUTOMATED  PVC className: fast ── ►  SC ── ►  Provisioner ▼ builds real storage (EBS volume etc.)  PV aut o-created ── ►  PVC ── ► 﫛 Pod mounts it zero PV s hand-written · the SC name in the claim is the only thing a developer must know PVC's storageClassName Result names a class ( fast ) dynamic provisioning from that class — manual PVs of the same name are bypassed unless matching perfectly field omitted + a default class exists uses t

CH 07  StorageClasses — continued  6 MIN · CORE  One sentence: a StorageClass is a named recipe — provisioner + parameters + policy — that builds PVs on demand ; claims name the recipe, the default class catches the lazy, and "" is the explicit "I brought my own warehouse." ⏭ The two settings that separate toy classes from production ones — CH 08: Class T uning ↑ back to top  Book 05 · S torage ◀ prev · ▤ TOC · next ▶ Page 10

CH 08 ⚙ Class Tuning — Binding Modes & Expansion  6 MIN · CORE ⏱ volumeBindingMode — WHEN to bind IMMEDIATE (DEFAULT) Bind the instant the PV C exists — before any P od exists . Simple, but with zoned storage the disk may be born in zone A while y our Pod later schedules to zone C → attach impossible → P od wedged. 0/1 nodes available: volume node affinity conflict # ← this error = bound to the wrong zone WAITFORFIRSTCONSUMER ✅ The PV C waits in Pending until a Pod that uses it is scheduled — then provisions the dis in the P od's zone . Topology-correct by construction. Production default for zoned clouds. # PVC waits... pod schedules to zone-c... # disk born IN zone-c — attach just works  allowVolumeExpansion — grow, never shrink # class must allow it (CH 07)... then just edit the claim: $ kubectl patch pvc db-data -p '{"spec":{"resources":{"requests":{"storage":"10Gi"}}}}' $ kubectl get pvc db-data NAME CAPACITY STATUS db-data 10Gi Bound # filesystem resized online (most drivers) # SHRINKING IS IMPOSSIBLE — storage can only ever grow. plan headroom. Setting Recommended Why volumeBindingMode WaitForFirstConsumer (zoned clouds) disk and Pod land in the same zone, always allowVolu

CH 09 着 StatefulSets — Why Identity Matters  6 MIN · CORE A Deployment's P ods are interchangeable cattle — random names, any replica can serve any request. Databases are not cattle : replica 0 is the primary, replica 1 is its follower, and each owns its own data. Enter the S tatefulSet.  DEPLOYMENT IDENTITY web- 7d9f-x7k2p random web- 7d9f-bbbba random die → replaced by NEW random names any pod can serve anything no "which one owns the data?"  STATEFULSET IDENTITY db- 0 PRIMARY — born first db- 1 follower — waits for 0 db- 2 follower — waits for 1 die → RESURRECTED WITH THE SAME NAME + same storage (CH 10) + same DNS  The headless service — per-Pod DNS apiVersion : v1 kind : Service metadata : { name : db } spec : clusterIP : None # HEADLESS — no VIP, no balancing selector : { app : db } ports : [{ port : 5432 }] # instead of one VIP, DNS returns EACH POD's address: # db-0.db.shop.svc.cluster.local → db-0's IP (the primary!) # followers find the primary BY NAME — no IPs in any config  Ordered by default: 0 → Ready → then 1 → R eady → then 2; deletion runs in reverse (2 → 1 → 0). The bootstrap sequence a database needs, built in  Name = contract: replication configs say "foll

CH 10  volumeClaimTemplates — Storage Per Replica  6 MIN · CORE The StatefulSet's killer storage feature: instead of one shared claim, you embed a templat e — and each replica gets its own PV C stamped fr om it , named after the P od it belongs to. apiVersion : apps/v1 kind : StatefulSet metadata : { name : db } spec : serviceName : db # the headless service (CH 09) replicas : 3 selector : { matchLabels : { app : db } } template : # the pod stamp metadata : { labels : { app : db } } spec : containers : - name : db image : postgres:16 volumeMounts : - { name : data, mountPath : /var/lib/postgresql/data } volumeClaimTemplates : # ★ THE COOKIE CUTTER FOR CLAIMS - metadata : { name : data } spec : accessModes : [ ReadWriteOnce ] resources : { requests : { storage : 10Gi } } storageClassName : fast StatefulSet db (replicas: 3) ├── pod db-0 ⇄ PVC data-db-0 ⇄ PV (own disk) ├── pod db-1 ⇄ PVC data-db-1 ⇄ PV (own disk) └── pod db-2 ⇄ PVC data-db-2 ⇄ PV (own disk) naming law: <template-name>-<statefulset>-<ordinal> ✅ SCALE UP → CLAIMS BORN 3 → 4 replicas: data-db-3 dynamically provisioned (CH 07!), mounted by db-3 . Fresh disk, zero setup. ⚠ SCALE DOWN → CLAIMS RETAINED 4 → 2: Pods db-3 ,

CH 11  CSI — The Universal Plug  5 MIN Every provisioner you've met ( ebs.csi.aws.com , minikube's hostpath , Ceph...) speaks CSI — the Container Storage Int erface : a vendor-neutral gRPC contract that lets any storage backend plug into any Kubernetes.  BEFORE CSI (IN-TREE ERA) Driver code lived inside the k8s sour ce tree Vendors begged SIGs for inclusion; releases tied to k8s cycles k8s shipped hundreds of drivers it couldn't all test  AFTER CSI Drivers are container s you install (Helm charts) Vendors release on their schedule, any k8s version In-tree drivers: frozen & deprecated — CSI is the only growth path Pod ⇄ PVC ⇄ StorageClass.provisioner = "ebs.csi.aws.com" │ ▼ CSI driver — two halves, both just Pods: ├── Controller plugin (Deployment) — CreateVolume, DeleteVolume, Expand └── Node plugin (DaemonSet — one per node, Book 04 CH 10 skips these!) └── NodeStageVolume / NodePublishVolume → the disk appears at the mountPath  Credentials, o f course, are Secrets (Book 02 · CH 05–06): the driver's chart consumes a Secret holding cloud API keys / backend tokens 里 volumeMode: Filesystem (default — a formatted dir) vs Block (raw device handed to the P od — databases that manage

LAB 1  Manual PV ↔ PVC Binding  12 MIN · HANDS-ON STEP 1 · Provision supply by hand $ kubectl apply -f - <<EOF apiVersion : v1 kind : PersistentVolume metadata : { name : pv-manual-1, labels : { tier : lab } } spec : capacity : { storage : 1Gi } accessModes : [ ReadWriteOnce ] persistentVolumeReclaimPolicy : Retain storageClassName : "" hostPath : { path : /data/pv-manual-1 , type : DirectoryOrCreate } EOF $ kubectl get pv pv-manual-1 # STATUS: Available (2 of the 4 checks pre-passed) STEP 2 · Demand + consume $ kubectl apply -f - <<EOF apiVersion : v1 kind : PersistentVolumeClaim metadata : { name : lab-claim } spec : accessModes : [ ReadWriteOnce ] resources : { requests : { storage : 500Mi } } storageClassName : "" # match the PV's "" — CH 04 rule 3 selector : { matchLabels : { tier : lab } } EOF $ kubectl get pvc lab-claim # Bound → pv-manual-1 (smallest fitting PV) $ kubectl run writer --image=busybox:1.36 --restart=Never --rm -it \ --overrides= '{"spec":{"containers":[{"name":"w","image":"busybox:1.36", "command":["sh","-c","echo persistent rocks > /data/hello.txt; sleep 5"], "volumeMounts":[{"name":"d","mountPath":"/data"}]}], "volumes":[{"name":"d","persistentVolumeClaim"

LAB 2  Dynamic Provisioning + Reclaim Proof  10 MIN · HANDS-ON STEP 1 · Zero PVs — just a claim $ kubectl get storageclass NAME PROVISIONER RECLAIMPOLICY BINDINGMODE standard k8s.io/minikube-hostpath Delete Immediate # default ✓ $ kubectl apply -f - <<EOF apiVersion : v1 kind : PersistentVolumeClaim metadata : { name : dyn-claim } # no className → default class (CH 07) spec : accessModes : [ ReadWriteOnce ] resources : { requests : { storage : 1Gi } } EOF $ kubectl get pvc dyn-claim # Bound — and NOBODY wrote a PV: $ kubectl get pv | grep dyn-claim # pvc-xxxx... auto-created by the provisioner! STEP 2 · Feel the Delete policy bite $ kubectl patch pv <auto-pv-name> \ -p '{"spec":{"persistentVolumeReclaimPolicy":"Retain"}}' # arm the trap first $ kubectl delete pvc dyn-claim $ kubectl get pv <auto-pv-name> STATUS Released # Retain: data held hostage (CH 06) — admin must clear claimRef or delete # WITHOUT the patch: PV + backing storage would be GONE. Delete is the default.  Proved: dynamic provisioning needs zero PV authorship — and the default Delete policy is one delete pvc away from data annihilation unless you Retain first. Teardown: kubectl delete pv <auto-pv-name> ↑ back to

LAB 3  StatefulSet — Identity & Per-Replica Data  15 MIN · HANDS-ON STEP 1 · Headless service + StatefulSet with a claim template $ kubectl apply -f - <<EOF apiVersion : v1 kind : Service metadata : { name : web } spec : { clusterIP : None , selector : { app : webs }, ports : [{ port : 80 }] } --- apiVersion : apps/v1 kind : StatefulSet metadata : { name : web } spec : serviceName : web replicas : 2 selector : { matchLabels : { app : webs } } template : metadata : { labels : { app : webs } } spec : containers : - name : nginx image : nginx:1.25 volumeMounts : [{ name : data, mountPath : /usr/share/nginx/html }] volumeClaimTemplates : - metadata : { name : data } spec : { accessModes : [ ReadWriteOnce ], resources : { requests : { storage : 100Mi } } } EOF $ kubectl get pods -w # web-0 Running → THEN web-1 (ordered! CH 09)  IDENTITY + STORAGE $ kubectl get pvc NAME STATUS CAPACITY data-web-0 Bound 100Mi ← per replica! data-web-1 Bound 100Mi $ kubectl run d --rm -it --image=busybox:1.36 \ --restart=Never -- wget -qO- web-0.web # per-pod DNS via the HEADLESS svc (CH 09) ⚙ WRITE PER-REPLICA DATA $ kubectl exec web-0 -- sh -c \ 'echo i-am-zero > /usr/share/nginx/html/i.txt' $ kubectl

LAB 3  StatefulSet — continued  15 MIN · HANDS-ON STEP 2 · Kill web-0 — resurrection, not reincarnation $ kubectl delete pod web-0 $ kubectl get pod web-0 # SAME NAME, back after reschedule $ kubectl exec web-0 -- cat /usr/share/nginx/html/i.txt i-am-zero # ← its OWN data survived: data-web-0 reattached STEP 3 · Scale down — the claims stay behind $ kubectl scale sts web --replicas=1 $ kubectl get pvc # data-web-1 STILL BOUND — retained by design (CH 10) Teardown: kubectl delete sts web && kubectl delete svc web && kubectl delete pvc data-web-0 data-web-1 — the PV Cs never go with the ST S. ↑ back to top  Book 05 · S torage ◀ prev · ▤ TOC · next ▶ Page 18

LAB 4 離 The Data-Survival Gauntlet  12 MIN · HANDS-ON One claim, three disasters. Which data survives? Run each round and predict before looking: SETUP · Claim + writer (reuse Lab 1's PV or Lab 2's dynamic claim) $ kubectl run g1 --image=busybox:1.36 --restart=Never -- \ sh -c 'echo round-one > /data/state.txt; sleep 9999' $ kubectl patch pod g1 --type =merge -p \ '{"spec":{"volumes":[{"name":"d","persistentVolumeClaim":{"claimName":"surv"}}]}}' 2>/dev/null \ || kubectl run g1 --image=busybox:1.36 --restart=Never \ --overrides= '{"spec":{"containers":[{"name":"g","image":"busybox:1.36", "command":["sh","-c","echo round-one > /data/state.txt; sleep 9999"], "volumeMounts":[{"name":"d","mountPath":"/data"}]}], "volumes":[{"name":"d","persistentVolumeClaim":{"claimName":"surv"}}]}}' Round Disaster Prediction Verdict 1 kubectl delete pod g1 data...? SURVIVES — it lives in the PV, not the Pod (Lab 3 proved the pattern) 2 kubectl delete pvc surv — while a Pod uses it instant gone? Terminating... hangs — the pvc-protection finalizer (CH 06). Delete the Pod first, then it proceeds 3 PVC gone + PV policy... data...? Retain → Released , bytes intact on the node ( minikube ssh ls /data/... )

QUIZ ✅ Self-Check Quiz ☑ 10 questions Q1. A container crashes and is restarted inside its Pod. Data written to an emptyDir volume... A. survives — emptyDir lives with the Pod B. is lost with the container layer C. moves to another node D. becomes read- only Q2. Which object is cluster-scoped ? A. PersistentVolumeClaim B. StatefulSet C. PersistentVolume D. Service Q3. ReadWriteOnce actually restricts mounting to... A. one Pod B. one NODE (any number of its Pods may share) C. one container D. one namespace Q4. Which is NOT a criterion the PV controller uses to match a claim? A. capacity ≥ request B. access modes ⊇ requested C. storageClassName equality D. the claiming Pod's name Q5. Retain policy, PVC deleted. The PV... A. enters Released — data kept until an admin intervenes B. is deleted with its backing disk C. immediately becomes Available for reuse D. enters Failed Q6. A PVC omits storageClassName ; a default class exists. Result? A. Pending until a manual PV matches B. validation error C. dynamically provisioned from the default class D. binds only PVs labeled default Q7. volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer exists to... A. slow down provisioning for safety B. delay binding

KEY  Answer Key + Scoring grade yourself Q Ans Why — one line 1 A emptyDir outlives containers, dies with the Pod — the whole three-lives ladder (CH 01–02) 2 C PV = supply = cluster-wide; PVC/StatefulSet/Service are namespaced — Book 01 · CH 11 (CH 03) 3 B The unit is NODES — same-node Pods may share one RWO volume (CH 05) 4 D Pod names never enter matching: capacity, modes, class, selector only (CH 04) 5 A Retain = Released, data hostage; clearing claimRef re-opens it (CH 06) 6 C Omitted field + default class = dynamic provisioning; "" would opt out (CH 07) 7 B Wait for the consumer → disk born in the Pod's zone; fixes node-affinity conflict wedges (CH 08) 8 D Data-safety by design: claims outlive scaled-down replicas (CH 10, Lab 3) 9 C Template = cookie cutter: data-<sts>-<ordinal> per replica (CH 10) 10 B Standard interface + installable driver containers; in-tree frozen (CH 11)  9–10 Ready for Book 06  6–8 Re-read missed chapters'  boxes  <6 Re-run Labs 1–4, then retake  Missed Q3? The RWO-is-a-node lie is the most common storage misconception in interviews — drill it. Missed Q8 or Q9? StatefulSet storage behavior (claims outlive scale-down) is exactly what "stateful" mea

GLOSS  Glossary  REFERENCE Volume — a Pod-level directory mounted into containers; lifespan set by its type (emptyDir, hostPath, configMap, PVC...). emptyDir — scratch volume sharing the Pod's life; survives container restarts, dies with the Pod; optional sizeLimit. hostPath — node-local path; couples Pods to nodes and can expose the whole filesystem — daemon-only territory. PersistentVolume (PV) — cluster-scoped piece of real storage with capacity, accessModes, reclaimPolicy; the supply. PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC) — namespaced request (capacity + modes + class + selector); the only thing Pods mount. Binding — 1:1 PV↔PVC match: capacity ≥, modes ⊇ , class ==, selector match; smallest fitting PV wins. Access modes — RWO (one NODE!), ROX, RWX (many nodes, shared filesystem), RWOP (one Pod, GA 1.29). Multi-Attach error — a block volume refusing simultaneous attach to two nodes; the RWO-wedge signature. PV phases — Available → Bound → Released (Retain holds here) → Failed; Released never auto-rebinds. Reclaim policy — Retain (keep data, admin intervenes) / Delete (PV + backing storage destroyed; dynamic default) / Recycle (removed). pvc-protection finalizer — keeps a PVC Terminating

CHEAT  One-Page Cheat Sheet  print me  STORAGE — COMMANDS $ kubectl get pv,pvc,sc $ kubectl get pvc # Pending? check 4 match rules $ kubectl describe pv X # node affinity = its zone $ kubectl patch pv X -p \ '{"spec": {"persistentVolumeReclaimPolicy":"Retain"}}' $ kubectl patch pv X -p '{"spec": {"claimRef":null}}' # Released→Available $ kubectl patch pvc P -p \ '{"spec":{"resources":{"requests": {"storage":"10Gi"}}}}' # grow only  PRODUCTION STORAGECLASS provisioner : ebs.csi.aws.com parameters : {type: gp3} reclaimPolicy : Retain # not Delete! allowVolumeExpansion : true volumeBindingMode : WaitForFirstConsumer # default class annotation: storageclass.kubernetes.io/is-default-class: "true" 着 STATEFULSET STORAGE SKELETON serviceName : db # headless: clusterIP None volumeClaimTemplates : - metadata : {name: data} spec : {accessModes: [ReadWriteOnce], resources: {requests: {storage: 10Gi}}} # → data-db-0, data-db-1 ... # scale-up: born · scale-down: RETAINED # delete STS: claims survive — manual cleanup  TRIAGE TABLE Symptom Meaning PVC Pending class/capacity/mode/selector mismatch Pod Pending + node affinity conflict disk in wrong zone → WaitForFirstConsumer Multi-Attach error

FINALE  What You Can Do Now  Book 05 complete Book 01 built the machine, 02 dressed it, 03 connected it, 04 placed it — Book 05 gave it memor y that sur vives death .  STORAGE — fully mapped: ├── Ladder container layer → emptyDir → PV (three lives of data) ├── PV / PVC cluster supply ⇄ namespaced demand · 4-rule binding ├── Access modes RWO = one NODE · RWX needs shared backing ├── Reclaim Available→Bound→Released→{Retain | Delete} ├── StorageClass dynamic recipes · WaitForFirstConsumer · grow-only ├── StatefulSets identity + per-replica claims that outlive scale-down └── CSI drivers as containers — the universal plug ✅ You can now... Trace any byte of cluster data through its three lives and say exactly which disaster erases it Bind claims by hand AND provision dynamically — and explain the four matching rules when a PV C goes P ending Decode RWO/RWX correctly, diagnose Multi-Attach wedges, and pick the right backing per workload Write production S torageClasses: R etain policy, zone-correct binding, grow-only expansion Run a S tatefulSet knowing precisely which disks belong to which replica — and what survives scale-down Read any provisioner: ...csi... line and know the whole

texts: OBSERVABILITY & OPERATIONS Book 07 of the series — knowing what your cluster is doing: Probes (the health question Kubernetes can't answer alone), Metrics Server & Prometheus, the exporter cast, log architecture & Loki, Grafana, PromQL/LogQL, events & audit — and the cluster-wide failure playbook. 喙 Probes liv eness · r eadiness  Metrics ser v er · t op  Prometheus pull model  Exporters node · stat e · cAd  Logs /v ar/log/pods 蝹 Loki labels only  Grafana the p ane  Playbook clust er triage K 8 S K N O W L E D G E B A S E · B O O K 0 7 · C O N T I N U E S B O O K S 0 1 – 0 6 · 2 0 2 6

 Contents — click any row 7 parts · 23 chapters PART I · PROBES — THE HEALTH QUESTION CH 01 Running ≠ Healthy p.3 CH 02 Liveness Probes — Restart the Stuck p.4 CH 03 Readiness — The Traffic Gate p.5 CH 04 Startup Probes & Probe Mechanics p.6 PART II · METRICS CH 05 Metrics Server & kubectl top p.7 CH 06 Prometheus — The Pull Model p.8 CH 07 The Exporter Cast — Who Exposes What p.9 PART III · LOGS CH 08 Where Logs Actually Live p.10 CH 09 Collection Patterns — DaemonSet · Sidecar p.11 CH 10 Loki — Prometheus for Logs p.12 PART IV · SEE IT & QUERY IT CH 11 Grafana — The Unified Pane p.13 CH 12 PromQL & LogQL — First Queries p.14 PART V · OPERATIONS CH 13 Events & Audit Logging p.15 CH 14 The Cluster-Scope Failure Playbook p.16 PART VI · LABS LAB 1 Probes That Bite p.17 LAB 2 Top & Events Triage p.18 LAB 3 Install the Stack (Helm Preview) p.19 LAB 4 Query Everything p.20 PART VII · PROVE IT QUIZ Self-Check Quiz p.21 KEY Answer Key + Scoring p.22 GLOSS Glossary p.23 CHEAT One-Page Cheat Sheet p.24 FINALE Where to Next → Book 08 p.25  Assumes Books 01–06. Book 01's self-healing restarts dead processes — this book's Part I handles the ones that are aliv e but broken . Book 06's HPA alr

CH 01 喙 Running ≠ Healthy  4 MIN · THE HOLE Book 01 · CH 06 taught self-healing: a P od dies → reconciliation replaces it. But look closer at what triggers it — process death . A deadlocked, memory-leaking, or infinitely-hung application never dies. It just keeps Running . Forever. Serving garbage. WITHOUT PROBES — THE LIE OF THE STATUS COLUMN NAME STATUS RESTARTS api-7d9f Running 0 # looks perfect... # reality: deadlocked since Tuesday. # holds connections open, serves timeouts. # self-healing will NEVER touch it — # the process is alive. k8s can't see # "working" — only "not crashed". WITH PROBES — YOU TEACH K8S WHAT "HEALTHY" MEANS NAME STATUS RESTARTS api-x7k2 Running 37 # restarts = the probe # KILLING broken containers. # 37 restarts looks scary — # it's the system working.  The three pillars this book covers (and the fourth)  Metrics how much / how fast  Logs what happened, exactly 喙 Probes is it working NOW  Traces where time w ent — Book 09' s horizon  Probes vs monitoring: probes are reflexes — automated, per-Pod, inside the cluster (restart / gate traffic). Metrics and logs are awareness — stored, queried, human-facing. You need both; reflexes without awareness is

CH 02  Liveness Probes — Restart the Stuck  6 MIN · CORE A liveness probe asks one question on a timer: "ar e y ou w orking?" Fail it enough times and the kubelet kills the container — and the restart policy (Book 01) brings it back fresh. Deadlock → cured by machine, not by 3am pager. spec : containers : - name : api image : myapi:2.0 livenessProbe : httpGet : path : /healthz # YOUR endpoint — cheap, local, self-contained port : 8080 initialDelaySeconds : 10 # let the app boot first periodSeconds : 10 # ask every 10s failureThreshold : 3 # 3 consecutive fails → RESTART  FOUR WAYS TO ASK Mechanism Healthy when... httpGet response 200–399 tcpSocket TCP connect succeeds exec command exits 0 grpc gRPC health check passes ⚙ THE TIMING KNOBS initialDelaySeconds grace before first check periodSeconds ask interval (default 10) timeoutSeconds answer deadline (default 1) failureThreshold consecutive fails → act successThreshold fails needed to heal (liveness: always 1) ⚠ The #1 liveness mistake — checking dependencies: if /healthz verifies "can I reach the database?", then one DB blip makes every Pod's liveness fail → the entire fleet restart-loops simultaneously — you converted a databa

CH 03  Readiness — The Traffic Gate  6 MIN · CORE Liveness answers "keep or kill?" — readiness answers a different question entirely: "send this P od cust omers right now?" A failing readiness probe restarts nothing ; it just removes the P od from the Service's endpoints (Book 03 · CH 11 machinery). livenessProbe : httpGet : { path : /healthz , port : 8080 } readinessProbe : httpGet : { path : /ready , port : 8080 } periodSeconds : 5 failureThreshold : 2 # pull from rotation fast successThreshold : 1 # but return instantly when it recovers WHAT A FAILING READINESS PROBE ACTUALLY DOES 﫛 web-1 Ready ✓ 﫛 web-2 NotReady — gated ▼ Service selector gathers endpoints ▼ $ kubectl get endpoints web NAME ENDPOINTS web 10.244.1.5:8080 # web-2 GONE from the list — # no restarts, no logs, just no traffic 喙 Liveness  Readiness Question are you alive, or kill you? should traffic reach you? On failure container RESTARTED removed from endpoints — nothing else Recovers by fresh process probe passing again — instant re-admission Use for deadlocks, hopeless states warming caches, loading models, overload shedding , DB reconnection  Rolling updates already depended on this: Book 01 · CH 20's "new P

CH 04  Startup Probes & Probe Mechanics  5 MIN Some apps boot slowly — a JVM loading 4GB of heap, a model loading weights. Liveness starts checking at initialDelaySeconds ... and if the app needs 90 seconds, you either set a huge delay (slow restarts forever) or watch it restart-loop dur ing every boot . The startup probe solves the dilemma: it disables the other pr obes until the app is up once. startupProbe : # runs FIRST — liveness/readiness wait httpGet : { path : /healthz , port : 8080 } failureThreshold : 30 # 30 × 10s = up to 5 minutes to boot periodSeconds : 10 livenessProbe : # takes over ONLY after startup succeeds httpGet : { path : /healthz , port : 8080 } periodSeconds : 10 failureThreshold : 3 Boot sequence with all three probes: container starts ──► startupProbe asks every 10s │ one success (or 30 fails → container killed) ▼ readiness + liveness activate from this moment ├── readiness fails → out of endpoints (traffic gate) └── liveness fails → RESTART (and startup runs again first!) Probe Fires On failur e One-line job startup from container start restart (after threshold) guard the boot — protect slow starters from eager liveness readiness after startup passes ou

CH 05  Metrics Server & kubectl top  4 MIN The lightest rung of the metrics ladder: metrics-server — a small in-cluster component that scrapes resource usage from every kubelet and serves it through the Metrics API. It's what makes kubectl top work and what fed Book 06's HP A. $ minikube addons enable metrics-server $ kubectl top nodes NAME CPU(cores) CPU% MEMORY(bytes) MEMORY% minikube 347m 17% 1823Mi 47% $ kubectl top pods -n shop NAME CPU(cores) MEMORY(bytes) web-x7k2 480m 210Mi # vs its REQUEST (Book 02 · CH 14) — 96% of 500m! ⚠ Know its ceiling: metrics-server keeps only the latest ~15 minutes of samples. No history, no graphs, no alerts, no dashboards. It answers "how much is it using righ t now ?" — long-term awareness is Prometheus's job (CH 06). top numbers also lag reality by ~1 minute (scrape + aggregation).  Its two customers: kubectl top (you) and the HPA's Resource metrics (Book 06 · CH 07) — no metrics-server, no autoscaling on cpu/memory 燐 top shows actual usage ; compare against requests to spot right-sizing candidates — that comparison is exactly what VPA automates (Book 06 · CH 08)  One sentence: metrics-server is the short-term pulse — live CPU/memory per no

CH 06  Prometheus — The Pull Model  6 MIN · CORE Prometheus is the de-facto metrics database of the Kubernetes world. Its defining choice: it pulls — it scrapes each target's /metrics HTTP endpoint on an interval, storing every measurement as a time ser ies . # a target's /metrics endpoint is just text — self-describing: $ curl localhost:8080/metrics http_requests_total {method= "POST" ,code= "200" } 1027 http_request_duration_seconds {quantile= "0.99" } 0.14 # metric NAME + LABELS (dimensions) + current VALUE — # scraped over time, each combo becomes a time series  Time Ser ies name + labels + timestamped values — the only data shape. Labels are the dimensions you'll slice by.  PromQL query language built for rates, aggregation, and math over series (CH 12).  Alerting PromQL conditions → Alertmanager → Slack/P agerDuty/email routing.  Why pull wins here: the scraper controls the pace and the target list; apps just expose /metrics and need zero knowledge of where Prometheus lives. Bonus: a dead target doesn't vanish — its up metric becomes 0 , so you can query wh ether the monitoring itself sees the target : up == 0 is the oldest trick in the Prometheus book. IN A CLUSTER — W

CH 07  The Exporter Cast — Who Exposes What  6 MIN · CORE Prometheus only scrapes — someone must expose the numbers. Three built-in exporters cover the whole cluster, each answering a different "is it healthy?" question: Exporter Runs as Exposes Answers  node- exporter DaemonSet (Book 06 · CH 01!) host-level: CPU, memory, disk, network of the machine "is the machine healthy?" ⚙ cAdvisor embedded in the kubelet per-container actual usage: CPU, memory, restarts "which contain er eats resources?"  kube-state- metrics Deployment, watches the API Server object states: replicas desired vs ready, pending pods, PVC capacity "does Kubernetes think all is well?"  The layer trick: the same Pod can be healthy in all three views at once — or exactly one. High node CPU (node-exporter) + low pod CPU (cAdvisor) = something else on the machine. Pod Running + kube_pod_status_phase{phase="Pending"} climbing (kube-state-metrics) = scheduling trouble (Book 04!). Three lenses, one truth.  ServiceMonitor — declarative scrape config apiVersion : monitoring.coreos.com/v1 # a CRD — Book 08 previews CRDs kind : ServiceMonitor metadata : { name : web, labels : { release : mon } } spec : selector : { mat

CH 08  Where Logs Actually Live  6 MIN · CORE Every container's stdout and st derr is captured by the container runtime and written to a plain file on the node . That's the entire native logging story — and its limits define everything else in P art III. $ kubectl logs web-x7k2 # the API reads node files FOR you... $ minikube ssh $ ls /var/log/pods/ default_web-x7k2_ e1a2... /api/0.log # ns_pod_UID/container/N.log # (N = restart count — --previous reads N-1! Book 01 · CH 24) $ ls /var/log/containers/ web-x7k2_default_api- e1a2... .log # symlinks — stable names for collectors Fact Consequence Logs are node-local files kubectl logs must ask the kubelet of that node — Pod gone from node = logs gone Runtime rotates them (containerd: 10Mi × 5 default) chatty apps wrap around; old logs vanish silently Survives container restarts (per-Pod dir), dies with the Pod Book 05's three-lives ladder, log edition Survives nothing else — no cluster-wide store exists node loss / eviction (Book 04 drain!) = history gone — hence collectors (CH 09)  The logging manifesto, 12-factor style: your app writes unbuffered to stdout/stderr — no log files inside the container, no rotation logic. The platform

CH 09  Collection Patterns — DaemonSet · Sidecar  6 MIN · CORE Node files don't walk to your database by themselves. T wo production patterns move them — and you already know the machinery of both. PATTERN 1 · NODE-LEVEL AGENT (DAEMONSET) ★ DEFAULT every node: 﫛 agent (Promtail / Fluent Bit) ├── reads /var/log/pods/** (hostPath mount) ├── attaches metadata: ns, pod, container, node └── ships → Loki / ES / cloud one agent covers EVERY pod on the node — zero per-app config, app stays ignorant PATTERN 2 · SIDECAR STREAMER one pod: 﫛 app ──writes──► emptyDir volume (Book 05 · CH 02!) 﫛 sidecar ──tails file──► ships to backend app CAN'T use stdout? per-app config, filtering, multiple destinations? the sidecar is app-owned plumbing  DaemonSet agent 欄 Sidecar Setup once per cluster every Pod that needs it Resource cost one agent per node (shared) multiplied per Pod Coverage everything on stdout/stderr — automatic only Pods you modified Special needs none possible per-app file-based logs, per-app parsing, routing Verdict start here — 90% of clusters escape hatch for stubborn apps ⚠ Pattern 3 exists and is usually a trap: the app pushes directly to the logging backend (embedded client, a

CH 10 蝹 Loki — Prometheus for Logs  6 MIN · CORE Loki (Grafana Labs) is log aggregation with one radical idea: index the labels, nev er the t ext. Full-text engines (ELK) index every word — powerful, expensive. Loki asks: "wh y index what y ou nev er quer y?"  THE TRADE 10–20× cheaper storage — only metadata is indexed Log lines stored compressed as chunks in cheap object storage Search = filter by labels first , then grep the few surviving lines at query time Trade-off accepted: free-text search across everything is weaker than ELK — in Kubernetes, labels are so good it rarely matters  THE SHARED LABEL MODEL Promtail labels a line with: namespace · pod · container · node — the SAME labels your metrics carry (Book 03 · CH 11's service DNS model) — CPU spike on pod X in Grafana → jump to logs of pod X — zero config Promtail's four-step pipeline (your DaemonSet agent from CH 09, Loki edition) ├── 1️⃣ Discover via k8s Service Discovery — every pod on my node ├── 2️⃣ Tail /var/log/pods files (CH 08!) ├── 3️⃣ Label attach ns/pod/container/node metadata └── 4️⃣ Ship HTTP PUSH batches → Loki's Distributor inside Loki: Distributor → Ingester (chunks) → Store → Querier — a Log Stream = o

CH 11  Grafana — The Unified Pane  4 MIN Grafana stores nothing . It's a stateless query-and-render layer over your data sources — the glass pane in front of Prometheus (metrics) and Loki (logs). Empty datasources = empty dashboard; the data always lives in the backends. THE CLASSIC DEBUG FLOW — ALL SIGNALS, ONE PANE  Metric alert "error rate jumped" ── ►  Prometheus p anel confirm · since when ── ► 蝹 Loki panel same labels → the ex ception line label jump: {namespace="shop", pod="api-x7k2"} — metric query and log query share the selector  Datasour ces — Prometheus, Loki, and dozens more; kube-prometheus-stack wires them in at install (Lab 3)  Dashbo ards — panels of PromQL/LogQL; community dashboards (node full-coverage, k8s cluster views) import by ID in seconds  Dashbo ards as code — export JSON, version in Git next to your manifests — observability joining your declarative world  Alerting UI — Grafana can evaluate alert rules too; deep setups keep alerting in Prometheus/Alertmanager (CH 06) and use Grafana for visualization + triage ⚠ The datasources-conflict trap: kube-prometheus-stack deploys Grafana itself (it's part of the bundle) and auto-configures its Prometheus

CH 12  PromQL & LogQL — First Queries  6 MIN · CORE Both query languages share DNA (that's deliberate — Loki's LogQL is designed to feel like PromQL). Learn the four moves and you can interrogate both signals.  PromQL — four moves # 1 · SELECT — by name + label matchers container_cpu_usage_seconds_total{namespace= "shop" } # 2 · RATE — counters need a rate over a window rate (http_requests_total[ 5m ]) # 3 · AGGREGATE — sum/avg by label dimension sum by (pod) ( rate (container_cpu_usage_seconds_total {namespace= "shop" , container!= "" } [ 5m ])) # 4 · CONDITION — the alert-shaped question sum by (pod) ( rate (http_requests_total{code=~ "5.." }[ 5m ])) / sum by (pod) ( rate (http_requests_total[ 5m ])) > 0.05 蝹 LogQL — same shape, logs # selector (LABELS ONLY — CH 10) then line filters then parse: {namespace= "shop" , pod=~ "web-.*" } |= "ERROR" # line contains != "health" # exclude noise # metrics FROM logs — count matches per minute: sum by (pod) ( rate ({namespace= "shop" } |= "Timeout" [ 5m ])) # and the correlation close (CH 11): # panel 1: rate(http_requests_total{pod=~"web-.*"}[5m]) # panel 2: {pod=~"web-.*"} |= "ERROR" ← same pod regex!  Counter law: counters only go up

CH 13  Events & Audit Logging  5 MIN Two different diaries. Events : what the controllers did to your objects (you've read them in every describe since Book 01). Audit log : what humans and clients did to the API — the who-did-what record.  EVENTS — THE CONTROLLER CHRONICLE $ kubectl get events --sort-by= .lastTimestamp LAST SEEN TYPE REASON OBJECT 12s Warning BackOff pod/web-x7k2 4m Normal Scheduled pod/web-x7k2 # Normal = information · Warning = attention # TTL ~1 hour — they EXPIRE. not an archive. # per-namespace scope (Book 01 scoping!) Every debugging chapter used them — now you know their lifecycle: generated by controllers/kubelet, aggregated per object, ephemeral . For incident forensics, ship them (EventExporter → Loki) or lose them. 着 AUDIT LOG — THE API DASHCAM # apiserver feature — OFF by default. # you supply a policy (stages): who : user / serviceaccount (Book 02!) what : verb + resource delete secrets... when : timestamp + source IP result : allowed / denied (RBAC verdicts) # policy levels: None → Metadata → # Request → RequestResponse (noisy!) The record that answers "who deleted the production namespace?" — RBA C says who may ; audit says who did . Compliance s

CH 14  The Cluster-Scope Failure Playbook  6 MIN · FINALE Books 01–06 debugged one P od . Real incidents are cluster-shaped: whole namespaces P ending, every DNS lookup dying, a node evacuating itself. The playbook — first move for each signature (every row is a callback): Signatur e Probable cause First mov e Everything in one ns → Pending ResourceQuota exhausted (B02) or no node fits (B04 funnel) kubectl describe quota -n ns · read a Pod's events All pods ImagePullBackOff, one ns imagePullSecrets missing/wrong (B02 · CH 06) kubectl get sa default -o yaml → check secret One node NotReady, pods evacuating kubelet/heartbeat lost → NoExecute taints (B04 · CH 05) kubectl describe node N → conditions + taints ALL DNS failing cluster-wide CoreDNS pods down (B03 · CH 11–12) kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-dns Ingress: everything 404/timeout controller Pod down, or rulebook orphaned (B03 · CH 04) kubectl get pods -n ingress-nginx · get ingress → ADDRESS? Random OOMKills across teams node memory pressure → eviction by QoS (B02 · CH 15) kubectl top nodes · check node memory-pressure taint API slow/5xx for everyone etcd struggling / quorum at risk (B01 · CH 08) check static

LAB 1  Probes That Bite  15 MIN · HANDS-ON STEP 1 · A pod whose health is a file — liveness $ kubectl apply -f - <<EOF apiVersion : v1 kind : Pod metadata : { name : probe-lab } spec : containers : - name : c image : busybox:1.36 command : [ sh , -c , 'touch /tmp/healthy; sleep 9999' ] livenessProbe : exec : { command : [ cat , /tmp/healthy ] } periodSeconds : 5 failureThreshold : 2 EOF $ kubectl get pod probe-lab # Running, READY 1/1, 0 restarts STEP 2 · Break it — the kubelet fights back $ kubectl exec probe-lab -- rm /tmp/healthy $ kubectl get pod probe-lab -w probe-lab Running 0 probe-lab Running 1 # 2 fails → KILLED & restarted (fresh file! CH 02) $ kubectl describe pod probe-lab | grep -A2 Events | tail -2 Container c failed liveness probe, will be restarted  READINESS — THE GATE $ kubectl patch pod probe-lab \ --type =merge -p '{"metadata":{"labels":{"app":"g"}}} $ kubectl expose pod probe-lab \ --port=80 --name=gate $ kubectl get endpoints gate gate 10.244.0.5:80 # remove the health file again → # readiness (same probe) fails → $ kubectl get endpoints gate gate <none> # GATED — pod still # Running, zero restarts! # (readiness ≠ liveness, CH 03)  READ THE RESTART STORY $

LAB 2  Top & Events Triage  10 MIN · HANDS-ON STEP 1 · The pulse — metrics-server $ minikube addons enable metrics-server $ kubectl top nodes # give it ~60s after enabling NAME CPU(cores) CPU% MEMORY(bytes) MEMORY% minikube 350m 17% 1800Mi 46% $ kubectl top pods -A --sort-by=memory | head -5 # the whole cluster, ranked by appetite — # your right-sizing shortlist (Book 06 · CH 08) STEP 2 · Cause a failure, then read the chronicle $ kubectl create deploy ghost --image=nginx: 1.999 $ kubectl get events --sort-by= .lastTimestamp | grep -i ghost Warning Failed Failed to pull image "nginx:1.999" Warning BackOff Back-off pulling image # the incident wrote its own report — # BEFORE you ran a single describe (CH 13) STEP 3 · The scope-first reflex (CH 14) $ kubectl get nodes # 1 · fleet healthy? $ kubectl get pods -A | grep -v Running # 2 · blast radius? $ kubectl get events -A --sort-by=.lastTimestamp | head -8 # 3 · chronicle # three commands, scope identified, playbook row selected — # the CH 14 reflex, now muscle memory Proved: live usage via top, self-writing incident chronicles via events, and the universal triage reflex. Teardown: kubectl delete deploy ghost . ↑ back to top  Book

LAB 3  Install the Stack (Helm Preview)  15 MIN · HANDS-ON  Honesty first: the stack ships as Helm charts — Book 08's subject. Today you run four commands as a preview ; Book 08 explains what every flag did. Needs ~3GB free in minikube: minikube start -- memory=6144 if tight. STEP 1 · Metrics + logs + pane — four commands $ curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/helm/helm/main/scripts/get-helm-3 | bash $ helm repo add prometheus-community https://prometheus-community.github.io/helm-charts $ helm repo add grafana https://grafana.github.io/helm-charts && helm repo update $ helm install mon prometheus-community/kube-prometheus-stack $ helm install loki grafana/loki-stack \ --set promtail.enabled= true # ← the CH 09 DaemonSet agent! $
