The full taints & tolerations system, node/pod affinity, topology spread, priority & preemption, and the maintenance discipline: cordon, drain, static P ods.  Scheduler filter → scor e → bind  Taints all 3 effects  Tolerations the k eys 鱗 Affinity node & pod ⚖ Spread zones & sk ew  Priority + pr eemption  Drain maint enance 直 Static P ods kubelet -born K 8 S K N O W L E D G E B A S E · B O O K 0 4 · C O N T I N U E S B O O K S 0 1 – 0 3 · 2 0 2 6

 Contents — click any row 7 parts · 20 chapters PART I · THE SCHEDULER'S MIND CH 01 How Scheduling Works p.3 CH 02 The Scheduling Toolbox p.4 PART II · TAINTS & TOLERATIONS — FULL SYSTEM CH 03 Taints — Effects & Use Cases p.5 CH 04 Tolerations — Operators & tolerationSeconds p.6 CH 05 Well-Known Taints — The Cluster's Own p.7 PART III · AFFINITY & SPREAD CH 06 nodeSelector & Node Affinity p.8 CH 07 Pod Affinity & Anti-Affinity p.9 CH 08 topologySpreadConstraints p.10 PART IV · PRIORITY & EVICTION CH 09 Priority Classes & Preemption p.11 PART V · NODE OPERATIONS CH 10 Cordon, Drain & Uncordon p.12 CH 11 Static Pods p.13 PART VI · LABS LAB 1 Node Affinity — Required vs Preferred p.14 LAB 2 Anti-Affinity — Prove the Separation p.15 LAB 3 Priority & Preemption Live p.16 LAB 4 The Maintenance Cycle p.17 PART VII · PROVE IT QUIZ Self-Check Quiz p.18 KEY Answer Key + Scoring p.19 GLOSS Glossary p.20 CHEAT One-Page Cheat Sheet p.21 FINALE Where to Next → Book 05 p.22  Assumes Books 01–03. Book 01 · CH 07 + Lab 5 gave you taints' first taste; CH 23 showed Pending = "the Scheduler said no". This book opens the black box: every reason the Scheduler says yes or no, and every knob you own . 

CH 01  How Scheduling Works  6 MIN · CORE The Scheduler is a control loop (Book 01 · CH 02) with one job: for each unscheduled Pod, pick the best feasible Node and bind the Pod to it. Every decision is a three-stage funnel: THE FUNNEL — EVERY POD, EVERY TIME  Pod appear s schedulerName: default ── ► 1 · FILTER ── ► 2 · SCORE ── ► 3 · BIND filter kills nodes that can't take the P od · score ranks nodes that can · the highest score wins 1 · FILTER — HARD CONSTRAINTS Pod's requests fit the node's allocatable (Book 02 · CH 14) Taints tolerated? (P art II of this book) nodeSelect or / required affinity match? Ports, volumes, hostNetwork conflicts Zero nodes sur vive → Pod stays P ending. This is the #1 cause. 2 · SCORE — SOFT PREFERENCES Preferred affinity/anti-affinity weights Spreading vs packing balance (CH 08) Image locality (image already pulled?), pod spread across zones... Every plugin votes 0–100; sum decides. Ties → random. # the binding is a real API object — you can see the decision: $ kubectl get pod web -o jsonpath= '{.spec.nodeName}' minikube ⚠ Scheduling is one-time, not a lease: once bound, the Scheduler never reconsiders. If the node degrades, the kubelet and node-li

CH 02 藺 The Scheduling Toolbox  5 MIN Five mechanisms decide placement. Knowing which st age each one acts in tells you which to reach for: Tool Stage Hard or soft? One-line job Resources (requests) Filter + Score hard (capacity) "this Pod needs 500Mi / 250m somewhere" Taints + Tolerations Filter hard (node repels) "keep ordinary Pods OFF this node" Node affinity / nodeSelector Filter / Score both (required / preferred) "this Pod WANTS certain nodes" Pod (anti-)affinity Filter / Score both "co-locate / separate from other Pods" topologySpread Score (+ filter) soft or hard "spread evenly across zones/nodes"  taints node pushes away ⇄ 鱗 affinity pod pulls t oward ⇄ ⚖ spread distribution discipline  Direction matters — the classic confusion: taints are node-side repulsion (the node refuses visitors without keys). Affinity is pod-side attraction (the Pod states its preferences). They never do each other's job — taints can't attract, affinity can't evict.  Dedicat e nodes GPU / memory-huge → taints + tolerations  Pin to hardware SSD, region, zone → node affinity  Resilience lay out HA across zones → spread + anti-affinity  Decision shortcut: keeping things OFF nodes → taints. Get

CH 03  Taints — Effects & Use Cases  6 MIN · CORE A taint is a node-side r epulsion field : key=value:effect . Book 01's Lab 5 proved the mechanics — this page is the full strategic picture. $ kubectl taint node node1 gpu=nvidia : NoSchedule node/node1 tainted $ kubectl taint node node1 gpu=nvidia :NoSchedule- # trailing dash = remove Effect Running Pods New Pods Use case NoSchedule stay blocked unless tolerated dedicate nodes (GPU, SSD, prod-only) PreferNoSchedule stay avoided if alternatives exist soft segregation — "try not to" NoExecute EVICTED now blocked unless tolerated remove workloads when a node degrades  The three strategic uses 1 · Dedication dedicated=ml:NoSchedule — only ML team's P ods (which tolerate) may land. A reservation without reserving capacity. 2 · Special har dware gpu=nvidia:NoSchedule — prevents accidental placement of Pods that can't use the GPU... and of Pods that would waste it. 3 · Node condition → eviction The control plane itself taints sick nodes with NoExecute — workloads flee a dying node automatically (CH 05). ⚠ Two traps: (1) taints don't attract — a tolerated Pod may land elsewhere; to pin it, combine taints with node affinity (CH 06). (2)

CH 04  Tolerations — Operators & tolerationSeconds  6 MIN · CORE A toleration is a Pod-side per mission : "I may land on (or survive on) nodes carrying this taint." Match rule: key + operat or (+ v alue) + effect . spec : tolerations : - key : gpu operator : Equal # default — value must match exactly value : nvidia effect : NoSchedule - key : "dedicated" operator : Exists # ANY value, as long as key exists effect : NoSchedule - key : "" operator : Exists effect : "" # tolerate EVERYTHING (use with fear) Operator Matches Value field Equal default key exists and value is identical required Exists key exists, any value (wildcard) must be empty ⏱ tolerationSeconds — the grace timer (NoExecute only) tolerations : - key : node.kubernetes.io/not-ready operator : Exists effect : NoExecute tolerationSeconds : 300 # if the taint lasts > 5 min → THEN evict me  The resilience dial: a transient blip (< 5 min) → your Pod rides it out. A real outage → eviction after the grace period. This is exactly how the default tolerations on Deployments behave — it's why brief node hiccups don't mass-evict your fleet.  No tolerationSeconds + NoExecute tolerated = survive forever on the tainted node 里 Eff

CH 05  Well-Known Taints — The Cluster's Own  6 MIN · CORE The node-lifecycle controller and kubelet taint nodes aut omatically as conditions change. These aren't your taints — they're the cluster's immune response, and recognizing them is a diagnostic superpower. Taint Effect Meaning node.kubernetes.io/not-ready NoSchedule/NoExecute node's Ready condition = False (kubelet heartbeat lost) node.kubernetes.io/unreachable NoExecute/NoSchedule node unreachable (network partition) — later becomes not-ready node.kubernetes.io/disk-pressure NoSchedule disk running out — no NEW pods (existing keep running) node.kubernetes.io/memory-pressure NoSchedule memory scarcity on the node node.kubernetes.io/network- unavailable NoSchedule networking not configured yet (some clouds) node.kubernetes.io/unschedulable NoSchedule added by kubectl cordon — CH 10 node-role.kubernetes.io/control- plane NoSchedule the brain-protection taint (Book 01 · CH 07) Node degrades → NotReady / Unreachable NoExecute taint applied │ ├─ pods without toleration → evicted (grace per tolerationSeconds) ├─ deployments recreate them on healthy nodes ← Book 01 · CH 06 loop └─ node recovers → taint removed → schedulable agai

CH 06 鱗 nodeSelector & Node Affinity  6 MIN · CORE Pod-side attraction to specific nodes. nodeSelector is the simple ancestor; node affinity adds operators, weights, and soft preferences. spec : nodeSelector : # the simple form: hard, exact-match only disk: ssd affinity : nodeAffinity : requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution : # HARD (filter) nodeSelectorTerms : - matchExpressions : - { key : disk, operator : In , values : [ ssd , nvme ] } preferredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution : # SOFT (score) - weight : 80 # 1–100 — a vote, not a veto preference : matchExpressions : - { key : zone, operator : In , values : [ east ] } Operators Meaning In · NotIn value is / is not in the list Exists · DoesNotExist key present / absent (any value) Gt · Lt numeric greater/less than (node labels as numbers) ⚠ Decode the long names — they're the whole contract: required... = filter (no match → Pending). preferred... = score (hint). IgnoredDuringExecution = if the node's labels change after your Pod is running, the Pod stays — affinity is checked at scheduling time only. (The mirror concept RequiredDuringExecution exists for pod affinity — live re-evaluation.) label node: kubectl labe

CH 07  Pod Affinity & Anti-Affinity  6 MIN · CORE Node affinity asks "which nodes ?" — pod affinity asks "near which other P ods ?", measured through a topology domain (same node? same zone? same region?). spec : affinity : podAffinity : # CO-LOCATE — "keep me near my cache" requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution : - topologyKey : kubernetes.io/hostname # same NODE labelSelector : matchLabels : { app : cache } podAntiAffinity : # SEPARATE — "never put replicas together" preferredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution : - weight : 100 podAffinityTerm : topologyKey : topology.kubernetes.io/zone # different ZONES labelSelector : matchLabels : { app : web } topologyKey (common) Domain = "together means..." kubernetes.io/hostname same physical node topology.kubernetes.io/zone same availability zone topology.kubernetes.io/region same region ✅ AFFINITY (CO-LOCATE) web + its cache on one node → localhost-fast calls, one bill. Latency-sensitiv e pairs that talk constantly. ✅ ANTI-AFFINITY (SEPARATE) 3 replicas o f web on 3 zones → one zone dies, 2/3 survive. Never stack the blast radius. ⚠ required anti-affinity is a placement cliff: more replicas than topology domains → the extra

CH 08 ⚖ topologySpreadConstraints  6 MIN · CORE Anti-affinity answers "are any P ods here?" — spread answers a better question: "is the distr ibution ev en ?" One constraint replaces a pile of weights. spec : topologySpreadConstraints : - maxSkew : 1 # max allowed imbalance topologyKey : topology.kubernetes.io/zone whenUnsatisfiable : DoNotSchedule # or: ScheduleAnyway (soft) labelSelector : matchLabels : { app : web } # — maxSkew = (most pods in one domain) − (fewest) # — domains with ZERO pods count too (they pull new pods!) MAXSKEW: 1 IN ACTION — 6 REPLICAS, 3 ZONES zone-a zone-b zone-c 2−2−2 → skew 0 ✅ · 3−2−1 → skew 2 ❌ next P od forced to zone-c · 3−3−0 → skew 3, but 0-domain "pulls" until fed whenUnsatisfiable Behavior when the rule can't hold DoNotSchedule hard — Pod waits (Pending) until it can comply ScheduleAnyway soft — place anyway, but the score penalty steers future Pods  Spread vs anti-affinity — when which? Anti-affinity: boolean togetherness, per-Pod-pair relationships, cheap on small sets. Spread: numeric evenness across N domains, scales to hundreds of replicas, and — the killer feature — counts empty domains , so a fresh zone always receives traffic first. 

CH 09  Priority Classes & Preemption  6 MIN · CORE When nothing fits anywhere, a high-priority P od may evict low er-priority Pods to make room. Priority is the cluster's pecking order under scarcity. apiVersion : scheduling.k8s.io/v1 kind : PriorityClass metadata : { name : high-priority } value : 1000000 # higher = more important globalDefault : false # one class MAY be the default preemptionPolicy : PreemptLowerPriority # default; or Never spec : priorityClassName : high-priority # attach to the Pod Built-in class Value Reserved for system-node-critical 2,000,001,000 kubelet-essential: CNI, kube-proxy system-cluster-critical 2,000,000,000 CoreDNS, metrics — cluster functions your Pods (no class) 0 everything below the system floor  How preemption actually fires High-prio Pod → Pending (no node fits — filter fails on resources) │ scheduler tries placement ▼ Preemption attempt : find node where evicting lower-prio victims would free enough for the whole Pod (incl. its requests!) ▼ victims deleted gracefully (their owners recreate them — elsewhere, later) ▼ high-prio Pod scheduled into the gap ✅ ⚠ Two honesty notes: (1) preemption is resource-arithmetic, not revenge — the schedu

CH 10  Cordon, Drain & Uncordon  6 MIN · CORE Node maintenance (kernel upgrades, hardware swaps) without downtime = a three-verb dance. Cordon stops new arrivals; drain evacuates; uncordon reopens. $ kubectl cordon node1 # 1 · add unschedulable taint (CH 05) node/node1 cordoned $ kubectl drain node1 --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data node/node1 cordoned # drain cordons for you too evicting pod shop/web-7d9f # graceful eviction — PDB-aware! pod/web-7d9f evicted $ # ...do the maintenance... $ kubectl uncordon node1 # 3 · reopen node/node1 uncordoned Flag Why it exists --ignore-daemonsets DaemonSet Pods are node-bound by design (log agents, CNI) — drain skips them; without the flag drain aborts --delete-emptydir- data Pods with emptyDir lose data on eviction — drain refuses by default; the flag says "ephemeral, go ahead" --force evict Pods not managed by a controller (standalone Pods die with no replacement — you were warned, Book 01 · CH 15) --grace-period / -- timeout tune eviction grace; PDBs can block indefinitely → drain waits/times out ⚠ Drain respects PodDisruptionBudgets (PDBs) — "keep ≥ 2 web replicas alive" pauses drain until it can evict safely. Production rule: d

CH 11 直 Static Pods  5 MIN Static Pods are created and managed directly by the kubelet , from manifest files on the node's disk — no Deployment, no Scheduler, no controller. The Scheduler's total bypass. kubelet flags: --pod-manifest-path=/etc/kubernetes/manifests │ watches the dir (default on kubeadm) ▼ file appears → kubelet runs the Pod no API call needed file edited → Pod updated file IS the spec file deleted → Pod dies kubectl delete → Pod briefly dies → kubelet recreates it (undeletable!) $ kubectl get pods -n kube-system NAME READY STATUS etcd-minikube 1/1 Running # ← static! kube-apiserver-minikube 1/1 Running # ← static! kube-controller-manager-minikube 1/1 Running # ← static! kube-scheduler-minikube 1/1 Running # ← static! coredns-7db6d8ff4b-abcde 1/1 Running # ← Deployment  The bootstrap paradox, solved: the Control Plane runs as static Pods because something must run the API Server before the API Server exists . The kubelet + a folder of YAML boot the entire brain — chicken, meet egg. (The -minikube / -nodename suffix: kubelet also creates a read-only mirror Pod in the API so you can kubectl get them.) 離 Your own static P od: drop a valid P od manifest into the manife

LAB 1  Node Affinity — Required vs Preferred  12 MIN · HANDS-ON STEP 1 · Label the node + hard affinity $ kubectl label node minikube disk=ssd $ kubectl create deploy aff --image=nginx --replicas=2 $ kubectl patch deploy aff --type =merge -p '{"spec":{"template":{"spec":{ "affinity":{"nodeAffinity":{"requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution": {"nodeSelectorTerms":[{"matchExpressions":[{"key":"disk","operator":"In", "values":["ssd"]}]}]}}}}}}}' $ kubectl get pods -o wide # all on minikube ✓ (label matches) STEP 2 · Break the label — watch required bite $ kubectl label node minikube disk- $ kubectl scale deploy aff --replicas= 3 $ kubectl get pods aff-xxx 1/1 Running # old pods: IgnoredDuringExecution — STAY aff-yyy 0/1 Pending # new pod: no node matches → filter fails $ kubectl describe pod -l app=aff | grep -A2 Events | tail -2 0/1 nodes are available: 1 node(s) didn't match ... affinity STEP 3 · Switch to preferred — same break, different outcome $ kubectl delete deploy aff && kubectl create deploy soft --image=nginx --replicas=2 $ kubectl patch deploy soft --type =merge -p '{"spec":{"template":{"spec":{ "affinity":{"nodeAffinity":{"preferredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringEx

LAB 2  Anti-Affinity — Prove the Separation  10 MIN · HANDS-ON STEP 1 · Required anti-affinity on a ONE-node cluster $ kubectl create deploy sep --image=nginx --replicas=3 $ kubectl patch deploy sep --type =merge -p '{"spec":{"template":{"spec":{ "affinity":{"podAntiAffinity":{"requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution": [{"topologyKey":"kubernetes.io/hostname", "labelSelector":{"matchLabels":{"app":"sep"}}}]}}}}}}' $ kubectl get pods sep-aaa 1/1 Running # fits — node is empty of "sep" sep-bbb 0/1 Pending # node already has one! sep-ccc 0/1 Pending # same hostname domain — no second one exists  WHY (events) $ kubectl describe pod sep-bbb | tail -2 0/1 nodes are available: 1 node(s) didn't match pod anti-affinity rules.  THE LESSON # required anti-affinity: # replicas > topology # domains = permanent # Pending. 3 replicas # × 1 node = 2 orphans. STEP 2 · Soften it — everyone fits $ kubectl patch deploy sep --type =merge -p '{"spec":{"template":{"spec":{ "affinity":{"podAntiAffinity":{"preferredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution": [{"weight":100,"podAffinityTerm":{"topologyKey":"kubernetes.io/hostname", "labelSelector":{"matchLabels":{"app":"sep"}}}}]}}}}}}' $ kubectl ge

LAB 3  Priority & Preemption Live  12 MIN · HANDS-ON  Setup note: preemption needs resource pressure . We fill the node with low-priority Pods holding real memory requests, then ask for a big high-priority Pod. Adjust sizes to your cluster's free memory. STEP 1 · Two classes + a filled floor $ kubectl create priorityclass low --value =100 $ kubectl create priorityclass high --value =1000 $ kubectl create deploy filler --image=polinux/stress --replicas=6 \ -- stress --vm 1 --vm-bytes 10M --timeout 6000s $ kubectl set resources deploy/filler --requests =memory= 500Mi $ kubectl patch deploy filler --type =merge -p \ '{"spec":{"template":{"spec":{"priorityClassName":"low"}}}}' $ kubectl get pods -l app=filler # 6 Running — floor is loaded STEP 2 · The VIP arrives — preemption fires $ kubectl run vip --image=polinux/stress --restart=Never \ --overrides= '{"spec":{"priorityClassName":"high","containers":[{"name":"s", "image":"polinux/stress","args":["--vm","1","--vm-bytes","50M"], "resources":{"requests":{"memory":"1500Mi"}}}]}}' -- stress --vm 1 --vm-bytes 50M $ kubectl get pods -w filler-xxx Terminating # ← a low-prio VICTIM was chosen vip Running # ← took its place STEP 3 · Read th

LAB 4  The Maintenance Cycle  12 MIN · HANDS-ON STEP 1 · Cordon — close the door $ kubectl cordon minikube $ kubectl get nodes NAME STATUS ROLES minikube Ready,SchedulingDisabled control-plane,master $ kubectl describe node minikube | grep Taints node.kubernetes.io/unschedulable:NoSchedule # ← the cordon taint (CH 05!) $ kubectl scale deploy web --replicas=3 # (any deployment) $ kubectl get pods -w # 3rd pod → Pending: nowhere to land STEP 2 · Drain — empty the room $ kubectl drain minikube --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data node/minikube cordoned evicting pod kube-system/coredns-... evicting pod default/web-aaa pod/web-aaa evicted $ kubectl get pods -A | grep -v Running # (single-node cluster: evicted pods go Pending — they have # nowhere else to go. on a 3-node cluster they'd REAPPEAR # on the healthy nodes — Book 01 · CH 06 in action.) STEP 3 · Uncordon — reopen $ kubectl uncordon minikube $ kubectl get nodes # Ready — SchedulingDisabled gone $ kubectl get pods -w # Pending pods schedule immediately  Proved: cordon = a NoSchedule taint you typed; drain = graceful, PDB-respecting evacuation; uncordon = instant refill. Teardown: scale your deployment back and delete lef

QUIZ ✅ Self-Check Quiz ☑ 10 questions Q1. The Scheduler processes a Pod in which order? A. Score → Filter → Bind B. Filter → Score → Bind C. Bind → Filter → Score D. Filter → Bind → Score Q2. Which taint effect evicts already-running Pods that don't tolerate it? A. NoSchedule B. PreferNoSchedule C. NoExecute D. None — taints never evict Q3. tolerationSeconds applies to which effect? A. NoExecute B. NoSchedule C. PreferNoSchedule D. All three equally Q4. A Pod with required node affinity for disk=ssd is running. The node's label is removed. The Pod... A. is evicted immediately B. reschedules to another node C. crashes D. keeps running — IgnoredDuringExecution Q5. required pod anti-affinity on kubernetes.io/hostname , 3 replicas, a 1-node cluster: A. all 3 co-located B. 1 Running, 2 Pending C. the Deployment is rejected D. round-robin placement Q6. maxSkew in a topologySpreadConstraint defines... A. minimum Pods per domain B. number of allowed domains C. max difference between the most- and least-loaded domains D. the eviction threshold Q7. A high-priority Pod is Pending for lack of memory. The Scheduler... A. may evict lower-priority Pods (minimum victims) to make room B. waits unti

KEY  Answer Key + Scoring grade yourself Q Ans Why — one line 1 B Filter (feasible) → Score (rank) → Bind — CH 01 2 C NoExecute evicts existing non-tolerating Pods now — CH 03 3 A The grace timer only makes sense for eviction — NoExecute — CH 04 4 D Affinity is scheduling-time only; label changes never evict — CH 06 5 B 1 hostname domain < 3 replicas → extras Pending forever — CH 07, Lab 2 6 C skew = max(domain count) − min(domain count), capped at maxSkew — CH 08 7 A Preemption = scheduler-driven, minimum-victim eviction — CH 09, Lab 3 8 D DaemonSet pods belong to their node; drain skips, flag acknowledges — CH 10 9 B kubelet + manifest dir = source of truth; API deletion is overridden — CH 11 10 C Cordon adds unschedulable taint — blocks placement, never evicts — CH 10, Lab 4  9–10 Ready for Book 05  6–8 Re-read missed chapters'  boxes  <6 Re-run Labs 1–4, then retake  Missed Q4 or Q10? They're the same fact wearing two hats: scheduling-time constraints never touch running Pods — only NoExecute taints and controller reconciliation do. Missed Q5? The topology-domain count is a hard ceiling for required anti-affinity. ↑ back to top  Book 04 · Scheduling & Node Management ◀ p

GLOSS  Glossary  REFERENCE Filter / Score / Bind — the Scheduler's funnel: feasible → ranked → written to the Pod's nodeName. Taint — node-side repulsion, key=value:effect ; effects NoSchedule / PreferNoSchedule / NoExecute. Toleration — Pod-side permission past a taint; operators Equal (exact) and Exists (wildcard, empty value). tolerationSeconds — grace period before a NoExecute eviction takes effect. Well-known taints — not-ready, unreachable, disk-pressure, memory-pressure, network-unavailable, unschedulable, control-plane — the cluster's automatic immune taints. nodeSelector — simple hard label match on nodes. Node affinity — required (filter) / preferred (score, weight 1–100) node matching with In/NotIn/Exists/DoesNotExist/Gt/Lt. IgnoredDuringExecution — affinity evaluated at scheduling time only; later label changes never evict. Pod (anti-)affinity — co-location / separation rules relative to other Pods, scoped by topologyKey. topologyKey — the domain label defining "together": kubernetes.io/hostname, topology.kubernetes.io/zone|region. topologySpreadConstraints — keep distribution even: maxSkew + topologyKey + whenUnsatisfiable (DoNotSchedule / ScheduleAnyway); empty doma

CHEAT  One-Page Cheat Sheet  print me  TAINTS & TOLERATIONS $ kubectl taint node N gpu=nvidia:NoSchedule $ kubectl taint node N gpu=nvidia:NoExecute $ kubectl taint node N gpu=nvidia:NoSchedule- # remove tolerations : - {key: gpu, operator: Equal, value: nvidia, effect: NoSchedule} - {key: gpu, operator: Exists, effect: NoExecute, tolerationSeconds: 300} effects: block-new / prefer-avoid / evict-now 鱗 AFFINITY & SPREAD node: required.../preferred...DuringScheduling IgnoredDuringExecution ops: In NotIn Exists DoesNotExist Gt Lt pod: podAffinity / podAntiAffinity + topology (hostname | zone | region) topologySpreadConstraints : - {maxSkew: 1, topologyKey: zone, whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule, labelSelector: {matchLabels: {app: web}}}  PRIORITY $ kubectl create priorityclass hi --value=1000 spec : {priorityClassName: hi} system-node-critical 2000001000 system-cluster-critical 2000000000 default pods: 0 · preemption = min victims also drives kubelet eviction order (with QoS)  MAINTENANCE $ kubectl cordon N $ kubectl drain N --ignore-daemonsets \ --delete-emptydir-data [--force] [--timeout=...] # evicts gracefully, respects PDBs # DaemonSet pods skipped $ kubectl uncordon N stati

FINALE  What You Can Do Now  Book 04 complete Book 01 built the machine, 02 dressed it, 03 connected it — Book 04 taught you where everything is allow ed to live, and how t o mov e it safely .  SCHEDULING — fully mapped: ├── Funnel filter (can) → score (should) → bind (done) ├── Taints NoSchedule · PreferNoSchedule · NoExecute ├── Tolerations Equal/Exists · tolerationSeconds ├── Affinity node + pod, required vs preferred, topologyKey ├── Spread maxSkew across zones — empty domains attract ├── Priority pecking order + preemption under scarcity └── Node ops cordon → drain (PDB-aware) → uncordon · static pods ✅ You can now... Explain any P ending P od: read the event, name the failing stage, name the knob that fixes it Dedicate nodes with taints + tolerations and pin workloads with affinity — without confusing the two directions Design replica layouts for HA (spread/anti-affinity) and know exactly when required becomes a P ending trap Set a priority hierarchy and predict who preempts whom under memory scarcity Run the full maintenance dance on a production node and describe what each flag protects Explain how the control plane boots itself with static P ods — and why you can't kube

format.title: Cluster Lifecycle & Production Readiness — Kubernetes Book 09

texts: CLUSTER LIFECYCLE & PRODUCTION READINESS Book 09 — the finale. Building and maintaining the cluster itself: kubeadm bootstrap, etcd backup & restore (where every object you've ever applied actually lives), the upgrade choreography, GKE · EKS · AKS compared, multi-cluster thinking, and the exam map that turns nine books into three certifications. ⚙ kubeadm bootstrap  etcd the book o f recor d  Snapshot backup + r estore  Upgrade the chor eography ☁ GKE·EKS·AKS the big thr ee  Multi-clust er fleet thinking  Exam map CKA·CKAD·CKS ✅ Readiness the checklist K 8 S K N O W L E D G E B A S E · B O O K 0 9 · T H E F I N A L E · 2 0 2 6

 Contents — click any row 6 parts · 18 chapters PART I · BIRTH & MEMORY CH 01 How a Cluster Is Born — kubeadm p.3 CH 02 etcd — The Book of Record p.4 CH 03 Backup & Restore — The Sacred Drill p.5 PART II · GROWING OLD GRACEFULLY CH 04 Cluster Upgrades — The Choreography p.6 PART III · THE MANAGED QUESTION CH 05 Managed vs Self-Hosted p.7 CH 06 GKE · EKS · AKS — The Big Three p.8 CH 07 Multi-Cluster & Fleet Thinking p.9 PART IV · THE FINISH LINE CH 08 The Exam Map — CKA · CKAD · CKS p.10 CH 09 The Production Readiness Checklist p.11 PART V · LABS LAB 1 etcd Snapshot & Restore Drill p.12 LAB 2 The Upgrade Rehearsal p.13 PART VI · PROVE IT QUIZ Self-Check Quiz p.14 KEY Answer Key + Scoring p.15 GLOSS Glossary p.16 CHEAT One-Page Cheat Sheet p.17 FINALE The Series Complete p.18  Assumes Books 01–08. Book 08's finale promised this book would visit "where Helm's release receipts and every object ever applied actually live" — that's etcd , and CH 02–03 hand you its backup drill (the single most-tested CKA skill). Book 04's drain and Book 01's quorum both return as upgrade prerequisites.  Book 09 · Cluster Lifecycle ◀ cover · start ▶ Page 2

CH 01 ⚙ How a Cluster Is Born — kubeadm  6 MIN · CORE Eight books assumed a cluster existed. Now: who builds it? A cluster is just machines r unning sev en binar ies (Book 01's cast) with a shared CA and a wired network. kubeadm is the official tool that does this plumbing — not a product, just a disciplined bootstrap. $ kubeadm init \ --control-plane-endpoint = "k8s-api.example.com:6443" \ --pod-network-cidr = 10.244.0.0/16 # output: root CA · certs · static-pod manifests · the join command $ kubectl apply -f calico.yaml # kubeadm does NOT install a CNI — you do $ kubeadm join k8s-api.example.com:6443 --token ... --discovery-token-ca-cert-hash ... # run on each worker → kubelet starts → node registers → Ready What kubeadm init actually does ├── generates PKI: CA, certs for apiserver/etcd/scheduler... ├── writes static-pod manifests → /etc/kubernetes/manifests │ (Book 04 · CH 11: kubelet boots the control plane!) ├── starts etcd + CP components as static pods ├── writes kubeconfig → /etc/kubernetes/admin.conf └── prints the join command (token + CA hash = trust on first use)  The bootstrap paradox, revisited: kubeadm doesn't "run" the control plane — it drops manifest files on di

CH 02  etcd — The Book of Record  6 MIN · CORE Book 01 called etcd "the memory." Sharper: it's the single sour ce of truth — every Deployment spec, every Secret, every Helm release receipt (Book 08 · CH 01!), every ServiceMonitor ever applied. Back it up or y ou don 't have a cluster — you hav e a clust er-shaped amnesia waiting t o happen.  etcd gone, no b ackup every object lost; nodes keep running P ods that nobody can change; rebuild = re-declare everything from Git (if you have it...) ⚠ etcd slow every API call waits — the whole cluster feels it (Book 07's "API slow" playbook row) ✅ etcd healthy + b acked up quorum serving (Book 01 · CH 08) · snapshots on a schedule · tested restores  etcd holds Secr ets in plaint ext by default (Book 02 · CH 07) — encryption-at-rest + locked-down PKI are etcd hygiene, not options ⚖ Quorum math r ules here too: 3 members tolerate 1 failure; a 2-member et cd is the w orst number (Book 01's table, life-or-death edition)  State separation (Book 05, finale-lev el): etcd = cluster state (specs, wishes). PV s = app data. Back up BOTH — an etcd restore with empty PV s is a database cluster full of empty databases # talking to etcd directly — mTL

CH 03  Backup & Restore — The Sacred Drill  6 MIN · CKA-CRITICAL Two commands. Guaranteed exam points. Career-saving muscle memory. T ake the shot: # BACKUP — one snapshot file, consistent point-in-time: $ ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl \ --endpoints =https://127.0.0.1:2379 \ --cacert =/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \ --cert =/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \ --key =/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key \ snapshot save /backup/etcd-snapshot-$(date +%F).db Snapshot saved at /backup/etcd-snapshot-2026-01-15.db # VERIFY — never trust an unverified backup: $ ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl --write-table =json \ snapshot status /backup/etcd-snapshot-2026-01-15.db HASH TOTAL KEYS TOTAL SIZE 4a2c... 1842 6.2 MB ⚠ Restore is not "put the file back": snapshot restore builds a new etcd data directory (new cluster identity, written to a fresh --data-dir ). The dance: stop the API Server → stop etcd → restore to a new data-dir → point etcd at it → restart everything . On a kubeadm cluster that means moving the static-pod manifests out, restoring, and moving them back — the API Server must be down during restore , because it would keep writing to the old, broken reality. The restore choreography (single-CP)

CH 04  Cluster Upgrades — The Choreography  6 MIN · CORE Kubernetes ships three releases a year; running a stale cluster means unsupported APIs and a painful jump eventually. The upgrade is a fixed dance — learn it once, perform it forever. Rule Why One minor at a time (1.28 → 1.29, never → 1.30) skew guarantees only hold between adjacent versions API Server first, kubelets after skew policy: kubelet may lag the API Server (up to 3 minors) — never lead it Control plane before workers new kubelets must speak to a new-or-equal API Server Read the "Upgrade notes" deprecated APIs get removed — your Book 08 CRDs and Helm charts may need version bumps before the cluster jumps $ kubeadm upgrade plan Components that must be upgraded: etcd · kubelet ×3 You can now apply: v1.29.x $ kubectl get nodes -o wide # watch versions march node-by-node: # CP 1.29 while workers still 1.28 — HEALTHY SKEW (expected!)  Workloads ride through untouched: the upgrade moves the plat form . Your Pods keep running — drain just asks them to walk across the street (Book 04). Only two things interrupt workloads: API removals (fix manifests first) and drain windows (spread workers, one at a time). ⚠ On managed c

CH 05 欄 Managed vs Self-Hosted  5 MIN The industry's default answer to CH 04's workload: buy the contr ol plane . But "managed" is a spectrum — knowing exactly which r esponsibilities tr ansfer is the interview-grade question. Responsibility Self-hosted (kubeadm) Managed (GKE/EKS/AKS) etcd — backup, quorum, encryption you (CH 02–03) vendor — invisible, SLA-backed API Server / CP upgrade you (CH 04's dance) vendor performs CP; you upgrade node pools CP availability (multi-master, LB) you (Book 01 · CH 08's 3-node math) vendor — regionally replicated Cert rotation, security patching (CP) you vendor Nodes, kubelets, node pools you you — still your drain/upgrade cycle CNI, CSI, admission policy, workloads YOU — Books 01–08, unchanged  The one-line division: managed = "we run the brain " (CP + etcd). The body is still yours — nodes, networking policy, RBAC, workloads, observability. Everything from Books 01–08 except CH 02–03's etcd drills transfers over; and even there, you own the data-residency and RBAC-around-etcd questions in regulated environments. ✅ GO MANAGED WHEN... your team is small; Kubernetes isn't your product; you want SL A-backed CP + integrated cloud IAM/storage (CH 0

CH 06 ☁ GKE · EKS · AKS — The Big Three  OVERVIEW Same Kubernetes, different clouds — the differences that actually bite live in three places: networking model, IAM integration, node pools .  GKE (Google)  EKS (A WS)  AKS (Azur e) Default networking VPC-native — Pod IPs are real VPC alias-IPs AWS VPC CNI — Pod IPs drawn from the subnet (ENI limits!) Azure CNI or kubenet — same IP-from-VPC tradeoff IAM integration Google IAM + Workload Identity IRSA (IAM Roles for Service Accounts) Entra ID + Workload Identity Standout Autopilot (Pod-level billing, no nodes to manage) largest ecosystem; ALB controller pairs with Book 03's Ingress smoothest Entra/AD enterprise fit  Why the IAM piece matters to YOU: it's Book 02's ServiceAccount story, cloud edition. A Pod that needs S3 access shouldn't hold static keys in a Secret (Book 02 · CH 07's risk) — it should assume a cloud role via its ServiceAccount (IRSA/Workload Identity). Workload identity = the SA token exchanged for short-lived cloud credentials. Same principle: ide ntity for workloads , scoped tigh t .  Networking consequence: VPC-native models mean Pod IPs ar e routable cloud resources — beautiful (no overlay) but subnet- sized

CH 07  Multi-Cluster & Fleet Thinking  OVERVIEW A single cluster is a blast radius . Bad deploys, bad upgrades (CH 04), regional outages — one control plane means one shared fate. Multi-cluster splits it. Honest framing: true "federation" (one API over many clusters) never won; today's practice is independent clust ers + shar ed tooling .  Blast radius prod-canary cluster takes the upgrade first (CH 04); a bad release never touches everything at once  Regions & r esidency latency (route to nearest), data laws (EU data stays EU — a hard wall, not a preference)  Environments the Book 08 overlay story, per- cluster instead of per-namespace Challenge Today's answer (concept lev el) Deploy to many GitOps fleet: ArgoCD ApplicationSets / Flux multi-cluster — one Git commit, N clusters reconcile (Book 08's pull model, fleet edition) One DNS across clusters global load balancing / multi-cluster Ingress (cloud LB + health checks steering between cluster edges — Book 03's LB at fleet level) Trust between clusters shared/mirrored CA or service-mesh identity — cross-cluster Service calls are an advanced, opt-in pattern , not default Consistency Git as the single spec (Book 08) + Book 09's

CH 08  The Exam Map — CKA · CKAD · CKS  SERIES CAPSTONE Nine books map cleanly onto the three CNCF certifications. This page is your study r oute converter : each cert's domain list, the books that own it, and the lab skills to drill. Cert Focus Series map Drill these labs CKAD developer build & run workloads B01 (Pods→Deployments) · B02 (config/secrets/probes...) · B05 (PVCs) · B06 (Jobs/HPA) B01 L1–4 · B02 L1–4 · B05 L1 · B06 L2–3 CKA admin operate clusters B01 (architecture, quorum) · B04 (taints/drain) · B05 (PV lifecycle) · B03 (networking/CNI) · B09 (kubeadm, etcd, upgrades) · B07 triage B09 L1–2 · B04 L4 · B05 L1–2 · B03 L3 CKS security (CKA prerequisite) harden at runtime B02 (RBAC, SecurityContext, PSS, Secret hygiene) · B03 (NetworkPolicy) · B07 (audit) · B08 (policy webhooks) + runtime security (falco, seccomp — beyond this series) B02 L2–3 · B03 L3 · re-read B02 CH 12–13  All three are hands-on, terminal-based, ~2h exams — no multiple choice. The skills this series drilled as runnable commands are literally the exam tasks: etcdctl snapshot save , kubectl auth can-i --as , NetworkPolicy YAML, drain/uncordon, kubectl taint . Speed comes from the Lab muscle memory, not

CH 09 ✅ The Production Readiness Checklist  THE SERIES IN ONE PAGE Nine books, compressed into the questions an SRE asks before saying "yes, ship it." Every line cites its owning book — this is the whole series as a gate.  CLUSTER & ETCD (B01 · B09) ☑ 3+ CP nodes — quorum math sane (B01·CH08) ☑ etcd snapshots scheduled AND restored once (B09·CH03) ☑ Secrets encrypted at rest (B02·CH07) ☑ Upgrade path rehearsed; versions ≤ 1 minor behind (B09·CH04) 着 IDENTITY & ACCESS (B02) ☑ No wildcard RBA C; least-privilege SAs per workload ☑ default SA cannot do anything (B02·CH11) ☑ PSS enforce on prod namespaces (B02·CH13) ☑ No raw Secrets in Git; external-secrets/SOPS  TRAFFIC & ISOLATION (B03) ☑ Ingress + TLS at the edge; no raw NodeP ort prod ☑ default-deny NetworkP olicy + named allows; DNS allowed first ☑ CNI actually enforces policies (verified, not assumed)  WORKLOADS & DATA (B04–06) ☑ Probes on everything (B07·CH02–04) ☑ requests/limits set → QoS deliberate (B02·CH14–15) ☑ Stateful data on PV Cs, Retain policy; PV backup story (B05) ☑ PDBs before the first real drain (B04·CH10)  OBSERVABILITY (B07) ☑ Metrics + logs central; dashboards exist ☑ Alerts route to humans who sleep in sh

LAB 1  etcd Snapshot & Restore Drill  15 MIN · HANDS-ON STEP 1 · Reach etcd inside minikube (docker driver) $ minikube ssh $ docker exec -it etcd-minikube sh # you're inside the etcd static-pod's container — # its certs are mounted at /etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ STEP 2 · Take + verify the snapshot $ ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl \ --endpoints =https://127.0.0.1:2379 \ --cacert =/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \ --cert =/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \ --key =/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key \ snapshot save /backup/snap1.db Snapshot saved at /backup/snap1.db $ ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl --cacert=... --cert=... --key=... \ snapshot status /backup/snap1.db --write-table TOTAL KEYS TOTAL SIZE ~1800 ~6 MB # keys = every object you've ever applied!  PROVE IT'S REAL ST ATE # exit container; from host kubectl: $ kubectl create ns snapshot-proof $ kubectl get ns | grep proof snapshot-proof Active # this ns exists NO W but not in # the snapshot taken a moment ago — # a restore would erase it. that's # "point-in-time," felt firsthand ⚠ RESTORE — THE HONEST P ART # full restore on minikube = rebuild # (single- node CP, static pods). # the DRILL to know cold: 1 · mv manifests out (CP dies) 2 · etcd

LAB 2  The Upgrade Rehearsal  10 MIN · HANDS-ON  Honest scope: minikube won't perform a real kubeadm upgrade — but the surrounding choreography (inventory, skew reading, drain discipline, pre-flight snapshot) is 80% of the real dance and fully drillable here. STEP 1 · Version inventory — the skew table $ kubectl get nodes -o wide NAME STATUS VERSION OS-IMAGE minikube Ready v1.2x.x Ubuntu... $ kubectl version --short 2>/dev/null || kubectl version # read it like CH 04: is any kubelet NEWER than # the API server? (that's the forbidden direction) STEP 2 · Pre-flight snapshot (the step-0 of every upgrade) $ # LAB 1's snapshot command, rerun — labeled for the upgrade: # /backup/pre-upgrade-$(date +%F).db # rule: no snapshot, no upgrade. ever. STEP 3 · The node-march, rehearsed $ kubectl cordon minikube && kubectl get nodes STATUS Ready,SchedulingDisabled # step 2 of the dance (B04·CH10) $ kubectl uncordon minikube $ kubectl get pods -A --no-headers | wc -l # your workload census — after a REAL upgrade you'd # re-run this and the Book 07 triage reflex to verify # everything survived the march Proved: skew reading, snapshot-before-change discipline, and the cordon→uncordon march. The r

QUIZ ✅ Self-Check Quiz ☑ 10 questions Q1. kubeadm init starts the control plane by... A. running apiserver as a systemd service B. writing static-pod manifests the already-running kubelet picks up C. installing Docker images manually D. calling the cloud API Q2. What does an etcd snapshot contain? A. All PV data B. Cluster state — every object's spec & metadata C. Container images D. Only RBAC rules Q3. Before snapshot restore , you must... A. delete all namespaces B. upgrade kubeadm first C. stop the API Server (and etcd), then restore to a new data-dir D. nothing — restore is hot Q4. Upgrading a cluster 1.28 → 1.30 in one step is... A. recommended B. fine for managed clusters C. forbidden — one minor version at a time D. required for kubeadm Q5. Valid version skew during an upgrade? A. kubelet newer than API Server B. kubelet older than API Server (never newer) C. kubelet equal always D. skew doesn't matter Q6. On a managed cluster (EKS), who upgrades the node pools' kubelets? A. the vendor, automatically always B. nobody — not needed C. you — via managed node-group upgrades (drain discipline still yours) D. the CNI Q7. EKS/AKS/GKE's "workload identity" is the cloud edition of...

KEY  Answer Key + Scoring grade yourself Q Ans Why — one line 1 B The bootstrap paradox: kubelet + manifest files conjure the CP — CH 01 2 B Specs & metadata only; PV bytes need their own backup — CH 02/03 3 C Restore = quiesce, restore to NEW data-dir, boot — CH 03, Lab 1 4 C Skew guarantees hold only between adjacent minors — CH 04 5 B kubelet may lag, never lead, the API Server — CH 04 6 C Vendor does CP; node pools stay your drain-cycle duty — CH 05/06 7 B SA → cloud role, short-lived creds — Book 02's identity model, cloud edition — CH 06 8 B Federation never won; fleets + steering won — CH 07 9 B mTLS by design + v3 API — the anonymous-client trap — CH 02, Lab 1 10 B CKA = operate: etcd, upgrades, network, triage — CH 08's map  9–10 Series mastered — exam-ready  6–8 Re-read missed chapters'  boxes  <6 Re-run Labs 1–2, then retake  Missed Q3? The restore choreography is the CKA etcd task — order matters more than flags. Missed Q6? "Managed" moving-but-not-deleting the choreography is the conceptual hinge of Part III. ↑ back to top  Book 09 · Cluster Lifecycle ◀ prev · ▤ TOC · next ▶ Page 15

GLOSS  Glossary  REFERENCE kubeadm — official bootstrap tool: generates PKI, writes static-pod manifests, prints join tokens. Join token / CA hash — trust-on-first-use credentials letting a worker's kubelet register securely. etcd — the cluster's key-value source of truth; quorum-based (odd members); holds every object incl. Helm receipts. etcdctl — etcd client; v3 API required for snapshots; mTLS flags mandatory. snapshot save / status / restore — consistent backup → verify → rebuild data-dir (new identity, API Server down during). Version skew — supported mixing during upgrades; kubelet ≤ API Server, adjacent minors only. kubeadm upgrade apply / node — CP-side / worker-side upgrade commands; one minor per hop. Managed Kubernetes — vendor runs CP + etcd (GKE/EKS/AKS); you own nodes, CNI/CSI choices, workloads. Node pool — a group of like nodes (per taints/labels/size) managed as a unit — the drain/upgrade unit in clouds. Workload Identity / IRSA — ServiceAccount-assumed cloud roles; short-lived creds instead of static keys. VPC-native / VPC CNI / Azure CNI — Pod IPs drawn from the cloud network (no overlay) — routable but subnet-bound. Multi-cluster — many independent clusters;

CHEAT  One-Page Cheat Sheet  print me  ETCD — THE SACRED COMMANDS ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl \ --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 \ --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \ --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \ --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key \ snapshot save /backup/snap.db $ ... snapshot status snap.db --write-table restore: stop APISERVER → snapshot restore --data-dir=/var/lib/etcd-new → repoint etcd → boot. multi-CP: same snapshot on ALL members.  UPGRADE CHOREOGRAPHY 0 · SNAPSHOT (no snapshot, no upgrade) 1 · CP: kubeadm upgrade plan kubeadm upgrade apply v1.X upgrade kubelet+kubectl, restart 2 · drain CP → uncordon 3 · per worker (one at a time): drain → kubeadm upgrade node → kubelet → uncordon → verify ONE MINOR per hop · kubelet never newer than apiserver · read API-removal notes BEFORE jumping ☁ THE BIG THREE Network Workload ID GKE VPC-native Workload Identity EKS AWS VPC CNI IRSA AKS Azure CNI/kubenet Entra + WI managed = vendor runs CP+etcd; YOU run node pools, CNI policy, workloads — Books 01–08 skills transfer 100%  EXAM MAP CKAD: B01·02·05·06 (build) CKA: + B03·04·07·09 (operate — etcd/upgrades/network/triage) CKS: B02·03·08-webhooks + runtime secu

FINALE  The Series Complete  9 OF 9 ☸ THE NINE-BOOK ARC — one machine, taught layer by layer: ├── 01 Architecture brain + muscle · reconcile loop · namespaces ├── 02 Config & Access configmaps · secrets · RBAC · QoS ├── 03 Networking services · ingress+TLS · policies · DNS ├── 04 Scheduling taints · affinity · priority · drain ├── 05 Storage PV/PVC · classes · stateful data · CSI ├── 06 Workloads daemonsets · jobs · canaries · autoscaling ├── 07 Observability probes · prometheus · loki · triage ├── 08 Delivery helm · kustomize · CRDs · operators · gitops └── 09 Lifecycle kubeadm · etcd · upgrades · clouds · exams You started with "what is a cluster?" — a brain and muscle. Y ou end able to build the brain, back it up, upgrade it, place workloads on the muscle, connect them, observe them, and let Git keep the whole story true. That is the complet e operat or's arc. 吝 Where to go from here  Certify: CH 08's map — sit CKAD, then CKA; add runtime security reading for CKS  Practice: rebuild a multi-node cluster with kubeadm (3 VMs) — CH 01's ceremony, felt for real; then break it and restore from Lab 1's snapshot  Ship: run one real project the full Book-08 way — Helm or Kustomize +

You've been using this book's contents all series without knowing: Book 07 · Lab 3 installed two charts, ServiceMonitor/VPA/HTTPRoute were CRDs (Books 07/06/03), ResourceQuota and PSS were admission controllers (Books 01/02), and cert-manager was an operator. Now the theory catches up.  Book 08 · P ackaging, GitOps & Extending K8s ◀ cover · start ▶ Page 2

CH 01  Helm — The Package Manager  6 MIN · CORE Book 07 · Lab 3: you typed four Helm commands and got Prometheus, Alertmanager, Grafana, Loki and Promtail — dozens o f objects — from four lines. Time to decode the machinery. $ helm repo add prometheus-community https://prometheus-community.github.io/helm-charts # ↑ the APP STORE ↑ where the store lives $ helm install mon prometheus-community/kube-prometheus-stack # ↑ RELEASE name ↑ CHART from that repo # one command → dozens of objects. how?  Chart — the pack age : a folder of templated Y AML + default values. The recipe card.  Repository — the store : a URL serving charts. The cookbook shelf (apt/brew/homebrew vibes).  Release — an inst alled inst anc e with a NAME and its own config. A cake you baked — receipt kept. ⚠ The problem Helm solves: raw YAML can't be parameterized. "Deploy Postgres, but with my password, our storage class, 3 replicas" without Helm = copy-paste-edit 500 lines and pray. With Helm: the chart holds templates, you supply values , the engine renders your personalized YAML. Same recipe, your kitchen.  Release names matter: Book 07's mon release named everything mon- grafana , mon-kube- state- metrics — o

CH 02  Charts, Values & Templating  6 MIN · CORE mychart/ ├── Chart.yaml # metadata: name, version, appVersion ├── values.yaml # DEFAULTS — the chart author's opinions ├── templates/ │ ├── deployment.yaml # Go-templated YAML │ ├── service.yaml │ └── _helpers.tpl # reusable snippets (naming conventions...) └── charts/ # sub-charts (dependencies) # templates/deployment.yaml — the templating you'll actually read: metadata : name : {{ .Release.Name }}-web # ← release name injected spec : replicas : {{ .Values.replicaCount }} template : spec : containers : - image : "{{ .Values.image.repository }}:{{ .Values.image.tag }}" # .Values = merged values tree · .Release = install metadata  Values precedence — LAST WINS Source Wins ov er Example chart's values.yaml — (the floor) replicaCount: 1 your file -f myvals.yaml chart defaults replicaCount: 3 --set replicaCount=5 everything (the ceiling) CI one-liners $ helm install web ./mychart -f prod-values.yaml --set image.tag= v2.1 $ helm template ./mychart -f prod-values.yaml # render WITHOUT installing — review the YAML! $ helm install web ./mychart --dry-run --debug # same idea, plus install mechanics  Why helm template is a superpower: the

CH 03  Releases — Lifecycle & Rollback  6 MIN · CORE A release isn't a one-shot install — it's a tracked lifecy cle with numbered revisions. If this feels familiar, it should: it's Book 01 · CH 21's rollout story, reborn at package level. $ helm upgrade web bitnami/nginx --set replicaCount= 3 $ helm history web REVISION STATUS DESCRIPTION 1 superseded Install complete 2 deployed Upgrade complete $ helm rollback web 1 $ helm history web 2 superseded Upgrade complete 3 deployed Rollback to 1 # ← NEW revision — history moves forward only! Command Job Callback helm upgrade --install N chart create-or-update — idempotent ; the CI/CD workhorse declarative wish, Book 01 style helm rollback N REV re-render an old revision as a new one Book 01 · CH 21: undo ≠ rewind helm uninstall N delete the release's objects namespaced cascade — Book 01 · Lab 3 helm get values N / helm list audit config / inventory releases —  The pro flags: --atomic — if an upgrade fails its health checks, auto-rollback (the Deployment-safety net from Book 01 · CH 20, applied to the whole package). --wait — block until all objects are ready. helm upgrade --install --atomic --wait is the CI one-liner worth memorizing.

CH 04  Kustomize — Overlays Without Templates  6 MIN · CORE Kustomize answers the same need as Helm — "same app, different environments" — with the opposit e philosophy : no templating language. Y our base Y AML stays valid, applyable, plain ; variants are declared as patches and transfor mers on top. base/ # the honest, deployable baseline ├── deployment.yaml # real YAML — no {{ }} anywhere ├── service.yaml └── kustomization.yaml # resources: [deployment.yaml, service.yaml] overlays/prod/kustomization.yaml resources : [ ../../base ] # inherit the baseline namespace : prod # TRANSFORMER: rewrite all namespaces namePrefix : prod- # TRANSFORMER: prefix every name images : - { name : nginx, newTag : "1.26" } # transformer: swap the tag replicas : - { name : web, count : 5 } # transformer: scale $ kubectl kustomize overlays/prod # PREVIEW — render the final YAML, change nothing $ kubectl apply -k overlays/prod # apply the overlay — BUILT INTO kubectl $ kubectl get deploy -n prod NAME READY IMAGE prod-web 5/5 nginx:1.26 # prefix ✓ ns ✓ tag ✓ replicas ✓  Helm  Kustomize Mechanism template + values → new YAML patch + transform valid base YAML Shines at distributing software to strange

CH 05 溺 CRDs — Teaching the API New Kinds  6 MIN · CORE You've spent seven books using kinds that don't exist in cor e Kuber netes : ServiceMonitor (Book 07), VP A (Book 06), Gateway & HT TPRoute (Book 03). Someone taught the API those kinds — with a Custom R esource Definition. apiVersion : apiextensions.k8s.io/v1 kind : CustomResourceDefinition metadata : name : crontabs.stable.example.com # plural.group — THE API path spec : group : stable.example.com versions : - name : v1 served : true schema : # OpenAPI validation — BUILT INTO the API openAPIV3Schema : type : object properties : spec : type : object required : [ cronSpec , image ] # the API enforces this! properties : cronSpec : { type : string } image : { type : string } scope : Namespaced # or Cluster (Book 01 · CH 11 scopes!) names : { plural : crontabs, singular : crontab, kind : CronTab } $ kubectl apply -f crontab-crd.yaml $ kubectl get crontabs # ← the API now SPEAKS your kind. RBAC protects it, # etcd stores it, kubectl explain crontab.spec works — # first-class citizen, indistinguishable from built-ins. ⚠ The crucial boundary: a CRD is schema-validated storage — nothing more . Your CronTab gets validated, versioned,

CH 06 烙 Operators — Runbooks as Code  6 MIN · CORE The series' spine returns one more time. Book 01's reconciliation loop — wat ch actual, c omp are desir ed, act — ran on built-in kinds. An Operat or is that same loop, running on your CRD, with your software's domain knowledge encoded inside. The Operator pattern 溺 CRD e.g. kind: PostgresCluster (CH 05) │ human writes the WISH: replicas: 3, version: "16", backup: daily ▼ 烙 Operator = custom controller (a Deployment) watching the CR │ reconciliation loop — with postgres expertise hardcoded: ▼ ⚙ ACTS via the k8s API: creates StatefulSet (Book 05!), headless Service (per-Pod DNS!), PVCs (volumeClaimTemplates!), configures replication, runs backups as CronJobs (Book 06!) ▼  reports status back onto the CR — Ready ✅ WHAT AN OPERATOR AUTOMATES Everything a skilled DBA does at 3am by hand : bootstrap a cluster, add replicas, promote on failover, take consistent backups, rolling-upgrade postgres 15→16 with the right switchover order. The runbook, written in Go, executed forever.  OPERATORS YOU'VE ALREADY MET prometheus-operator taught the API ServiceMonitor (B07) cert-manager B03 · CH 06: "the cert just appears" — an operator for Certi

CH 07  Admission Webhooks — The Last Gate  6 MIN · CORE Every request this series has made — kubectl apply , controllers, operators — crosses the API Server's bouncer line: AuthN → AuthZ (Book 02) → Admission → per sist (etcd) . Admission is the final, programmable checkpoint — and you've been living under it all along. ✅ BUILT-IN ADMISSION YOU'VE MET ResourceQuota B01 · CH 06 — "checked at the door, not on the floor" — admission! PodSecurity B02 · CH 13 — PSS enforce/warn/audit IS an admission controller LimitRange defaults injected per-pod NamespaceLifecycle rejects objects into terminating namespaces (B01 · Lab 3)  EXTENSIBLE: CALL YOUR CODE MutatingWebhookConfiguration → API Server calls your HTTPS service; webhook RETURNS A PATCHED object. (inject sidecars, defaults, labels) ValidatingWebhookConfiguration → webhook says allow / deny+reason. ("no :latest tags" → 403 with your policy message) The webhook flow kubectl apply pod.yaml → AuthN (who?) → AuthZ (may you?) → MUTATE sidecar injected, resources defaulted → VALIDATE sees the MUTATED object — order matters! → etcd  policy engines (Kyverno, OPA Gatekeeper) = prebuilt validating/mutating layers driven by policy CRDs (CH 0

CH 08  GitOps — The Pull Model  6 MIN · CORE The classic delivery flow: CI runs kubectl apply or helm upgrade . Two quiet problems: your pipeline holds cluster credentials (Book 02's threat model, aimed at your own automation), and drift is invisible — someone hand-edits a Deployment, and Git says one thing while the cluster does another. Forever. ❌ PUSH (CI APPLIES) CI ──kubectl──► cluster creds live in CI · hand-edits = silent drift · nothing reconciles · "who changed prod?" ✅ PULL (GITOPS) Git ◄──pull── in-cluster AGENT ──apply──► cluster no creds flow OUT · agent reads Git (pull), watches cluster, reconciles the diff · hand-edits get REVERTED (or alerted)  The four GitOps principles (OpenGitOps): ① the entire system is declarative (this whole series trained you for it) · ② desired state is versioned in Git , immutable history · ③ changes are pulled by an approved agent — nothing pushes in · ④ the agent continuously reconciles , not just at deploy time. The spine, r evealed: Book 01 taught wat ch actual → c omp are desir ed → act for Pods. Book 06 aimed it at replica counts. Book 08 aims it at your entir e cluster's configuration : Git is the spec, the cluster is the reality,

CH 09  ArgoCD & Flux — Concept Level  OVERVIEW Two CNCF-graduated implementations of the pull model, same reconciliation core, different personalities:  ArgoCD 襁 Flux Personality UI-first — watch diffs, click sync, app-of-apps dashboards toolkit of lean controllers, no required UI Extension model Application CRD (yes — an operator whose CRD describes "keep ns X matching Git path Y"!) GitOps Toolkit CRDs (Kustomization, HelmRelease, Source) Know it for visual drift triage, multi-cluster apps, sync waves/hooks modularity, OCI artifact sources, bootstrap-from-nothing Both reconcile Git→cluster, detect drift, support Helm charts and Kustomize overlays natively (CH 03 + CH 04 compose!) # the ArgoCD Application — a CR describing one GitOps deployment: apiVersion : argoproj.io/v1alpha1 kind : Application spec : source : { repoURL : https://github.com/acme/fleet , path : apps/web/overlays/prod } destination : { server : https://kubernetes.default.svc , namespace : prod } syncPolicy : automated : { prune : true , selfHeal : true } ⚠ The two powerful switches, handled with respect: selfHeal — manual kubectl edit is reverted automatically (drift becomes impossible; so does your emergency h

LAB 1  Helm Lifecycle — Upgrade & Rollback  15 MIN · HANDS-ON STEP 1 · Install — and name the release $ helm repo add bitnami https://charts.bitnami.com/bitnami && helm repo update $ helm install web bitnami/nginx --set replicaCount= 2 $ helm list NAME REVISION STATUS CHART APP VERSION web 1 deployed nginx-x.y.z 1.25.x $ kubectl get deploy # → web-nginx — RELEASE NAME prefixes everything (CH 01) STEP 2 · Upgrade — history only moves forward $ helm upgrade web bitnami/nginx --set replicaCount= 3 $ helm history web REVISION STATUS DESCRIPTION 1 superseded Install complete 2 deployed Upgrade complete $ helm rollback web 1 && helm history web 3 deployed Rollback to 1 # NEW revision — Book 01 · CH 21's law $ kubectl get deploy web-nginx # replicas back to 2 ✓  AUDIT THE RECEIPTS $ helm get values web USER-SUPPLIED VALUES: replicaCount: 2 # your overrides only; # add -a for the FULL tree (CH 02) $ kubectl get secrets | \ grep sh.helm.release sh.helm.release.v1.web.v 1 ... # the receipts live in Secrets — # Book 02's safe, holding Helm's # paperwork (CH 01!)  SEE WHAT ONE COMMAND MADE $ kubectl get all \ -l app.kubernetes.io/instance=web # deployment · service · (pods...) — # one char

LAB 2  Kustomize Overlays  12 MIN · HANDS-ON STEP 1 · An honest base $ mkdir -p base overlays/prod && cd base $ kubectl create deploy web --image=nginx:1.25 --replicas=1 \ --dry-run=client -o yaml > deployment.yaml $ cat > kustomization.yaml <<EOF resources : [deployment.yaml] EOF $ kubectl kustomize . # renders EXACTLY the base — no templating, just valid YAML STEP 2 · The prod overlay — four transformers $ cd ../overlays/prod $ cat > kustomization.yaml <<EOF resources : [ ../../base ] namespace : prod namePrefix : prod- images : - { name : nginx, newTag : "1.26" } replicas : - { name : web, count : 3 } EOF $ kubectl kustomize . | grep -E 'name:|image:|replicas|namespace' namespace: prod # transformed name: prod-web # prefixed image: nginx: 1.26 # retagged replicas: 3 # scaled STEP 3 · Apply the overlay $ kubectl create ns prod $ kubectl apply -k overlays/prod $ kubectl get deploy -n prod NAME READY IMAGE prod-web 3/3 nginx:1.26 # every transformer, live Proved: base stays valid Y AML; the overlay is pure declaration; kubectl -k needs no extra binary. Teardown: kubectl delete ns prod (cascade — Book 01!). ↑ back to top  Book 08 · P ackaging, GitOps & Extending K8s ◀ prev · ▤ TO

LAB 3  Build Your Own API Kind  12 MIN · HANDS-ON STEP 1 · Teach the API CronTab (CH 05's CRD, condensed) $ kubectl apply -f - <<EOF apiVersion : apiextensions.k8s.io/v1 kind : CustomResourceDefinition metadata : { name : crontabs.stable.example.com } spec : group : stable.example.com versions : - name : v1 served : true schema : openAPIV3Schema : type : object properties : spec : type : object required : [ cronSpec , image ] properties : cronSpec : { type : string } image : { type : string } scope : Namespaced names : { plural : crontabs, kind : CronTab } EOF  THE API SPEAKS YOUR KIND $ kubectl apply -f - <<EOF apiVersion : stable.example.com/v1 kind : CronTab metadata : { name : my-cron } spec : cronSpec : "*/5 * * * *" image : my-cron-img:1.0 EOF $ kubectl get crontabs NAME AGE my-cron 5s # first-class! $ kubectl explain crontab.spec # schema docs — generated # from YOUR openAPIV3Schema  THE API ENFORCES *YOUR* SCHEMA $ kubectl apply -f - <<EOF apiVersion : stable.example.com/v1 kind : CronTab metadata : { name : bad } spec : { image : x:1 } EOF The CronTab "bad" is invalid: spec.cronSpec: Required value # rejected at the door — # YOUR required field, enforced # by the API S

QUIZ ✅ Self-Check Quiz ☑ 10 questions Q1. helm install mon chart-x creates... A. a chart B. a repository C. a named release with tracked revisions D. a namespace called mon Q2. After helm rollback web 1 from revision 3, helm history shows... A. history trimmed to one entry B. a NEW revision 4, "Rollback to 1" — forward-only history C. revision 1 re-marked deployed, 2–3 deleted D. an error — rollback is Deployment-only Q3. Values precedence, last-wins: A. --set < -f file < chart defaults B. chart defaults < --set < -f file C. they merge randomly D. chart defaults < -f file < --set Q4. Kustomize differs from Helm fundamentally because it... A. patches and transforms valid base YAML — no templating language B. requires a separate binary C. stores releases in Secrets D. only works with charts Q5. A CRD by itself provides... A. a running controller B. schema-validated, RBAC-protected storage — with no behavior C. automatic backups D. a new namespace Q6. The ServiceMonitor kind (Book 07) exists because... A. it's built into core k8s B. kubectl installed it C. the prometheus-operator taught the API via a CRD D. Grafana created it dynamically Q7. Order at the API Server's admission line: A

KEY  Answer Key + Scoring grade yourself Q Ans Why — one line 1 C Install = named release instance, revisions tracked in Secrets — CH 01 2 B Rollback re-renders as a new revision; history never rewinds — CH 03, Lab 1 3 D Defaults lose, file beats them, --set beats everything — CH 02 4 A No templates: transformers/patches over valid YAML, built into kubectl — CH 04 5 B CRD = storage + validation only; Lab 3's CronTab sat there — CH 05 6 C Every non-core kind you've used came from someone's CRD — CH 05/06 7 A Mutation first, so policy validates what will actually persist — CH 07 8 C "Checked at the door" — Quota (B01) and PSS (B02) ARE admission — CH 07 9 B Pull direction kills credential exfil + drift — CH 08 10 D selfHeal = reconcile live state back to Git; hotfixes must go through Git — CH 09  9–10 Ready for Book 09  6–8 Re-read missed chapters'  boxes  <6 Re-run Labs 1–3, then retake  Missed Q5 or Q6? The CRD/Operator split is THE extension-model question — data vs behavior. Missed Q8? Realizing Quota and PSS were admission all along is this book's biggest "oh" — the built-in world already ran the pattern you're now extending. ↑ back to top  Book 08 · P ackaging, GitOps &

GLOSS  Glossary  REFERENCE Chart — Helm package: templated templates/ + default values.yaml + Chart.yaml metadata. Repository — URL serving charts; helm repo add subscribes you to the store. Release — a named installed instance of a chart; every object labeled and tracked together. Revision — numbered snapshot of a release state; upgrades and rollbacks append (forward-only). values precedence — chart defaults < -f file < --set ; last wins. helm template / --dry-run — render before install; review the exact YAML that will hit the cluster. --atomic / --wait — auto-rollback on failed upgrade / block until ready; the CI-safe install flags. Kustomize — template-free customization: base (valid YAML) + overlays of patches/transformers; kubectl -k . Transformers — namespace, namePrefix, images, replicas — declarative rewrites applied at render time. CRD — CustomResourceDefinition: teaches the API a new kind (group/version/kind, schema, scope); cluster-scoped itself. Custom Resource (CR) — an instance of a CRD; inert data without a controller. Operator — CRD + custom controller: domain-expert reconciliation loop that manages the software's full lifecycle. Operator capability levels — inst

CHEAT  One-Page Cheat Sheet  print me  HELM — COMMANDS $ helm repo add X URL && helm repo update $ helm install N chart [-f v.yaml] [--set k=v] $ helm upgrade N chart [--install] [--atomic --wait] $ helm rollback N REV # new revision! $ helm history N · list · get values N [-a] $ helm template ./chart -f v.yaml # preview $ helm uninstall N # receipts gone too  KUSTOMIZE — SKELETON base/kustomization.yaml: resources : [deployment.yaml, service.yaml] overlays/prod/kustomization.yaml: resources : [../../base] namespace : prod · namePrefix : prod- images : [{name: nginx, newTag: "1.26"}] replicas : [{name: web, count: 3}] $ kubectl kustomize overlays/prod # preview $ kubectl apply -k overlays/prod 溺 CRD MINIMUM + WEBHOOK FLOW kind : CustomResourceDefinition spec : { group, versions[].schema, scope, names{plural,kind} } # CRD = data only · +controller = Operator flow: authn → authz → MUTATE → VALIDATE → etcd Quota · LimitRange · PSS = built-in admission Kyverno/Gatekeeper = policy CRDs on webhooks failurePolicy: Fail = webhook down ⇒ API down  GITOPS — ARGOCD APPLICATION spec : source : {repoURL, path} destination : {server, namespace} syncPolicy : automated : { prune : true , self

Decode and safely operate any chart — upgrade with --atomic, audit values, roll back knowing history never rewinds Structure a fleet repo: Helm for third-party software, Kustomize overlays for your environments Extend the API with your own CRD and explain precisely what an operator adds to it Read the API Server's full request path — authn → authz → mutate → validate → etcd — and place every Book 02 concept on it Set up GitOps with eyes open: what selfHeal and prune really promise, and what never belongs in Git  Where to next — Book 09 · Cluster Lifecycle & Production Readiness — the finale: everything so

PART I · DAY 1 · CH 01  What is Infrast ructure as Co de?  6 MIN · T1 Manual server setup is the chef who "just knows" the dish — until they quit, and nobody can remake it. Infrastructure as Code (IaC) replaces tribal knowledge with a written recipe anyone can follow, with the same taste every time. main.tf is the blueprint; terraform apply is the construction crew.  THE RULE Idempotence. Apply the same code ten times → same infrastructure every time. f(f(x)) = f(x) . The property that makes IaC safe to retry, safe in CI, safe to share across teams. ▣ The 5-step loop (memorize) 1 · Write .tf in Git → 2 · Review PR + fmt → 3 · Plan +/−/ ∼ diff → 4 · Apply API calls → 5 · Monitor drift alarm Code says where to go · state remembers where you've been · refresh checks where you are. ▣ Why it exists — a real story Startup: 3 devs, 1 EC2 made by clicking. Works. Team grows to 20, need dev/staging/prod + 50 servers. Without IaC: nobody remembers the security-group rules, dev works / prod fails, the engineer who built it left, audit can't trace port openings, region outage = 3 weeks of clicking. With IaC: same company rebuilds prod in 12 minutes via terraform apply -var-file=prod.tfvars

PART I · DAY 1 · CH 02  What is Terrafo rm + T he 6 Pillars o f W hy  7 MIN · T2 + T3 Terraform (HashiCorp, 2014, Go, MPL 2.0, open source) is a multi-cloud standard that builds, changes, and versions infrastructure safely. It manages existing providers (AWS, GCP, Azure, 3000+ more) and your own in-house solutions. Six reasons it wins, each with the objection already answered.  2023+: new releases are BUSL — the MPL line continues as OpenTofu .  TERRAFORM IN ONE SENTENCE Learn once, manage anything, with the best preview and biggest ecosystem. 3000+ providers. The community has answered every error you'll hit. ▣ The 6 pillars 1 · IaC done right Code replaces clicks; Git replaces memory. git log --oneline -- infra/ git revert <sha> && terraform apply Objection "scripts do that" → scripts aren't idempotent/previewable; Terraform is. 2 · Platform-agnostic resource "aws_s3_bucket" "a" { bucket = "x" } resource "azurerm_resource_group" "b" { name = "rg" } resource "github_repository" "c" { name = "infra" } One apply touches 3 APIs. Both, configured before the second human exists.  THE 3 PAINS OF LOCAL STATE ① Teammate applies from their laptop → your state is stale → resources duplicated. ② Two apply at once → corrupt JSON or half-written resources. ③ Laptop dies / file deleted → management history gone. PART I · DAY 1 · CH 11  State Locking — The Mutex Explained  7 MIN · T13 Two engineers + concurrent apply = corrupted state. The fix: a DynamoDB lock table holds a single row per backend key. First apply grabs it (conditional-write), others fail fast, lock releases when apply finishes. The contract: only one writer to state at a time, ever.  THE LOCK LIFECYCLE apply starts → conditional-write LockID → if row exists, fail fast with who/when/operation → if acquired, do work + write new state to S3 → on success, delete the lock row . The lock is a row, not a file. ▣ What the lock error looks like $ terraform apply │ Error: Error acquiring the state lock │ │ Error acquiring the state lock: ConditionalCheckFailedException: │ Conditional Write failed: LockID = my-bucket/dev/terraform.tfstate │ │ Lock Info: │ ID: abc-123-def-456 │ Path: my-bucket/dev/terraform.tfstate │ Operation: OperationTypeApply │ Who: teammate@laptop │ Created: 2026-09-07 10:02:11 UTC │ Version: 1.5.0 │ │ Terraform acquires a state lock to protect the state from being │ written by multiple users at the same time. Please resolve the issue │ by removing the lock manually. ▣ Force-unlock — the danger zone # Step 1: r

PART III · LEVEL 2 · CH 18  Provisioners — Do ctrine: Last Resort  7 MIN · T22 Provisioners run scripts after resource creation or before destruction. They're the escape hatch when the provider doesn't have a feature — and the doctrine is use them last . user_data, Packer, Ansible cover 95% better. ⚠ THE CRITICAL CAVEAT Provisioners run ONLY on the resource's first creation . Re-apply with an unchanged resource does NOT re-run them. They re- run only after destroy + recreate. State never knows if the script succeeded — only that Terraform "tried". PART II · DAY 2 · CH 05  count vs for_each — The Rename Trap ⏱ 8 MIN · META Both copy a resource N times. count = index identity, for_each = key identity. Remove from the middle and count shifts every later copy; for_each kills only the removed key. That's the whole chapter in two sentences — the rest is proof.  THE RULE for_each for anything with a meaningful identity (servers by name, subnets by AZ). count for "N identical copies" or 0/1 toggles. Never mix both in one block. §1 The difference, demonstrated count — index-based resource "aws_instance" "web" { count = 3 tags = { Name = "web-${count.index}" } } # → web[0] web[1] web[2] # count 3→2 destroys web[2]. # Remove the MIDDLE? Later indexes # SHIFT — downstream refs break. for_each — key-based resource "aws_instance" "web" { for_each = toset(["web-a","web-b"]) tags = { Name = each.key } } # → web["web-a"] web["web-b"] # Remove "web-c": ONLY it dies. # Rename: old key dies, new key # born, everything else untouched. §2 5 copy-ready patterns # 1 — subnets per AZ (map: AZ → netnum, best of both) resource "aws_subnet" "public" { for_each = { for i, az in var.azs : az => i } cidr_block = cidrsubnet("10.0.0.0/16", 8, each.value)

SOLUTIONS · BOSSES ✅ sol-37 · sol-38 · sol-39  BAND sol-37 CIDR, not SG refs + both-side DNS ingress { from_port = 5432 to_port = 5432 protocol = "tcp" cidr_blocks = ["10.20.0.0/16"] # ← data VPC CIDR, not the SG id } # + aws_vpc_peering_connection_options BOTH sides: # allow_remote_vpc_dns_resolution = true 易 WHY — SG identity stops at the peering boundary, but routes carry CIDRs fine; DNS needs its own explicit opt-in per side or names stay dark. ⚠ TRAP — opening 0.0.0.0/0 "to make it work" (works, and invites the internet to the database).  EXAM — cross-peering: CIDR sources + both-side DNS flag. sol-38 Contract out, data source in, graph ordered # network/outputs.tf output "vpc_id" { value = aws_vpc.main.id } output "private_subnet_ids" { value = aws_subnet.private[*].id } # app/data.tf data "terraform_remote_state" "network" { backend = "s3" config = { bucket = "tfstate-prod" key = "network/terraform.tfstate" } } resource "aws_instance" "app" { subnet_id = data.terraform_remote_state.network.outputs.private_subnet_ids[0] } # CI: network job → app job (needs: network). 易 WHY — outputs publish the contract, the data source subscribes, and the pipeline orders what Terraform can

SOLUTION · FINAL BOSS ✅ sol-40 — t he full chain, worked  BLACK BELT provider "aws" { region = "us-east-1" } # (+ emulator creds/endpoints) resource "aws_vpc" "main" { cidr_block = "10.0.0.0/16" } resource "aws_subnet" "a" { vpc_id = aws_vpc.main.id cidr_block = "10.0.1.0/24" availability_zone = "us-east-1a" } resource "aws_subnet" "b" { vpc_id = aws_vpc.main.id cidr_block = "10.0.2.0/24" availability_zone = "us-east-1b" } resource "aws_security_group" "web" { # 443 in, all out vpc_id = aws_vpc.main.id ingress { from_port=443 to_port=443 protocol="tcp" cidr_blocks=["0.0.0.0/0"] } egress { from_port=0 to_port=0 protocol="-1" cidr_blocks=["0.0.0.0/0"] } } resource "aws_instance" "web" { for_each = toset(["a1","a2","b1","b2"]) subnet_id = startswith(each.key,"a") ? aws_subnet.a.id : aws_subnet.b.id vpc_security_group_ids = [aws_security_group.web.id] provisioner "local-exec" { command = "echo ${each.key}=${self.private_ip} >> ips.txt" } } output "ips" { value = { for k,i in aws_instance.web : k => i.private_ip } } # $ init → plan (8 add) → apply → output shows 4 IPs → destroy → state empty 易 WHY — every chapter fires once: provider auth, graph-ordered VPC→subnets, SG by reference, ke

Any red returns to next week's rotation with its Book 1 chapter.
